title: The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: Revival Begins with the “Heart”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, let’s begin by doing something very small: lay your hand gently on the left side of your chest, be still for three seconds, and listen to the sound that began before you were born and has never once stopped since.

That is your heartbeat.

At rest, an adult heart beats about seventy times a minute, around a hundred thousand times a day, and over a lifetime more than two billion times. Every minute it pumps about five litres of blood around the body — some seven and a half thousand litres a day. It never takes a holiday and never asks anyone to cover its shift. In a hospital, when a doctor must decide whether a person is alive or dead, the last thing he looks at is still that line on the ECG.

This is a profound metaphor: whether a person truly lives or dies comes down to the heart.

We often pour a great deal of effort into the outward things — appearance, qualifications, position, gifts, the fruits of our ministry, other people’s opinion of us. We invest all our time in what can be seen. But from the very first day, God’s eyes have looked past all of this and straight into one place: the human heart.

The theme of this lesson takes just a few words: the importance of the heart. But those few words are the backbone of the whole Bible, and the starting point of the end time revival.

If we truly long for the end time revival to come, we can’t stop at crying out in prayer and waiting expectantly; we also need to begin preparing at the level of the heart. Because revival has never been an outward wave of enthusiasm, but an inward turning-around of life; not activity in outward form, but the return of human hearts.

There’s a saying that puts it exactly: revival is a change in people’s lives that brings about a transformation of society. Notice the order — first the change of life, and only then the transformation of society. If our lives are to change, the first step must be letting God win our “heart.” Because whoever wins a person’s heart wins that whole person and that whole life; without the heart, everything else is just work around the edges.

Today’s theme verse is very short — just one sentence: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

This is the end of the Transfiguration. Moses withdrew, Elijah withdrew, the cloud dispersed, the voice fell silent. The disciples lifted their heads, and on the mountain only one remained — Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the truest picture of a heart the Lord has won: in my heart, after all the clamouring voices, only Jesus remains; in my heart, after all the figures have faded, I see only Jesus there.

The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not circumstances. This morning, I’d like to invite you to quietly ask yourself one question: if my heart were opened up right now, who would be the biggest one inside it?

sections.heading: 1. Scripture Background: The Glory on the Mountain and “Jesus Alone”
sections.html:
Before we come to the three key points of the lesson, let’s first get clear on the background to our theme verse, because the background to a text is often the key to the text.

Author, date and audience

Church history is unanimous that the author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, originally named Levi, a former tax collector in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9). That a man whose whole job was counting money and poring over account books should later write a Gospel all about “the heart” and “the Kingdom of Heaven” is grace in itself.

It is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, that is, around the time the temple in Jerusalem was destroyed. It was written mainly for Jewish Christians. That is why Matthew keeps saying, “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet,” and quotes the Old Testament so extensively throughout, with one aim alone: to prove that this Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the King of the Kingdom of Heaven.

The phrase “the Kingdom of Heaven” appears more than thirty times in Matthew; it is the book’s central thread. And what a king cares about most is whether people’s hearts have truly bowed beneath his authority — not shouting “Long live the king!” with their lips, but enthroning him in their hearts. This is precisely one of what 321 calls the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King.

The context: from the failure of the “heart” to the reordering of the “heart”

The Transfiguration isn’t a passage dropped in out of nowhere. It follows straight on from Matthew 16, and chapter 16 is all about a test of the “heart.”

In the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked the disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). Full marks. It was a revelation from the Holy Spirit, and Jesus commended him for it.

But only a few verses later: “From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up” (Matthew 16:21). Peter took him aside and rebuked him. Jesus turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men” (Matthew 16:23).

Notice the key phrase in Jesus’ diagnosis: “not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” “Setting your mind” in the original is φρονέω (phroneō), meaning “the orientation of the mind,” “the direction in which the heart sets its value and makes its plans.” The same Peter, the same mouth: one moment speaking a revelation from heaven, the next speaking the words of Satan. The difference wasn’t knowledge or eloquence; it was which way his heart was facing in that moment.

This is what 321 calls the shift of perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Peter’s failure in that moment wasn’t a moral failure but a failure of perspective; and perspective lives in the heart.

On the mountain: everything must point to that One

“After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.” (Matthew 17:1–2)

“He was changed” in the original is μεταμορφόω (metamorphoō). This word is well worth remembering, because Paul uses the very same word in Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” That “transformed” is the same as “changed” here. Jesus’ transformation on the mountain revealed the glory that was his all along; the transformation within us reveals the life he has placed in us. And the channel for both is the heart.

Next, “Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him” (Matthew 17:3). Moses represents the Law, Elijah the Prophets. The two great pillars of the Old Testament were standing there together.

Then Peter spoke up again: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17:4).

Peter spoke very devoutly, and his motive wasn’t bad. But the problem lay in the “three tents” — he had put Jesus on a level with Moses and Elijah. Again, it’s a matter of the heart: in his heart, Jesus was still only “one third.”

So the Father himself stepped in: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him’” (Matthew 17:5). When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces and were very afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid” (Matthew 17:7).

And then comes our theme verse: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

Moses was gone, Elijah was gone. The Law and the Prophets weren’t abolished; they were fulfilled — the One they had pointed to all their lives was now standing before them. Every signpost in the Old Testament finally converges on one name: Jesus.

The action of “lifting up their eyes” is fascinating too. The eyes are the outlet of the heart. Wherever your eyes are fixed, there your heart belongs; and conversely, whoever your heart belongs to, your eyes will instinctively look for. That is why the Lord Jesus said, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

Brothers and sisters, this is the lesson we must learn our whole lives long: let the tents in our heart go from three to one; let the figures before our eyes go from many to One. Seeing no one but Jesus — this is letting Jesus be King; this is letting Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: 2. What God Values Most Is “Our Heart”
sections.html:
Now we come to the first key point of the lesson.

From Genesis to Revelation, the Bible mentions the “heart” more than a thousand times. That number is itself a declaration: how much God cares about the state of the human heart. He doesn’t look at appearance, he doesn’t look at talent, he doesn’t look at achievement; he looks at the heart.

Scripture: God looks at the heart

“But Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.’” (1 Samuel 16:7)

The scene is vivid. Samuel had been sent to Bethlehem to anoint a new king in the house of Jesse. As soon as the eldest son, Eliab, stepped forward, Samuel said to himself: surely Yahweh’s anointed stands before him. Why? Because he was tall and handsome — he looked every inch a king.

And God said: not him.

Seven sons passed by one after another, and not one of them was the one. Finally Samuel asked: are these all your sons? Only then did Jesse remember there was still the youngest, out in the wilderness keeping the sheep — the boy who hadn’t even been called home for the family feast: David.

Notice: even the prophet Samuel could misjudge. Looking at outward appearance is human instinct, not human wickedness; but looking at the heart is God’s very nature.

The original: what is the Hebrew “heart”?

The Hebrew word for “heart” is לֵב (lev) or לֵבָב (levav), and it appears more than eight hundred times in the Old Testament. One thing needs special explanation here: the Chinese word for heart leans towards the emotions; when we speak of “putting our heart into something,” we mostly mean “having feelings.” But the Hebrew “heart” covers far more — it includes thought, will, decision, conscience, motive and judgements of value.

In other words, the Hebrew “heart” isn’t the emotional corner of a person; it’s the person’s central control room. So when God says he “looks at the heart,” he isn’t looking at whether you felt moved today or shed a tear; he is looking at who sits in the commander’s chair in the control room of your whole being.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture: three confirmations

First, David was chosen by God not because of his credentials but because of his heart. Our lesson says David was “a man after God’s own heart.” That description is right, but the reference needs correcting: “after God’s own heart” isn’t in 1 Samuel 16:7 but in 1 Samuel 13:14 — “Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and Yahweh has appointed him to be prince over his people”; and in the New Testament, Acts 13:22 also says, “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.”

Look at how Acts explains “a man after my heart”: “who will do all my will.” So being after God’s own heart isn’t about feeling passionate; it’s about a surrendered will. David was by no means a perfect man; he fell very far and committed great sins. But every time he fell, his heart turned back to God. He didn’t defend himself; he said, “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). What God wants isn’t people who have never fallen, but people whose hearts are always turned towards him.

Second, Jesus rebuked the Pharisees not because they kept too little of the law, but because their hearts were far from God. “These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me. And in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrine rules made by men” (Matthew 15:8–9). Here the Lord Jesus is quoting Isaiah 29:13.

The Pharisees tithed down to the last leaf of mint, dill and cumin, fasted twice a week, and knew the law by heart. As far as outward religious performance went, they were top of the class. But Jesus’ verdict came in two words: “in vain.” So worship can be perfectly correct and at the same time utterly hollow; service can be extremely busy and at the same time far, far away.

Third, God’s greatest longing for us is wholehearted love. “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5).

These two verses are the Shema, which Jews recite every morning and evening. Notice that word “all” — in Hebrew it is “with your whole heart,” nothing held back, not one corner hidden. God doesn’t accept love paid in instalments, nor surrender with a shareholding kept in reserve.

An illustration: the control tower and the heart

There’s a picture I often think of: an airport control tower.

An international airport may have the longest runways in the world, the newest aircraft, the most luxurious terminals; but if the control tower fails for just ten minutes, the whole airport is instantly paralysed, and planes dare not take off or land. Because the tower doesn’t do the flying; the tower is responsible for “deciding the direction.”

The human heart is the control tower. Gifts are the aircraft, opportunities are the runways, achievements are the terminals — all important, but none of them is the tower. If the tower fails, the more aircraft there are, the more dangerous it becomes.

Now look at the scientific side. In 1991 J. Andrew Armour, a researcher in neurocardiology, put forward the concept of the “heart brain,” showing that the heart itself has a complex intrinsic nervous system that can sense and process information independently and communicate with the brain in both directions. In other words, the heart isn’t just a passive pump; it interacts genuinely and closely with our thoughts and emotions.

Of course, the “heart” the Bible speaks of isn’t the same as the anatomical heart; but it is truly wonderful that when God made us, he wrote this concept of a “centre” into both our bodies and our spirits. When the physical heart stops, a person dies; when the spiritual heart goes astray, a life collapses.

A famous saying

In Book One of his Confessions, Augustine wrote words that have been repeated down the ages: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

That sentence names the root of all human restlessness. The human heart was made in the image of God; it is a seat prepared for God. When that seat is empty, people try to fill it with work, achievement, relationships, entertainment, religious activity; and the fuller they stuff it, the more restless they become. Because that seat is the size of only One.

Applying the 321 vision

The Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Notice that not one of these three statements is head knowledge; every one of them is a surrender of the heart.

“Jesus is my role model” — not admiring Jesus as a great figure of history, but following him as the one standard in my heart. “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5) — in the Chinese Union Version’s wording, “let the heart of Christ Jesus be your heart,” a sentence that sets the “heart” right into the text.

“The Bible is my standard” — not storing up the Bible as knowledge, but letting it come into the heart and wield the knife. “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12).

“The Holy Spirit is my guide” — not working things out by our own cleverness, but letting the Holy Spirit lead the way in our hearts. 321 has a wonderfully vivid saying: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Because “out of it is the wellspring of life.”

So whether our gifts are great or small, whatever our abilities, God has only one standard: do we love him with our heart, and have we given our heart wholly to him? What he wants isn’t worship from the lips, but a response from the heart.

sections.heading: 3. The Root of Many Problems Is a Problem of the “Heart”
sections.html:
Next comes the second key point of the lesson, and the one that cuts deepest.

When something goes wrong — in our relationship with God, in our relationships with others, in the unity of the church, in the fruitfulness of our ministry — our first reaction is usually: is it the wrong method? Does the system need changing? Do we need to run a few more events, hold a few more meetings?

Our lesson puts it bluntly: these are not technical problems, nor problems of structure, but problems of the “heart.”

Scripture: keep your heart

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Every word of this verse carries weight.

“Keep” in Hebrew is נָצַר (natsar), whose basic meaning is “to watch over, to guard, to keep watch,” a word used for guarding a city or watching over a vineyard. It isn’t passively “being a bit careful”; it’s actively posting sentries.

“With all diligence” (in the Chinese, “above all else you guard”) literally means “more than everything that must be guarded,” and that “guard” is מִשְׁמָר (mishmar), meaning a sentry post, a guardhouse, the watch over a prison. In other words, Solomon is saying: there are many things in life that need sentries posted over them — your money, your reputation, your health, your family — but if you have only one company of guards, send them all to guard your heart.

“Wellspring” in Hebrew is תּוֹצָאוֹת (totsa’ot), from the root “to go out,” meaning an outlet, a source, the place where water springs up. So the picture in this verse is: your heart is the spring, and your whole life is the river flowing out from it.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture: the order from inside out

Proverbs chapter 4 is a father’s counsel to his sons: “Listen, sons, to a father’s instruction. Pay attention and know understanding” (Proverbs 4:1). And after verse 23 speaks of the “heart,” the verses that follow are crucial — the father goes on to speak of the mouth, the eyes, the feet. The order is crystal clear: first the heart, then the mouth, then the eyes, then the feet. From the inside out, not from the outside in.

This is exactly the Lord Jesus’ diagnosis: “For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts, covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and defile the man” (Mark 7:21–23).

Look: the Lord Jesus lists thirteen things and then says that all of them “come from within.” He doesn’t say they were caused by circumstances, or by other people, or by the times.

Luke 6:45 also says, “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.” Our mouth is the tap of the heart. What comes out of the tap doesn’t depend on the tap; it depends on the water tank.

And Jeremiah goes straight to the point: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). In the next verse God himself answers: “I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart” (Jeremiah 17:10). We can’t see through our own hearts, but God can. That’s why we need to hand our hearts over to him every day for him to search.

Three scenes from the lesson

Our lesson points to three of the most common scenes; let’s look at them one by one.

First, when we drift apart from people, it often isn’t because the other person really is bad, but because the prejudice, pride and hurt in our hearts haven’t been dealt with. The same sentence, spoken by someone we like, is concern; spoken by someone we’re prejudiced against, it’s mockery. It isn’t the sentence that changes; it’s our heart.

Second, when we grow cold towards God, it often isn’t because the truth has stopped being true, but because our hearts have gradually drifted; busyness, weariness, bitterness and idols have bit by bit taken God’s place. The church in Ephesus was a good church; the Lord commended their toil, their endurance, their refusal to tolerate evil men. But the Lord said, “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4). A church whose ministry calendar is completely full may still have a cold heart.

Third, when we grow weary in serving, it may not be because we’re too busy, but because our hearts are no longer willing, no longer simply serving the Lord. Washing the same hundred dishes: wash them out of love, and the more you wash the sweeter it gets; wash them out of duty, and the more you wash the more bitter it gets; wash them to make an impression, and the more you wash the more resentful you get. The task is the same; the heart is different, and so the outcome is completely different.

An illustration: the spring upstream

Imagine a village whose stream suddenly turns muddy. The villagers work very hard: they put nets across the stream downstream, fish out the rubbish, sprinkle in purifying agents, busy until midnight every day, yet the water never runs clear. Until one day someone walks three kilometres upstream and discovers that a stretch of earth has collapsed beside the spring.

Dealing with the spring takes a day; dealing with the downstream takes a lifetime.

So many of our “problems” are downstream: our temper, our words, our relationships, our weariness in ministry. Yet we keep trying to fish things out downstream. Proverbs 4:23 is God’s counsel to us: go upstream, and look at your heart.

The help of psychology, and how the Bible goes beyond it

On this point psychology actually gives us a very useful supporting witness. In the 1960s the American psychiatrist Aaron T. Beck developed cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and its central finding is this: our emotions and behaviour are not determined directly by events themselves, but by how we interpret those events — by “automatic thoughts” that flash by almost instantly, so fast we don’t even notice them. The same thing happens to two people and their reactions are worlds apart; the difference lies in the interpretation, and the interpretation lies in the heart.

This echoes exactly what 321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

But we must be clear: psychology is only a help; it cannot override the Bible. Cognitive therapy can help a person “swap out a thought,” but the gospel “swaps out a heart.” God’s promise goes far beyond any therapy: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).

The difference between a heart of stone and a heart of flesh isn’t how hard it is, but whether it can feel and whether God can touch it. God doesn’t give the stone counselling; God replaces the heart. That is something no human can do; only God can.

Applying the 321 vision

321 speaks of fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Notice the order — problems often break out in the last two: ministry runs into trouble, relationships turn sour; but the roots are usually buried in the first two: mindset and life.

That’s why 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. If we turn the order upside down, trading life for ministry and relationships for results, in the end both sides lose.

And the problem of the heart, when all is said and done, comes down to one thing: “self.” The old self is “self-centred”; the new self is “selfless.” The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? It is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? It is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Look back at that scene with Peter and it becomes even clearer. Peter urged the Lord not to go to the cross. He meant well, yet the Lord called him “Satan.” Why so severe? Because in that moment his heart put “the things of men” above “the things of God” — that is, “self” had taken a seat that didn’t belong to it.

So if we can overcome the problems of the heart, the outward problems will no longer be hard problems.

sections.heading: 4. Love Is a Response from the Heart, Not a Rational Choice
sections.html:
We now come to the third key point of the lesson.

Scripture: he loved us first, with his heart

God’s love for us was never calculated; it was given from the heart.

“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

See how there’s no “rational condition” anywhere in this sentence. He didn’t wait for us to improve before loving us; he didn’t assess whether we’d give him a return on his investment before loving us. “While we were yet sinners,” he gave up his Son. By rational calculation, this was a thoroughly bad bargain; but love never happens inside a calculation.

That’s why John says, “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). All our love is a response, not an invention.

Scripture: we must love him with all our heart

In the same way, our love for God must also come from the heart. Our lesson lists three passages; let’s look at them one at a time.

First, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Mark 12:30).

This was the Lord’s answer when a scribe asked Jesus, “Which commandment is the greatest of all?” The Lord quoted Deuteronomy 6:5 and added “with all your mind.” Each of these four “with all” phrases is ἐξ ὅλης in Greek, meaning “out of the whole of.” Heart, soul, mind and strength — emotions, life, thought and physical energy: the whole person, all the time, with all our might, nothing held back.

Second, “These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15:8).

How far apart can the lips and the heart be? As far apart as heaven and earth. This is the most frightening religious condition of all: completely up to standard on the outside, completely blank on the inside.

Third, “My son, give me your heart; and let your eyes keep in my ways” (Proverbs 23:26).

A small correction needs noting here: in the Chinese Union Version this verse reads simply “My son, give me your heart,” not “O my son, you must give me your heart.”

“Give me” in Hebrew is נָתַן (nathan), simply “to give.” God says: “give” me your heart. Not lend it to me, not rent it to me, not entrust it to me for two hours on Sunday morning, but give it to me.

And the second half is even more striking: “Let your eyes keep in my ways.” Whoever your heart belongs to, your eyes will follow. This sentence carries us all the way back to today’s theme verse — “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8). When the heart belongs to the Lord, lift up your eyes and you will naturally see only Jesus.

What love becomes if it doesn’t begin in the heart

Our lesson puts it well: if love doesn’t begin in the heart, it turns into religious duty, into formal behaviour, even into the heavy burden of the law.

The household in Luke chapter 10 is the best illustration. Martha “was distracted with much serving”; her hands were serving Jesus, but her heart was complaining about her sister. What did the Lord say? “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:41–42).

The Lord didn’t rebuke Martha for serving; the Lord’s heart went out to Martha in her “anxiety and trouble.” Serving itself wasn’t wrong; what was wrong was that her heart had left the very Lord she was serving.

Paul also says, “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision amounts to anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Outward marks amount to nothing; only the faith that works itself out in love from the heart counts.

But if it begins in the heart, everything is different: it brings willing and joyful obedience, sincere and simple worship, and service full of love. The same ministry with a different heart has a completely different flavour.

An illustration: a bouquet that became a bill

There was a brother who gave his wife a bouquet of flowers every month without fail, never forgot an anniversary, and never fell a penny short on the housekeeping. From the outside, he was beyond reproach. But one day his wife, her eyes red, said: “I’ve received every bunch of flowers you’ve given me, but I’ve never once received you.”

When love is reduced to duty, flowers become a bill; when marriage is reduced to a contract, a home becomes a company.

It’s the same with our relationship with God. Every box on the Bible-reading plan ticked, perfect attendance at meetings, offerings always on time — if the heart isn’t in it, all of this in God’s eyes is like that bouquet with no one behind it.

A famous saying and some research

The French mathematician and thinker Blaise Pascal left us a famous line in his Pensées: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” The realm of love was never something reason could fully measure. This doesn’t mean faith ignores reason — the Christian faith has the most solid rational foundations; it means that the deepest surrender happens in a place deeper than reason.

Psychology also offers us a weighty confirmation. The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, making it one of the longest studies of adult life ever conducted. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, sums up the study’s clearest finding: what keeps people healthy and happy throughout their lives isn’t wealth, isn’t fame, isn’t achievement, but good relationships.

This is exactly what 321 says: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And the quality of every relationship depends on how much “heart” we put into it.

Applying the 321 vision

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Many people have the order reversed: busy with tasks first, then busy with people, thinking of themselves only last of all — and as for God, he can wait until they have time. The result is that the heart grows ever drier and the work grows ever heavier.

The 920 practice of 321 is exactly how love is lived out every day: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before each “2,” we practise living out the selfless (0) life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice that fruit isn’t squeezed out by effort; it grows out of life. You can’t order a tree to bear fruit; all you can do is let it put down roots, take in water and turn towards the sunlight. When the heart is turned towards the Lord, fruit grows naturally.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: A Heart the Lord Has Won
sections.html:
Set today’s message within the 321 framework, and we’ll see it even more clearly.

The Three Foundations all live in the heart

Jesus is my role model — “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). A role model isn’t hung on the wall to be looked at; it’s carried in the heart to be learned from.

The Bible is my standard — the word of God “is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). The standard isn’t kept on the bookshelf but on the tablet of the heart: “not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh” (2 Corinthians 3:3).

The Holy Spirit is my guide — “because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5:5). The Holy Spirit doesn’t issue orders over our heads; he pours love into our hearts.

The Two Core Values: the throne of the heart has room for only One

Let Jesus be King — the human heart is a throne, not a long bench. Peter wanted to make three tents, but the Father said, “Listen to him.” There is only one King.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when our hearts truly surrender, what people see is no longer our gifts, our eloquence or our ability, but that One. Seeing no one, except Jesus alone.

The Goal: establish God’s system

God’s system isn’t an organisational chart; it is a living network made up of people whose hearts the Lord has won. The smallest unit of the system isn’t a department; it’s a heart. If the hearts belong to God, the system belongs to God; if the hearts still belong to “self,” even the most beautiful structure is just a copy of the Worldly system.

From self-centred to selfless

The old self is “self-centred”; the new self is “selfless.” “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Notice that selflessness isn’t erasing yourself down to zero, nor denying yourself until you have no worth. Selflessness is yielding up the “self” that fights for the throne and letting Christ come in — so selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The shift of perspective

The renewal of the heart shows itself concretely in four shifts:

From the human perspective to God’s perspective — Peter’s failure lay precisely in “setting your mind … on the things of men” (Matthew 16:23).

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective — “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective — “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

From a worldly perspective to a godly perspective — not a change of vocabulary, but a change of heart.

The Path of Serving and the 235 relationships

The 321 Path of Serving is: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Notice that this path begins with “Spirit,” not with “Service.” Many people skip the first three stations and rush straight to the fourth, and so the more they serve, the emptier their hearts become.

And the 235 relationships remind us: don’t walk alone. Become a “2” with someone who is selfless, serving as one another’s spiritual companion, able to examine each other’s hearts honestly; go on to build a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that life is passed on; and finally become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, serving together. The lessons of the heart are never learned behind closed doors on our own; they are learned in real relationships, where we are refined, loved and healed.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Three Ways to Turn the Heart Back to the Lord
sections.html:
Our lesson has prepared three very practical exercises for us. 321 has the “eight stages of changing our mindset”: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. We’ll work these eight stages into the three exercises, so that each exercise isn’t something done once, but something that truly changes our lives.

Exercise 1: Take stock of your “heart” every day

Every evening, spend three minutes asking yourself three questions:

1. Today, has my heart drifted away from God?

2. Have I harboured resentment, bitterness or pride towards anyone?

3. Did what I did today come from a heart that loves the Lord, or from duty or a desire to impress?

Let this devotional exercise become the thermometer of your soul.

Deepen it with the eight stages:

Information — first learn Proverbs 4:23 by heart: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” Without information, there is no starting point.

Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit himself to shine his light on you; don’t rely on self-examination alone. David’s prayer is worth praying every day: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). Self-examination easily stops at self-blame; revelation brings freedom.

Conviction — truly believe that “out of it is the wellspring of life,” and stop pushing the problem onto circumstances and other people.

Implementation — start tonight: three minutes, three questions, no more and no less.

Evaluation — choose one day each week to look back over the week’s record: on which day did my heart drift? Where did it drift? Who or what was the trigger?

Correction — not self-blame, but turning back. When you see bitterness, forgive that same day; when you see pride, confess it that same day; don’t let the sun go down while you are still angry.

Repetition — there’s no crash course in the lessons of the heart. Keep it up for thirty days, ninety days, until it becomes a habit; and a habit kept long enough becomes character.

Multiplication — find a brother or sister to be your “2,” do it together, and share with each other once a week. You’ll find that the moment you say it out loud, strength comes.

Exercise 2: Worship with your heart, not just with your mouth

This week, in every time of worship, don’t just sing; speak to the Lord, open your heart, and say to him: “Lord, my heart is here; please come and win it.”

Worship isn’t a singing technique; it is the entrusting of the heart and union with him.

The Lord Jesus said to the Samaritan woman, “But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers” (John 4:23). Notice that the Father wants such people — not that the Father “accepts” them, but that the Father “seeks” them. What God is looking for is a heart that is truly open.

Deepen it with the eight stages: Information is understanding what worship is; Revelation is being suddenly touched by the Lord during a particular hymn; Conviction is admitting that much of our past worship was only a movement of the lips; Implementation is, starting this week, making at least one line of every song something you “sing to him” — not to yourself, and not to the person beside you; Evaluation is asking yourself how many times this week you truly came into the Lord’s presence; Correction is adjusting — if you habitually get distracted, arrive five minutes early and be still first; Repetition is doing this week after week; Multiplication is bringing your family along, so that worship in your home comes alive as well.

Exercise 3: Write a “letter of the heart” to Jesus

Find a quiet moment and write a letter to Jesus, including:

1. How you want to love him.

2. The attitudes of heart you want to adjust for him.

3. The heart you are willing to offer him.

When you write it out, it is also a declaration: “Lord, my heart is here; may you win it.”

Why “write”? Because when we write, vague feelings are forced into clear sentences; and only clear sentences can become a commitment we can examine and come back to check against.

Paul says, “being revealed that you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh” (2 Corinthians 3:3). We write to the Lord with a pen; the Lord writes on the tablets of our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

Deepen it with the eight stages: once it’s written, put it away and set a date — take it out and read it through again in three months’ time; that is Evaluation and Correction. Renew it once a year; that is Repetition. Look for a chance to invite a friend to write one too; that is Multiplication.

A Gentle Reminder: God wants not performance but the “heart”

Don’t rush to serve more, learn more, do more; first ask one question: is my heart still with the Lord?

Revival doesn’t begin with action; it begins with a heart willing to respond to God.

God has never been short of workers; what God is looking for is people of one heart with him. “If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14). Notice these four actions — humbling, praying, seeking, turning — not one of them is running an event; every one is an action of the heart.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: When the Heart Is Right, Life Is Right; When the Heart Drifts, Direction Drifts
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we set out today from one verse, and we return to it now: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

When the disciples went up the mountain, their hearts were full of people: Moses, Elijah, their own plans, the idea of three tents, the fear of being overwhelmed by glory. When they came down the mountain, only One remained in their hearts.

That is the whole meaning of a heart won by the Lord. It isn’t that we become more impressive; it’s that the figures before our eyes grow fewer, and only that One grows greater.

When the heart is right, life is right; when the heart drifts, direction drifts. If a ship’s heading is off by one degree, the faster it sails, the further it gets from its goal. We don’t lack speed; what we lack is correction.

So the call the prophet Joel sounded to his generation still rings out today: “Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness” (Joel 2:13). Tearing your garments is an outward act; tearing your heart is an inward brokenness. What God wants has always been the latter.

The change in our lives begins with the “heart”; the coming of revival also begins with the “heart.” May we all become people whose hearts the Lord has won, so that God’s glory may be revealed through us.

Because whoever wins a person’s heart wins that person; and when the hearts of the whole church are won, revival will come to this land!

This morning, I want to issue this call to you: give him your heart. Not your time, not your talents, not your service — first give him your heart. Because once the heart is given, everything else naturally follows.

Let Jesus reign as King in your heart; let Jesus receive all the glory from your life.

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)
declarations: Lord, I want to give my heart wholly to you,
no longer seeking to please you only by my actions,
but letting all I say, all I do and all I think flow from sincere love for you!
practices: Take stock of your “heart” every day
Worship with your heart, not just with your mouth
Write a “letter of the heart” to Jesus
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, thank you. While I was still a sinner, you loved me first, with all your heart.

Lord, please search my heart. I confess that I often honour you with my lips while my heart quietly drifts far from you; I am often busy doing things, yet forget for whom I am doing them. Please forgive me.
Take away the heart of stone within me and give me a heart of flesh; take down the three tents in my heart until only one is left, and let you alone sit upon that throne.
May the Holy Spirit shine his light on me day by day, so that I can keep my heart above all else. May every outcome of my life flow from a heart that loves you.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). This week, have you spent most of your energy cultivating your “outward appearance” or your “heart”? Name one specific thing, and share how you want to adjust.

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Right now, which gateway of your heart most needs a guard posted — bitterness, pride, comparison, or busyness? Pray for one another, asking the Lord himself to reign as King at that very point.
