sections.heading: Introduction: We Always Look Outside for the Answer
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to face together a subject that is very close and very real, and yet one we so often walk around.

Think back to the last thing that brought your spirits low. Perhaps it was a remark at home, perhaps an unfair decision at work, perhaps a piece of service at church that nobody understood. As we replay that thing in our minds, have you noticed a common pattern? Our explanations nearly all point outward. The circumstances were too hard, that person was too awful, the resources were too thin, the timing was wrong, people don’t understand me. We are like someone standing in front of a mirror who sees a smudge on the face in the glass — and reaches out to wipe the mirror. We wipe and wipe; the mirror gets shinier and shinier, and the smudge on our face hasn’t shrunk one bit.

Picture this. A child keeps coughing. The parents change hospitals, change doctors, buy more expensive medicine, and still the child coughs. At last one doctor asks, “Does anyone at home smoke?” The problem was never in the child’s throat; it was in the air of the living room. Brothers and sisters, our spiritual life is so often like this: we work desperately to treat the cough of our “behaviour”, yet refuse to deal with the air of the “heart”.

The Lord Jesus sees deeper than we do. While the crowd argued about whether to wash hands before eating, how many times to wash and how much water to use, the Lord Jesus pointed to a place no one wanted pointed at. He said that what goes into a person from outside cannot defile him; it is what comes out from within that defiles. He was not discussing hygiene. He was performing surgery. He laid the scalpel on the human heart and said: the problem is here.

The moment those words were spoken, every excuse expired. We can no longer say, “The circumstances forced me into it.” We can no longer say, “He’s the one who made me like this.” For the Lord put it very plainly: evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts, covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride and foolishness — of these thirteen, not one flies in from outside. Every one of them “comes from within”. Circumstances are not the manufacturer; circumstances are only the developing fluid. They do not put anything new inside us; they simply bring to light what was already there.

Solomon saw this secret long ago. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The sense of the original is this: of everything you must guard, the first place to post a sentry and set a watch is your heart. Not your reputation, not your possessions, not your health — your heart. For the outcome of a whole life does not flow from circumstances; it flows “out of” the heart.

So the goal of today’s lesson is simple, yet far from easy. We are learning to stop wiping the mirror and wash our face instead; to stop merely treating the cough and change the air; to stop merely correcting behaviour and hand our heart to God. We want to grow quiet before the Lord, let him shine his light, let him work, and let him once again reign as King in our hearts. Because every problem begins in the “heart” — and only in the “heart” can it truly be solved.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An Argument About Hand-Washing
sections.html:
To feel the full weight of the Lord Jesus’ words, we first need to stand where it happened.

The Gospel of Mark was written by Mark — the man Acts 12:12 calls “John who was called Mark”. The tradition of the early church consistently identifies Mark as the co-worker and interpreter of the apostle Peter, who set down the life of Jesus as Peter preached it. In 1 Peter 5:13 Peter calls him “Mark, my son”, which shows how close the two were. This Gospel is generally thought to have been written between the late 50s and the 60s AD, mainly for Gentile believers in Rome. The evidence is in the book itself: Mark often has to explain Jewish customs, and in this very passage he stops to spend two whole verses telling his readers the Jewish rules about washing hands, cups and pitchers (Mark 7:3–4). If his readers had been Jews, none of that would have needed saying.

How did it all come about? Mark 7:1–2 tells us that Pharisees and some of the scribes came from Jerusalem and gathered around Jesus. They saw some of his disciples eating with “defiled”, that is, unwashed, hands. Notice that “defiled” hands here are not dirty hands. This was not a question of hygiene but of ritual. The oral law of the Jews had drawn up very detailed rules for the purification rites priests performed before entering the sanctuary, and later laid those same rules on ordinary people: before a meal you poured a set amount of water over your hands in a set order, wiped them, and poured again. None of this was commanded in the Law of Moses. It had been added by later generations, and the text calls it “the tradition of the elders”.

So these religious experts from Jerusalem came with the eyes of inspectors. They challenged Jesus: “Why don’t your disciples walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat their bread with unwashed hands?” (Mark 7:5). On the surface they were asking about rules; underneath, they were challenging his authority.

The Lord Jesus’ answer was razor-sharp. He first drew on Isaiah 29:13: “Because this people draws near with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught.” In Mark 7:6–7 the Lord quotes this passage to expose their most basic disease: lips and heart had parted company. The lips were worshipping; the heart was far away. Then the Lord gave a concrete example — “Corban”. The word korban means “an offering given to God”. A person could declare his property Corban, meaning it now belonged to God, and so, quite properly, he no longer had to use it to support his parents. With one spiritual-sounding word, the fifth commandment was cancelled. So the Lord said, “Full well do you reject the commandment of God, that you may keep your tradition” (Mark 7:9).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? This is the key to the whole chapter: religion can be used to gift-wrap a heart that refuses to obey. A person can keep the hand-washing ritual scrupulously while letting his parents go hungry. Washed spotless on the outside, and inside too filthy to be seen.

So the Lord Jesus called the crowd to him and spoke the words that shook the whole gathering: “Hear me, all of you, and understand. There is nothing from outside of the man, that going into him can defile him; but the things which proceed out of the man are those that defile the man” (Mark 7:14–15). The disciples didn’t understand and asked him privately. And there in the house, to this circle of his closest friends, the Lord laid the answer out in full — our key passage today. The source of defilement is not food but the human heart; not the table but the mind; not the outside but the inside.

Mark adds a comment of great significance: “making all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). In a single phrase he declares that the purity laws of the Old Testament have completed their task for their time, and that the focus of the new covenant has shifted from diet to the heart. From then on, God’s people are called not to “wash their hands” but to “wash their hearts”.

Once we understand this background, we can see that the three key points of this lesson are really the three incisions of the Lord Jesus’ heart surgery. The first cut opens up the root of sin; the second strips away the disguise of behaviour; the third deals with the way our thinking erodes the heart.

sections.heading: 1. The Origin of Sin: It Starts in the Heart
sections.html:
In Mark 7:21–23 the Lord Jesus says, “For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts, covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and defile the man.”

Notice the verbs the Lord uses: “proceed” and “come from”. The Greek ekporeuomai means “to walk outward, to go out”. Sin is not a visitor that creeps in from outside; sin is a resident that walks out from within. The direction of this word matters enormously: at a single stroke it overturns humanity’s oldest self-defence.

We are used to saying, “I was perfectly fine until he provoked me.” The Lord says: no — it came out from within.

The Bible’s word for “heart” is lev or levav in Hebrew and kardia in Greek. It never means only the emotions. In Scripture the heart is the centre of the person, the command post, taking in thought, will, emotion, conscience and choice. So when God says he looks at the heart, he is not merely checking whether you’re in a good mood today; he is looking at which way the command centre of your whole person is facing. 1 Samuel 16:7 puts it plainly: “I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

The first murder the Bible records was an event of the heart. Genesis 4 tells us that when Cain’s offering was not accepted, he became very angry and his face fell. God himself came to warn him. Genesis 4:6–7: “Yahweh said to Cain, ‘Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.’” God gave him a warning, and he also gave him a chance: sin was only crouching at the door; it had not yet come in; you must master it. Sadly, Cain did not deal with the jealousy in his heart. The text goes on: “Cain said to Abel, his brother, ‘Let’s go into the field.’ While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him” (Genesis 4:8). Between “angry, his face fallen” and “rose up and killed him” there stood no circumstance — only a heart that had never been dealt with.

Trace it further back, and the very first occurrence of sin was also an event of the heart. Isaiah 14:13–14 records the fallen one’s soliloquy: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” Count them: in these two short verses there are five “I will”s. Ezekiel 28:17 says too, “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” The origin of sin was not some external temptation; it was a heart that left its originally intended position and wanted to take God’s place. Pride is the root of the problem; the self-centred life is where the fall of humanity began.

So the Lord Jesus brought the standard back to the heart. He said, “But I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). And again, “But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment” (Matthew 5:22). Brothers and sisters, how solemn these words are. The Lord is not raising the moral bar so that we will despair; he is showing us where the disease is lodged, so that we can be healed. A doctor who would treat only the swelling you can see, but refuse to scan for the tumour inside, would not be kind — he would be negligent. The Lord loves us, and so he brings the truth about our inner life into the light.

Jeremiah 17:9 gives an even more direct diagnosis of the human heart: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” The next verse follows straight on: “I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.” We cannot see through our own hearts, but God can. That is why we need to pray: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

Let me use an everyday picture. Have you ever had a leak in your house? A water stain appears on the ceiling. You paint over it, and next month it’s back — bigger. The problem isn’t in the ceiling; it’s in the pipe upstairs. The paint deals with the “symptom”; the pipe is the “source”. Our behaviour is the stain on the ceiling; our heart is the pipe. Dealing with behaviour without dealing with the heart makes us like someone forever repainting the ceiling: spending a fortune, worn out, and the stain comes back year after year.

On this point psychology offers us some confirmation from the side. In the 1960s Dr Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania put forward the theory of cognitive therapy. He found in his clinical work that what makes patients suffer is often not the event itself but the “automatic thoughts” that flash, almost unnoticed, between the event and the emotion. Two people interpret the same event differently, and their emotions are entirely different. Beck therefore argued that to change emotion and behaviour, you must go back to that thought furthest upstream. That is exactly what the Bible said long ago: the outcome of a whole life flows from the heart. Of course, we must be clear about the difference: Beck dealt with patterns of thought; the Bible deals with whom our life belongs to. Psychology can help people see the power of their thoughts, but it cannot give a person’s heart back to God. Only the Holy Spirit can renew the human heart.

From the standpoint of the 321 vision, this is the starting point of all our practice. The first of the Three Foundations is: Jesus is my role model. The Lord Jesus’ lifelong obedience did not come from gritting his teeth and suppressing his behaviour; it flowed from a heart wholly surrendered to the Father. In Gethsemane he said, “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). That is a selfless heart. And the mark of the old self is the self-centred life — I want, I think, I feel I’ve been short-changed. Those five “I will”s are the very language of Satan.

Brothers and sisters, this morning we need to admit honestly: my problem is not my circumstances, not my spouse, not my colleagues, not my church. My problem is my heart. Admitting it is very uncomfortable, yet it is the first step towards healing. For when we take the finger we’ve been pointing at others and lay it on our own chest, grace finally has room to work.

sections.heading: 2. Behaviour Cannot Cover a Wrong Heart
sections.html:
The first cut laid open the root; the second must strip away the disguise.

There is a deep instinct in us: when the heart is wrong, we don’t go and repair the heart — we go and patch up our behaviour. We use more service, more giving, more pious language to soothe the unease inside, and even hope to buy God’s approval with it. But the Bible is very clear: God does not look at the surface of our behaviour; he looks at the motive behind it.

King Saul is the most painful example. Through Samuel, God commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but he spared the best of the sheep and cattle and kept King Agag alive. When Samuel arrived, Saul’s first words were, “You are blessed by Yahweh! I have performed the commandment of Yahweh” (1 Samuel 15:13). But the bleating of the sheep and the lowing of the cattle gave him away. At once he changed his story, shifted the blame onto the people, and found the most spiritual of reasons for what he had kept back: it was to be sacrificed to Yahweh. Samuel’s reply is one of the weightiest sayings in the Old Testament — 1 Samuel 15:22–23: “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.’”

Notice: the sacrifice Saul meant to offer was a real sacrifice, the animals were real animals, the fire would have been real fire. His “religious behaviour” was a hundred per cent correct. But God said: I don’t want it. Because it wasn’t obedience; it was a cover-up. God puts rebellion on a level with witchcraft because the two are the same at heart: both want to manipulate the outcome according to my own will; both say, “I’m going to be in charge.”

The New Testament has an equally sobering example. Acts 5 tells of Ananias and Sapphira. At that time the church was full of love and generosity; Barnabas had sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet. Ananias and his wife also sold a property, also brought a sum of money, also laid it at the apostles’ feet. From the outside the gift was beyond reproach: the money was real, the land was real, the action was real. But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land?” (Acts 5:3). And Peter went on, “While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God” (Acts 5:4).

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to Peter’s logic. Their sin was not “not giving enough”. Peter says it outright: whether to sell, how much to give — that was entirely up to them. Their sin was that they had “conceived this thing in their heart” — wanting the praise people would give, without paying the whole price; wanting a spiritual reputation without the spiritual reality. The problem wasn’t the amount; it was the motive. Ananias fell down dead on the spot, and about three hours later so did Sapphira. Great fear came on the whole church and on all who heard of it (Acts 5:11). Through this event God set a lasting mark on the early church: in God’s house we may be imperfect, but we may not be fake.

In Matthew 23 the Lord Jesus rebukes the scribes and Pharisees seven times for hypocrisy. The Greek for “hypocrite” is hupokrites, which originally meant “an actor wearing a mask”. In the ancient Greek theatre an actor held a mask over his face; the audience saw the character, not the man. When the Lord Jesus uses this word, he is in effect saying: your piety is a performance; the audience below applauds, but the one on stage has no real face. He also said, “For you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness” (Matthew 23:27).

We must beware of a misunderstanding here. The Bible is not saying behaviour doesn’t matter. The book of James says clearly that faith without works is dead. What the Bible is saying is that behaviour must be the fruit of the heart, never a substitute for it. Fruit has to grow on the tree. You could tape an apple onto a dead branch, and from a distance it would look very much like a fruit-bearing tree. Come closer and you’ll see: the tree is dead, and the apple will rot. Fruit that grows from life and fruit that has been tied on may look alike on the outside, but they are utterly different in nature.

1 Timothy 1:5 gives us the positive standard: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.” Look at these three phrases: a pure heart, a good conscience, sincere faith. Love is not behaviour put on for show; love “grows out of” these three things. The order cannot be reversed.

Psychology has also observed our human disguises. In 1957 the Stanford University social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when a person’s behaviour doesn’t match his beliefs, an uncomfortable tension builds up inside, and to relieve it people often don’t change their behaviour — they revise their explanation, finding themselves a reason that sounds reasonable. Saul saying “it’s to sacrifice to Yahweh”, Ananias keeping some back yet saying it was everything — these are ancient versions of that same mechanism. We are very good at finding a spiritual coat to put on our disobedience. And that is exactly why we need God’s light. We can fool ourselves; we cannot fool God.

In his Institutes of the Christian Religion Calvin says that the human heart is “a factory of idols”. That is precisely this lesson’s reminder: the factory inside us is always running, and without God’s light we don’t even know what we are producing.

From the standpoint of the 321 vision, this goes straight to the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. What was Saul’s problem? He wanted to be king. He spared Agag to save face; he offered sacrifice to save his position. What was Ananias’s problem? He wanted the glory. He wanted the church to see him as generous as Barnabas. Brothers and sisters, before every piece of service we can ask ourselves two simple questions: in this, who is King? In this, who is the glory going to? If the answer is “me”, then however fine the behaviour, before God it is only a performance.

The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The order cannot be turned round. When ministry runs ahead of life, we start using ministry to cover the emptiness of our life; when performance runs ahead of relationships, we start using busyness to cover the distance in our hearts. What God wants first is not our hands but our heart. Hands without a heart are just a machine.

sections.heading: 3. When the Brain Controls the Heart, the Heart Goes Bad
sections.html:
The third cut deals with the way our thinking erodes the heart.

When reason replaces faith, when fear replaces trust, when calculation replaces simplicity, we no longer love God by “relying on the heart”. We start relying on the brain: assessing, scheming, guarding, comparing, controlling. The brain itself is not bad; God made us with reason so that we would use our reason to serve the truth. The problem is one of order: when the brain sets out to control the heart, the heart begins to go bad.

Moses warned the Israelites of this in advance in Deuteronomy 8. They were about to enter Canaan, the land flowing with milk and honey, and Moses said, “Beware lest you forget Yahweh your God, in not keeping his commandments, his ordinances, and his statutes, which I command you today” (Deuteronomy 8:11). Then he described the dangerous process: “lest, when you have eaten and are full, and have built fine houses and lived in them; and when your herds and your flocks multiply, and your silver and your gold is multiplied, and all that you have is multiplied; then your heart might be lifted up, and you forget Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage” (Deuteronomy 8:12–14). Finally Moses spoke out loud the deadliest words of the heart: “and lest you say in your heart, ‘My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth’” (Deuteronomy 8:17). Then came the antidote: “But you shall remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers, as it is today” (Deuteronomy 8:18).

Notice that Moses did not say “you will go and worship idols”. He said “you say in your heart”. The fall begins with a sentence in the heart that no one else hears. “I earned this” — three short words, and God has been shown off his throne.

And it isn’t only prosperity. The lesson reminds us that hatred, pornography, greed and envy, if they are thought about and indulged over and over in the mind, will in the end devour the heart. James 1:14–15 describes the process like time-lapse photography: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” Drawn away, enticed, conceived, bears, full grown, death — not one link in the chain is sudden. Every collapse has a long incubation, and the place where it incubates is in our minds.

Brothers and sisters, we can honestly ask ourselves a few questions. When I’m driving, when I’m washing the dishes, when I lie down at night — what is my mind replaying? Is it replaying, yet again, the thing that person said to me? I’ve replayed it hundreds of times, and each time I’ve become more certain that I’m right and he’s wrong. Or am I turning some impure image over and over in my mind, comforting myself that “at least I didn’t do anything”? Proverbs 23:7 in the Chinese Union Version reads, “as he thinks in his heart, so is he”; the World English Bible renders it, “as he thinks about the cost, so he is.” Whatever you think about over and over, you gradually become.

Science offers some powerful supporting evidence here. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb put forward an important principle of neuroplasticity, which later generations boiled down to a famous phrase: “Neurons that fire together wire together.” In other words, when the same pathway of thought is activated again and again, the neural connection is strengthened, and in time it becomes an automatic response. That is why bitterness grows deeper the more we think about it, and why desire grows bigger the more we feed it. You are not “just thinking for a moment”; you are laying a road. The first time it’s a footpath; the hundredth time it’s a tarmac road; the thousandth time it’s a motorway — the car gets on and, without touching the accelerator, rolls straight down it.

Research by the American psychologist Susan Nolen-Hoeksema at Stanford University also shows that “rumination” — chewing over negative events and our own feelings again and again — significantly prolongs and deepens depression, and makes it harder to solve problems. Her response styles theory (1991) has been deeply influential in psychology. Brothers and sisters, this bears out the wisdom of the Bible exactly: going over and over a hurt will not bring justice; it will only bring bondage.

So what should we do? The Bible’s answer is not “think about nothing” but “put in its place what you should think about”. 2 Corinthians 10:5 says, “throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” The phrase “bringing into captivity” carries the battlefield sense of “taking prisoner, marching a captive off”. When a thought comes, we don’t debate with it; we march it before Christ for judgement. And Philippians 4:8 gives us the replacement list: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.”

This is also the point of this lesson’s “Gentle Reminder”: learn to cut it off at the moment the thought stirs. When a train is doing three hundred kilometres an hour you can’t hold it back, but while it’s still standing at the platform, all you have to do is not get on. In Walter Mischel’s famous marshmallow experiments at Stanford University in the 1970s, the children who were able to delay gratification often did it not by “trying harder to hold out” but by “turning their attention elsewhere” — covering the sweet, singing, looking somewhere else. Spiritual warfare is the same: don’t stare at the temptation and wrestle with it; turn to Christ.

The 321 vision puts it very clearly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. For the direction of the “heart” determines the outcome of a whole life. The 321 vision also says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When your focus is on the person who hurt you, your heart is controlled by him; when your focus turns to Jesus, your heart is won by the Lord. The same event, seen from man’s point of view, is an injustice; from God’s point of view, it is building us up. From the earthly point of view it is a loss; from heaven’s point of view it is treasure stored up. From the temporary point of view it is humiliation; from the eternal point of view it is glory. Turn the point of view, and the heart turns with it.

Brothers and sisters, this is the battlefield every morning. What was your first thought when you woke up today? To whom did you hand your heart? If we let our thoughts control our hearts, the heart goes bad — and that is where every problem begins. But if every morning we realign our hearts with God, everything in that day will be different.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From a Self-Centred Heart to a Selfless Heart
sections.html:
Put these three key points side by side, and we see the road of life the 321 vision speaks of.

The Three Foundations remind us how the heart is to be built. Jesus is my role model: the Lord’s heart was turned wholly towards the Father; he said, “I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The Bible is my standard: a heart without a standard will follow its feelings; God’s word is the light that shines into the deepest places. The Holy Spirit is my guide: the renewal of the heart does not come by willpower but by the Holy Spirit. Ezekiel 36:26 says, “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” God doesn’t repair the old heart; he gives a new one.

The Two Core Values show us whom the heart belongs to. Let Jesus be King — the heart has room for only one throne; if he isn’t sitting on it, I am. Saul’s tragedy was that he would not come down off the throne. Let Jesus receive all the glory — Ananias’s tragedy was that he wanted a share of the glory. The throne of the heart and the glory are something we must decide afresh every day.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. God’s system does not begin with organisation; it begins with hearts renewed one by one. When the heart is right, the home will be right; when the home is right, the church will be right.

The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The three key points of this lesson are really three faces of the self-centred life. First, the self-centred life shows itself as evil thoughts, because I have put myself at the centre, and anyone who gets in my way becomes my enemy. Second, the self-centred life shows itself as disguise, because I want to keep up a self-image that people approve of, so I use behaviour to cover my motives. Third, the self-centred life shows itself as control, because I don’t trust God to arrange things, so I rely on the brain and keep calculating, tying my heart up in anxiety.

And “selflessness” does not mean wiping yourself out, or becoming someone with no feelings and no views. Selflessness means no longer having myself at the centre, so that Christ can be the centre. It is not becoming nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. Paul puts it most clearly: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; those five “I will”s are the prototype of pride. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Think about it: when you condemn someone in your heart, your relationship begins to sour; when you bless that person in your heart, the wall begins to loosen. The heart is the source of our relationships.

The fivefold change stands out especially clearly in this lesson: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The mindset we need to change today is this — the problem is not outside, it is inside. Once that mindset changes, our life begins to change; when our life changes, the way we respond in daily living changes; when daily living changes, our relationships change; and when our relationships change, our ministry finally bears real fruit. Reverse the order, and we will get a great deal done without any real life.

The priority of relationships reminds us too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Most people turn the order round: first busy with things, then dealing with people, then reluctantly facing themselves, and only at the very end thinking of God. And so the heart grows busier and busier, harder and harder. This lesson calls us to put the order right again: the first thing every morning is to hand our heart to God.

For practice, this lesson is especially suited to 920. 920 says that every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; with that person we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23): not one of the nine is a behavioural technique; every one is fruit of the heart. While I still hold bitterness in my heart towards that person, however polite I am to him I will bear no fruit; when my heart has been won by the Lord, the fruit grows naturally.

And don’t forget the relationships of 235: with a selfless person, become a “2” — spiritual companions to each other, keeping watch over one another; within the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, be shepherded and shepherd others; and in the end become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. The lessons of the heart are never learned by hiding away on your own. You need a companion who can tell you the truth, because the thing we see least clearly is our own heart.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use the 321 vision’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into practice one by one.

Practice 1: quiet reflection. Set aside ten minutes each day to be quiet before God. Ask the Lord to shine his light so that you can see the true state of your heart, whether it’s pride, bitterness, fear or lust.

Information: first receive today’s truth — every problem begins in the heart. Revelation: don’t stop at having read it; ask the Holy Spirit to point out in you that name, that incident, that image. Conviction: when the light comes, don’t argue; say, “Yes, Lord, I admit it.” Implementation: today, fix a regular ten minutes and write down what the Lord has shown you. Evaluation: in the evening look back — in those ten minutes was I really quiet, or was I just scrolling on my phone? Correction: if you can’t manage ten minutes, start with three, but don’t skip it. Repetition: keep it up for twenty-one days in a row until it becomes a habit. Multiplication: take this practice to your “2”; invite a companion to do it with you, and report back to each other.

Practice 2: a prayer for a renewed mind. Read Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” Entrust your thoughts and intentions to God, and ask the Holy Spirit to help you be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you are not controlled by the desires in your head.

Information: understand that “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is, in the original, continuous and passive — it isn’t that I change myself; it’s that I let God change me. Revelation: ask the Lord to show you which clip your mind replays most often. Conviction: admit that the replay is not harmless. Implementation: every time it appears, replace it at once with a verse — for example Philippians 4:8, or Psalm 51:10: “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” Evaluation: after a week, count — how many times did it come this week? How many times did I cut it off? Correction: if you’re always attacked at a certain time or in a certain setting, change that time and that setting. Repetition: memorise the verse until you know it better than the clip. Multiplication: share with someone which verse helped you.

Practice 3: practise obedience that “relies on the heart”. The next time you are going to serve God, give, or make any decision of faith, first ask yourself: is this coming from the heart? Or from pressure, habit or fear?

Information: understand that God looks at motive more than behaviour (1 Samuel 15:22). Revelation: ask the Lord to shine a light on what really drives your service — is it love, the fear of being looked down on, or the wish to be praised? Conviction: once you have admitted it, don’t immediately resign from your service; hand your motive over to the Lord. Implementation: before every decision, be quiet for thirty seconds and ask these two questions: who is King? Who gets the glory? Evaluation: when this week did I say yes out of pressure? Correction: learn to say honestly, “I need to pray about it first,” instead of agreeing reluctantly and then complaining. Repetition: make “check the heart first” the fixed routine for your decisions. Multiplication: model this honesty in your small group, so that others dare to be honest too.

A Gentle Reminder: Cut It Off the Moment the Thought Stirs

Don’t make light of evil thoughts in your heart that have not yet been acted on; God looks at the heart rather than the outward appearance. When we think that “just thinking about it” doesn’t matter, that is precisely where corruption begins. Learn to cut it off at the moment the thought stirs — that is what truly overcoming temptation means.

The easiest moment to put out a fire is while it’s still a single match. Once the whole floor is ablaze, the cost is altogether different. Satan doesn’t set out to make you fall at the start; all he wants is for you to “take one more look, think about it one more time, replay it once more”. That is why the Lord Jesus taught us to pray, “Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:13).

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Reign as King in My Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we have taken a rather uncomfortable journey. The Lord Jesus’ scalpel has laid open the root of sin, stripped away the disguise of behaviour, and dealt with the erosion of our thinking. But please remember: when the Lord operates, it is never to condemn; it is to heal.

God does not want an outward piety; he wants a heart that he has won. Every problem begins in the “heart”, and only in the “heart” can it be solved. Man looks at the outward appearance; God looks at the heart. We wipe the mirror; God washes our face. This is the good news of the gospel: we don’t have to wash our hearts clean before we dare to come. We bring this soiled heart to him and let him wash it, let him exchange it. He has promised, “I will also give you a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).

At the opening of his Confessions Augustine says, “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Our hearts were made for God, so nothing but God can fill them. We try to fill them with achievement, with relationships, with shopping, with busyness, and in the end they are still empty. Because there is only One worthy to sit in that place.

So today’s call is very simple: let Jesus be King. Not one item on your calendar, not an adviser to your life, but King — seated on the throne of your heart, ruling your thoughts, your emotions, your motives, your decisions. And let him receive all the glory; keep not a scrap of it back for yourself.

The Lord Jesus said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). May we pray like this every day: Lord, my heart belongs to you; reign as King within me.

keyVerses: Mark 7:20–23 (World English Bible)

“He said, ‘That which proceeds out of the man, that defiles the man. For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts, covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and defile the man.’”
declarations: Lord, I give my heart to you. I will not let my thoughts rule me, I will not let my emotions control me; I will let you alone be the Lord of my heart!
practices: Quiet reflection
A prayer for a renewed mind
Practise obedience that “relies on the heart”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You don’t see as man sees; you look at the heart. You are not fooled by our surface, and you love us so much that you are willing to show us the deepest truth about ourselves.

Lord, I confess that I often look outside for the answer, blaming my circumstances and blaming others, yet refusing to face my own heart. I confess too that I have used right behaviour to cover wrong motives, and busy service to hide the emptiness inside. And I confess above all that I have let my thoughts replay hurts and replay desires, letting my heart grow harder day by day.

As the prayer of Psalm 51 asks, create in me a clean heart and renew a right spirit within me. Take away the stony heart out of my flesh and give me a heart of flesh. May the Holy Spirit be my guide, teaching me to rely on the heart and not the brain; may your word be my standard, so that I can cut a thought off the moment it stirs; may the Lord Jesus be my role model, so that I live out a selfless life.
Lord, today I give the throne of my heart back to you. Reign as King within me, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Mark 7:21 says, “For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts.” Take a quiet minute to think back to the last time something made you angry or hurt you. Whom did you blame at the time? If you turn your focus from your circumstances and other people back to your own heart, what do you see?

1 Samuel 15:22 says, “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” In your present service or giving, is there anything that actually comes from pressure, habit or the wish to be affirmed? How are you willing to hand the motive behind it over to the Lord this week?

l024.subtitle: Every Problem Starts in the Heart, and Only in the Heart Can It Be Solved

sections.heading: Introduction: That Day, They Forgot to Ask Counsel of Yahweh
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

I want to take you back first to a morning more than three thousand years ago.

The Israelites had just crossed the Jordan. Jericho had fallen, and Ai had been taken. The whole land of Canaan was shaking. Just then a group of visitors arrived. Their clothes were in rags, the sandals on their feet were worn out and patched, and the bread they carried was dry and mouldy. They said to Joshua: we have come from a very distant country; we heard of the fame of Yahweh your God, and we have come on purpose to make peace.

How did Joshua judge the matter? He looked. He touched. The leaders of Israel even tasted that dry bread. He used every power of observation and reasoning a commander of his day could use. On the evidence, the conclusion was perfectly reasonable: these men really had come from far away. So the leaders of Israel made a covenant with them and swore an oath to let them live.

Then the Bible writes a sentence so short it sends a chill through you: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth” (Joshua 9:14).

Brothers and sisters, notice that Joshua committed no great moral sin. He wasn’t greedy, he wasn’t immoral, he didn’t worship idols. He simply — relied on the brain and not the heart. He simply analysed the situation, felt he had thought it through, and so saw no need to ask God. Three days later the truth came out: those men lived right next door. That mistaken covenant followed Israel for centuries; even in the reign of David they were still paying the bill.

One failure to ask, and centuries of entanglement.

That is what we are going to talk about today.

Brothers and sisters, we often say we should do things “with our heart”, but in practice we far more often “work it out in our heads”. In the life of faith, the key is not how much we know or how much we think, but whether our heart is right before God.

Have you noticed something strange? When people do evil, it nearly always starts with a plan in the head. A lie needs its story worked out first; a theft needs its route worked out first; a betrayal needs its excuse worked out first. No one writes a letter designed to set people against each other “by accident”. Evil is very often the product of careful planning.

But what about the deeds that truly please God? The widow who dropped two small coins into the offering box did no financial planning. Mary, who broke the alabaster jar, did no return-on-investment analysis. The Samaritan saw a wounded man on the road, and the Bible says he “was moved with compassion” — his heart was moved first, and only then did he move into action.

Let me give you a modern scene.

A husband and wife argued for three months over whether to change jobs. The husband made a spreadsheet of salary, commute, pension and the children’s school catchment; the wife made another spreadsheet of the risks, her parents’ health and their service at church. The two spreadsheets lay on the dinner table; figure by figure they checked, reason by reason they argued, and neither could win the other over. Three months went by. The job hadn’t changed, but their hearts had already gone cold towards each other.

Until one evening the husband put the spreadsheets away and said one sentence: we haven’t prayed together for three months. They reached no conclusion at all that night, but when the two of them knelt down together, the tears came. A week later the answer surfaced of its own accord — and both of them had peace about it.

Brothers and sisters, do you see? When two heads reason against each other, the result is usually that both lose; when two hearts turn together towards God, the result is often that both win. This is exactly what the 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to ask you to put a question to yourself — and I suggest you carry it with you for a whole week:

Right now, am I relying on the heart, or relying on the brain?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Father’s Words Before His Son Leaves Home
sections.html:
To understand Proverbs 4:23, we first have to step into its setting.

The main author of Proverbs is Solomon. 1 Kings 4:32 records that “he spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs numbered one thousand five.” Solomon reigned from about 970 to 930 BC, and the contents of Proverbs took shape mainly in that period. Later, in the days of King Hezekiah (the late eighth century BC), Hezekiah’s men copied out and added a further section (Proverbs 25:1).

Proverbs is not a book of law, nor a book of prophecy. It belongs to the Old Testament’s “wisdom literature”. Wisdom literature has little to say about Mount Sinai with its thunder and lightning; it talks about the kitchen, the field, the market and the law court. It talks about how someone who fears God can live like someone who fears God on a Tuesday morning. The Hebrew word for “wisdom” is חָכְמָה (chokmah), a word that could originally describe a craftsman’s skill. In Exodus 31, speaking of Bezalel, God says, “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship.” So biblical wisdom is not lofty theory; it is the skill of living rightly.

Proverbs 1 to 9 is one long stretch of a father’s counsel to his son, very tender in tone, with “my son” coming again and again. Chapter 4 is all the more special, because here Solomon recalls his own childhood: “For I was a son to my father, tender and an only child in the sight of my mother. He taught me, and said to me: ‘Let your heart retain my words. Keep my commandments, and live’” (Proverbs 4:3–4). Do you see it? These are words handed down through three generations. David taught Solomon, Solomon taught his son, and now, through Scripture, they teach us.

Now look at the context. Proverbs 4:20–27 is a very complete paragraph, like a full-body health check:

“My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings. Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and health to their whole body. Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life. Put away from yourself a perverse mouth. Put corrupt lips far from you. Let your eyes look straight ahead. Fix your gaze directly before you. Make the path of your feet level. Let all of your ways be established. Don’t turn to the right hand nor to the left. Remove your foot from evil.” (Proverbs 4:20–27)

Ears, eyes, heart, mouth, feet — five parts of the body. Did you notice where the heart is placed? Right in the middle. Before it come the ears and eyes, the channels through which everything comes in; after it come the mouth and feet, the channels through which everything goes out — our words and our actions. The heart sits in the middle, the master switch.

That is why Solomon says “with all diligence” — above all else. Guard the heart, and you have guarded everything; lose the heart, and however tightly you control your mouth, however closely you watch your steps, you are only building embankments downstream.

Now look at two key words.

“Keep” is the Hebrew נָצַר (natsar), whose basic meaning is “to watch, to guard, to keep watch over” — a military term, the action of standing sentry. The word order of the original is even stronger: “More than all guarding, guard your heart.” And the word behind “all diligence”, “all guarding”, is מִשְׁמָר (mishmar), which means “a guard post” and can also mean “a prison” — in Genesis 40, when the cupbearer and the baker were put “in custody in the house of the captain of the guard”, it is this same root. In other words, Solomon is saying: of everything you guard in this world — your property, your reputation, your health, your future — none of it, all added together, needs you standing sentry day and night as much as one thing does: your heart.

“Wellspring” is the Hebrew תּוֹצָאוֹת (totsa’ot), meaning “outlet, source, the place where water flows out”. In the book of Joshua the word is often used for the point where a boundary “goes out” to some place. So the picture in this sentence is this: your heart is a spring, and every river of your whole life flows out of that spring.

There is one more thing worth noticing. From beginning to end Proverbs 4 talks about “the way” — “the way of wisdom” (4:11), “the path of the righteous” (4:18), “the way of the wicked” (4:19). Solomon talks about the way, and the way, and the way, and then at verse 23 he suddenly turns inward to talk about the heart. Why? Because the direction of the way is decided by the heart. People don’t take the wrong road first and then have a change of heart; they have a change of heart first and then take the wrong road.

Brothers and sisters, this is the foundation of the whole lesson. It’s not that God doesn’t care what you do; it’s that God cares about your heart first. For if the spring is bad, nothing can save the whole river downstream.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Make Decisions with the Brain, and the Heart Goes Bad
1. Whoever Relies on the Brain for Everything Easily Doubts God and Resists Him
sections.html:
“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

Notice that this verse does not say “don’t use your understanding”; it says “don’t lean on your own understanding”. “Lean” is the Hebrew שָׁעַן (sha’an): to put your whole weight on something, to rest against it. When Samson, at the very end, asked to feel the pillars on which the house rested, “that I may lean on them” (Judges 16:26), this is the very word: that is the action of leaning. The problem has never been that we have brains; the problem is that we put the whole weight of our person on our own brains.

Humanity’s first fall was a fall of relying on the brain.

The serpent said to the woman, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). And then the Bible records: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6).

Look at what Eve did. She carried out a complete assessment. Nutritional value — good for food. Sensory experience — a delight to the eyes. Self-improvement — to be desired to make one wise. All three indicators passed; the data was flawless. Her analysis wasn’t wrong, but her conclusion was fatal. For the tree was called “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” — to eat it meant that from then on she would use her own head to judge what is good and what is evil, and no longer look to the mouth of God.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. Relying on the brain and on ourselves is, at bottom, the self-centred life — I want to judge for myself, I want to be in charge, I don’t need to ask God. And once people are used to judging for themselves, the heart hardens inch by inch.

“A man’s heart plans his course, but Yahweh directs his steps.” (Proverbs 16:9) “There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.” (Proverbs 14:12) Notice: that way “seems right to a man”. Not an obviously crooked road, but a road that looks very straight. That is what makes it most dangerous.

sections.heading: 2. Evil Is Often the Product of Careful Planning
sections.html:
The lesson puts it accurately: many sins, such as lying, stealing and crime, are often committed only after careful planning and analysis in the head.

David is a living example. In 2 Samuel 11, David saw Bathsheba — and then what? First he “sent and inquired after the woman”; then he sent for her; then he wrote summoning Uriah back; then he laid on a meal and got him drunk; and finally he wrote that deadly letter and put it in Uriah’s own hand to carry back to the front. Every step was calculated, every step was logical, every step was a masterpiece of the brain. Even a man after God’s own heart could use his brain to push himself that far.

Genesis 6:5 says, “Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.” “Imagination” is the Hebrew יֵצֶר (yetser), whose basic meaning is “something a potter shapes”. In other words, the human heart is like a workshop, moulding, designing and devising day and night. In the generation before the Flood, everything that workshop turned out was evil.

Jeremiah saw even more deeply: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9).

sections.heading: 3. Supporting Evidence from Psychology: Reason Is Often Just the Defence Lawyer After the Fact
sections.html:
In 2001 the social psychologist Jonathan Haidt published a well-known paper entitled “The Emotional Dog and Its Rational Tail”. He proposed the “social intuitionist model”: in moral judgement, people often reach a conclusion first, and reason then catches up to find arguments for that conclusion. He used a picture — we think reason is the master and emotion the pet; in fact it’s more like the dog walking along with the tail wagging behind.

Earlier still, in 1957, Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when people’s behaviour doesn’t match their beliefs, they mostly don’t change their behaviour; they rewrite their beliefs so they can feel at ease.

Brothers and sisters, these two findings are really saying the same thing — our brains are extremely good at one job: finding a respectable way to describe what we already wanted to do.

So you hear sentences like these: “It’s not that I won’t forgive him; I’m waiting for the right moment.” “It’s not that I don’t give; I’m doing responsible financial planning.” “It’s not that I don’t come to fellowship; I’m keeping time free for my family.” Every one sounds smooth; every one makes sense. But brothers and sisters, smooth is not the same as acceptable to God.

Paul said it long ago: “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3). Even giving your body to be burned can profit nothing — if the heart is wrong.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight: Rely on the Brain, and You’ll Be Troubled
sections.html:
The 321 vision has a saying that captures it perfectly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

Why does relying on the brain bring trouble? Because the brain’s job is to calculate risks, project consequences and weigh gains against losses. The more you rely on the brain, the more variables you see; the more variables, the less you dare to move; the less you dare to move, the more anxious you become. It’s a downhill road, and you slide faster and faster.

What’s more, the focus of someone who relies on the brain is bound to drift. The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. But once you start calculating with your brain, your focus inevitably lands on yourself (will I lose out?), on others (what is he really up to?), on circumstances (is this the right moment?). The moment the focus leaves Jesus, the heart begins to go bad — not overnight, but a little colder each day, a little harder each day.

The lesson uses three words to describe the heart after relying on the brain: cold, rigid, drifting from God. The three come in order.

First, cold. The prayers are still there, only shorter; the meetings are still there, only now they’re appointments in the diary. You haven’t left; you’re just no longer moved.

Then, rigid. When someone gives you a word of caution, your first reaction is to defend yourself, not to examine yourself. You become quick to justify yourself — and very convincing at it.

Finally, drifting from God. By this stage people are often still serving, still preaching, still leading a small group. Outside, everything carries on as before; inside, the master has changed. That was Saul — right up to his death, he was still king of Israel.

Brothers and sisters, the heart doesn’t go bad suddenly. The heart cools slowly. Like a cup of hot tea left on the table: nobody pushes it, and it goes cold all by itself. To keep your heart is not to let it go cold by itself.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Make Choices with the Heart, and the Heart Will Be Kept
1. What Does It Mean to “Rely on the Heart”?
sections.html:
Let’s be clear first, so there’s no misunderstanding.

The “heart” the Bible speaks of, the Hebrew לֵב (lev), is not the same as what we mean today by “emotions”. In the Hebrew mindset the heart is the hub of the inner person, taking in reason, emotion and will — the whole inner self. So the Bible never tells us not to think. Psalm 119 says, “I will meditate on your precepts”; Paul says, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2); the Lord Jesus says, “you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Mark 12:30) — and “with all your mind” means bringing every thought we have to bear.

So what is the “relying on the brain” this lesson speaks of? It is reason that has left God, running independently, self-sufficient — the thinking of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And what is “relying on the heart”? It is the whole person — my reason included — surrendered before God, letting the Holy Spirit move and guide.

That is why the 321 vision says: let the heart control the brain; don’t let the brain control the heart. The brain is a very good servant but a very bad master. God gave us brains to serve love with them, not to replace love with them.

The lesson says: “When we act by ‘relying on the heart’, we let the heart obey the prompting of the Holy Spirit and let love be the starting point of what we do.” That sentence is the key to the whole lesson.

sections.heading: 2. Jesus is my role model: That One Sentence in Gethsemane
sections.html:
In the Garden of Gethsemane our Lord made the most important choice of “relying on the heart” in human history.

“He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.’” (Matthew 26:39)

Brothers and sisters, if the Lord had analysed it with his brain that night, what would the conclusion have been? The disciples were not yet fully trained, the gospel had not yet reached the Gentiles, the Jews badly needed a leader, and he was thirty-three, in the prime of life. By any calculation, the cross was the worst possible deal. But the Lord did no calculating. He said only this: not what I desire, but what you desire.

This is selflessness. The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. The cross looked like total defeat, yet three days later it brought eternal victory.

Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5).

sections.heading: 3. Love with the Heart, Worship with the Heart, Obey with the Heart
sections.html:
The lesson lists three things: loving others needs the heart, worship needs the heart, obedience needs the heart. Let’s look at them one at a time.

First, love others with the heart. “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). “Cheerful” in the original is ἱλαρός (hilaros), the root of the English word “hilarious” — not squeezed out under duress, but given with joy. It isn’t that God can’t get hold of the money; God wants the heart.

Second, worship with the heart. The Lord Jesus said, “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). He also quoted Isaiah to rebuke the religious people of his day: “These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15:8). Brothers and sisters, the lips can be present while the heart is absent. Our morning devotion is the same — the body may be sitting in front of the screen, but the heart is not necessarily there.

Third, obey with the heart. “To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). Saul kept back the fattest sheep and cattle, and his reason sounded noble: they were to be sacrificed to Yahweh. What a reasonable story! But God didn’t want sheep and cattle; God wanted a heart willing to listen.

sections.heading: 4. One Alabaster Jar, Two Ways of Counting
sections.html:
There is a scene in the Gospels that sets “relying on the heart” and “relying on the brain” in the same room, and the contrast is breathtaking.

Six days before the Passover, in Bethany, “Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12:3).

Mary didn’t say a word. She simply poured out the most precious thing she had, all at once.

Immediately someone in the room started doing the sums: “Why wasn’t this ointment sold for three hundred denarii, and given to the poor?” (John 12:5). Those words came from the mouth of Judas. Brothers and sisters, be honest — how reasonable that sounds! Care for the poor, concern for effectiveness, sensible allocation of resources. On the balance sheet, Judas was right; in the heart, Judas was the furthest from Jesus.

What did the Lord say? “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for me” (Mark 14:6). And he added, “She has done what she could” (Mark 14:8).

Brothers and sisters, “She has done what she could” — those few words are heaven’s highest commendation of a heart. Mary didn’t make the cleverest choice; she made the choice that loved the Lord most. And the fragrance filled the whole house.

Those who rely on the brain count how much the ointment is worth; those who rely on the heart know only that the Lord is worth it.

sections.heading: 5. An Example from Daily Life, and Some Supporting Evidence from Science
sections.html:
Let me describe a very small scene.

A sister made breakfast for her husband every day. One day she realised she hadn’t really “looked at” that breakfast for a long time — while frying the egg she was planning the day’s schedule in her head; while pouring the milk she was thinking about the messages she had to answer. The task got done, but the love didn’t get passed on. So she began to practise one thing: for the two minutes it took to fry the egg each day, she thought about nothing else and simply prayed one sentence for her husband. The egg was the same egg, she said, but the warmth of that home changed.

Brothers and sisters, the same task done relying on the brain is a chore; done relying on the heart, it is an act of love.

In his 1994 book Descartes’ Error, the neuroscientist Antonio Damasio describes a patient he calls Elliot. Surgery for a brain tumour had damaged his ventromedial prefrontal cortex. His IQ scores were still normal, his logical reasoning still intact, his memory unimpaired. Yet his life fell apart — he could not make decisions. Choosing a pen, he could analyse for ages; fixing an appointment, he could list endless reasons for comparison and still not decide. The reason: the link between emotion and value had been severed. Damasio therefore argued that pure reason is simply not enough for people to make good decisions.

Brothers and sisters, this is only supporting evidence; the Bible is our standard. But it is an interesting piece of evidence: even medicine tells us that a person left with nothing but the brain cannot really live.

The philosopher Pascal left a famous line in his Pensées: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” He himself was one of the foremost mathematicians of the seventeenth century, writing a treatise on conic sections at the age of sixteen. Yet this man, so skilled at using his brain, after his famous “Night of Fire” in 1654, sewed into the lining of his coat the parchment on which he had written, “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars”, and carried it with him for the rest of his life.

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: Rely on the Heart, and You’ll Be Glad
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. This is the third of the Three Foundations — the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Zechariah 4:6: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Might” and “power” are good things, but they cannot replace the Holy Spirit.

The 321 vision also says: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. The moment we rely on the brain, the order is reversed — first we think how to handle the “thing”, then how to manage the “people”, then we think about ourselves, and last of all about God, and often only once things have gone wrong. Those who rely on the heart have the order right: first be quiet before God; when the heart is right, the people fall into place, and the thing naturally finds a way forward.

So how does “letting the heart control the brain” work in daily life? Let me offer three very simple questions you can ask before any decision:

The first question: have I asked God? Not “I’ve thought about what God would think”, but really stopping, getting quiet, and asking him out loud. This is the very question on which Joshua failed.

The second question: is there love in this? If you take love out, what is left of this decision? If all that’s left is self-interest, then wait a little longer.

The third question: once it’s done, who will get the glory? If deep down I’m secretly hoping for other people’s praise, then however fine the decision, it was made relying on the brain.

Brothers and sisters, these three questions take less than three minutes, yet they can save you three years of wasted road.

Behaviour that truly pleases God is not the cleverest choice; it is the most obedient response.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Outcome of a Whole Life Flows from the Heart
1. Back to Our Key Verse
sections.html:
“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

This verse points to the core of faith — not what we do, but who we are; not how much fruit we produce, but whether the starting point of our heart is right.

The Lord Jesus made this truth very plain: “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45). And again: “For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19).

So life is not a contest of behaviour; life is the outflow of a spring. You cannot let the spring grow thick with moss and expect the water downstream to be clear.

Jeremiah paints the picture more fully. Just before his words “The heart is deceitful above all things”, the prophet says: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit” (Jeremiah 17:7–8).

Brothers and sisters, look at this tree. It doesn’t bear fruit because the weather is good; it bears fruit because its roots are by the water. Heat will come, drought will come — that is certain; but if the roots are in the right place, the fruit won’t fail.

And where the roots go down is decided by the heart. The “outcome” is the visible branches and leaves; the “heart” is the invisible root. We spend too much time pruning the branches and too little caring for the root.

sections.heading: 2. Two Kings: David and Saul
sections.html:
The lesson places David and Saul side by side, and the contrast carries great weight.

Outwardly, Saul was beyond reproach. 1 Samuel 9 calls him “an impressive young man; and there was not among the children of Israel a better person than he. From his shoulders and upward he was taller than any of the people.” He did religious things too — he offered sacrifice (1 Samuel 13:9), he built an altar (1 Samuel 14:35), he kept back the best of the sheep and cattle to sacrifice to God (1 Samuel 15:15).

Where did the problem lie? In the heart. Through Samuel, God said to him: “For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king” (1 Samuel 15:23).

More telling still is the way Saul admitted his wrong. First he said, “I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of Yahweh, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice” (1 Samuel 15:24) — shifting the blame even as he confessed. Then he said, “I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel” (1 Samuel 15:30) — what he cared about most was still saving face. Brothers and sisters, that is repentance that relies on the brain.

And David? In terms of what he did, David’s sin was far worse than Saul’s — adultery, and murder on top of it. Yet the moment the prophet Nathan said, “You are the man,” David said at once, “I have sinned against Yahweh” (2 Samuel 12:13). No explanation, no shifting of blame, no conditions. Then he wrote Psalm 51: “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart” (Psalm 51:17).

That is why God said, “Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart” (1 Samuel 13:14). The New Testament confirms it: “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will” (Acts 13:22).

Brothers and sisters, God has only ever had one standard for choosing: “I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

sections.heading: 3. The Heart Can Be Exchanged
sections.html:
At this point some of you may be feeling heavy inside: but my heart is simply hard — what can I do?

Here is the good news. God does not only require us to keep our hearts; God promises to give us a new heart: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).

What’s the difference between a heart of stone and a heart of flesh? Stone feels nothing; flesh can hurt. Only a heart that can ache over sin, ache for people, ache for what is on God’s heart, is a living heart.

This promise was fulfilled in the New Testament. Paul says, “and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5:5). “Poured” carries the sense of overflowing, of tipping out — not a few drops, but a downpour. And he prays for the Ephesian church “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love” (Ephesians 3:17).

Brothers and sisters, what great grace this is: we don’t squeeze love out of ourselves — God first pours his love into our hearts; we don’t keep a good heart by our own effort — Christ dwells in our hearts. So “keep your heart” is never a lone battle; it is working together with the One who lives within.

And David showed us how to keep this new heart: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). Brothers and sisters, keeping your heart doesn’t mean gritting your teeth and standing guard on your own; it means opening your heart every day and inviting God to search it.

sections.heading: 4. An Illustration from Science and Some Supporting Evidence from Psychology
sections.html:
The human heart beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day and never takes a day off in a lifetime. And the heart is not just a pump. In 1991 the cardiac scientist J. Andrew Armour proposed the concept of an “intrinsic cardiac nervous system”, showing that the heart itself has a network of neurons — the figure usually quoted is around forty thousand — so that it has even been called “the little brain in the heart”.

Brothers and sisters, I want to say this very carefully: this is only a physiological phenomenon and cannot be used as a basis for interpreting Scripture. The heart the Bible speaks of is not that muscle. But as an illustration it is beautiful — even in the Creator’s design, the heart does not just passively receive instructions; the heart itself can “speak”.

Psychology also has reliable observations on the practice of “keeping the heart”. In a study published in 2003, Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked participants to write down, over several weeks, things they were grateful for. This group scored clearly higher in well-being and satisfaction with life than the groups who recorded hassles or neutral events. A pen, a notebook and a few lines can change the angle from which a person sees the world.

How much more for us — what we hold in our hands is not merely a gratitude notebook; we have the word of God.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: The Fivefold Change
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Notice the order: the starting point is mindset, not ministry. We often do it backwards — to change our ministry we change our methods; to change our relationships we learn communication techniques. The result: the methods change, but the people don’t; the techniques are learned, but the heart doesn’t change.

This is exactly what Proverbs 4:23 is talking about: flowing out of the heart. The heart is where our mindset lives. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; and when relationships change, ministry naturally bears fruit.

The 321 vision also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. This is the most practical translation of “out of it is the wellspring of life”.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Let the Heart Return to Its Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s bring the 321 vision together and look at this lesson through it.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — in Gethsemane he obeyed with his heart, saying, “not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). The Bible is my standard — not my analysis, my experience, my intuition, but the word of God; whoever does not take the Bible as their standard will certainly take their own brain as their standard. The Holy Spirit is my guide — rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King: the most practical thing this lesson addresses is “who is King”. When the brain is king, the heart goes bad; when the heart lets Jesus be King, the brain returns to its proper place as a servant and becomes an instrument of love. Let Jesus receive all the glory: with things accomplished by relying on the brain, the glory often quietly shifts to ourselves; with things accomplished by relying on the heart, you know yourself that it wasn’t your own ability.
