The Goal. Establish God’s system — a system that flows out of the heart, where people love one another and let Jesus be King; not an organisation stacked up out of calculation, procedures and talent.

The self-centred life and selflessness. Relying on the brain and on ourselves is the self-centred life; relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit is selflessness. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Eve wanted to replace God’s judgement with her own — that is leaving our originally intended position. And pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Have you noticed that almost every quarrel at home starts like this: two heads each doing their own analysis, each convinced they’re right, and then both sides lose? If one person is willing to rely on the heart first, the whole situation changes at once.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

A change of viewpoint. Those who rely on the brain see what is human, earthly, temporary, worldly; those who rely on the heart see what is God’s, heavenly, eternal, godly. “‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts’” (Isaiah 55:8–9). Brothers and sisters, however brilliant our brains, they can only calculate at earth’s height; only a heart drawn close to God can reach the height of heaven.

The 920 practice. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; we practise living out the selfless (“0”) life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice that not one of these nine can be produced by relying on the brain. You can use your brain to fake patience, but you can’t fake joy; you can use your brain to put on a gentle expression, but you can’t put on real kindness. Fruit grows; it isn’t manufactured — and the fruit grows in the heart.

The relationships of 235. With a selfless person, become a “2”; build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, when you look for companions, don’t look only at gifts, ability and resources — that is choosing people by relying on the brain. God looks at the heart, and we must learn to look at the heart too.

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The first step on this path is “Spirit”. If the first step is wrong, however fast you go after that, you only end up further away.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Making “Relying on the Heart” Part of Every Day
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s place them within the 321 vision’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they are not just three good suggestions but a road we can walk to the end.

Practice 1: Reflect on the Motives Behind Your Actions

Ask yourself each day: “Was what I did today done relying on the heart, or was it just a decision calculated by the brain?” And record one thing you did today “relying on the heart” — how did it feel different?

Information: first memorise the key verse — Proverbs 4:23. Put it on your phone’s home screen or stick it on the mirror.

Revelation: as you read this verse, ask the Holy Spirit to shine a light on one specific matter. Don’t stop at having read it; let God point out, “It’s that one.”

Conviction: admit honestly — yes, I did that relying on the brain, and deep down I know it.

Implementation: today, pick one thing and deliberately do it relying on the heart.

Evaluation: in the evening spend three minutes looking back: how did the thing done relying on the heart feel inside, compared with the things done relying on the brain?

Correction: identify the situation where you most easily slip into relying on the brain — perhaps when money is discussed, perhaps when facing a particular person, perhaps when you’re criticised. Make your correction right there.

Repetition: seven days in a row. One thing a day, written down.

Multiplication: tell your “2” about this practice, do it together, and ask each other one question: did you rely on the heart today?

Practice 2: Learn to Obey from the Heart in Small Things

Start with the most ordinary actions — talking with people, handling chores, your times of prayer — and deliberately remind yourself to rely on the heart, rather than just getting by on the brain.

The Lord Jesus said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). The training of the heart has no grand occasions; the training of the heart all takes place in small things.

Make it this specific: today, when you talk with someone, look them in the eye for three seconds before you speak; today, before you reply to a message, pray one sentence for that person; today, as you do the housework, treat it as service offered to God.

Brothers and sisters, you will find that relying on the heart is actually slower — but it lasts longer. Relying on the brain runs fast, but it doesn’t run far.

Practice 3: Pour Out Your Heart to God

Use the psalms or words of prayer to pour out your heart to God. Tell him honestly what state your heart is in, and ask him to help you rely not on your own reason but on the Holy Spirit to guide your heart.

“Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us.” (Psalm 62:8) “Pour out your heart” in the original means just that — emptying the heart out, like turning a bottle completely upside down. Brothers and sisters, prayer is not giving God a briefing; prayer is turning the bottle upside down.

This week I suggest you read Psalms 51, 62 and 139, take one verse from them, put it in your own words and say it to God. Don’t polish it, don’t tidy it up; God doesn’t need a beautiful report — what God wants is a real heart.

Four Gentle Reminders from the Lesson

One: the heart is the key, not knowledge.

Two: true worship relies on the heart, not on form.

Three: the brain can help you understand, but only the heart can connect you with God.

Four: keep reminding yourself with this sentence: “Am I relying on the heart, or relying on the brain?”

Brothers and sisters, please don’t just hear these four sentences. Pick one of them and use it today.

I particularly want to explain the third one again, so that no one misunderstands: the brain can help you understand, but only the heart can connect you with God. So we are not against study, not against thinking, not against planning. Paul was one of the greatest thinkers of his age; he was educated at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and he could quote the Greek poets (Acts 17:28). But Paul said, “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ” (Philippians 3:7).

Brothers and sisters, it isn’t throwing the brain away; it’s putting the brain in its right place. When the brain kneels down, it becomes the best of servants.

Let me add one last very practical reminder: practising “relying on the heart” needs a quiet space. The human heart cannot hear God in the midst of noise. So keep this time every morning for yourself — just as we are doing now. Morning devotion is not a programme; morning devotion is a watchtower for the heart. “More than all guarding, guard your heart” — standing sentry takes a set time, a set place and discipline.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let the Heart Control the Brain
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we live in an age that exalts reason and efficiency. This age teaches us to assess, to optimise, to account for every minute. None of these is a sin in itself. But when reason takes the throne, the heart is pushed into a corner; when efficiency becomes the highest standard, love becomes a kind of waste.

So today we choose to return to God’s original intention — what he wants is our heart.

“My son, give me your heart; and let your eyes keep in my ways.” (Proverbs 23:26)

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? God didn’t say “give me your achievements”, nor did he say “give me your plans”. God said: give me your heart.

From today let’s learn together: relying on the heart brings us into line with God’s heart; relying on the brain may lead us off God’s way. From today, choose to let the heart control the brain, and let every action spring from love for God and trust in him.

Brothers and sisters, I know some of you are saying in your hearts right now: my heart has been cold for a long time — can I still go back?

I want to tell you: yes, you can. Because God has never been looking for a perfect heart; God is looking for a heart that is willing to turn back. David’s heart was broken, Peter’s heart was shattered, the prodigal son’s heart wandered very, very far — but the father was still waiting at the end of the road. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart” (Psalm 51:17). If this morning you are willing to give your heart to him again, that is a new beginning.

Let Jesus reign as King in your heart. Once the heart lets Jesus be King, the brain will grow quiet, return to where it belongs, and become a good servant of love. On that day, all that flows out of your whole life will be for his glory — because the outcome of a whole life flows from the heart.

Brothers and sisters, this morning let’s give our hearts back together. Not handing over our intelligence, but handing over our throne. Let man be man and let God be God. Let the heart control the brain, and let Jesus control the heart.

keyVerses: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

“But Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.’” (1 Samuel 16:7)
“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)
declarations: The lesson leaves us with a declaration. Please join me and say it from the heart:
I choose to love God from the heart and to act from the heart, so that the outcome of my whole life wells up from my heart!
Say it once more, a little slower, and let your heart catch up:
I choose to love God from the heart and to act from the heart, so that the outcome of my whole life wells up from my heart!
practices: Reflect on the motives behind your actions
Learn to obey from the heart in small things
Pour out your heart to God
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We come before you and confess that we are far too used to relying on the brain and far too unused to relying on the heart. We are used to analysing, calculating and assessing, yet we seldom stop to ask you: Lord, what is your will? Lord, forgive us for being like Joshua long ago — we thought things through, but we didn’t ask counsel of you.

Lord, create in me a clean heart and renew a right spirit within me. Take away the stony heart out of my flesh and give me a heart of flesh. Search me and know my heart; try me and know my thoughts; see if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.

Lord, teach me to keep my heart above all else. Teach me to rely on the heart in small things, in my words, in loving others, in worship and in obedience. May the Holy Spirit guide me every day, so that I do not lean on my own understanding but trust in you with all my heart.

I am willing to let you reign as King in my heart. I am willing to let the heart control the brain, and no longer let the brain control the heart. May everything that flows out of my whole life glorify your name.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth.” (Joshua 9:14) Think back over the past month: was there something you “thought through and then just went ahead with”, without first asking God? How did it turn out? If you could do it again, at which step would you stop and pray first?

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) In your life right now, which situation or which relationship most easily makes your heart grow cold and hard? This week, what specific action will you take in that situation to “rely on the heart” rather than “rely on the brain”?
l025.title: Let the Heart Govern the Brain
l025.subtitle: Rely on the Heart and the Heart Stays Good; Rely on the Brain and the Heart Goes Bad
l025.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: The Morning a Prophet Misjudged
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the peace of the Lord come upon you this morning.

Let’s begin by going back three thousand years, to an ordinary morning in Bethlehem.

The old prophet Samuel, a horn of anointing oil in his hand and the dust of the road still on him, walks into this little town. The elders of the town come out to meet him, trembling, and ask him, “Do you come in peace?” Samuel says, “In peace.” Then he invites Jesse and his sons to come with him to the sacrifice.

The door opens, and the firstborn, Eliab, walks in. Scripture doesn’t spend a single extra word on it; it simply records what happened in Samuel’s heart: “When they had come, he looked at Eliab, and said, ‘Surely Yahweh’s anointed is before him.’” (1 Samuel 16:6)

Brothers and sisters, notice that phrase — the Chinese Union Version reads, “he said in his heart.” Samuel wasn’t making small talk; he had reached a verdict inside himself. And he reached it very fast — so fast that Scripture doesn’t even have time to record a conversation. One look, and the matter was settled.

What did Eliab have going for him? He was tall, he was handsome, he was the firstborn, the face of the family. From a human point of view, if a man like that doesn’t become king, who will?

But then God spoke. His answer was like a bucket of cold water, and also like a shaft of light: “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

That sentence was the most important sentence of that morning, and it is the most important sentence of our devotion this morning too.

Notice who it was spoken to. Not to a brand-new believer, not to someone spiritually immature, but to Samuel — the great prophet who had served in the tabernacle since childhood, who had heard God’s voice all his life, who had anointed Israel’s very first king. Even Samuel could misjudge. Even Samuel needed God to remind him: you are looking at the outward appearance; I am looking at the heart.

And what about us?

Brothers and sisters, every single day we are “looking.” We look at people’s degrees, their job titles, their incomes, their clothes, the number of likes on their Facebook posts. In church we “look” as well — at whose prayers are longer, at who gives more, at who stands on the platform and who sits in the corner. We even turn that same gaze on ourselves: I’m not good enough, I’m not capable enough, I have no gifts, I probably don’t even rank in God’s eyes.

But God says: I don’t see as man sees.

In this lesson we are going to face together a truth that cuts deeper than almost any other, and sets us freer than almost any other: God looks at the heart. It cuts deep, because before God we cannot pretend; it sets us free, because before God we don’t need to. We will look at it from three angles: first, God does not look at outward appearance, only at the heart; second, if the heart is right, the deeds will be right, and if the heart is wrong, even the rightest deeds are useless; third, how to discern the state of the heart — seeing the essence by its fruit.

sections.heading: 1. Scripture Background: The History Behind a Horn of Oil
sections.html:
To really hear 1 Samuel 16:7, we first need to stand inside that piece of history.

In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Samuel were originally a single book, counted among the “Former Prophets.” Jewish tradition holds that Samuel was the main recorder, and that the part after Samuel’s death was continued by the prophet Nathan and the prophet Gad. That view rests on 1 Chronicles 29:29: “Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the history of Samuel the seer, and in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the history of Gad the seer.” The book is generally thought to have reached its final form after the kingdom divided and before the exile, written for a people who were asking, “How did Israel end up where it is today?”

The central question the book sets out to answer is this: what kind of king is the king God wants?

Here is the background. The Israelites were dissatisfied with God’s rule through judges and prophets, and they demanded, “Make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” (1 Samuel 8:5) “Like all the nations” — those few words are the root of the problem. What they wanted was not God’s system but the system of the nations; not a king after God’s own heart, but a king who looked like a king.

So God gave them Saul. What kind of man was Saul? Scripture describes him in detail: “an impressive young man; and there was not among the children of Israel a better person than he. From his shoulders and upward he was taller than any of the people.” (1 Samuel 9:2) Brothers and sisters, that was exactly the people’s specification sheet for a “king”: tall, handsome, imposing. Saul met every requirement.

And the result? Saul failed twice at the critical moment. The first time was at Gilgal: unable to wait any longer for Samuel, he offered the burnt offering on his own authority, and the prophet said to him, “But now your kingdom will not continue. Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and Yahweh has appointed him to be prince over his people.” (1 Samuel 13:14) The second time was the campaign against the Amalekites. God had commanded that everything be utterly destroyed, but Saul spared King Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle — and claimed he meant to sacrifice them to Yahweh. Samuel answered him with words that have echoed down the ages: “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22)

By the end of chapter 15, Saul has been rejected. Chapter 16 opens with God saying to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.” (1 Samuel 16:1)

So 16:7 is not an isolated proverb; it is the turning point of the whole book. Here God declares: last time I gave you a king according to your way of seeing, and you saw how that turned out; this time I will choose, according to my way of seeing, a man after my own heart.

There is one word here that deserves our close attention. 1 Samuel 15:23 says, “Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.” 16:1 says, “I have rejected him,” and in 16:7 the Chinese Union Version has God say, “I have not chosen him.” In all three places, the word for “reject” is the same Hebrew word — מָאַס (ma’as), meaning to refuse, to disdain, to cast away. In other words, the Hebrew of 16:7 is far blunter than “I have not chosen him”: it says, as the World English Bible renders it, “I have rejected him.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see the thread? Saul rejected God’s word, so God rejected Saul; Eliab was a fine figure of a man, yet God said, “I have rejected him.” From beginning to end, God’s choosing had nothing to do with height, nothing to do with looks, nothing to do with birth order. God wanted only one thing: the heart.

In the end, the one God chose was David, the youngest son, out in the wilderness keeping the sheep — so overlooked that his own father hadn’t even called him home. “Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the middle of his brothers. Then Yahweh’s Spirit came mightily on David from that day forward.” (1 Samuel 16:13)

A boy his own family had left out was remembered by God. Because God looks at the heart.

sections.heading: 2. God Does Not Look at Outward Appearance, Only at the Heart
sections.html:
1. Two Ways of Seeing, Two Worlds

Let’s read our key verse once more: “For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

The original uses two key words here. “Outward appearance” is מַרְאֶה (mar’eh), whose root is simply “to see”; it means what is seen — the look, the exterior, the image a person presents. And “heart” is לֵבָב (lebab).

Brothers and sisters, it’s worth pausing to explain this: the “heart” in the Bible is not quite what we usually mean by the word. When we speak of the heart, we lean towards the emotions — heartbroken, light-hearted, heart-stirred. But the Hebrew “heart” is the central control room of the whole person: it takes in our thoughts, our will, our motives, our conscience and our choices. When God says he looks at a person’s “heart,” he doesn’t only mean “I know how you feel.” He means, “I know what you really think, I know your real motives, and I know what you will decide when no one is watching.”

So this verse is really contrasting two worlds. Man lives in the world of appearances; God lives in the world of what is real. Man sees the résumé; God sees the motive. Man sees the stage; God sees backstage. Man sees the photograph; God sees the heartbeat.

The writer of Hebrews puts it even more piercingly: “There is no creature that is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open before the eyes of him to whom we must give an account.” (Hebrews 4:13) The word for “laid open,” τραχηλίζω (trachēlizō), carries the picture of a neck bent back and wholly exposed. Before God we have no good side, no filter, no retouching.

2. Scripture Interprets Scripture: What Is Real Is Done Within

The lesson text links this passage to Romans 2, and the connection is exactly right. Here is what it says: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, neither is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit not in the letter; whose praise is not from men, but from God.” (Romans 2:28–29)

Paul is performing major surgery here. For the Jews, circumcision was their identity card — the visible proof, the evidence that “I belong to God.” But Paul says that if the sign never reaches the heart, it is merely “the letter” — in the original γράμμα (gramma), meaning “what is written.” The letter is there; the life is not.

Pay special attention to the last phrase: “whose praise is not from men, but from God.” Brothers and sisters, that phrase settles whom we will live for all our lives. If what we want is people’s praise, we have to keep working on the outside; if what we want is God’s praise, we have to keep working on the inside. You cannot play to two audiences at once.

The Lord Jesus put the same truth even more sharply: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.” (Matthew 23:27) The word “hypocrite” is ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs) in the original — originally “an actor wearing a mask.” The Lord Jesus is saying: you are acting a part, and you act it very well — so well that you’ve come to believe it yourself.

He also quoted Isaiah: “These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.” (Matthew 15:8) Brothers and sisters, this is one of the most chilling conditions of all: the lips are in the temple, but the heart is somewhere else. People hear praise; God hears emptiness.

And the inner life that God treasures — Peter describes it beautifully: “in the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in the sight of God.” (1 Peter 3:4) So in God’s eyes, the most precious adornment of all is the one no one can see.

3. Pictures from Life: The Iceberg, the Root and the Backstage

Our lives are like an iceberg. The physics is simple: sea ice has a density of about 917 kilograms per cubic metre and seawater about 1,025, so roughly nine-tenths of an iceberg lies below the waterline and only one-tenth shows above it. People see the one-tenth; God sees the nine-tenths. And a ship is never sunk by the tenth that shows — it is sunk by the nine-tenths beneath the surface.

Our lives are like a tree as well. Walk down the street after a typhoon, and the trees that have been blown over are often not the shortest ones, but the ones whose roots didn’t go deep enough. However lush the branches above, if there are no roots below, one strong gust and it’s all over.

Psychology has observed the same thing. In 1959 the sociologist Erving Goffman, in The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, set out his theory of “front stage and backstage”: on the front stage we perform the role that is expected of us, and only backstage do we take it off. Later, in 1974, the psychologist Mark Snyder introduced the idea of “self-monitoring” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. He found that some people are highly sensitive to “how others see me” and constantly adjust their behaviour to fit what each situation expects.

Brothers and sisters, people who self-monitor highly do very well in social settings. But before God, the front stage and the backstage are one and the same stage. God doesn’t look at your front stage; he looks at your backstage. Or more precisely, God has never thought you had two stages at all.

One more number. An adult heart beats on average about seventy times a minute — more than a hundred thousand times a day, around thirty-six and a half million times a year. That heart began beating while we were still in our mother’s womb, and it will go on beating until the day we see the Lord face to face, and no one has ever once applauded it. It does a lifetime of work with no audience. Brothers and sisters, the inner life God treasures is work just like that — no applause, yet it is the very thing that keeps us alive.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus Is the Focal Point, the Bible Is the Standard

The Three Foundations of the 321 vision are, first, “Jesus is my role model”; second, “the Bible is my standard”; and third, “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” This passage shines a light on all three.

First, our perspective must shift. 321 often says we must move from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. When Samuel looked at Eliab, his perspective was human, earthly, temporary and worldly; when God said, “I look at the heart,” his perspective was divine, heavenly, eternal and godly. Brothers and sisters, morning devotion isn’t about learning one more story; it’s about receiving a new pair of eyes.

Second, our focus must be aligned. 321 says Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The reason we care so much about appearances and about how others see us is that our focus has drifted. Focus on other people, and you will perform; focus on yourself, and you will wear yourself out; focus on your circumstances, and you will panic. Only when Jesus is the focal point will you be at peace.

Third, our standard must be consistent. The Bible is my standard — not other people’s praise, not the likes of my own echo chamber. “Whose praise is not from men, but from God.” (Romans 2:29) When we move our standard from people back to God, we walk off the stage and back to the altar.

sections.heading: 3. If the Heart Is Right, the Deeds Will Be Right; If the Heart Is Wrong, Even the Rightest Deeds Are Useless
sections.html:
1. The Same Fall, Two Different Endings

The lesson text sets two men side by side, and they make one of the most thought-provoking contrasts in all of Scripture: Saul and David.

Both were anointed kings, both sinned — and, in all fairness, by human reckoning David’s sin was the heavier. Saul’s fault was failing to carry out the command fully and offering a sacrifice he had no right to offer; David’s was adultery, and the plotted murder of his loyal commander Uriah. Weigh them on human scales, and Saul should have stayed while David should have been deposed.

Yet God’s verdict was the exact opposite. Why?

Look at David first. The prophet Nathan used the parable of a little ewe lamb to bring David face to face with himself, then pointed at him and said, “You are the man.” Scripture records David’s response in just a handful of words: “David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against Yahweh.’ Nathan said to David, ‘Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.’” (2 Samuel 12:13)

Brothers and sisters, notice: no explanation, no shifting the blame, no “however,” no “but the situation at the time was very complicated.” One sentence — I have sinned against Yahweh. And forgiveness came in that very same verse.

David wrote that experience into Psalm 51. He said, “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10) And again, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

Now look at Saul. When Samuel confronted him with his sin face to face, Saul answered, “I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of Yahweh, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” (1 Samuel 15:24)

On the surface, Saul also said, “I have sinned” — in words almost the same as David’s. But there’s a fatal clause in the middle: “because I feared the people.” What that means is: it wasn’t that I wanted to do it; the people forced me. In the very act of confessing his sin, he pushed it off onto someone else.

Even more telling is what he said next: “I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and come back with me, that I may worship Yahweh your God.” (1 Samuel 15:30) Brothers and sisters, did you hear it? What he cared about was saving face in front of the people. And he said “Yahweh your God,” not “my God.” God was no longer in his heart; God was only in his public show.

So God’s verdict was: “Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.” (1 Samuel 15:23)

The same fall — but one man fell towards God and the other fell towards people. The one who fell towards God was lifted up; the one who fell towards people fell further and further away.

2. Scripture Interprets Scripture: The Difference between Admitting Sin and Repenting

Hebrew has a key verb: שׁוּב (shuv), meaning “to turn back, to return.” True repentance is not an emotion; it is a change of direction. A person can weep bitterly without moving one step in a new direction; and a person can quietly shed a single tear and, from that moment, turn round and head for home.

The New Testament word is μετάνοια (metanoia), literally “a change of mind” — first the mindset changes, then the behaviour. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 teaches: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Repentance begins with the mindset.

Paul distinguishes sharply between two kinds of sorrow: “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.” (2 Corinthians 7:10) David’s was godly sorrow; Saul’s was the sorrow of the world — what grieved him was not that he had sinned against God, but that he was losing his position.

That is why Samuel said, “To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22) That day Saul had in fact offered sacrifices; there was religious activity, there was the look of devotion. But God didn’t want the sheep; God wanted the heart.

Paul says something of equal weight: “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:3) Brothers and sisters, this is a frightening verse. Giving away everything you own, giving up your very body — what could be more “right” than that? Yet if the heart is wrong, the verdict is three words: profits me nothing.

The Lord Jesus warns us too: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1) Doing good is right, but doing it “to be seen by them” uses the reward up on the spot. If the heart is wrong, even the rightest deeds are useless.

3. An Illustration: A Flight Path One Degree Off

A piece of simple arithmetic shows just how dangerous it is when “the heart is wrong.”

Suppose a plane takes off with its heading one degree off. One degree is tiny; you can hardly see it on the instruments, and no one on board feels a thing. But a one-degree error will put you about 1.7 kilometres off course after a hundred kilometres; about 17.5 kilometres off after a thousand; and after ten thousand kilometres, 175 kilometres off — enough to land you at an airport in a different country.

Brothers and sisters, a deviation of the heart is that one degree. A little self-pity today, a little comparison tomorrow, a little “I’m only doing this for the good of the church” the day after — you feel none of it at the time, yet ten years on you touch down somewhere completely foreign.

Saul didn’t become Saul in a day. The reason he gave for his first unauthorised sacrifice sounded perfectly reasonable: “Because I saw that the people were scattered from me … and that the Philistines assembled themselves together at Michmash.” (1 Samuel 13:11) Every time there was a reason; every time he drifted one more degree.

The Reformer John Calvin is generally credited with describing the human heart, in his Institutes of the Christian Religion, as “a factory of idols.” A factory never shuts down; it keeps on producing. That is why Jeremiah says, “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it? I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.” (Jeremiah 17:9–10) Who can know it? We can’t even understand our own hearts. That is why we need, every day, to hand our hearts over to the Lord who searches them.

Psychology confirms just how good we are at finding excuses for ourselves. In 1957 the psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when our behaviour conflicts with our beliefs, we seldom change the behaviour; instead we tend to adjust the belief so that we can feel at ease. And in a 1975 study, Miller and Ross summed up what is called the “self-serving attribution bias”: when we succeed, we credit ourselves; when we fail, we blame our circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that Saul exactly? When he succeeded, he set up a monument to himself at Carmel (1 Samuel 15:12); when he failed, he said, “I feared the people.” It isn’t that people can’t confess sin; it’s that we are very good at confessing half of it.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness

The 321 vision puts it with great precision: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

Saul’s problem can be summed up in a single phrase: the self-centred life. In his heart there was a “self” that no one was allowed to touch — a self that wanted face, wanted position, wanted to be honoured by people. So when God’s command collided with that self, he chose to sacrifice God’s command. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take God’s place. Saul left his originally intended position as the anointed servant, seized the power of the king — and in the end even grabbed Samuel’s robe and tore it (1 Samuel 15:27).

What made David precious can also be summed up in a single phrase: before God he was selfless. When he was rebuked he did not reach for his royal power; he simply said, “I have sinned against Yahweh.” Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Saul’s pride provoked more and more pride, until he was hunting David down, and he lost his kingdom and his family fell apart — that is both sides losing. David’s humility drew a whole kingdom into worship, and Psalm 51 is still lifting up countless fallen people to this day — that is both sides winning.

Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus — and living that fullness out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) When the “I” who wants to save face steps down, Christ comes alive within. When the heart is right, the deeds are right.

sections.heading: 4. How Can We Discern the State of the Heart? Seeing the Essence by Its Fruit
sections.html:
1. An Invisible Heart, Visible Fruit

We may well ask: if the heart can’t be seen, how can I know whether my heart is right?

The Lord Jesus gave us a very practical method: “By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” (Matthew 7:16) He went on: “Even so, every good tree produces good fruit; but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit. A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit.” (Matthew 7:17–18)

“Fruit” in the original is καρπός (karpos). The nature of fruit is that it isn’t squeezed out by effort; it grows naturally out of life. No apple tree has ever said to itself in spring, “This year I’m going to try really hard to produce apples.” As long as it is alive, as long as it is joined to its roots, as long as it has sunlight and water, the fruit comes.

So fruit is not a performance; fruit is the outward showing of what something is. That is exactly the test the Lord Jesus gives us: don’t examine your performance; examine your fruit.

Luke’s Gospel states the principle even more plainly: “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.” (Luke 6:45)

Brothers and sisters, remember this phrase: “Out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.” Your mouth is the outlet of your heart. You don’t need to go digging into your heart; just listen to what you’ve said this past week.

2. Pressure Is the Most Honest Test

The lesson text puts it well: especially in a crisis or under pressure, a person’s true self is laid bare.

It’s like a tea bag. Leave a tea bag on the table and it looks clean and dry; drop it into hot water and the water changes colour at once. The hot water didn’t “put” the colour into the tea bag; the hot water simply drew out what was already inside.

Brothers and sisters, the person who drives you up the wall, the situation that keeps you awake at night, did not put bitterness into you. It is only hot water. What it draws out is what was already inside you.

So the lesson text asks three questions that cut deep, and this morning we need to answer them honestly:

When I’m angry, do I blame others, or do I examine myself?

When I’m offended, do I choose to forgive, or do I nurse a grudge?

When no one is watching, am I still the same person?

Scripture gives us two contrasting examples. Joseph was sold by his brothers, falsely accused by his master’s wife and forgotten by the cupbearer. After thirteen years steeping in hot water, what came out? “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” (Genesis 50:20) That was sweet.

Peter, in the high priest’s courtyard, had hot water splashed over him, and what came out was three denials of his Lord. But thank the Lord — the Lord Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and that one look sent him outside weeping bitterly. In that moment Peter’s fruit was bitter, but his heart was right — he wept, and he turned back. That is why, beside the Sea of Tiberias, the Lord entrusted him with his charge all over again.

Brothers and sisters, bad fruit is not a reason for despair; bad fruit is an alarm. When the alarm goes off, what we need to do is not rip the alarm off the wall, but go back to the root.

3. Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology

Brain science offers a fascinating confirmation. In his 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman divided human thinking into “System 1” and “System 2.” System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive; System 2 is slow, effortful and deliberate. He pointed out that the great majority of the judgements we make in daily life are made by System 1.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: where does your quickest reaction come from? It comes from what has already been shaped and formed inside you. When you have time to think, you can be very spiritual; when you have no time to think, what comes out is the real you. That is exactly what the Lord Jesus meant by “the abundance of the heart.”

So change can’t happen only in “System 2” — only when we have the time, when we’re in the mood, when we’re sitting in morning devotion. Change has to go deep enough to reach “System 1,” down into our reflexes. And only the Holy Spirit can work that deep. God says, “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 36:26)

A heart transplant isn’t self-cultivation; it’s grace. God isn’t asking us to polish our heart of stone; he means to replace it.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, and Bear Fruit through 920

The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will be glad, rely on the brain and you will be troubled. The whole outcome of a life flows from the heart.

The scriptural basis for this is Proverbs: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Brothers and sisters, the Chinese Union Version reads, “Keep your heart above all else that you keep.” Your health needs guarding, your finances need guarding, your reputation needs guarding — but Scripture says: guard your heart above all of these.

The lesson text reminds us that when we “rely on the heart” and live a life that truly fears God, we will bear good fruit; when we “rely on the brain,” calculating and settling for appearances, the heart decays. Those who rely on the brain are always calculating: how will people see me if I do this? Will I lose out? Will my effort pay off? The more they calculate, the more troubled they become. Those who rely on the heart ask just one question: Lord, does this please you? Then they go and do it, and their heart is set free.

And what does good fruit look like? Paul lists it clearly: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

This is exactly the 321 “920 practice”: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before each “2,” we practise living out a selfless life (0) and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Brothers and sisters, notice the wisdom of “920”: fruit isn’t borne in a mountain cave; it’s borne in relationships. Your patience has to grow on that co-worker who is always late; your kindness has to grow on that family member who speaks so harshly; your gentleness has to grow on the very person who most easily makes you angry. Without a “2,” there is no “9.”

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: When the Heart Is Right, Everything Is Right
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if we set today’s lesson within the 321 blueprint, we see a complete picture.

1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are all lessons of the heart. Jesus is my role model — he said, “I am gentle and humble in heart” (see Matthew 11:29); the Lord himself is the heart that is perfectly right. The Bible is my standard — not other people’s opinions, not fashionable values, but God’s word measuring my heart. The Holy Spirit is my guide — because only the Holy Spirit can reach the depths of the heart; it is he who pours God’s love into our hearts (see Romans 5:5).

The Two Core Values are also a matter of whom the heart belongs to. Let Jesus be King — the place where the King sits is not a pulpit but a throne, and that throne is in the heart. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when there is no “I” in the heart wanting to make a name for itself, the glory naturally returns to the Lord.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, God’s system does not begin with organisation; it begins with one heart after another being aligned with God. The reason 1 Samuel 16 is a turning point is that God decided no longer to build according to the “like all the nations” specification, but to start again with a man after his own heart.

2. Fivefold Change: It Begins with the Mindset

321 says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Today’s lesson is precisely the first of these — a change of mindset: from the mindset that “man looks at the outward appearance” to the mindset that “God looks at the heart.” Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “Transformed by the renewing of your mind” — renewal starts in the mind, in our mindset.

Once the mindset changes, the life changes: I no longer have to perform. Once the life changes, daily living changes: I no longer have to compare. Once daily living changes, relationships change: I am able to forgive. Once relationships change, ministry changes: I serve because I love the Lord, not because I need applause.

That is why 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Saul had the order upside down — he put ministry first (winning against the Amalekites), then relationships (pleasing the people), and life last of all, and he lost everything. David had the order right — he was first a shepherd boy, he first had a relationship with God, and only after that came the throne.

3. The Priority of Relationships: First with God, Then with Ourselves, Then with Others, and Last with Things

When the heart is aligned with God, the priority of relationships falls back into place: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

First with God — that is why David said, “I have sinned against Yahweh.” (2 Samuel 12:13) He knew that every sin is first of all a sin against God.

Then with ourselves — no self-deception, no self-pity, no self-boasting. Saul’s greatest problem was that he refused to face himself; he wanted Samuel to “honour” him. A person who dares not face himself cannot truly face God either.

Then with others — “By their fruits you will know them.” (Matthew 7:16) Our relationships with others are the orchard of the heart.

Last with things — service, work and achievement all come last. Not because they don’t matter, but because they must not come first.

4. 235 Relationships: A Heart That Is Not Alone

The 321 “235” tells us: become a “2,” a spiritual companion, with someone who is selfless; build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and become the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, why does the work of the heart need a “2”? Because the heart deceives itself. “The heart is deceitful above all things” (Jeremiah 17:9); we cannot see ourselves clearly. The reason David was able to turn back was that God sent a Nathan to stand before him. Saul had Samuel beside him too — sadly, he treated the prophet as a prop for his public image rather than a mirror for his heart.

Do you have a “Nathan”? Do you have a spiritual companion who can tell you the truth without you turning on them? If not, ask the Lord to give you one today. If you do, thank the Lord for them today — and open your heart.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Walking the Truth into Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three practices. Let’s take each of them a layer deeper using the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Hand My Heart to the Lord Every Day

The first thing on waking is not to look at your phone, but to say to the Lord, “Lord, I give you my heart for today. Please search it, cleanse it, and guide my motives and decisions all day long.”

Information: First take in this passage — “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to show you what you reach for first when you wake each day — that is the true king of your heart.

Conviction: Truly believe that “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23), rather than merely agreeing that it’s a sensible saying.

Implementation: From today, don’t keep your phone by the bed; let the first words you speak on waking be spoken to the Lord.

Evaluation: Spend three minutes every evening asking the Lord: how many hours today was my heart aligned with you?

Correction: Which part of the day do I most easily lose ground? Commit that part of the day to him in particular.

Repetition: Keep going for forty days in a row, until the decision becomes a habit and the habit becomes life.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister and invite them to practise with you, checking in on each other and reminding each other.

Practice 2: Examine the Heart Behind My Reactions

When I react strongly in the middle of an emotion (anger, sadness, pride, a sense of inferiority), I don’t rush to explain or act; first I quietly pray and ask the Lord, “What is the heart behind this reaction of mine?”

Information: “Out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.” (Luke 6:45)

Revelation: Emotions aren’t the enemy; emotions are the dashboard. They aren’t the problem itself — they are reporting the problem.

Conviction: Believe that my reactions will honestly expose my heart, and that God allows that exposure in order to heal, not to condemn.

Implementation: Set yourself a “ten-minute rule” — whenever a strong emotion rises, be still for ten minutes before you respond; and in those ten minutes do only one thing: give your heart to the Lord.

Evaluation: How many times this week did I hold to the ten minutes? The times I failed — what did they have in common?

Correction: If I find that one particular person, or one particular remark, always sets me off, there is usually an unhealed wound there; bring it before the Lord and ask him to heal it.

Repetition: Put “ten minutes” on your phone’s wallpaper as a daily reminder.

Multiplication: When someone comes to you with a complaint, don’t rush to judge who’s right; first help them ask, “What is the heart behind this reaction of mine?”

Practice 3: Practise Actions That Flow from the Heart

This week, choose one thing to do — not because you ought to, or because others expect it, but out of love for the Lord. It might be an act of service for the Lord, a choice to deny yourself, or simply time spent drawing near to him.

Information: “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:3)

Revelation: So motive determines worth. The same act done out of love is eternal; done out of fear, it simply wears you out.

Conviction: Believe that God looks at motives more than at results.

Implementation: This week, do one good deed that “no one will ever know about” — no posting, no mentioning it, no hinting.

Evaluation: While you were doing it, was there even a slight longing in your heart to be seen? Admit it honestly.

Correction: If there was, offer that longing up as a sacrifice, and say to the Lord: this time the praise belongs to you.

Repetition: At least one a week, until “good deeds no one knows about” become the rhythm of your daily living.

Multiplication: Share the principle of this practice in your small group (not what you did), and lead your brothers and sisters to “act from the heart” together.

sections.heading: 7. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
God isn’t looking at your performance, but at whether you truly depend on him.

Doing the right thing is not the same as having a right heart; only reverence and obedience that come from deep within are acceptable to God.

Before people you may be able to put on a show, but before God everything is naked and laid open. Rather than working on the surface, love God with all your heart.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call: When the Heart Is Right, Life Is Right
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, let’s come back together to the closing words of the lesson text.

What God treasures is not our outward appearance, nor everything we do on the surface, but our hearts. May the Lord help us live out, every day, a heart that truly fears him — not calculating with the brain, not acting by appearances, but simply coming back before him, so that our hearts are always aligned with him. When our hearts are right, everything in our lives will be right too.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to give you three calls.

First, let Jesus be King — King of your heart. Not King of your calendar, not King of your ministry, but King of your motives. When he reigns as King in your heart, everything outside falls into place by itself.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. The reason we perform is that we want a little of the glory to land on us. But brothers and sisters, that little bit of glory is so small — far too small to be worth a lifetime of weariness. Give all the glory back to the Lord, and you’ll find you suddenly feel very light.

Third, hand over your heart. God says, “My son, give me your heart; and let your eyes keep in my ways.” (Proverbs 23:26) What God wants first is not your time, your money or your service; what God wants first is your heart. Once your heart is his, everything else goes along with it.

The Lord Jesus promises us, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8) Brothers and sisters, may every one of us be pure in heart — not perfect people, but honest people; not sinless people, but people whose hearts are open to God.

On that morning three thousand years ago, God said to Samuel, “Man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7) On this morning three thousand years later, God says the very same thing to you and to me.

He isn’t looking at your score sheet; he is looking at your heart. And right now, your heart is in his hands.

keyVerses: “But Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.’” (1 Samuel 16:7)
declarations: Lord, I give my heart to you; may I please you both inside and out!
practices: Hand my heart to the Lord every day
Examine the heart behind my reactions
Practise actions that flow from the heart
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you that you don’t see as man sees. People look at our outward appearance; you look at our hearts. People look at our performance; you look at our motives. Before you we cannot pretend, and we don’t need to.

Lord, we confess that we so often live by the opinions of others. We do things in order to be seen, we say things in order to be praised, and we cover things up so as not to lose face. Please forgive us. Like David, we say before you today: I have sinned against the Lord.

Create in us clean hearts, and renew a right spirit within us. Take away our hearts of stone and give us hearts of flesh. Holy Spirit, help us keep our hearts above all else, so that the whole outcome of our lives flows from the heart.
Help us, in every relationship, to live out a selfless life and bear the fruit of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.
Lord, I give my heart to you; may I please you both inside and out.
Reign as King in my heart, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “By their fruits you will know them.” (Matthew 7:16) Think back over this past month. Under pressure, or when you were offended, what was your first reaction? What did that reaction show you your heart is full of right now?

“Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10) David fell and turned back; Saul fell and shifted the blame. In your present situation, is there something you keep explaining away but have never truly confessed to God? Are you willing to hand it to the Lord today?
l026.title: God Looks at the Heart
l026.subtitle: Get the Heart Right and Life Comes Right
l026.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: The Measuring Rod of “Wholeheartedness” — Who Gets to Decide?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re going to reflect together on a word that seems ordinary but is remarkably hard to pin down — “wholehearted,” or as we say in Chinese, “using the heart.”

In church we often hear praise like this: “That sister serves so wholeheartedly.” “That brother prepared with real heart.” And we often hear sighs like this: “Well, he did it, but his heart wasn’t really in it.” The strange thing is that if we press the question — “So what exactly does it mean to do something wholeheartedly?” — ten people will probably give you ten different answers.

Some say being wholehearted means spending time. The longer you spend, the more wholehearted you are. So we start comparing who arrives earliest, who leaves latest, who has pulled the most all-nighters. Some say wholeheartedness is measured by results. If you do it beautifully and get results, you were wholehearted; if you mess it up, you weren’t. So we treat results as the scales on which the heart is weighed. Others say being wholehearted means emotional investment: the more tears you shed and the faster you’re moved, the more wholehearted you are.

There’s some truth in each of these, but none of them is the Bible’s answer. Time can be time spent going through the motions; results can be results earned for yourself; and tears may just be the tide of an emotion coming in and going out. A chef can stand in a kitchen for twelve hours thinking only about the day’s takings; a mother may spend just ten minutes sewing a button on her child’s shirt, and those ten minutes are filled to the brim with love. Length of time, size of results, rise and fall of emotions — none of them equals “wholeheartedness.”

So how should wholeheartedness be measured in God’s eyes?

In 1 Timothy 1:5 Paul gives us an accurate measuring rod: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.” The purpose of all God’s commands, the destination of all truth, is “love.” And this love doesn’t appear out of nowhere; it has a source, and the source has three streams: a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith.

In other words, when God measures whether we are wholehearted, he doesn’t measure how much we’ve done; he measures whether our love truly flows from these three sources. These three sources are like the three filters in a water-treatment plant: the first filters out the impurities of motive, the second filters out the failings of conduct, the third filters out the pretence of faith. Only when all three are clear does what flows out become living water — the love God is looking for.

In this lesson we’ll begin with the first filter: a pure heart — that is, a simple heart.

Why start with the simple heart? Because it is the source of the source. Conscience deals with “Did I do the right thing?” Faith deals with “Is what I believe genuine?” But the simple heart deals with “Why am I doing this?” Once the motive goes crooked, everything after it goes crooked too. It’s like a river: however much you clean up the mouth, if the source is muddy, the whole river is muddy. Solomon said it long ago: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Brothers and sisters, this morning we’re not going to measure anyone else’s heart; we’re going to let God measure our own.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter to a Young Pastor
sections.html:
To understand the measuring rod of 1 Timothy 1:5, we first need to know the circumstances in which Paul handed it over.

The author of 1 Timothy is the apostle Paul. It is generally thought that the letter was written after Paul’s release from his first imprisonment in Rome, somewhere between AD 62 and 64 — a work of his later years. Its recipient, Timothy, was Paul’s spiritual son: he probably came to faith when Paul passed through Lystra on his first missionary journey, and on the second journey Paul took him from Lystra to work alongside him. Acts 16:1–3 records that Timothy’s mother was a Jewish woman who believed, and his father was a Greek. 2 Timothy 1:5 goes further and mentions the “sincere faith” of his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice — and notice that the word “sincere” is the very word Paul uses in 1 Timothy 1:5. Paul is saying: Timothy, that unadulterated faith handed down through three generations of your family is exactly what I want you to hold onto in Ephesus.

The situation behind the letter is very concrete. 1 Timothy 1:3 says, “As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine.” Ephesus was the capital of the province of Asia and home to the temple of the goddess Artemis — one of the most prosperous religious and commercial centres of the Mediterranean world at the time. Paul had ministered there for three years (Acts 20:31), and the church had deep foundations; but precisely because they were deep, the enemy’s attacks were all the more sophisticated.

Paul goes on to say that those men were “not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes, rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith.” (1 Timothy 1:4) Where was the problem? It wasn’t that anyone was openly denying Christ; it was that some had turned the faith into a never-ending knowledge contest. They researched genealogies, argued about the law and showed off esoteric speculation. On the surface they were zealous, but at the core they were “desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm.” (1 Timothy 1:7)

Paul puts his finger right on it: this kind of zeal only “causes disputes.” The sense of the original is generating an endless chain of questions with no way out. You’ll notice that these people weren’t lazy — they were extremely diligent; they weren’t uncommitted — they were extremely committed. They spent more time than anyone and read more widely than anyone. By the world’s standard of “wholeheartedness,” they would certainly count as wholehearted.

But Paul says: you’ve taken the wrong road. Because “the goal of this command is love.”

The word for “goal” is telos in Greek, meaning the end point, the purpose, the outcome finally to be reached. Paul is saying: God did not give all his commands to produce a crowd of people who are good at arguing, but to shape a people who know how to love one another. The end point of the law is love, the end point of truth is love, and the end point of all service is love. If you read the Bible all your life and never learn to love people, you haven’t really understood a single page.

And the first source of this love, Paul says, is “a pure heart.” The Greek for “pure” is katharos, which basically means clean, unadulterated, unmixed; from it eventually came the English word “catharsis” (cleansing). In the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, katharos is often used to describe the offerings presented to God, which had to be “without blemish,” and the vessels of the temple, which had to be “clean.” By using this word, Paul is in effect saying: your heart, too, is a vessel — a vessel brought to God’s table — and there must be nothing dirty in it.

There is also a parallel usage in Paul that deserves our attention. 2 Corinthians 11:3: “But I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.” The Greek word for “simplicity” here is haplotēs, meaning singleness — not forked, not folded, the same inside and out. A simple heart is a heart that has only one direction.

Brothers and sisters, this is our theme today. A pure heart is a simple heart; a simple heart is a heart facing in one direction only. The nineteenth-century Danish thinker Søren Kierkegaard wrote a book titled Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. That title alone is the finest footnote to 1 Timothy 1:5.

sections.heading: 1. A Pure Heart: Simple Love That Flows from the Heart
sections.html:
1. Pure Means “Unmixed”

What the original means by “a pure heart” is a clean heart, a simple heart — a heart with nothing mixed in, a heart free of bad motives. Love like this doesn’t calculate gain and loss; it isn’t after recognition or reward. It loves for the sake of love itself.

What does “unmixed” mean? Modern technology gives us a very fitting example. At the core of every phone and every computer in our hands today is a silicon wafer. The polysilicon used in semiconductor manufacturing has to reach a purity known as “9N” or even “11N” — that is, 99.9999999 per cent or higher. Put another way, that means no more than one impurity atom in every billion silicon atoms. Why demand such an extreme level of purity? Because if even a little more impurity gets in, the flow of electrons is disrupted and the whole wafer has to be scrapped.

Brothers and sisters, God cares about our hearts in just the same way. Not because God is a nitpicker, but because the heart is where the current of life flows. Mix in a little vanity, and love short-circuits; mix in a little comparison, and our service overheats and crashes; mix in a little resentment, and our prayers can’t get through. Solomon put it precisely: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

2. Mary: A Broken Jar of Ointment

Scripture gives us a portrait of a simple heart. Mark 14:3 records: “While he was at Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at the table, a woman came having an alabaster jar of ointment of pure nard — very costly. She broke the jar, and poured it over his head.” John 12:3 tells us the woman’s name: “Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.”

Notice three actions: she took it, she broke it, she poured it out.

“She took it” — this was her most precious possession. Pure nard came from the Himalayan regions of northern India and had to travel long trade routes to reach Palestine; at the time it was an extremely expensive luxury. By Judas’s own valuation in John 12:5 it was worth “three hundred denarii,” and one denarius was a labourer’s wage for a day. In other words, this one jar of ointment was worth a whole year’s wages for an ordinary labourer who spent nothing at all.

“She broke it” — this means she held nothing back. Once the jar is broken, it can’t be sealed again; once the ointment is out, it can’t be gathered back. Mary didn’t pour out half and keep half; she smashed every way of retreat.

“She poured it out” — this means she gave everything. She poured it over Jesus’ head, anointed his feet, and wiped them with her own hair. In Jewish culture a woman’s hair was her glory (1 Corinthians 11:15), and not something she would lightly let down in front of others. Yet she took her own glory and used it to wipe the Lord’s feet.

In her eyes there was only Jesus — no thought of other people’s opinions, and nothing held in reserve. That is a simple heart.

And what did Jesus say? “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for me.” (Mark 14:6) “She has done what she could.” (Mark 14:8) The Lord didn’t say she had done the most; the Lord said she had “done what she could.” God never compares our abilities; God only looks at whether we have given him everything we could.

3. Judas: A Calculated Righteousness

In the same house there was another heart. John 12:5 records Judas’s words: “Why wasn’t this ointment sold for three hundred denarii, and given to the poor?”

At first hearing, how reasonable that sounds, how socially concerned! But Scripture immediately lays his cards on the table: “Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it.” (John 12:6)

Brothers and sisters, this is one of the most chilling verses in the whole Bible. Because what Judas said was perfectly correct in principle. Three hundred denarii really could have helped a great many poor people, and helping the poor really was what the law commanded. What he got wrong was not the content; it was the heart.

Mary relied on the heart; Judas relied on the brain. Mary saw Jesus; Judas saw a price tag. Mary asked, “What can I give the Lord?” Judas asked, “What’s in this for me?” His starting point was not love, but outward righteousness and inward greed; he was looking at an exchange of value, and so he missed seeing the glory of Jesus.

This is exactly what the 321 vision reminds us again and again: rely on the heart and you will be glad; rely on the brain and you will be troubled. Those who rely on the heart see the Lord and break the jar with joy and gladness; those who rely on the brain calculate gain and loss — the whole house is full of fragrance, yet they can’t smell it; all they can smell is money.

4. The Science of Motivation: How Rewards Kill Passion

Psychology confirms the Bible’s insight from another angle. In 1973 the Stanford psychologists Lepper, Greene and Nisbett carried out a famous experiment. They took a group of nursery-school children who already loved drawing and divided them into three groups: the first was told in advance that they would receive a lovely “Good Player” certificate when they finished drawing; the second was not told, but unexpectedly received a certificate when they finished; the third received no reward at all.

Two weeks later the researchers observed whether the children would still choose to draw during free-play time. The result was surprising: the first group, the children who had “drawn for the certificate,” spent markedly less time drawing of their own accord, while the children who had received no reward, or only an unexpected one, were as keen as ever.

Psychologists call this the “overjustification effect.” Later, the “self-determination theory” that Deci and Ryan developed at the University of Rochester (1985) took this further: when external rewards replace inner motivation, a person’s drive to do the very same thing is actually hollowed out.

Brothers and sisters, this is what makes “mixing” so dangerous. Rewards in themselves are not bad, but once the reward becomes the reason, love is no longer love; it becomes a transaction. And as soon as the applause stops and the returns dry up, we can’t keep going. Conversely, the reason a simple heart can last is precisely that, from the very start, it never lived on applause.

5. Blessed Are the Pure in Heart

Jesus states it with absolute certainty: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)

“They shall see God” doesn’t mean they will one day see some image; it means that here and now their eyes are able to recognise God. Psalm 24:3–4 says: “Who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill? Who may stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.” Only those with a pure heart can climb the hill; those whose hearts are muddied cannot see him even standing on the hill.

Do you long to see God? Then begin by practising a simple heart.

This is also the first of the Three Foundations of the 321 vision: Jesus is my role model. Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus is on ourselves, we become like Judas, calculating what we’ll get out of the situation; when the focus is on other people, we fret about how they’ll rate our jar of ointment; when the focus is on our circumstances, we feel that now is not the time to break the jar. Only when Jesus is the focal point can we, like Mary, quietly pour our very best upon the Lord while everyone else is frowning.

The old self is self-centred, so it has to enter everything into its own accounts; the new self is selfless, so it can pour out, break open, and leave no way of retreat. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus — and living that fullness out. On Judas’s abacus a jar of ointment was worth only three hundred denarii; on the lips of Jesus it became a memorial to be told wherever the gospel is preached throughout the whole world (Mark 14:9).

sections.heading: 2. The Prodigal’s Father: Love Takes the Initiative
sections.html:
1. A Father Who Ran

In the parable of the prodigal son, the father’s actions show us what love from the heart looks like. Luke 15:20: “He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”

Hidden in this one verse are four actions, and each of them says the same thing: love takes the initiative.

The first is “saw.” “While he was still far off, his father saw him” — the younger son was still out on the horizon, and the father recognised him. How did he recognise him? Because he was watching every day. Only someone who watches every day can pick out that familiar figure at the furthest distance. Love is a long, steady gaze.

The second is “moved with compassion.” The Greek word is splanchnizomai, from the root splanchna, which refers to a person’s inward parts, the very innards. To the Greek ear this isn’t a faint sympathy; it is a compassion that churns up from deep in the gut. The Gospels use this word for Jesus when he saw the harassed and scattered crowds (Matthew 9:36), and they use it for this father too. The father’s love wasn’t a judgement of the head; it was a shaking of the bowels.

The third is “ran.” In Middle Eastern culture, an elder of standing does not run. The Middle Eastern biblical scholar Kenneth Bailey, drawing on his many years of research in Middle Eastern villages, pointed out that for an elderly patriarch to run he would have to hitch up his long robe and expose his legs — a deeply undignified thing to do. But this father ran. He would rather lose his own dignity in front of the whole village than let his son be humiliated by anyone on the road into the village.

The fourth is “kissed him.” The original is kataphileō, a word stronger than an ordinary kiss — kissing again and again, fervently, the kind that can’t stop.

Saw, moved with compassion, ran, kissed him again and again — not one of these actions was demanded, not one was an obligation. None of it came from moral duty or from a calculated choice; it came from love’s being “moved with compassion.”

2. Love Moved Him to Act, Love Moved Him to Forgive, Love Moved Him to Welcome Completely

Notice a detail in this parable that is often overlooked: the younger son had prepared a speech. Luke 15:18–19: “I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.’”

But he only got halfway through it. The father didn’t wait for him to finish “Make me as one of your hired servants”; he turned and instructed his servants, “Bring out the best robe, and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand, and sandals on his feet.” (Luke 15:22)

The robe was status, the ring was authority, the sandals were the mark of a free man — slaves went barefoot. In one breath the father restored his son’s standing, authority and freedom in full, without a moment’s hesitation.

This is a simple heart: love moved him to act, love moved him to forgive, love moved him to welcome completely.

There’s a very deep spiritual principle here. The 321 vision says that humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. This father had every “right”: the right to make his son kneel and confess first, the right to make him repay the inheritance he had squandered, the right to put him on probation for a while and see. But he laid down all those rights. He didn’t stand waiting at the door; he ran out onto the road. He didn’t settle accounts first; he handed over the robe first.

Now look at the elder son. Luke 15:29: “But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.’”
