Brothers and sisters, did you hear it? “These many years I have served you” — he had reckoned a father-son relationship as an employment contract; “I never disobeyed a commandment of yours” — he had reckoned obedience as performance; “you never gave me” — he had reckoned love as wages he was owed. The elder son was in the house, but his heart had left home long ago. He did every single thing right, and had every bit of his heart wrong.

Judas relied on the brain to reckon the price of the ointment; the elder son relied on the brain to keep accounts over a young goat. It is the same disease. On the surface they both stood on the side of “what’s reasonable,” but inside there was no love.

3. The Same Kiss, Two Different Hearts

Scripture contains a contrast that makes you shudder.

In Luke 15:20, the father “kissed him.” Matthew 26:49: “Immediately he came to Jesus, and said, ‘Hail, Rabbi!’ and kissed him.”

In the Greek, both places use the same verb, kataphileō — to kiss fervently, again and again. The action is identical; the hearts are worlds apart. The father’s kiss was a welcome that welled up from his very bowels; Judas’s kiss was the product of cold calculation, a “sign” agreed in advance for the purpose of betraying Jesus. Matthew 26:48 spells it out: “Now he who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, ‘Whoever I kiss, he is the one. Seize him.’”

How heartbroken the Lord Jesus’ reply was: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48)

When a kiss doesn’t come from a pure heart, it spoils, it rots — it can even become a curse.

This reminds us that even actions that look right have to be driven by a simple heart, or they lose their worth. The same act of giving can be Mary’s ointment, or it can be Ananias’s deceit (Acts 5:1–4); the same act of prayer can be the tax collector beating his breast, or it can be the Pharisee’s boasting (Luke 18:10–14); the same kiss can be a father’s welcome, or it can be Judas’s signal.

Paul said it long ago: “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:3) Give away every possession, put your very life on the line — if there is no love, what is written in God’s ledger is zero.

4. Relationships Matter More Than Things, People Matter More Than Tasks

Harvard University has a “Study of Adult Development” that began in 1938 and continues to this day — one of the longest-running studies of human lives ever undertaken. One of its directors, the psychiatrist Robert Waldinger, after sifting through decades of data, pointed out that the strongest predictor of who lives healthy, happy and long is not wealth, not fame and not cholesterol levels, but good relationships and close connection with others.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

The younger son valued “things” above “relationships,” so he demanded his share of the estate and went off to a distant country. The elder son also valued “things” above “relationships,” so he quibbled over a young goat. Only the father, from beginning to end, valued the relationship — “for this, my son, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.” (Luke 15:24) In the father’s eyes, that the person had come back mattered ten thousand times more than whether the money ever did.

Our Heavenly Father is exactly that kind of father. While we were still sinners, he ran towards us first. The apostle John says, “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) Brothers and sisters, your simple love and mine has never been something we squeezed out of ourselves; it is drawn out of us by the Father who ran towards us first.

sections.heading: 3. A Simple Heart Brings Forth Genuine Love
sections.html:
1. Love Is the Goal of Everything

Back to our key verse: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.” (1 Timothy 1:5)

Love is the goal of everything. Only love that flows from “a pure heart” can move people, honour God and change the world.

Why? Because people can smell mixed love. Children are the most sensitive of all — they know deep down whether their parents really care about them or just want a good-looking report card. Church members are sensitive too — everyone knows deep down whether a co-worker really cares about them or just wants to add them to his ministry tally. Mixed love can last for a while, but not for a lifetime; it can fool people’s eyes, but it can’t fool their hearts, and still less can it fool God.

God made this plain through the prophet Samuel: “For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

2. A Single Eye, a Focused Light

In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus uses a wonderful image: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” (Matthew 6:22)

The Greek word for “sound” is haplous — the adjective form of haplotēs (singleness, simplicity), which we met earlier — meaning single, undivided, healthy. Jesus isn’t talking about eyesight; he’s talking about focus. If a person’s eye looks in one direction only, their whole body is full of light; if their eyes dart this way and that, their whole body is in darkness. That’s why Jesus goes straight on to say, “No one can serve two masters … You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

Physics gives us a superb illustration. A hundred-watt light bulb scatters its light in every direction and can only light up one room. But the same energy, organised into laser light — one wavelength, one direction, one phase — can cut steel plate, perform eye surgery and carry data across oceans. Where’s the difference? Not in the amount of energy, but in whether it is “single” or “scattered.”

Brothers and sisters, we often feel we lack the ability to serve God. In fact what we lack is often not energy but simplicity. When our hearts want to please God and also be liked by people, want to glorify the Lord and also keep a little glory for ourselves, our light scatters. But once the heart becomes single, that very same life becomes a light that can cut through the darkness.

3. Examine Your Own Heart

In this complicated age it is very easy for our motives to become mixed: we do things to gain an advantage, to save face, to prove ourselves, to win applause. But what God values is not what we do, but whether the heart with which we do it is “pure.”

So let me gently lay three questions on your heart:

Has anything else been mixed into your love?

Is your service to others driven by love, or by duty?

Is your worship of God about getting blessings, or simply about wanting to draw near to him?

These three questions are not meant to condemn us; they are meant to help us return to the root of “wholeheartedness” and learn to respond to God with a simple heart.

Paul himself often asked himself questions like these. He told the Galatians, “For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” (Galatians 1:10)

Jesus brought the matter right down to practical detail: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1) “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:3–4)

The nineteenth-century evangelist D. L. Moody is generally credited with a famous saying: “Character is what you are in the dark.” In the dark there is no audience, no applause, no record. What you are there is what you are.

4. Where a Pure Heart Comes From

At this point, some of you may feel your heart sinking: so what do I do? The moment I examine myself, I find my heart is hopelessly mixed.

The prophet Jeremiah told the truth on our behalf long ago: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9) By self-examination alone we can’t even see through our own hearts, let alone wash them clean.

So a pure heart is never something we manufacture; it is something God creates. How did David pray after his great sin? “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10) The Hebrew verb “create” is bara’ — the very word for “create” in Genesis 1:1, “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” — a creating out of nothing that only God can do. David wasn’t asking God to patch up his heart; he was asking God to create a new one.

And God has promised: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 36:26)

So our practice is not to grit our teeth and scrub our hearts white, but to hand our hearts to God every day for him to search and renew. That is exactly the psalmist’s prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

5. Love Everyone around You with a Simple Heart

The 321 vision includes a very practical exercise called “the 920 practice”: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before each “2,” we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice: the first of the nine graces is love. And the fruit of the Spirit is “fruit,” not a “product.” Products are churned out in a factory against a deadline; fruit grows from life within. A simple heart is the tree, and love is the fruit. Get the tree right, and the fruit will naturally be right.

So the first person you meet tomorrow morning is your “2.” Your spouse, your children, your colleagues, that brother who so often annoys you — they are all “2s” whom God has placed in your life. Live out selflessness before them, and you are walking in the order of “life first, then relationships, then ministry.”

And a change of life brings about the fivefold change: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. What is the mindset we need to change today? It is this one sentence: what measures wholeheartedness is not how much I do, but where my love comes from.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: A Simple Heart Is a Selfless Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s take what we’ve received today and look at it within the 321 framework.

1. The Three Foundations: Giving Simplicity Its Roots

Jesus is my role model. Who is the supreme model of a simple heart? The Lord himself. “Who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6–7) “Emptied himself” — he poured himself out. Mary poured out a jar of ointment; the Lord poured out himself. To learn simplicity is to learn from him.

The Bible is my standard. The measuring rod for “wholeheartedness” isn’t in my hands, nor on other people’s lips; it is in God’s word. 1 Timothy 1:5 is today’s measuring rod. If our standard isn’t the Bible, we’ll use time, results and applause as our rod instead — and at the end of all that measuring, what we’ll have measured out is an exhausted, proud self.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. A pure heart is created by the Holy Spirit, not cultivated by me. Our responsibility is to open up and let the Holy Spirit shine his light on us every day.

2. The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King, Let Jesus Receive the Glory

Judas had two kings in his heart: Jesus and money — and in the end money became king. The elder son also had two kings in his heart: his father and his own merit — and in the end merit became king. Mary had only one King in her heart, and so she could break the jar.

A heart that isn’t simple is really a heart whose throne hasn’t yet been cleared. To let Jesus be King is to ask the “self” on that throne to step down. And when our service no longer needs applause to vouch for us, the glory will naturally all go to Jesus.

3. The Old Self Is Self-Centred, the New Self Is Selfless

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Judas’s “self” made him leave his originally intended position as a disciple and become one who sat in judgement on his Lord; the elder son’s “self” made him leave his originally intended position as a son and become a hired hand counting his wages. But the prodigal’s father laid down a patriarch’s dignity and rights and returned to the simplest originally intended position of all — “father” — and that is why he was able to run.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s greatest skill is not getting us to stop doing things, but getting us to do them while quietly keeping a little name for ourselves on the side; he doesn’t need to stop our hands, only to mix our hearts. So when a person is truly selfless, Satan has nowhere to get a grip.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. At the moment the jar was broken, the disciples’ pride stirred up more and more criticism, but the Lord’s humility brought out a house full of fragrance — a fragrance that lingers to this day and has spread throughout the whole world.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living that fullness out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) A simple heart is a heart that says, “It is no longer I.”

4. A Shift in Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective: man looks at the outward appearance, but God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective: three hundred denarii is an earthly price tag; “a good work” is heaven’s assessment.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective: applause is temporary; God’s reward for what is done in secret is eternal.

From a worldly perspective to God’s perspective: the world asks, “Is it worth it?” God asks, “Who are you doing this for?”

5. The Goal: Establish God’s System

A simple heart is not merely a matter of personal cultivation; it is the foundation of a system. In a team whose hearts are mixed, even the best plans will be quietly worn down by people working against one another; but when a group of people who simply love the Lord come together, they can carry the great things God entrusts to them. That is why 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When the life is simple, the relationships are clean; when the relationships are clean, the ministry has roots.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Living Simplicity Out
sections.html:
The lesson text has prepared three practices for us. Let’s use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work them through solidly.

Practice 1: Meditation and Prayer

Spend time every day in quiet before God and say to him, “Lord, please shine your light on me, so that I can see whether my heart is pure.” Then answer honestly: what is my motive for doing this? Does it come from simple love, or do I want a return or recognition?

Information: First copy 1 Timothy 1:5 and Psalm 139:23–24 onto the first page of your notebook, and read them once every morning.

Revelation: Don’t just read them; stop and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you. Information is what I know; revelation is what God tells me.

Conviction: When the Holy Spirit points out a mixed motive, don’t argue back; just say, “Lord, you’re right.”

Implementation: Write down the most important thing you’ll do that day, and next to it write, “Why am I doing this?”

Evaluation: Look at it again in the evening, and ask yourself whether your motives drifted today.

Correction: If they drifted, confess it, and ask God to create a clean heart in you (Psalm 51:10).

Repetition: Keep practising for forty days in a row. Habits of the heart aren’t formed in a day, and they aren’t broken in a day either.

Multiplication: Find a spiritual companion to do it with you, and share with each other once a week.

Practice 2: A Small Action Challenge

This week, deliberately do one thing purely to please God, without letting anyone know, so as to practise “loving God simply” rather than seeking people’s praise.

This is exactly what the Lord commanded: “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:3–4)

What might it be? Taking out your neighbour’s rubbish without saying a word; praying for forty days for someone who has wronged you, without telling them; arriving at the meeting place half an hour early to set out the chairs, then sitting down quietly. And once you’ve done it, be sure to resist the urge to “let someone know” — the moment that urge is resisted is the moment the heart is cleansed.

Practice 3: A Motive Check

Whenever you’re about to do something, stop first and ask yourself three questions:

Am I doing this because I love God or love people?

Am I expecting something in return, or applause?

If no one ever knew, would I still be willing to do it?

If the answers to these questions help you see your heart clearly, you can practise a pure heart step by step.

These three questions are three filters you can carry with you everywhere. When you first start practising, it will feel very unnatural, even a bit deflating — because you’ll discover just how many of the things you do are mixed. Don’t lose heart; being able to see the mixture is already the Holy Spirit’s grace. It’s the people who can’t see it who are truly in danger.

A Gentle Reminder

A pure heart isn’t something we’re born with; it is formed through practice.

Don’t be afraid to admit that your heart isn’t simple enough; God delights to help a heart that sincerely repents.

Simplicity is not foolishness; it is choosing to rely on the heart rather than relying on the brain to calculate gain and loss.

The Lord Jesus said, “Be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.” (Matthew 10:16) The word translated “harmless” is akeraios in the original, meaning unmixed, pure. So simplicity has never meant naïveté; simplicity is wisdom carried to its very height, still choosing to love cleanly.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we set out today from a question: what does it mean to be “wholehearted”?

Now we have an answer. What God values is our “heart,” not our outward behaviour. As we learn to practise a simple heart, we can truly love God and love people “wholeheartedly.”

The jar of ointment Mary broke was, on Judas’s abacus, a waste; but in the Lord’s eyes it was “a good work,” a memorial to be told wherever the gospel is preached throughout the whole world (Mark 14:6, 9). That is the arithmetic of the kingdom of heaven. What you offer simply to the Lord, the world may laugh at as a bad bargain — but the Lord remembers, and the Lord remembers for ever.

The road the prodigal’s father ran down was, in the villagers’ eyes, a loss of dignity; but in the Heavenly Father’s purposes it was a miniature of redemption. Our God is exactly that kind of God — a God who runs to us first.

So this morning the Lord extends an invitation to you and to me: clear the throne of your heart, and let Jesus be King. Not “the achievements of my service,” not “other people’s approval,” not “how much I’ve done” — let Jesus be King.

And let Jesus receive all the glory. When our love no longer needs to keep a little name for ourselves, God’s glory will fill everything.

In the next lesson we will go on to explore the second dimension by which “wholeheartedness” is measured: “a good conscience.” May we practise step by step, and build a heart that is honest and pure.

Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. (Matthew 5:8) May you see him today.

keyVerses: 1 Timothy 1:5: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.”
declarations: I choose to practise a pure heart, to love Jesus simply — nothing mixed in, nothing calculated — desiring only to please him.
practices: Meditation and prayer
A small action challenge
A motive check
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You know our hearts more deeply than we know them ourselves. You see how many impurities are mixed into our love — wanting to be seen, wanting to be affirmed, wanting to be remembered. Lord, today we will no longer cover it up; we confess it before you.

Create in us clean hearts, and renew a right spirit within us. Take away our hearts of stone and give us hearts of flesh. Make us like Mary, with eyes for you alone, able to break the jar and offer our very best, leaving no way of retreat. Make us like that father, loving first, loving completely, loving without calculation.
Lord, we also ask you to keep us from falling into Judas’s condition — saying the right words with our lips while keeping our own accounts in our hearts.
May the Holy Spirit shine his light on us every day; help us rely on the heart and not the brain, and keep our focus on you — not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances.
May all we do throughout our lives flow out of a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith; may Jesus reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Mark 14:8: “She has done what she could. She has anointed my body beforehand for the burying.” In your life right now, is there an “alabaster jar not yet broken” — something you have long wanted to offer to the Lord, yet always felt was too costly or too precious to give up? What has been holding you back?

Luke 15:20: “But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” Share a moment when you experienced God “running towards you” first. This week, whom is God asking you to run towards first?
l027.title: A Simple Heart
l027.subtitle: How to Measure Whether We Rely on the Heart (Part 1)
l027.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: The Window That Divided Two Lives
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the grace and peace of the Lord Jesus be with us this early morning.

Let’s begin by stepping into a scene together. It is Jerusalem, three thousand years ago, on a day of jubilation. The ark of the covenant is at last being carried into the City of David. Trumpets sound, harps and lyres ring out, and the whole house of Israel shouts and leaps for joy. At the very front of the procession walks the king of the nation. He has taken off his splendid royal robes and put on a linen ephod — the garment of a priest — and he is dancing before the Lord with all his might. Sweat runs down his cheeks, and his heart holds only one thing: God has come; God’s presence has returned to the midst of his people.

At that same moment, in that same city, one person is not out in the street. She is inside the house, watching through a window. The Bible records: “As Yahweh’s ark came into David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out through the window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before Yahweh; and she despised him in her heart.” (2 Samuel 6:16)

Brothers and sisters, notice where these two people are standing. One is inside the celebration, the other outside it. One is in the crowd, the other behind a window. One is drenched in sweat, the other without a speck of dust on her. One is worshipping, the other is analysing. And all that separates them is a single window.

But that window is not really in a wall. It is in the heart.

It is a pane of glass between “relying on the heart” and “relying on the brain”. Through the glass you can see everything, yet feel nothing. You can hear the music, yet you cannot enter the joy. You can describe the scene in perfect detail, even critique it with great eloquence, yet you remain outside the whole time.

In the last lesson we reflected together on “a simple heart”. In this lesson we go a step further and ask a very practical question: how do we measure whether we are truly “relying on the heart”?

It is a question that cuts deep. Because when we have been in church long enough, we all become very good at “looking spiritual”. We know the language of prayer, the gestures of worship, the order of service, the formulas for sharing. Our heads are full of Bible knowledge, theological terms and spiritual vocabulary. But deep down we know perfectly well: knowing is not the same as relying on the heart; proficiency is not the same as love; attendance is not the same as presence.

Obeying God’s word “from the heart” is the key to every believer’s growth in life. Yet amid busy lives and complicated rational thinking, can we still keep that simple heart?

Today we will explore three things together from the Bible: first, how to follow God “from the heart”; second, how a simple heart produces joyful obedience; and third, how to avoid the traps of rational analysis and spiritual hypocrisy. May the Holy Spirit this morning invite us out from behind the window and bring us back to simple faith and love, to enjoy our relationship with God and his joy all over again.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Passages, One Message
sections.html: Before we come to the three key points, let’s first plant our feet firmly on the scriptural foundation. Today’s two theme passages, one from the historical books of the Old Testament and one from the Gospels of the New, stand about a thousand years apart, yet point to the same truth.

sections.heading: 1. The Setting of 2 Samuel 6–7
sections.html:
First and Second Samuel were originally a single book in the Hebrew Bible; they were divided into two only when the Septuagint translation was made in the third century BC. The book records Israel’s transition from the era of the judges into the era of the monarchy, and according to Jewish tradition and internal evidence, its authorship is linked to the records of three prophets: Samuel, Nathan and Gad (see 1 Chronicles 29:29).

David reigned from roughly 1010 to 970 BC. He first reigned as king of Judah in Hebron for seven and a half years; then all Israel anointed him king, and he captured Jerusalem from the Jebusites and made it his capital. The first great thing he did next was not to build a palace, expand his army or repair the city walls, but to “bring the ark of God back home”.

This point is enormously important. The ark was the sign of God’s presence; inside it were the two tablets of the law, Aaron’s rod that had budded, and a jar of manna. Throughout the years of Saul’s reign the ark lay neglected at Kiriath Jearim; even before Saul became king it had already been there for twenty years (see 1 Samuel 7:2). The whole nation had a king, an army and a government, yet it did not put God’s presence at the centre. As soon as David became king, he set out to put that order right.

The first attempt to move the ark failed. They carried it on a new cart, copying the Philistines’ method, instead of having the Levites carry it on poles as God had commanded through Moses. The oxen stumbled, Uzzah reached out his hand to steady the ark, and God struck him down on the spot (2 Samuel 6:6–7). David was afraid, and he left the ark at the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite for three months. Three months later, hearing that God had blessed Obed-Edom’s whole household, he joyfully went again, and this time, in the right way, they offered sacrifices after every six steps, shouting, sounding the trumpet and dancing all the way as they brought the ark into the City of David.

So the worship of 2 Samuel 6 was not a momentary loss of emotional control. It was joy from the depths of the heart of a man who had been through failure, been through holy fear, and been set alight again by grace.

Michal was the daughter of Saul. She had once loved David deeply and had saved his life (1 Samuel 19:11–17). Later Saul gave her in marriage to another man, and after David became king he took her back. Her whole life was caught between her father’s dynasty and her husband’s. The religion she knew was Saul’s kind of religion — all about decorum, all about image, all about “a king ought to look like a king”. So when she saw her husband dancing before the people, her first reaction was not to be moved, but to be ashamed.

Right after that, in chapter 7, God made an everlasting covenant with David through the prophet Nathan: “Your house and your kingdom will be made sure forever before you. Your throne will be established forever.” (2 Samuel 7:16) God also promised: “I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place, and be moved no more.” (2 Samuel 7:10) This is the famous “Davidic covenant” of biblical theology, finally fulfilled in David’s descendant, Jesus Christ.

Brothers and sisters, look at the order: chapter 6 is worship, chapter 7 is blessing. In chapter 6 David lays himself down before God; in chapter 7 God gives him an everlasting throne. And chapter 6 ends with another, chilling sentence: “Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.” (2 Samuel 6:23) One man bore everlasting fruit; the other left no descendants. This is no coincidence. This is the Bible speaking to us.

sections.heading: 2. The Setting of Matthew 11
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector, mainly for Jewish readers, probably in the AD 60s. The whole book sets out to prove that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David.

What is the setting of chapter 11? Rejection. John the Baptist sends messengers from prison to ask, “Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3) Then the Lord Jesus rebukes Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum — towns that had seen him perform most of his mighty works with their own eyes, yet did not repent.

Right in the middle of all this rejection, doubt and indifference, the Lord Jesus suddenly lifts up his head and prays: “At that time, Jesus answered, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.’” (Matthew 11:25) When Luke records the same event, he adds that the Lord Jesus “rejoiced in the Holy Spirit” (Luke 10:21).

The background to these words is that the scribes and Pharisees — the people who knew the Scriptures best in that day — shut the Messiah out, while fishermen, tax collectors, women and little children followed him with joy.

Brothers and sisters, two passages, two eras, two scenes — and they say the same thing: God is not found by a clever brain; God is met by a simple heart.

sections.heading: 1. Obeying God’s Word from the Heart Is Simple
sections.html:
The Scriptural Foundation

The Lord Jesus quoted the words of Isaiah to rebuke the religious leaders of his day: “These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me. And in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrine rules made by men.” (Matthew 15:8–9)

Notice the three contrasts here. Lips against heart; rules made by men against the word of God; worship against “in vain”.

The word for “in vain” in Greek is matēn, meaning “empty, futile, without effect”. In other words, an act of worship can get everything right — the right place, the right time, the right ritual, the right Scripture — and the result can still be zero. Why? Because “their heart is far from me”.

Brothers and sisters, what a sobering reminder this is. It is not that God doesn’t value what we do; it is that God values the heart that does it. “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

A simple heart “believes first, understands later”

A simple heart acts from within, out of love, without tangled motives.

We often have a habit: God speaks a word, and our first reaction is “why?” Why should I forgive him? He hasn’t even apologised. Why should I give? Money is already tight this month. Why should I go and care for that person? I hardly know him. We want to send God’s word into the courtroom of reason first, to cross-examine it, debate it thoroughly and make sure it’s worth our while, before we are willing to carry it out.

But God does not want us to understand and analyse his word thoroughly before we act; he wants us simply to believe and to do it — that is what an “act of faith” is.

The Lord Jesus said: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:31–32)

Look at the order: first “remain in my word”, then “you will know the truth”, and only last “the truth will make you free”. We don’t first know and then obey; we first obey and then come to know. Understanding happens in obedience; freedom is gained in action.

The Lord Jesus also said: “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” (John 7:17) The resolve to do comes first; the knowing comes after. This is the Bible’s consistent way of knowing: truth is not researched into being; it is obeyed into being.

James puts it even more bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) “Deluding your own selves” — in the original the sense is to talk yourself, by plausible-sounding reasoning, into a false conclusion. Brothers and sisters, the person we deceive most easily is ourselves. We hear a great many sermons and think we’ve come a long way, when in fact we haven’t moved a single step.

An Example from Daily Life

I often think of a picture. A child is learning to swim, and the coach says, “Relax, give your body to the water, and the water will hold you up.” The child stands at the side of the pool thinking for a long time: what is the density of water? What is the formula for buoyancy? Will my body weight be more than the buoyancy? The more he analyses, the tenser his body becomes; and the tenser his body becomes, the more he sinks. Next to him is another child who understands none of this but simply trusts the coach. With a splash he jumps in, spreads out his arms and legs — and floats.

Brothers and sisters, the principle of buoyancy was learned on the water by the child who floated, not worked out on the poolside by the one who calculated.

Think of an even more everyday picture. A mother is teaching her child to ride a bicycle. The child asks, “Mum, why don’t two wheels fall over?” The mother says, “Start pedalling — once you’re moving, you won’t fall.” If the child insisted on understanding the gyroscopic effect and the conservation of angular momentum before he would get on the bike, he would probably never learn to ride in his life. But as long as he is willing to push down on the pedal the first time, his body will find its own balance.

Faith is just like that. God’s word does not take effect only once we have thought it through; it is when we step out that we discover he has been holding us up all along.

Reason and Faith Are Not Enemies

Here I want to say a word of balance. Evangelical faith has never been anti-intellectual. We believe “You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5), and when the Lord Jesus quoted it he also added “with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37). God gave us reason so that we would use it to love him, to know him, to discern heresy, and to search the Scriptures diligently.

The problem is not “having a brain”; the problem is “using the brain in place of the heart”, putting reason in the place of the Holy Spirit. Paul says: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1) Knowledge itself is not sin; the problem is knowledge without love.

The Portuguese-American neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, in his 1994 book Descartes’ Error, records a famous case. A patient he called “Elliot” suffered damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex during surgery for a brain tumour. His IQ scores remained excellent, his memory intact, his logical reasoning flawless, yet he had completely lost the involvement of emotion. The result? He could not make any decision at all. Just deciding which pen to use, or whether to file documents by date or by subject, could keep him comparing back and forth for hours, and in the end he accomplished nothing; his career and his marriage collapsed one after the other. From this Damasio argued that pure reason does not lead to better decisions; on the contrary, it paralyses a person.

Brothers and sisters, in science this is called the “somatic marker hypothesis”; in the Bible it is called “the heart”. Solomon said it three thousand years ago: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The wellspring of life does not flow from the brain; it flows from the heart.

The French mathematician and thinker Blaise Pascal left a famous saying in his Pensées, generally held to be number 423 of that work: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” He himself was an outstanding mathematician, yet he understood that reason has its limits.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The Three Foundations of Kingdom 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Notice that it says “standard”, not “reference book”. A standard means this: it does not first need the approval of my reason; it is itself the highest authority. When I treat God’s word as my standard, my response is “Yes, Lord”; when I treat God’s word as a reference, my response is “Wait a moment, Lord, let me think about it.”

And the difference between “relying on the heart” and “relying on the brain” is exactly what 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart and you are glad; rely on the brain and you are troubled. Because when we rely on the brain, the focus is on ourselves — is this worth it for me, will I lose out, what about my face? When we rely on the heart, the focus is on Jesus — he has spoken, so I go.

This is also the starting point of the “fivefold change”: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. Today’s lesson sets out to change one mindset: I do not understand first and then believe; I believe first and then understand.

sections.heading: 2. Rely on the Heart and You Will Be Joyful; Rely on the Brain and You Will Be Troubled
sections.html:
David’s Dance and Michal’s Eyes

“Relying on the heart” brings forth joyful worship; “relying on the brain” brings burdens, criticism and judgement. 2 Samuel 6 portrays this vividly through one dramatic contrast.

First, look at David: “David danced before Yahweh with all his might; and David was clothed in a linen ephod.” (2 Samuel 6:14)

The phrase “with all his might” is in Hebrew bekol-‘oz, literally “with all strength”. This was no graceful court dance; this was celebration with total abandon, dripping with sweat, with no thought for his image. He took off his royal robes and put on a linen ephod. The royal robe stands for status; the ephod stands for service. He did not stand before God in his identity as “king”; he bowed before God in his identity as “worshipper”.

Now look at Michal: “Michal the daughter of Saul looked out through the window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before Yahweh; and she despised him in her heart.” (2 Samuel 6:16)

“Despised” — in Hebrew bazah — means “to regard as worthless, to look down on”. The same word is used when Esau despised his birthright (Genesis 25:34). Brothers and sisters, the essence of judging is putting a very low price on someone else’s actions.

That evening, when David returned home to bless his household, Michal came out to meet him and said: “How glorious the king of Israel was today, who uncovered himself today in the eyes of his servants’ maids, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!” (2 Samuel 6:20)

Those words are full of analysis: she analysed the setting (in the eyes of his servants’ maids), analysed the status (the king of Israel), analysed the gains and losses (how glorious he was today). Every word was precise; every sentence was cutting. Once reason departs from love, it turns into a knife.

David’s reply is our theme text for today: “It was before Yahweh, who chose me above your father, and above all his house, to appoint me prince over the people of Yahweh, over Israel. Therefore I will celebrate before Yahweh. I will be yet more vile than this, and will be worthless in my own sight. But the maids of whom you have spoken will honor me.” (2 Samuel 6:21–22)

Notice the first thing David says: “It was before Yahweh.” In the original, the phrase “before Yahweh” appears again and again in this chapter. David had only one audience in his heart. In Michal’s eyes there were many audiences — servants, maids, the people, public opinion. The more audiences a person has in his heart, the less free he can be.

Then notice David’s second statement: “I will be yet more vile than this, and will be worthless in my own sight.” Brothers and sisters, what an astonishing reply. You humiliate me, and not only do I not defend myself — I will go lower still. This is exactly what 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Did David lay down his position as king? No — he was returning to his originally intended position as a creature. Before God, the king and the infant alike are dust.

The Distance of One Window

Brothers and sisters, think about that window again.

It wasn’t that Michal didn’t know how important the ark was. She was Saul’s daughter, raised in the palace from childhood; her knowledge of religious ritual was probably richer than that of anyone out in the street. The problem was that she was “inside” — inside the house, yet outside the worship.

This is the most dangerous place for a spiritual life to be: you are very close to where it’s happening, yet you never go in; you see most clearly, yet you feel the least; your commentary is the most accurate, yet your experience is the shallowest.

Are there Michals in the church today? There are. Some sit in the back row and never miss a meeting, yet never raise a hand, never open their mouth, never shed a tear. In their hearts they’re thinking: the theology of this song is off; that speaker’s illustration was inappropriate; the sound desk is too loud today. They are right about everything — except that their heart never went in.

I want to say this very carefully: discernment is necessary; the Bible commands us to “test all things” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). But the difference between discernment and judging is this: discernment is for protecting the community; judging is for raising ourselves up. Discernment builds up; judging breeds bitterness.

Joy Carries Weight

“Rely on the heart and you will be joyful” — this is not just a word of encouragement; it is a fact with both spiritual and physiological grounds.

Nehemiah said to the returned exiles: “Don’t be grieved, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.” (Nehemiah 8:10) Joy is not the result of strength; joy is the source of strength.

The psalmist also says: “Serve Yahweh with gladness. Come before his presence with singing.” (Psalm 100:2) “Gladness” is not an optional extra; it is the very essence of worship.

On the scientific side, Gunter Kreutz and fellow researchers at the University of Frankfurt in Germany published a study in 2004 in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine comparing amateur choir members in two conditions: “singing” a piece and “listening to the same piece”. They found that while singing, the secretory immunoglobulin A in their saliva (s-IgA, associated with mucosal immunity) rose significantly, and their positive emotions rose significantly too; merely listening did not produce the same effect.

Brothers and sisters, this study gives us a vivid reminder: taking part and looking on do not have the same effect. With the same hymn, those who sing it receive something; those who only watch do not. In the same service of worship, those who go in are strengthened; those who stand behind the window come away with nothing but opinions.

A classic 2003 study by the American psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, also showed that participants assigned to record “things to be grateful for” each week did markedly better — in mood, in physical symptoms and in optimism about the future — than the group assigned to record “hassles”.

Gratitude and grumbling are two different neural circuits, and two different spiritual states. David walked the road of gratitude; Michal walked the road of grumbling.

Two Endings

The text goes on to record a heartbreaking sentence: “Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.” (2 Samuel 6:23)

The Bible doesn’t say plainly whether this was God’s direct punishment or the result of husband and wife living as strangers from then on. But the Bible puts this sentence right here so that we will see: judging cannot bring forth life. A cold heart bears no fruit.

By contrast, David, because he worshipped from the heart, not only gained God’s pleasure but, straight afterwards in chapter 7, entered the destiny and blessing God had prepared for him and his descendants (2 Samuel 7:10–16). God said: “Your house and your kingdom will be made sure forever before you. Your throne will be established forever.” (2 Samuel 7:16)

Brothers and sisters, to the man who danced before God, God gave an everlasting throne. The woman who sneered from behind the window did not leave behind even one child.

Later God assessed David like this: “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.” (Acts 13:22) “A man after my heart” — what God wants has never been people after his brain, but people after his heart.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Michal stirred up conflict with her contempt. Had David struck back with his royal authority, that household would have been utterly destroyed. Instead David chose to be “yet more vile”. This is exactly the selfless life — selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me (see Galatians 2:20).

321 also says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

David’s focus was “before Yahweh”, so he was free. Michal’s focus was “in the eyes of his servants’ maids”, so she was bound. Brothers and sisters, this morning ask yourself one question: who is the audience in my heart?

321’s “920 practice” reminds us: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we are to practise living out the “0” (selfless) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Michal was David’s closest “2” — and also his hardest. The people hardest to love are often the people closest to us. In that moment David did not bear the fruit of revenge; he bore the fruit of gentleness and self-control.

sections.heading: 3. God Delights in a Simple Heart, Not a Clever Brain
sections.html:
The Thanksgiving of the Lord Jesus

“At that time, Jesus answered, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.’” (Matthew 11:25)

There are two key words in this verse.

The first is “the wise and understanding”. In Greek it is sophōn kai synetōn, referring to people who are wise, learned and able to grasp things thoroughly. In the setting of that day it meant the scribes and Pharisees — the people who could recite the Five Books of Moses and were experts in the law.

The second is “infants”. In Greek it is nēpiois, literally “little children who cannot yet speak”. What marks an infant? No knowledge, no ability, no resources, no bargaining chips — only one instinct: to reach out its arms to be held.

The Lord Jesus thanked the Father for hiding spiritual things from the first group and revealing them to the second. This does not mean God dislikes clever people; Paul was one of the most learned men of his day. It means this: the door into God’s kingdom is not opened for the head but for the heart; that door is very low, and you have to stoop down to go through it.

Elsewhere the Lord Jesus says it even more directly: “Most certainly I tell you, unless you turn, and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.” (Matthew 18:3) “Turn” in the original is straphēte, meaning “to turn round, to change direction”. As people we grow older and older and know more and more, yet the way into the kingdom of heaven asks us to walk back — back to that starting point of simple trust.

Paul says: “But God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong.” (1 Corinthians 1:27)

Spiritual Things Are Not Calculated

Spiritual things are not gained by analysis and calculation; it is the simple heart that can enter God’s kingdom.

Think of examples in the Bible.

When Abraham was called, “He went out, not knowing where he went” (Hebrews 11:8). Had he first demanded a map, a geological survey and a full risk assessment, he would have stayed in Ur for ever.

Peter had toiled all night in his boat and caught nothing. The Lord Jesus — a carpenter — told him to put out into deep water and let down the nets. From the point of view of a professional fisherman, this was an amateur instructing an expert, and casting nets in deep water in broad daylight made no sense. Peter said: “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.” (Luke 5:5) “But at your word” — with that one phrase, the net was full.

When General Naaman wanted the prophet to heal his leprosy, Elisha told him to go and wash seven times in the Jordan. He flew into a rage: were not the rivers of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel? His analysis was entirely correct: the water really was better. But cleansing was not in the water; it was in obedience. Only when he went down and “dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God” was his flesh restored, “like the flesh of a little child” (2 Kings 5:14). Brothers and sisters, notice that description — like the flesh of a little child. Obedience makes the old young again.

A Simple Heart Is Trust, Not Naivety

Here I need to make an important distinction. A simple heart is not a muddled heart.

Paul says: “Brothers, don’t be children in thoughts, yet in malice be babies, but in thoughts be mature.” (1 Corinthians 14:20) The Lord Jesus also said: “Be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.” (Matthew 10:16)

So simplicity is not ignorance; simplicity is being “uncomplicated”. This simplicity is exactly what Paul feared would be stolen: “But I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.” (2 Corinthians 11:3)

“Simplicity” in the original is haplotēs, meaning “single, unfolded, with no hidden layers”. The first thing Satan did in the Garden of Eden was to add a hidden layer to Eve’s heart: “Has God really said …?” (Genesis 3:1) From then on the human heart was no longer one piece but several layers: a layer on the surface, a layer underneath, and yet another layer at the very bottom.

The Preacher says: “Behold, I have only found this: that God made man upright; but they search for many schemes.” (Ecclesiastes 7:29) “Many schemes” — that is complication. What God made was simple; what humans added was complication.

That simple heart is like an infant trusting its parents — not doubting, not bargaining, simply depending. The psalmist describes it like this: “Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.” (Psalm 131:2) Notice: it is a “weaned child”, not a baby still at the breast. A nursing baby is in its mother’s arms in order to get milk; a weaned child is in its mother’s arms simply for the mother. A simple heart does not seek God to get something from him; it simply wants God himself.

The Wall of Knowledge and the Door of Faith

The lesson text contains a very precious reminder: don’t let theological knowledge become a wall around our hearts; let simple faith become the door to our worship.

Brothers and sisters, walls and doors are built from the same bricks. The same body of theological knowledge can be built into a wall that shuts God out, or laid into a doorway that brings us before God. Where is the difference? In whether that knowledge has passed through the “heart”.

Paul warns of the state of things in the last days, saying some will be “always learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 3:7). He also says: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6)

The American psychologist Barry Schwartz, in his 2004 book The Paradox of Choice, drew together research by himself and his colleagues showing that people can be divided into “maximizers” and “satisficers”. Maximizers must find the very best option in everything; they gather as much information as possible and compare again and again. Satisficers set a reasonable standard and decide once it is met. The research showed that the choices maximizers make are not necessarily any worse objectively, but they have more regret, lower satisfaction and less happiness.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a spiritual reminder. In the matter of following God, if we keep “maximizing” — always trying to find the most cost-effective way to obey, the safest amount to give, the least costly degree of forgiveness — we will find that the more information we have, the less joy we have.

The Danish thinker Søren Kierkegaard wrote a book in 1847 whose very title is Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. He was right: we are complicated because we want many things at once.

The missionary Hudson Taylor served in China for more than fifty years, and he is generally credited with this widely quoted saying: God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply. At the heart of that saying is simplicity — no detours, no shortcuts, no hidden layers.

Simplicity Makes Life Grow

A heart like this leads a person to know God and experience God, and makes our spiritual life keep growing, being renewed and gaining power.

The early church was a group of people just like this: “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.” (Acts 2:46–47)

Notice “gladness and singleness of heart”: the original is aphelotēti kardias — “a simple heart”. These people had no seminaries, no systematic theology textbooks, no buildings; what they had was a simple heart, and the result was that “the Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.”

Harvard University’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, is one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in the world. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has pointed out publicly many times that the most consistent finding of this study, spanning more than eighty years, is not that wealth or fame brings health and happiness, but “good relationships”.

Brothers and sisters, this confirms exactly the order 321 teaches: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Michal put “things” (decorum, image, royal dignity) ahead of “people” and “God”, and her relationships shattered. David put “God” first, and his other relationships were healed instead.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

What Michal wanted was “David looking like a king”; what David wanted was “Yahweh reigning as King in this city”. That is the difference. When we rely on the brain, we are really defending a tiny king — ourselves; when we rely on the heart, we are welcoming the true King — Jesus.

321 also says: our perspective must shift — from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly.

Michal’s perspective was man’s, earthly, temporary and worldly: what will people think? What about the royal family’s dignity? David’s perspective was God’s, heavenly, eternal and godly: this was before Yahweh. The same event, two perspectives, two lives.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Brain to the Selfless Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we place this lesson within the whole picture of 321, we see it even more clearly.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Jesus is my role model — he says: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Notice that this verse comes right after “revealed them to infants” in 11:25. The Lord first thanks the Father for revealing things to infants, and then immediately calls the weary and burdened to come to him. These are two sides of the same speech: the simple heart receives revelation, and the simple heart also receives rest.

The Bible is my standard — a standard means I don’t send God’s word into the courtroom of reason to be tried; I bring myself before God’s word to be tried.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Michal relied on her own judgement; David relied on being “before Yahweh”.

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The moment David took off his royal robe was the moment he let Jesus be King. He gave up the glory, and God gave him an everlasting throne.

The Goal is: establish God’s system. God’s system is not established by cleverness; it is established by a company of people who obey simply.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

321 says: the old self is “self-centred”; the new self is “selfless”. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem.

What lies deep beneath “relying on the brain”? The self-centred life. I want to understand because I want to be in control; I want to be in control because I don’t feel safe handing myself over; I don’t feel safe because, in my heart, I am still the king.

Michal’s problem was not cleverness; it was the self-centred life. Her ego needed decorum to prop it up, so her husband’s lowliness became her humiliation.

When David said, “I will be yet more vile than this, and will be worthless in my own sight,” that was selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me (see Galatians 2:20). Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan cannot attack a person who has no ego left to be offended. If you don’t care about your own face, Satan can find nothing to grab hold of.

The Fivefold Change

321 speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Today’s lesson starts precisely with mindset. The old mindset is: I must understand first before I can obey. The new mindset is: I obey, and then I truly understand.

Once the mindset changes, the life changes — I am no longer tense; I begin to rest.

Once the life changes, daily living changes — when I finish reading the Bible in the morning, I no longer just underline it; I go and do one thing straight away.

Once daily living changes, relationships change — I no longer look at my spouse, my children or my co-workers with an analysing eye; I look at them with the eyes of love.

Once relationships change, ministry changes — I no longer serve with my abilities; I serve with my life.

235 Relationships and the 920 Practice

321’s “235 relationships” teach us: become a “2” — spiritual companions — with selfless people; build “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, do you have a “2”? A spiritual companion you can say this to: “Lately I seem to be serving with my brain”? A simple heart is hard to guard alone; it needs companions. In the wilderness David had Jonathan; Paul had Barnabas; Timothy had Paul.

And the “920 practice” reminds us: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we are to practise living out the selfless life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (see Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice: the second of the nine graces is joy. Joy is not a personality type; joy is a fruit. And fruit isn’t squeezed out by effort; it grows naturally from life. Those who rely on the heart bear fruit; those who rely on the brain only produce verdicts.

The Shift in Perspective

321 says: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly.

Brothers and sisters, this lesson gives us a very simple test. When you are hesitating over whether to obey something God has already made clear, ask yourself four questions:

First, are the considerations I’m weighing right now from man’s point of view, or from God’s?

Second, am I calculating earthly gains and losses, or heavenly rewards?

Third, what I care about right now — is it temporary face, or eternal fruit?

Fourth, is my motive right now worldly security, or God’s commission?

Once you’ve asked those four questions, the answer is usually very clear.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Practical Exercises, Eight Stages to Go Deeper
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices for daily living. Let’s look at them one by one, and use 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep into our lives.

Practice 1: Act on One Thing Straight after Reading the Bible

After your devotions each day, don’t just reflect or take notes — “act at once” and put into practice one sentence you read today. Even if it’s something as simple as forgiving someone, encouraging a brother or sister, or treating your family more lovingly, as long as it comes from a simple heart that loves God, God accepts it with pleasure.

How do you actually do this? When you finish reading, don’t close your Bible and rush off. Stop for thirty seconds and ask: “Lord, from today’s passage, what one thing do you want me to do today?” Then write that thing down, as a sentence with a time and a person in it. Don’t write, “I want to be more loving.” Write, “Today at twelve noon, I will phone so-and-so.”

James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

Practice 2: Learn to Worship as David Did

In private or in a meeting, try laying aside your inhibitions and your image, and simply sing for God and dance for God, regardless of what others think. Write down how one time of worshipping from the heart felt and what fruit it bore.

Brothers and sisters, I know that for many people this is the hardest of the three. Especially for us Chinese, who were taught from childhood to be reserved, to be proper, to “know our limits”. But remember David’s words: “It was before Yahweh.”

You can begin in the most private place. In your own room, shut the door, put on a worship song, lift your hands and sing to God. No one sees but God — and he is your only audience.

The Lord Jesus said: “But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.” (John 4:23)

Practice 3: Repent Before God of Worship and Service Driven by Reason

Be still and ask God: “Lord, am I more often serving you with my brain rather than with my heart?” Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and bring renewal.

Repentance is not self-blame. Self-blame looks inward at ourselves, and the more we look, the deeper we sink; repentance turns round to look at God, and the more we look, the brighter it gets. “Repentance” in the original is metanoia — precisely “a change of mind, a turning round”.

The psalmist says: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

Using the Eight Stages to Deepen These Three Practices

Stage one, Information. Today’s lesson is the information: the difference between relying on the heart and relying on the brain, the contrast between David and Michal, the Lord Jesus’ praise of infants. Copy these verses into your notebook; copying them once beats reading them ten times.

Stage two, Revelation. For information to become revelation, it must pass through the Holy Spirit. Ask the Lord to show you: where is that “window” in my life? In what matter have I been standing outside, just watching? Ask the Lord to point out one specific person, one specific matter.

Stage three, Conviction. For revelation to become faith, there has to be an “Amen”. Say before God: Lord, I trust your word more than my analysis; I believe that obedience comes first and understanding follows, not understanding first and obedience after.

Stage four, Implementation. Starting today, do three things: act on one thing straight after your morning devotions; worship at least once a day in a way that “only God sees”; and each evening examine before God whether today you relied on the heart or on the brain.

Stage five, Evaluation. After a week, get out your notebook and look back: in these seven days, how many things did I actually carry out? Which day was most joyful? What was I doing that day? Joy will usually mark the moments when you relied on the heart.

Stage six, Correction. When you find yourself slipping back into analysing and putting things off, don’t lose heart — correct course at once. It might mean moving your devotional time ten minutes earlier; it might mean shrinking “the one thing to do” to something you are sure you can do. The aim is not greatness; the aim is reality.

Stage seven, Repetition. A simple heart is not won by a single decision; it is formed by repeated practice. An action repeated for forty days becomes a habit; a habit repeated for forty months becomes character.

Stage eight, Multiplication. Share what you’ve experienced with your “2”. Tell them: this week I tried doing one thing straight after reading the Bible, and here’s what happened. If a changed life isn’t multiplied, it stops with us; once it multiplies, it enters God’s system.

A Gentle Reminder

We often think that “reading more and understanding more” will please God more, yet we overlook the fact that what God values is a simple heart.

Brothers and sisters, this is not telling us not to study or not to pursue truth. It is reminding us: knowledge that has not passed through the heart turns into a wall. Don’t let theological knowledge become a wall around our hearts; let simple faith become the door to our worship.

The theologian A. W. Tozer opens his book The Knowledge of the Holy by writing that what comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us. Notice — he is not speaking of how much information about God we have stored up, but of what kind of God truly rises up within us when we think of him.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Are You Relying on the Brain, or on the Heart?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that window.

Are you following the Lord by “relying on the brain” or by “relying on the heart”? This is not a question of knowledge; it is a choice about a relationship.

A question of knowledge can be looked up, studied in a class, asked of an expert. A choice about a relationship can only be made by you. No one can walk out of the room for you; no one can push open that door for you.

What God is looking for is a simple heart like David’s, not a rational gaze like Michal’s.

Three thousand years ago, that king in a linen ephod danced in the streets of Jerusalem. A thousand years later, his descendant Jesus Christ laid aside not a royal robe but the glory of heaven. Paul says he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), and in the end he humbled himself, “becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8).

Brothers and sisters, our Lord is the one who relied on the heart most completely of all. He did not bargain with the Father; in the Garden of Gethsemane he said only this: “Nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39)

He is our role model.

So this morning I want to issue you a call: come out. Come out from behind the window, come out of your analysis, come out of “I’ll do it once I’ve thought it through”. God’s word has already been made clear enough; what remains is not a problem of understanding but a problem of the will.

Let us choose to worship from the heart, obey from the heart, and love the Lord from the heart, because that is the life that can truly enter into the heart of God.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: At that time, Jesus answered, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.” (Matthew 11:25)

David said to Michal, “It was before Yahweh, who chose me above your father, and above all his house, to appoint me prince over the people of Yahweh, over Israel. Therefore I will celebrate before Yahweh. I will be yet more vile than this, and will be worthless in my own sight. But the maids of whom you have spoken will honor me.” (2 Samuel 6:21–22)
declarations: Let us declare together:
I declare: I will love God and worship God with a simple heart; I will no longer analyse the Lord’s commands with my brain, but obey his word from the heart!
practices: Act on one thing straight after reading the Bible
Learn to worship as David did
Repent before God of worship and service driven by reason
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Lord, you search the human heart; you know how many hidden layers there are within us. We confess that we often serve you with our brains rather than with our hearts. We are familiar with your word, yet we do not obey it; we critique worship, yet we do not enter into it; we stand behind the window, seeing very clearly, yet living very coldly.
Lord, forgive us. Take Michal’s gaze out of us, and give us David’s heart. Make us become like little children — not doubting, not bargaining, simply depending on you.
Holy Spirit, shine your light on us, and point out the one thing we have kept putting off, kept analysing, yet still refused to obey. Give us strength to go and do it today.
Lord Jesus, you are our role model; the Bible is our standard; the Holy Spirit is our guide. Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 2 Samuel 6:16 says: “As Yahweh’s ark came into David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out through the window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before Yahweh; and she despised him in her heart.” In your life right now, what is one thing you have kept “watching through the window” but have never stepped into? What has been holding you back?

Matthew 11:25 says: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.” Share a time when you “obeyed first and understood later”. What side of God did that act of obedience help you come to know?
l028.title: A Simple Heart
l028.subtitle: How to Measure Whether We Rely on the Heart (Part 2)
l028.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: The Lane No One Was Watching
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. In this morning’s devotion, let’s begin with a scene many of us have been through.

Have you ever gone through customs at an international airport? You come out with your luggage, and ahead of you there are usually two lanes: a green one marked “Nothing to declare” and a red one marked “Goods to declare”. Very often there is no one beside those two lanes keeping an eye on you, no one opening your bags, no one asking you a single question. You could stride out through the green lane, quickly and naturally, and no one would ever know.

But one person would know. That person is you.

In those few short seconds, what decides which lane you walk through is not the camera in the ceiling, nor the customs officer in uniform, but a voice inside you. That voice is not loud and not noisy, yet it is very hard to fool. After you have walked through, it will keep following you — out of the airport, into the car, all the way home — and even at night, when you lie down, it will still be there, speaking softly.

The Bible gives this voice a name. It is called “conscience”.

Brothers and sisters, throughout this series of morning devotions we have been learning one thing: to “rely on the heart”, not “rely on the brain”. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you are glad, rely on the brain and you are troubled. But here a question arises: how do I know whether I am really “relying on the heart”, or merely “relying on the brain”? How do I know whether I am truly wholehearted, or merely look very zealous?

This is a very practical question, because zeal can be faked. Our serving can be very busy, our attendance very punctual, our giving very generous, our praying very loud — all these outward, visible things can be faked convincingly. The Lord Jesus quoted the words of Isaiah: “These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.” (Matthew 15:8) Lips very close to God, and a heart very far from him — what a frightening kind of distance that is.

So “relying on the heart” is not outward zeal but inward sincerity. What, then, do we measure it by?

This lesson gives us a very accurate measuring rod: “a clear conscience”. Paul says: “But the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.” (1 Timothy 1:5) Notice the order in this verse: the sum of every command is love, and this love has three sources — a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. All three are inward; not one is outward. God never looks first at what we have done; he looks first at what kind of heart we did it from.

Incidentally, the title of today’s lesson speaks of “a clear conscience” — literally, a conscience without shame — which is a very vivid way of putting it; while the Chinese Union Version, at both 1 Timothy 1:5 and Acts 24:16, renders the phrase as a conscience “without deficiency”. The two ideas are closely related: when there is nothing owing before God, there is no shame in the heart. Today, whenever we quote Scripture, we follow the wording of the Bible text itself (in English, “a good conscience” and “a conscience void of offense”), while in our teaching, practices and declarations we keep this lesson’s own phrase, “a clear conscience”.

Today we will look at three things together: first, where a clear conscience comes from; second, how a clear conscience becomes the standard for measuring whether we are “relying on the heart”; and third, what God does when a person lives by conscience and yet is misunderstood.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Paul, Peter and a Ship That Can Founder
sections.html:
To read our theme passages accurately, let’s first get to know their setting.

The author of 1 Timothy is the apostle Paul. According to the common view among evangelical scholars, Paul was released after his first house arrest in Rome (about AD 60–62) and travelled further; 1 Timothy was probably written between AD 62 and 64, to Paul’s spiritual son Timothy. Paul says: “As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine,” (1 Timothy 1:3) — which shows that Timothy had stayed on in Ephesus at the time.

Ephesus was the most important city of the Roman province of Asia, home of the temple of the goddess Artemis. It was steeped in religion and bustling with commerce, a crossroads of every kind of philosophy, superstition, occultism and false teacher. In an environment like that, the church’s greatest danger was not persecution from outside but deviation from within. So Paul deals with “different doctrine” right at the start. He says those people “have turned away to vain talking”, “desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm.” (1 Timothy 1:6–7)

Notice how Paul corrects them.
