He does not debate the details of doctrine point by point; he pulls the conversation straight back to the root: the goal of the command is love, and love comes out of a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. In other words, whether a person’s teaching goes astray often begins not in the head but in the conscience.

This is exactly the warning at the end of the same chapter: “holding faith and a good conscience, which some having thrust away made a shipwreck concerning the faith.” (1 Timothy 1:19) Paul’s picture is a ship breaking apart. Conscience is like a ship’s ballast and rudder: it is not the engine and supplies no power, but without it, however fast the ship goes, it will capsize. Brothers and sisters, what a fitting picture — so many people fail not because their gifts are lacking, but because they have thrust away their conscience.

Now consider the word “conscience” itself. In New Testament Greek it is συνείδησις (syneidēsis), made up of σύν (together) and εἴδησις (knowing); literally it means “knowing together”. The Latin conscientia and the English conscience are built in exactly the same way. The word itself tells us something: when you do something, there is someone besides yourself who “knows it together” with you. Paul puts it clearly in Romans: “I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 9:1).

The word behind “good” in 1 Timothy 1:5 is in Greek ἀγαθή (agathē), simply “good”; while the word in Acts 24:16, rendered “void of offense”, is a different word, ἀπρόσκοπος (aproskopos), meaning “not stumbling, not causing others to stumble”. Taken together, the good conscience the Bible speaks of has two sides: good towards God, and causing no one to stumble towards others.

The scene of Acts 24 is Caesarea, around AD 57. Paul has been accused by the Jews and is on trial before the governor Felix. In that courtroom, falsely accused and framed with trumped-up charges, Paul states the discipline of his whole life: “In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.” (Acts 24:16) The original word behind “practice” carries the sense of “training, striving hard” — a clear conscience is not something we are born with; it is built by daily practice.

As for 1 Peter, it was written at around the same time as 1 Timothy, about AD 62–64, to believers living as exiles scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia. They were facing exclusion from society and harsh treatment from their masters. Peter tells them: “For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience toward God.” (1 Peter 2:19)

Three books, three settings: one in a city overrun by false teachers, one in a courtroom of false accusation, one in a foreign land of exile and suffering. Through these three passages God tells us the same thing: in the places no one else can see, conscience is the most honest line between us and God.

Teaching 1: A Clear Conscience Comes from the Precious Blood of Jesus

sections.heading: 1. A Numb Conscience Is the Most Dangerous Kind of Health
sections.html:
The lesson begins by pointing out a fact: before we came to faith, our conscience was gradually numbed by sin, even to the point of ceasing to function. Paul’s words are shocking: “through the hypocrisy of men who speak lies, branded in their own conscience as with a hot iron” (1 Timothy 4:2).

The word “branded … as with a hot iron” in Greek is καυστηριάζω (kautēriazō), the very word used in medicine for “cauterising”; the English cauterize comes from it. In ancient and modern surgery alike, searing a wound with intense heat can stop the bleeding, but it also destroys the nerve endings there, so that patch of skin loses its sense of pain for good. Paul’s meaning is this: a person’s conscience can be seared by sin again and again, until in the end — it no longer hurts.

No pain sounds like good news. In fact it is the most dangerous news of all.

The renowned twentieth-century hand surgeon Dr Paul Brand (1914–2003) treated patients with Hansen’s disease (leprosy) in India. One of the most important discoveries of his life was this: the loss of fingers and toes in Hansen’s disease is mostly not because the bacteria eat them away directly, but because damaged nerves lose the sense of pain. So patients would grip a scalding pot without pulling their hand away, or keep walking on a foot with a hole worn in it, injury upon injury, until they were crippled. He later co-wrote with the author Philip Yancey Pain: The Gift Nobody Wants (published in 1993), and the title itself is a sermon — pain is the gift nobody wants, yet everybody needs.

Medicine also knows a rare genetic disorder called “congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis” (CIPA). Children with this condition cannot feel pain from birth. They seem like superheroes, but in reality they often bite through their tongues, burn themselves or break bones without knowing it, and most do not live to adulthood.

Brothers and sisters, please take this to heart: what the sense of pain is to the body, conscience is to the soul. A conscience that can hurt is not a defect in your spiritual life; it is evidence that your spiritual life is still alive. What is truly frightening is the person who has done what should not be done and feels nothing at all.

sections.heading: 2. Why Does Conscience Go Numb?
sections.html:
A conscience does not go numb in a day; there is a process. Paul says to Titus: “To the pure, all things are pure; but to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their mind and their conscience are defiled.” (Titus 1:15) Sin does not only defile a person’s actions; it also defiles the very organ that judges those actions.

Psychology offers good supporting evidence for this process. In 1957 the social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance” (A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance). He pointed out that when a person’s behaviour is inconsistent with his own beliefs, an uncomfortable tension arises inside; and to remove that tension there are two routes — change the behaviour, or change the belief. Sadly, changing behaviour is harder and changing belief is easier. So people begin to find reasons for themselves: “Everybody does it,” “This time is an exception,” “I had no choice,” “Nobody gets hurt anyway.”

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely how a conscience is seared layer by layer. The first time, there’s a sharp sting in the heart; the second time, just a little discomfort; the third time, you find a very good reason; the fourth time, you feel entirely in the right. By the tenth time, that spot no longer hurts.

And here is the problem — people cannot wash their own conscience clean. You can suppress it, get round it, anaesthetise it, find reasons for it, but you cannot wash it clean. Hebrews says clearly of the Old Testament sacrifices: “This is a symbol of the present age, where gifts and sacrifices are offered that are incapable, concerning the conscience, of making the worshiper perfect” (Hebrews 9:9). The blood of bulls and goats could deal with ritual uncleanness, but it could not touch the stain deep in a person’s conscience.

sections.heading: 3. The Precious Blood Cleanses Not Only Sin, but Conscience Too
sections.html:
Thank the Lord, this is exactly what the precious blood of Jesus Christ accomplishes. Hebrews says: “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” (Hebrews 9:14)

Notice the word “conscience” here — the Chinese Union Version renders it “heart”, but adds a note in brackets that the original word is “conscience”. What the blood of Christ cleanses is precisely the place we cannot reach ourselves. Hebrews also says: “let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and having our body washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22). “Sprinkled from an evil conscience” — the debt that kept accusing you and kept you from lifting your head has been sprinkled away by the precious blood.

I often use a picture: conscience is like a window. A window doesn’t give off light by itself; its function is to let the light from outside shine through. When the window is dirty, the problem isn’t the sun; the glass needs washing. Trying to “be a good person” by our own efforts is like frantically adding lamps on the inside of the glass; only the precious blood washes the glass clean from the outside, so that God’s light can shine in.

And God does not only wash; he writes anew. God says: “I will put my laws into their mind, I will also write them on their heart. I will be their God, and they will be my people.” (Hebrews 8:10, quoting Jeremiah 31:33) Paul, speaking of the Gentiles, also says: “in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them” (Romans 2:15).

If even the Gentiles have a conscience within them testifying for them, how much more do we, who have been cleansed by the precious blood and indwelt by the Holy Spirit? The Holy Spirit will speak to us through this cleansed conscience. The Lord Jesus said: “When he has come, he will convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment” (John 16:8).

So when we obey the Holy Spirit and act according to conscience, that is truly “relying on the heart”.

sections.heading: 4. Applying the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness, from Numbness to Sensitivity
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, in the 321 vision we say the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The renewal of conscience is the starting point of all of this.

First, this is what “the Holy Spirit is my guide” looks like in practice. Among the Three Foundations, the guidance of the Holy Spirit is not some mysterious feeling; very often it happens in that quiet, inconvenient nudge of conscience that you would very much like to sidestep.

Second, this is the watershed between “the old self, self-centred, and the new self, selfless”. The old self’s conscience is led by the “self”: I want it, it suits me, I lose nothing. The new self’s conscience is led by Christ. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out.

Third, this is the shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. Man’s perspective asks, “Will I be found out?” God’s perspective asks, “Has God seen it?” — and the answer is always: he has.

David’s prayer is worth offering every day: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Teaching 2: A Clear Conscience Is the Standard for Measuring Whether We Rely on the Heart

sections.heading: 1. Not Everything Is Spelled Out in the Bible
sections.html:
The lesson puts it very plainly: not everything can be found as an explicit rule in the Bible, but we can use our conscience to judge.

This is not compromise; it is exactly what the New Testament teaches. The church in Corinth faced a very thorny problem at the time: much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered to idols. To eat, or not to eat? There is no law in the Bible that says, “You shall not eat beef sacrificed to Artemis.” So Paul spent three whole chapters, 1 Corinthians 8 to 10, dealing with it, and the principle he gives is this:

“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up.” (1 Corinthians 10:23)

Notice that Paul grants that “all things are lawful” — in Christ we really are free. But he immediately adds two measuring rods: is it profitable? Does it build up? Brothers and sisters, “May I?” is a question of law; “Should I?” is a question of conscience. A Christian who only asks “May I?” is still living at the level of law; a Christian who asks “Should I?” has entered the level of life.

So when we face a choice, we can ask ourselves one question — please write it down: “In this matter, can my conscience face God with boldness?”

The apostle John says: “Beloved, if our hearts don’t condemn us, we have boldness toward God” (1 John 3:21). Paul also says: “But he who doubts is condemned if he eats, because it isn’t of faith; and whatever is not of faith is sin.” (Romans 14:23) Notice this: if you have doubts in your heart and force yourself to do it anyway, then even if the thing itself is not wrong, it has become sin for you. Because you are already practising not listening to the voice of your conscience.

sections.heading: 2. Care Not Only for Our Own Conscience, but for Others’ Too
sections.html:
The lesson reminds us very well: we should consider not only whether our own conscience is at peace, but also have regard for the consciences of others.

Paul goes on in the same chapter: “Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.” (1 Corinthians 10:24) In chapter 8 he puts it even more strongly: “Thus, sinning against the brothers, and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.” (1 Corinthians 8:12)

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: to wound a brother’s weak conscience is to sin against Christ. In God’s eyes, a brother’s conscience is more precious than your freedom.

This is Paul’s summary: “In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.” (Acts 24:16) As we said earlier, the word behind “void of offense” here is ἀπρόσκοπος, meaning “not stumbling”. So the picture in this verse is this: as I walk, I don’t trip myself up, and I don’t become a stone in front of anyone else’s feet. Clear before God, clear before others, and clear before myself — only these three sides together make a complete clear conscience.

There are countless examples in daily life. Claiming a little extra on an expense report, since the company won’t check anyway; forwarding a very powerful but unverified message in a group chat, since everyone is forwarding it anyway; saying something half-true to your spouse, since it doesn’t really count as lying anyway. Each thing is small — so small that we say, “What does it matter?” But conscience doesn’t look at the size of the matter; conscience only looks at whether you listened to it.

sections.heading: 3. Conscience Is Not the Highest Standard — the Bible Is
sections.html:
Here a very important word must be said, lest we go astray: conscience is a measuring rod, but this rod itself needs to be calibrated. Conscience is not the highest standard; the Bible is our standard.

Why? Because conscience can be wrong. The strongest evidence is Paul himself. Standing before the council, he said: “Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until today.” (Acts 23:1) Yet this same man had once, in all good conscience, hunted down Christians, and in all good conscience approved of the stoning of Stephen. His conscience did not lie to him; the information loaded into his conscience was wrong.

I often use a sailing picture. A ship’s compass is a good thing, but it can be thrown off by the iron fittings of the hull and by magnetic interference, so navigators must regularly check it against the stars in the sky and against known reference points. Conscience is that compass; the Bible is the unmoving North Star. The compass must be checked against the star every day; conscience must be checked against God’s word every day.

That is why Paul says: “holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience” (1 Timothy 3:9). A pure conscience and the truth of the faith are bound together. A person who doesn’t read the Bible will find his conscience becoming more and more like this world; a person who reads God’s word every day will find his conscience becoming more and more like Christ.

Martin Luther is generally held to have said these words when he faced interrogation at the Imperial Diet of Worms in Germany in 1521: “My conscience is captive to the Word of God; to go against conscience is neither safe nor right.” Notice where the weight of that sentence falls — not “I go by my conscience”, but “my conscience is captive to the Word of God”. That is a Christian conscience.

sections.heading: 4. Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, then Relationships, then Ministry
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, in the 321 vision we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. This teaching puts that very order into practice.

Why was Paul willing to restrict his own freedom for the sake of a piece of meat? Because in his heart a brother’s life mattered more than his right to eat meat. This is selflessness: it is not that I have no freedom; it is that for love’s sake I am willing to lay my freedom down. Pride is seizing rights and leaving our originally intended position; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. A person who gives way out of regard for someone else’s conscience is practising selflessness.

This is the 920 practice too. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that not one of these nine graces can be borne where there are no “others”? When you are on your own, you have no chance to be patient and no one to be kind to. God puts our “2” beside us precisely so that we will bear fruit in relationships.

And the most honest measuring rod for whether we are truly “relying on the heart” in these relationships is this: when we lie down at night, is there peace in our hearts?

Teaching 3: God Vindicates the Person Whose Conscience Is Clear

sections.heading: 1. Abimelech: God Himself Restrains a Man of Integrity
sections.html:
The lesson gives two wonderful examples. Let’s look at them one at a time.

The first is Abimelech. Genesis 20 records that while Abraham was living as a sojourner in Gerar, out of fear he called Sarah his sister; and Abimelech, king of Gerar, took Sarah. Had this gone ahead, the consequences would have been unthinkable — for Isaac, the son of the promise, had not yet been born.

What did God do? God appeared to Abimelech in a dream by night. Abimelech pleaded that he was innocent, and the Bible records: “God said to him in the dream, ‘Yes, I know that in the integrity of your heart you have done this, and I also withheld you from sinning against me. Therefore I didn’t allow you to touch her.’” (Genesis 20:6)

Notice two things.

First, the word “integrity” in Hebrew is תֹּם (tom), meaning “complete, whole, unmixed”; it shares a root with the word for a “blameless” person (תָּמִים, tamim). What God saw was not Abimelech’s outward action but his inward motive — he did not know, and he meant no harm.

Second, and more precious still: God says, “I also withheld you.” Brothers and sisters, how comforting that is! When a person’s heart is upright, God not only sees him; God steps in to restrain him so that he does not fall. We often think that keeping our conscience is a lonely and costly thing; it isn’t so — when you keep a clear conscience before God, God himself will put on the brakes for you.

This passage also shows us the other side: Abraham, the one who lied, was actually the one whose heart was not upright. When God’s children make decisions out of “fear”, they will protect themselves with “lies”. Conscience’s first enemy is often not greed, but fear.

sections.heading: 2. David and Abigail: Both Sides Lose, or Both Sides Win
sections.html:
The second example is even more striking. In 1 Samuel 25, David is still on the run. He and his men had protected Nabal’s shepherds and flocks in the wilderness, taking nothing from them. When sheep-shearing time came, David sent men to ask Nabal for a little food — entirely reasonable in the culture of the day.

How did Nabal respond? He not only refused, but heaped insults on them. His very name says it all — “Nabal” (נָבָל, nabal) means “fool” in Hebrew. His wife Abigail later said: “Please don’t let my lord pay attention to this worthless fellow, Nabal; for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him” (1 Samuel 25:25).

And David’s reaction? He immediately ordered four hundred men to strap on their swords, set on wiping out every male in Nabal’s household. Brothers and sisters, this is the same David who had spared Saul in the cave, and who, having only cut off the edge of his robe, found that “David’s heart struck him” (1 Samuel 24:5). A man who had overcome temptation in a great matter very nearly destroyed himself over the small matter of a meal.

This is exactly what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. Nabal’s pride provoked David’s anger. Had David actually struck, Nabal’s whole household would have died, David’s conscience would have been ruined, and the hands that would one day hold the throne would have been stained with innocent blood — that is how both sides lose.

Right at that moment, God sent Abigail. She prepared gifts, hurriedly got down from her donkey, fell at David’s feet and spoke a speech of great wisdom. Its most crucial words were: “It will come to pass, when Yahweh has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel, that this shall be no grief to you, nor offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself. When Yahweh has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant.” (1 Samuel 25:30–31)

Brothers and sisters, look at the reason Abigail used to stop David. She didn’t say, “You can’t beat us,” nor did she say, “Murder is against the law.” What she said was: one day, when you are king, will your conscience trouble you? She drew David’s eyes away from the anger in front of him to the throne ahead; from man’s perspective to God’s; from the temporary to the eternal. What a wise sister she was!

And David’s response? He turned around at once: “David said to Abigail, ‘Blessed is Yahweh, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me! Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.’” (1 Samuel 25:32–33)

This is what 321 says: humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Abigail’s humility drew out David’s humility; one sister willing to bow low saved the lives of a whole household and preserved the conscience of a king.

And Nabal? “About ten days later, Yahweh struck Nabal, so that he died.” (1 Samuel 25:38) David did not lift his hand; God lifted his. This is the lesson’s main point: God vindicates the person whose conscience is clear.

Paul says it with absolute certainty: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.’” (Romans 12:19) Brothers and sisters, the reason we rush to avenge ourselves is that deep down we’re afraid God won’t deal with it; the reason we can let go is that we believe God surely will. Letting Jesus be King means that at the very moment we are wronged, we hand the authority to judge back to him.

sections.heading: 3. Jesus: A Perfectly Clear Conscience, yet Rejected
sections.html:
The lesson goes very deep here: even when outsiders cannot understand our choices, we must still live by conscience. Just like Jesus — his conscience was perfectly clear, yet he was rejected, and even crucified.

Peter, writing to believers suffering in the lands of their exile, says: “For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience toward God.” (1 Peter 2:19) “Commendable” in the original is χάρις (charis) — the very word for “grace”. In God’s eyes, a person who suffers wrongly for conscience’s sake carries the radiance of grace.

Peter then sets Jesus before us: “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21). “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23)

Brothers and sisters, look at how the Lord Jesus responded. He didn’t explain; he didn’t hit back; he “committed himself”. The original, παραδίδωμι (paradidōmi), means “to hand over, to give into another’s hands” — like handing what is most precious entirely into the keeping of the One who is most reliable. The Lord Jesus deposited his reputation and the wrongs done to him entirely with God the Father. Jesus is my role model — this is the first of the Three Foundations.

Psychology has a concept called “moral injury”, put forward by the psychiatrist Jonathan Shay in 1994 in his research on Vietnam veterans (Achilles in Vietnam). His observation was that what kept these veterans from healing for years was often not the fear of the battlefield, but having been forced to do things that violated their own moral convictions. In other words, what people really dread is not pain, but “I have betrayed what I myself believe.”

This confirms the Bible from the opposite direction: the pain of suffering unjustly can be borne; it is the burden of a guilty conscience that truly crushes a person. So it is better to suffer with a clear conscience than to prosper with a guilty one.

sections.heading: 4. A Gentle Reminder: Not a Conscience That Pleases People
sections.html:
The lesson ends with a very important reminder: a conscience that pleases people is not a clear conscience. Even if we suffer for it, as long as we have boldness before God, that is truly relying on the heart.

Paul asks it very pointedly: “For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” (Galatians 1:10)

Brothers and sisters, we need to distinguish between two kinds of “unease in the heart”. One is the Holy Spirit’s reminder in our conscience, because I have sinned against God; the other is simply fear that people will be unhappy, fear of being misunderstood, fear of losing applause — that is not conscience; that is face. The first must be obeyed; the second must be nailed to the cross.

God is the Lord who examines the heart. He said to Samuel: “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7) Man looks at the outward appearance; God looks at the heart — this is the most comforting, and also the most solemn, sentence of this whole morning devotion.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s connect today’s message with the 321 vision.

First, the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — his conscience was perfectly clear; when he was cursed, he didn’t curse back, but committed himself to him who judges righteously. The Bible is my standard — conscience is the measuring rod, and the Bible is the reference that calibrates it; the compass must be checked against the star every day. The Holy Spirit is my guide — very often the Holy Spirit speaks not through visions but through that one quiet, inconvenient nudge of conscience.

Second, the Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King: at the moment we are wronged, not avenging ourselves but handing the authority to judge back to him — that is letting him reign as King. Let Jesus receive all the glory: when people ask us, “Why are you being so foolish?”, we have the chance to speak of the Lord who searches the heart.

Third, the Goal: establish God’s system. The Worldly system measures by “whether you got caught”; God’s system measures by “being clear before God”. When a group of people who act with a clear conscience come together, that is God’s system in embryo.

Fourth, the self-centred life and selflessness. A self-centred conscience revolves around “me”: it suits me, I’m in the right, I lose nothing. A selfless conscience revolves around Christ: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan — Satan’s two favourite tactics are to numb our conscience, and to keep accusing a conscience that the precious blood has already washed clean. Both tactics fail before the precious blood.

Fifth, the fivefold change. The change of mindset: from “Is anyone watching?” to “God is always watching.” The change of life: the precious blood cleanses the conscience and removes dead works. The change of daily living: in every small decision, asking, “Is my conscience at peace?” The change of relationships: having regard for others’ consciences — people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. The change of ministry: only when a person with a clear conscience serves will God’s work stand firm.

Sixth, the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. A clear conscience is the very checklist for this order — clear before God, clear before ourselves, clear before others.

Seventh, 920 and 235. 920: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise selflessness (0) and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. 235: we all need an Abigail — a “2”, a spiritual companion who dares to stop us when we act on impulse. Brothers and sisters, do you have someone like that beside you? Are you willing to be someone else’s Abigail? Had there been no Abigail back then, David’s hands would have been stained with blood. Very often God doesn’t stop us with thunder; he stops us with a spiritual companion willing to speak the truth.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four practices. We will take them deeper using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Offer the Lord One Prayer Every Day

The lesson’s practice: each day, quiet your heart and pray this one sentence to the Lord: “Lord, shine your light on me, so that in everything I do today I may keep a clear conscience.”

Information: first put the Scriptures into your heart — Psalm 139:23–24 and 1 Timothy 1:5.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you truly see that God is searching your heart right now — this is not a theory; it is a fact.

Conviction: acknowledge from the heart that “God really is watching”, and that his searching comes from love, not to condemn me.

Implementation: set a time — ideally the first minute after you open your eyes in the morning — to say this prayer.

Evaluation: in the evening, think back: was there a moment today when you remembered this morning’s prayer?

Correction: if you didn’t remember it all day, put the prayer on your phone’s wallpaper or stick it on your mirror.

Repetition: keep it up for forty days in a row, until it becomes a habit.

Multiplication: share this prayer with your “2”, and do it together.

Practice 2: Stop and Ask One Question Before Everything

The lesson’s practice: practise small acts of “not going against conscience”. Before anything, stop and ask: “Will my conscience be at peace?” Whether it’s being honest, keeping your word or saying a single sentence, ask the Lord to help you act according to conscience.

Information: 1 Corinthians 10:23 and Romans 14:23.

Revelation: see the difference between “May I?” and “Should I?” — the level of law and the level of life.

Conviction: acknowledge that whatever is not of faith is sin; if you have doubts in your heart, don’t force yourself to do it.

Implementation: this week, pick three situations to practise deliberately — before you speak, before you press “send”, before you sign — and pause for three seconds first.

Evaluation: how many times did you pause those three seconds? Which time was hardest?

Correction: identify the kind of thing you most easily slide past, and guard it especially.

Repetition: make “pause for three seconds” a reflex of your body.

Multiplication: share in your small group one time when you “paused for three seconds”.

Practice 3: Write Down Something That Once Troubled Your Conscience

The lesson’s practice: write down something that once troubled your conscience, confess it to the Lord and ask for renewal, letting the precious blood of Jesus cleanse you once again, so that you regain peace.

Information: 1 John 1:9, Hebrews 9:14 and Hebrews 10:22.

Revelation: distinguish between “the Holy Spirit’s conviction” and “Satan’s accusation”. The Holy Spirit’s conviction is specific, points to the cross and brings hope; Satan’s accusation is vague, points to yourself and brings despair.

Conviction: believe that the cleansing of the precious blood is complete — conscience included.

Implementation: be still, write it on paper, and confess it to the Lord item by item.

Evaluation: after confessing, does your heart truly feel lighter? If it still feels heavy, is there something you haven’t yet handed over?

Correction: if needed, find a spiritually mature co-worker to pray with you.

Repetition: don’t treat this as a one-off activity; make it a regular self-examination.

Multiplication: when others are so weighed down by accusation that they can’t lift their heads, you will be able to show them this way out.

Practice 4: Take the Initiative to Do One Good Thing Your Conscience Is Urging You to Do

The lesson’s practice: take the initiative to do one good thing that “your conscience has been urging you to do” but you haven’t done before — such as apologising first, encouraging someone, or making amends for a wrong.

Information: Acts 24:16 and Matthew 5:23–24.

Revelation: conscience not only tells us “don’t do what is wrong”; it also urges us to “go and do the good thing you ought to do”. Good left undone builds up into a debt just the same.

Conviction: admit that the reason for putting it off is mostly face, not time.

Implementation: think of one name today and follow through within this week — a phone call, an apology, money you owe.

Evaluation: once it’s done, how much lighter is the burden on your heart?

Correction: if the other person responds badly, still thank the Lord, because your responsibility is a clear conscience, not controlling the outcome.

Repetition: make “act as soon as conscience nudges” your normal way of life; don’t let a backlog build up.

Multiplication: with your spiritual companion, each draw up your own list, and pray for each other and check on each other’s progress.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the question we started with: how do we measure whether we are “relying on the heart”?

The answer lies not in how much we have done, but in whether there is peace in our hearts as we do it; not in what others say, but in whether, in the dead of night when there is no one left but you and God, you dare to lift your head and look at him.

“Relying on the heart” is not outward fervour; it is inward honesty.

May we keep a clear conscience all our lives, never going against the prompting of the Holy Spirit, never numbing the reminders within, living every day in the attitude and conduct that please God, and becoming people he regards as upright. For God looks at the heart, not at the outward appearance.

So this morning I want to issue three calls to you, brothers and sisters.

First, let the precious blood wash your conscience clean once again. Don’t carry old debts forward; hand them over today.

Second, let the Bible calibrate your conscience every day. Conscience is the compass; God’s word is the North Star. A compass that is never checked against the star will steer the ship onto the rocks.

Third, let Jesus reign as King in the places where you have been wronged. Don’t avenge yourself; don’t rush to explain; commit yourself to him who judges righteously. He restrained Abimelech, he stepped in for David, and he will surely vindicate you too.

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) May everything that flows from our lives spring from a heart washed by the precious blood, calibrated by God’s word and bold before God, so that Jesus reigns as King — may all the glory be his.

keyVerses: “But the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.” (1 Timothy 1:5)
“In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.” (Acts 24:16)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:
I will act with a clear conscience every day, so that my heart is right before God and right before others.
My conscience has been washed by the precious blood of Jesus; I will no longer let sin sear it numb.
I take the Bible as my standard to calibrate my conscience, and the Holy Spirit’s reminders as my guide.
I will not avenge myself; I commit everything to him who judges righteously.
I do not seek to please people; I seek only to stand with boldness before God.
practices: Offer the Lord one prayer every day
Stop and ask one question before everything
Write down something that once troubled your conscience
Take the initiative to do one good thing your conscience is urging you to do
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
Your precious blood cleanses not only our sins but also our conscience, so that we can come before you with boldness.

Lord, shine your light on us. We confess that, out of fear of people, fear of loss and fear of trouble, we have often pressed down the reminders you give in our hearts; again and again, we have let our conscience grow dull. Today we come before you to confess, and we ask you to cleanse us once more with your precious blood, so that our hearts are sprinkled from an evil conscience.

Make us sensitive, so that at the Holy Spirit’s gentlest reminder we respond at once. Make us honest, so that before anything we first ask: in this matter, can my conscience face you with boldness? Make us mindful of others, so that we never cause a single brother or sister to stumble because of our own freedom.

Lord, when we are misunderstood and wronged, give us patience, so that like you, when we are cursed we do not curse back, but commit ourselves to him who judges righteously. We believe that vengeance belongs to you, and you will repay.
Prepare spiritual companions like Abigail beside us, and make us an Abigail for others — to stop them when they act on impulse, and to hold them up before they fall.

May we rely on the heart and not the brain all our lives, rely on the Holy Spirit and not on ourselves, keep a clear conscience, and be people you regard as upright. Let Jesus reign as King in our hearts; may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “through the hypocrisy of men who speak lies, branded in their own conscience as with a hot iron.” (1 Timothy 4:2) Think back: is there any area of your life that once made your heart sting but no longer hurts? How do you plan to let the precious blood cleanse that place again?

“that this shall be no grief to you, nor offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself.” (1 Samuel 25:31) Do you have a spiritual companion like Abigail beside you, who dares to tell you the truth? This week, whom could you approach and invite to become your “2”?
l029.title: A Clear Conscience
l029.subtitle: How to Measure Whether We Rely on the Heart
l029.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: Something No Instrument Can Measure
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Every year when we have a health check, we’re handed a report. Blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, liver function — rows and rows of figures that measure our bodies down to the last detail. Yet on that report there will never be a line called “faith”. No instrument in the world can show how deep and how genuine a person’s trust in God really is. And so we often live with an unanswered question: is my faith real, or is it fake? Am I actually trusting God, or only talking about him?

Today’s lesson sets out to answer exactly that question — how do we measure whether we are “relying on the heart”? The answer comes in three words: sincere faith.

What does it mean to “rely on the heart”? Relying on the heart is not straining hard. It isn’t clenching your teeth, tightening your fists and furrowing your brow to force yourself to believe. Relying on the heart is a heart that is simple and single-minded towards God. When we love Jesus with our hearts and keep his word with our hearts, our lives will naturally overflow with trust in God and obedience to him. What overflows naturally like that is “sincere faith”.

The word “sincere” here is a fascinating one. In New Testament Greek it is ἀνυπόκριτος (anypokritos), formed from the negative prefix ἀν- and ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs). The word ὑποκριτής was originally a technical term of the ancient Greek theatre: an actor who went on stage wearing a mask. Only later did it come to mean “a hypocrite”. So “sincere faith”, translated literally, is “faith without a mask”. Not faith performed for an audience, not faith that appears only with make-up on, the lights up and the camera rolling, but faith that takes off the mask and stands before God barefaced.

Brothers and sisters, what is our faith so often mixed with?

First, it’s mixed with being driven by circumstances. When things are going well, I say, “Thank the Lord, God is so good.” The moment things turn, I say, “Has God stopped caring about me?” Faith like that isn’t built on God; it’s built on the weather.

Second, it’s mixed with social pressure. Everyone in the small group says “Amen”, so I’d be embarrassed not to; everyone else raises their hands, so I’d be embarrassed not to raise mine. And so my mouth is singing hymns while my heart is doing sums.

Third, it’s mixed with rational analysis. If the numbers add up, I believe; if they don’t, I back off. If I understand it, I obey; if I don’t, I obey at a discount. My brain becomes a review committee for God’s word, and God’s promises have to pass my feasibility assessment before they can take effect.

All three of these mixtures “water down” our faith. Watered-down faith looks fine on ordinary days, but the moment the storm comes, it’s exposed for what it is.

Today the Holy Spirit wants to use the stories of three people to measure our hearts. One is a fisherman who stepped out of the boat in a midnight storm — Peter. One is an old warrior who followed God wholeheartedly for forty-five years in the wilderness — Caleb. One is a shepherd boy who went out to meet a giant in the Valley of Elah — David. They lived in different times, at different ages, with different gifts, in completely different situations. But inside them there was one thing the same: they did not rely on the brain to analyse God; they relied on the heart to trust God.

Before we go on, one thing needs to be made clear. This lesson is not about turning us into people who don’t think and don’t take responsibility. God made us with minds; the mind is God’s gift, not God’s enemy. The 321 vision puts it plainly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. The issue has never been “whether we have a brain” but “whether we rely on ourselves”. When the brain sits in the servant’s seat, it is a good steward; once the brain takes the throne, faith is pushed off it.

Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” Brothers and sisters, the wellspring of life does not flow from the brain; it flows from the heart. Let us return to simplicity, return to a single-minded trust in God, and live out a sincere faith.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three “Hearts” and Three Generations of Faith
sections.html:
Our key passages today come from Paul’s two letters to Timothy. To grasp the weight of the words “sincere faith”, we first need to know the man who wrote them, the man who received them, and the situation at the time.

Author, Date and Recipient

The author of both letters is the apostle Paul. First Timothy was written around AD 63 to 65, after Paul was released from his first house arrest in Rome; Second Timothy was written in AD 66 to 67, during his second imprisonment, before his martyrdom — the last letter he left to the world. In other words, the phrase “sincere faith” appears once in the mature years of Paul’s pastoral work and once at the very end of his life. This is not the slogan of a young preacher; it is the conclusion an old apostle reached by spending his whole life.

The recipient is Timothy. Acts 16:1 records: “He came to Derbe and Lystra: and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed; but his father was a Greek.” Timothy came from a mixed family: his father was Greek and his mother Jewish. From childhood he lived in the gap between two cultures. He seems to have been rather introverted and easily intimidated, and not physically strong either (1 Timothy 5:23 mentions his “frequent infirmities”). Yet Paul treated him as his own spiritual son, calling him “Timothy, my true child in faith” (1 Timothy 1:2).

Where was Timothy serving at the time? 1 Timothy 1:3 says, “As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine.” Timothy was pastoring the church in Ephesus. Ephesus was then the leading city of the province of Asia, home to the famous temple of Artemis, commercially thriving and ideologically chaotic. False teachers had arisen in the church who loved “myths and endless genealogies” (1 Timothy 1:4). They argued over words all day long; the more they debated, the livelier it got, and the colder their lives became.

Paul’s prescription: three “hearts”

Faced with this chaos, Paul didn’t try to out-argue them; he took the conversation straight back to the root. 1 Timothy 1:5: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.”

Brothers and sisters, notice the three things here. All three concern the inner life — though in the original only the first actually uses the word “heart” (kardia):

The first is “a pure heart” (καθαρὰ καρδία), meaning purity of motive, with no other purpose mixed in. This is exactly what the Lord Jesus said in Matthew 5:8: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

The second is “a good conscience”, meaning openness of conduct — nothing hidden and owing before God.

The third is “sincere faith”, meaning genuineness of trust — no mask, no performance.

Put these three together and you have what this lesson calls “relying on the heart”. So relying on the heart is not an emotional high; it is a state of life in which the motive is pure, the conscience is clear and the trust is real. Paul says that true love comes “out of” these three. The order cannot be reversed: first a pure heart, then sincere faith; first sincere faith, then love without pretence. This is exactly what 321 says — life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Faith Passed Down Three Generations

Now look at 2 Timothy 1:5: “having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois, and your mother Eunice, and, I am persuaded, in you also.”

In his prison cell, near the end, Paul remembered Timothy’s faith, and remembered where that faith came from: his grandmother Lois, his mother Eunice, and then Timothy. Three generations, one unbroken line.

There’s an important reminder here: faith is not a gene you inherit, but it is a legacy that can be received. Lois and Eunice could not “copy” their faith into Timothy, but they could plant the word of God in him. 2 Timothy 3:15 says, “From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus.” The words a child hears growing up become the foundation he stands on all his life.

This is precisely the “3” in what 321 calls the “235 relationships” — the passing on of life between spiritual parents and spiritual children. How far a person’s faith can go often depends not only on that person, but on whether someone behind them planted God’s word in them, and whether someone ahead of them is waiting for them to pass God’s word on. Brothers and sisters, is your faith going to stay in your generation, or be passed on to the third?

With this background, we can see that “sincere faith” is not an abstract term. It was Paul’s prescription for an Ephesus overrun with false teachers, and the legacy closest to his heart in a Roman prison cell. Now let’s follow the lesson into three real scenes and see what sincere faith looks like.

sections.heading: 1. The Response of Simple Trust: Peter Walks on the Water
sections.html:
Scripture

“But the boat was now in the middle of the sea, distressed by the waves, for the wind was contrary. In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea. When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, ‘It’s a ghost!’ and they cried out for fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, ‘Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.’ Peter answered him and said, ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.’ He said, ‘Come!’ Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’ Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matthew 14:24–31)

The Scene: A Night with No Way Back

This happened right after the miracle of the five loaves and two fish. Matthew 14:22 says, “Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, and to go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away.” The word “made” is a strong one — the Chinese Union Version says he “urged” them, pressed them. It was Jesus himself who sent his disciples into this storm. Brothers and sisters, remember this: some storms come not because we took the wrong road, but precisely because we took the right one. Sometimes the next step of obedience is a storm.

“The fourth watch of the night”, by Roman reckoning, was between three and six in the morning. In other words, the disciples had been battling a headwind in the dark for nearly nine hours. They were professional fishermen on the Sea of Galilee; rowing was their trade. But that night their expertise was no use at all. Our most helpless moments are often not when we know nothing, but when we have used up everything we know and still cannot move an inch.

Right then, Jesus came. He said one thing: “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.”

Key words: “It is I”

The words “It is I” are, in the Greek, ἐγώ εἰμι (egō eimi), literally “I am”. These are the very words the Septuagint uses in Exodus 3:14, where God says to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” At the height of the storm, Jesus declared himself with the name of God.

So, brothers and sisters, what the disciples really needed that night was not for the wind to stop, but to recognise that the One who is “I AM” was right there on the water. Standing above the storm was the Lord who created the storm.

Peter’s response was simple: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.”

Notice what Peter asked for. He didn’t say, “Lord, let me have a go.” He said, “Command me” — what he wanted was an order, a word. Peter’s faith was not a belief that “I can walk”, but a belief that “his word can hold me up”. Romans 10:17 says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” Faith is never courage conjured out of thin air; faith is a response to a word.

Jesus answered with a single word: “Come!”

And Peter stepped down from the boat.

Physically Impossible, Possible in Faith

Brothers and sisters, let’s think about how “unreasonable” Peter’s step really was. The surface tension of water at twenty degrees Celsius is about 72 millinewtons per metre. That’s enough to hold up a pond skater weighing a few milligrams, but it could never hold up a grown fisherman. In terms of physics, the foot Peter put out should have gone straight under, a hundred per cent of the time.

But he didn’t sink. Because what held him up was never the surface tension of the water; it was Jesus’ one word, “Come!”

Faith is not calculating the impossible into the possible. Faith is handing the impossible to the Lord for whom all things are possible. If Peter had first carried out a risk assessment, he would never have left that boat. And that night, only one man in the whole boat knew that walking on Jesus’ word was safer than sitting in his own boat.

Martin Luther, in his 1522 preface to Romans, is generally credited with describing faith as “a living, daring confidence in God’s grace”. Living, so it moves; daring, so it steps out. Faith that stays in the boat is a museum specimen; only faith that steps onto the water is alive.

Why did Peter begin to sink?

“But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink.”

Where did it go wrong? The text is precise: “when he saw that the wind was strong.” It wasn’t that the wind got stronger — the wind had been that strong all along; it was there before he got out of the boat. What changed was not the wind but Peter’s eyes. He had been looking at Jesus’ face; now he was looking at the size of the wind.

The word “saw” here is the Greek βλέπω, meaning to look intently, to fix one’s gaze on. The moment his focus shifted, the ground gave way beneath his feet.

A well-known psychology experiment helps us understand this. In 1999, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris at Harvard ran the “invisible gorilla” experiment (published in the journal Perception). Participants were asked to count the passes made by the players in white in a video, and about half of them completely failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walk into the frame, beat its chest and walk out again. The researchers called this “inattentional blindness”. Our attention is a limited resource; what we see depends on what we are focusing on.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the spiritual reality. When we fix our eyes on the storm, Jesus is right in front of us, yet we “can’t see” him. Peter’s problem was not that his faith suddenly vanished; it was that his focus changed channel. The 321 vision reminds us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

There is also a physical fact here. The neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux, in The Emotional Brain (1996), showed that fear signals can travel from the thalamus straight to the amygdala, a step faster than they reach the cerebral cortex for rational judgement. In other words, our “fear” runs faster than our “figuring it out”. So we can’t wait until we’ve “figured it out” before we believe — because fear always arrives before thought. Our only way is to seat God’s word on the throne of our hearts before fear has a chance to speak.

The lesson puts it well: rely on the heart and you have faith; rely on the brain and you will be afraid.

Even as He Sank, He Still Cried Out

Brothers and sisters, there’s a deeply tender detail here that we mustn’t miss. As Peter began to sink, he cried out three words: “Lord, save me!”

It is one of the shortest prayers in the Bible, and one of the most genuine. At his most humiliating moment, Peter’s first reaction was still to turn to Jesus. That tells us the heart in him that trusted wholeheartedly had not died.

And Jesus’ response? “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him.” “Immediately” — grace is faster than sinking. Brothers and sisters, you may sink, but you will not go under, because the Lord’s hand is faster than the water.

Then the Lord asked a question: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”

The Greek for “doubt” is διστάζω (distazō), whose root carries the idea of “two” — standing on both sides, wavering back and forth. James 1:6–8 explains this word perfectly: “But let him ask in faith, without any doubting, for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven by the wind and tossed. For that man shouldn’t think that he will receive anything from the Lord. He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.”

Little faith is not no faith. Little faith is faith split in two: half given to the Lord’s word, half given to the size of the wind.

An Everyday Illustration

Anyone who has learned to swim knows this: the more you thrash about in the water, the faster you sink; the more you relax and give your body over, the better you float. What makes a drowning person most dangerous is not that they can’t swim, but that they’re desperate to grab hold of something. Every lifeguard learns in training that being clutched by a drowning person is the most dangerous situation of all, because that person isn’t trusting you; they’re clinging to you.

The spiritual world is the same. The more we struggle with our brains, the deeper we sink; the more we entrust with our hearts, the more firmly we stand.

Applying the 321 Vision

Peter’s lesson is exactly the shift of perspective 321 talks about: from the earthly (how strong the wind is) to the heavenly (what the Lord has said); from the temporary (this one night’s storm) to the eternal (the One who is “I AM”).

It is also a lesson in the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. At the moment Peter began to sink, the whole order was turned upside down — first he looked at “things” (the storm), then at “himself” (I’m going under), and only last did he remember “God” (Lord, save me). Brothers and sisters, everyone who turns the order upside down will sink; everyone who puts God back in first place will find the Lord’s hand reaching out.

Rely on the heart and you’ll have joy; rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. When Peter relied on his heart outside the boat, he experienced something no one else in history has experienced; when he relied on his brain on the water, he experienced the three most humiliating seconds of his life.

sections.heading: 2. People Focused on God’s Promise: Caleb and Joshua
sections.html:
Scripture

“They brought up an evil report of the land which they had spied out to the children of Israel, saying, ‘The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that eats up its inhabitants; and all the people who we saw in it are men of great stature. There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.’” (Numbers 13:32–33)

“If Yahweh delights in us, then he will bring us into this land, and give it to us: a land which flows with milk and honey. Only don’t rebel against Yahweh, neither fear the people of the land; for they are bread for us. Their defense is removed from over them, and Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them.” (Numbers 14:8–9)

The Scene: The Crossroads at Kadesh Barnea

In the second year after leaving Egypt, the Israelites came to Kadesh Barnea. God told Moses to choose one man from each of the twelve tribes to spy out the land of Canaan. They were gone forty days (Numbers 13:25), travelled the length of the land, and brought back a single cluster of grapes that took two men to carry on a pole (Numbers 13:23).

The same land, the same journey, the same forty days. Yet when they got back, there were two completely opposite reports.

Caleb’s report was: “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30)

The report of the ten spies was: “We aren’t able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.” (Numbers 13:31)

Brothers and sisters, notice this: the facts they saw were exactly the same. The city walls really were strong; the Anakites really were huge. The difference was not in the information; the difference was in the focus. The ten measured the gap between “the enemy and me”; the two measured the gap between “the enemy and God”.

Key words: “evil report” and “grasshoppers”

Numbers 13:32 says they “brought up an evil report”. The Hebrew for “evil report” is דִּבָּה (dibbah), meaning slander, defamation, spreading a bad name. In the Bible this word is usually used of malicious, untrue talk. In other words, the ten spies weren’t just “a bit pessimistic”; they were giving a bad name to the land God had promised, which amounted to indirectly slandering the God who had promised it.

Then comes that heartbreaking line: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.”

Notice the order: first, “we were in our own sight as grasshoppers”, and only then the inference, “and so we were in their sight”. They shrank in their own eyes first, and then projected that self-image onto their enemies’ eyes. In fact, the Bible tells us later that the Canaanites at the time were scared to death. In Joshua 2:11, Rahab the prostitute says, “As soon as we had heard it, our hearts melted, and there wasn’t any more spirit in any man, because of you.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? While the Israelites thought they were grasshoppers, the Canaanites were frightened out of their wits. This is the greatest cost of “relying on the brain and ourselves” — shrinking our picture of God, magnifying our own fear, and then using that faulty assessment to overrule God’s promise.

Psychology Confirms, Scripture Corrects

The psychologist Albert Bandura (1977) put forward the theory of “self-efficacy”: whether a person believes they can accomplish something actually affects whether they are willing to try and how long they hold on when things get hard. This research helps us understand the psychology of the ten spies: when self-assessment collapses, action stops.

But, brothers and sisters, Scripture wants to correct us here at a deeper level. Caleb’s faith was never built on “I can”. He never said, “We’re strong enough.” What he said was: “If Yahweh delights in us, then he will bring us into this land.” The ground of faith is not “I am able”; the ground of faith is “God is able”. Psychology can explain why people shrink back, but it cannot produce sincere faith; only God’s promise can.

And look at how Caleb described those giants: “for they are bread for us.” In the eyes of the ten spies, it was “a land that eats up its inhabitants”; in Caleb’s eyes, it was those inhabitants who were Israel’s food. The very same giants — to the eyes of fear, they were the ones who devour; to the eyes of faith, they were the ones to be devoured.

Why Caleb Won God’s Praise

Numbers 14:24 records God’s verdict: “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and has followed me fully, him I will bring into the land into which he went. His offspring shall possess it.”

“Another spirit” — the Chinese Union Version renders it “another resolve” — is in Hebrew רוּחַ אַחֶרֶת (ruach acheret), literally “another spirit”. It wasn’t that Caleb had more nerve; it was that there was another spirit inside him — his inner world was governed by the Spirit of God, so his outward judgement was different from everyone else’s.

The phrase “followed me fully” means in the Hebrew “to follow after to the full” — following all the way, leaving nothing held back. This is the best commentary on “relying on the heart”. In Numbers 32:12 and Deuteronomy 1:36, the Chinese Union Version renders it “followed me wholeheartedly”. This was God’s own verdict on a man — brothers and sisters, wouldn’t you like God to describe you that way one day?

Forty-Five Years Without Changing Channel

Caleb’s story isn’t over. Forty-five years later, at eighty-five, he came to Joshua. Joshua 14:10–12 records: “Now, behold, Yahweh has kept me alive, as he spoke, these forty-five years … Now, behold, I am eighty-five years old, today. As yet I am as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me. As my strength was then, even so is my strength now for war, to go out and to come in. Now therefore give me this hill country, of which Yahweh spoke in that day …”

For forty-five years that promise didn’t fade in his heart for a single day. What he asked for wasn’t the plain but the hill country; not an easy place, but Hebron, where the Anakites still lived.

How hard is that today? In 2020, a team led by Jordan Poppenk at Queen’s University in Canada published a study in Nature Communications that used brain imaging to estimate that a person has around 6,200 “thought transitions” a day while awake. Our minds change channel more than six thousand times a day. And Caleb didn’t change channel for forty-five years.

Brothers and sisters, is there a promise God has given you that has been sitting in your hands for a long time? Don’t throw it away. God’s promises don’t expire; the only danger is that our hearts expire first.

Applying the 321 Vision

The ten spies represent the self-centred life: they put themselves at the centre, so the answer they came up with was “we are like grasshoppers”. Caleb represents selflessness: he put God at the centre, so the answer he came up with was “God will bring us in”. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred see giants; the selfless see the promise.

There’s one more thing we can’t overlook: Caleb didn’t stand firm alone; Joshua stood with him. Numbers 14:6 says Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes together. Ecclesiastes 4:9 says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.” This is exactly the “2” in 321’s “235 relationships” — becoming spiritual companions with someone who is selfless. When six hundred thousand men collapsed together, two people holding each other up kept the hope of a whole generation alive.

Brothers and sisters, who is your “2”? When everyone around is spreading an evil report, is there one person willing to stand with you and say, “We are well able to overcome it”?

sections.heading: 3. David Defeats Goliath: Words of Faith Are Acts of Faith
sections.html:
Scripture

“Then David said to the Philistine, ‘You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.’” (1 Samuel 17:45)

“and that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn’t save with sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh’s, and he will give you into our hand.” (1 Samuel 17:47)

The Scene: Forty Days of Stalemate in the Valley of Elah

The Philistines and the Israelites each held a hillside, with the Valley of Elah between them. Out of the Philistine camp came a champion named Goliath.

The Bible gives us very specific figures. 1 Samuel 17:4 says his height was “six cubits and a span” — about 2.9 metres. Verse 5 says his coat of mail weighed five thousand shekels of bronze; at roughly 11.4 grams to the shekel in those days, that’s about 57 kilograms. Verse 7 says the iron head of his spear weighed six hundred shekels — about 6.8 kilograms. With a man like that standing in front of you, any rational assessment reaches only one conclusion: impossible.

What’s more, he “came near morning and evening, and presented himself forty days” (1 Samuel 17:16). Forty days of intimidation had ground down the morale of an entire army. Verse 11 says, “When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid.”

Brothers and sisters, notice that Israel’s army had a king, warriors, weapons and battle lines. It lacked nothing — except a heart that trusted God wholeheartedly. And Satan’s favourite weapon has never been sword or spear; it is those same few sentences repeated in your ear every morning and every evening.

David Saw What No One Else Saw

Just then, a boy bringing bread and cheese for his older brothers arrived at the camp. He heard Goliath’s words and said something that turned the whole battle around:

“For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” (1 Samuel 17:26)

Brothers and sisters, it was the same giant. What everyone else saw was “how tall he is”; what David saw was “God is being insulted”. Everyone else measured the gap between the enemy and themselves; David measured the gap between the enemy and God.

This is the first mark of sincere faith: having eyes only for Jesus. When a person truly honours God as great in their heart, the enemy’s height automatically becomes an irrelevant number.

Faith Is Not a Leap into Thin Air

Some people think faith means shutting your eyes and jumping. It doesn’t. Look at 1 Samuel 17:34–37, where David says to Saul: “Your servant was keeping his father’s sheep; and when a lion or a bear came, and took a lamb out of the flock, I went out after him, and struck him, and rescued it out of his mouth … Yahweh who delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.”

This wasn’t the first time David had trusted God; it was the first time he had trusted God “in public”. Out in the wilderness where no one was watching, he had already fought several battles alongside God. The lion and the bear were God’s preparatory course for Goliath.

The phrase “leap of faith” is generally attributed to Kierkegaard, but a more biblical way to put it is this: faith is not a leap; faith is a walk — stepping on the faithfulness God has already proved, one step at a time. Brothers and sisters, what you build with God in secret today is what you’ll be able to stand on in the light tomorrow.

Taking Off Saul’s Armour

1 Samuel 17:38–39: Saul dressed David in his own tunic, put a bronze helmet on his head and clad him in a coat of mail. David tried to walk, but said, “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them.” Then David took them off.

This scene is full of meaning. Saul’s armour represents “human methods” — the best equipment available, fit for a king, but not what God had given David. Brothers and sisters, how often have we been defeated not because we lacked equipment but because we were wearing equipment that wasn’t ours? Other people’s gifts, other people’s models, other people’s ways of serving — on us, they only stop us from moving.

David took off the armour, picked up the sling he knew so well and chose five smooth stones from the brook (1 Samuel 17:40). This was a tool he had practised with thousands of times in the wilderness. Incidentally, a sling was no child’s toy. In David and Goliath (2013), the writer Malcolm Gladwell cites the calculations of the Israeli ballistics expert Eitan Hirsch, who showed that a stone hurled by a skilled slinger could reach a speed of about thirty-four metres per second. What God uses is very often the very thing already in our hands.

Words of Faith Are Acts of Faith

The most stirring moment is David’s declaration: “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.”

“Yahweh of Armies” in Hebrew is יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tsevaot), meaning Yahweh who commands the armies of heaven. Goliath brought one army; David brought the Commander of all armies.

Notice: David spoke first, then acted. Romans 10:10 says, “For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.” Believing in the heart, confessing with the mouth — words of faith are themselves acts of faith. The lesson could not have chosen a better heading for this point.

Brothers and sisters, our mouths often betray our hearts. We say, “God will make a way,” and then add, “but I think it’s going to be hard,” and the second sentence swallows up the first. Sincere faith means our words and our hearts agree — consistent from first to last, the same in public and in private.

Then David ran towards Goliath. 1 Samuel 17:48 says “David hurried, and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine.” For forty days a whole army had been retreating; only one man ran forward. That is faith’s sense of direction.

Testimony and Corroboration

Church history is full of “David-like” figures. George Müller of Bristol, England (1805–1898) cared for more than ten thousand orphans over his lifetime, yet he held to one principle: never ask anyone for money, only pray to God. His records include mornings when there was nothing on the orphanage tables, the children sat down and gave thanks anyway, and then the doorbell rang. He said he wanted to prove one thing to his generation — that God is a God who hears prayer. This is not legend; it is history recorded in the diaries and account books he left behind.

Applying the 321 Vision

David’s declaration is exactly 321’s Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. He handed over sovereignty of the battlefield — “the battle is Yahweh’s”; and he made the purpose of victory clear — “that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel” (1 Samuel 17:46).

This is also “humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan”. Goliath was pride incarnate: he left his originally intended position, seized rights and tried to take God’s place as the one to be feared. David was humility incarnate: he returned to his originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. In the end, what pride stirred up was fear across all Israel, and both sides lost; but what humility set in motion was courage through the whole army. 1 Samuel 17:52 says the men of Israel and of Judah rose up, shouted, and pursued the Philistines. One man’s humility led a whole army to victory.

Brothers and sisters, what is the Goliath in front of you today? A diagnosis? A debt? A relationship that won’t mend? Or an old self that hasn’t changed in forty years? Don’t start by measuring how tall it is; start by measuring how great God is.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Sincere Faith Is a Heart Returned to Its Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set these three stories within the 321 framework and see the whole picture.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. Hebrews 12:2 says, “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” The perfect model of sincere faith is not Peter, not Caleb, not David, but the Lord Jesus himself. He is the author of faith, and he is its perfecter.

The Bible is my standard. Peter’s feet could step onto the water because there was a word: “Come!” Caleb could stand firm for forty-five years because there was a promise. David could run towards the giant because he knew these were “the armies of the living God”. Faith has never been a feeling; faith is standing on a word.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Caleb had what the Chinese Union Version calls “another resolve” — in the original, “another spirit”. It wasn’t that his willpower was stronger than anyone else’s; it was that there was Another inside him, guiding him.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King. Peter sank because, in that moment, the storm became king; David won because Yahweh of Armies was King. The throne of our hearts has room for only one. If Jesus isn’t sitting on it, something else is.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. David made it very clear: he wanted “all the earth” to “know that there is a God in Israel”. The final landing point of sincere faith is not “I have great faith”, but “my God is truly great”.

The Goal: establish God’s system. One person relying on the heart is one person changed; a whole group relying on the heart becomes God’s system. Caleb and Joshua, two men standing firm, brought a whole generation into its inheritance forty years later.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Brothers and sisters, we need to ask ourselves an honest question: is relying on the brain and ourselves really just a habit? No. Underneath, it is very often pride — I have to understand first before I’ll obey; I have to work it all out before I’m willing to entrust it. That puts my own understanding above God’s word. It means I am auditing God.

The “grasshoppers” of the ten spies and the “giant” Goliath are really two sides of the same disease: one sees himself as too small and so doesn’t believe; the other sees himself as too big and so becomes arrogant. Both are the self-centred life. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and trying to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Goliath left his originally intended position, so he fell; David returned to his, so he stood.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

There is only one mindset this lesson sets out to change: the ground of faith is not in me; it is in God. Once that mindset changes, life moves from “I have to hold on” to “he is holding me up”; once life changes, daily living moves from worry to joy; once daily living changes, relationships move from defensive to open; once relationships change, ministry moves from forced to overflowing.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Peter’s sinking was the order turned upside down; Caleb’s standing firm was the order put right.

The Shift of Perspective

From the human to the divine: no longer asking “how much do I have?” but “who is God?”
