From the earthly to the heavenly: no longer staring at the height of the waves, but gazing at the height of the throne.

From the temporary to the eternal: 2 Corinthians 4:18 says, “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”

From the worldly to the godly: 2 Corinthians 5:7 says, “for we walk by faith, not by sight.”

The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living a selfless life (the “0”), we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (the “9”) of its expressions. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.”

Brothers and sisters, notice the seventh — “faith”, which the Chinese Union Version renders “faithfulness”. The Greek word is πίστις (pistis), the very same word as “faith”. In other words, genuine faith is not just one act of courage in a storm; it grows into a character in everyday life: dependable towards God, trustworthy towards others. Sincere faith will in the end bear fruit in “sincere dealings with others”. 1 Peter 1:22 says, “Seeing you have purified your souls in your obedience to the truth through the Spirit in sincere brotherly affection, love one another from the heart fervently.” When the heart is purified, love is without pretence; when faith is sincere, love is sincere too.

The 235 relationships: becoming a “2”, spiritual companions, with someone who is selfless — Caleb and Joshua; establishing the “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children — Lois, Eunice and Timothy; becoming the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades — the band of mighty men David later gathered in the wilderness. Brothers and sisters, sincere faith is never a one-man show. It needs companions, it needs a legacy, it needs a team.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We are going to work them through thoroughly using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication.

Practice 1: Recall a time when your faith “stepped across”

Has there been a time when you didn’t rely on your own analysis at all, but acted boldly simply because you trusted God? Write that experience down, and thank God for letting you trust him with your heart.

How do you go deeper? Information: write down clearly the time, the place, the difficulty you faced and God’s word to you — don’t just write “God was very gracious to me”. Revelation: quietly ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light — what was God really teaching you that time? Conviction: tell yourself that it wasn’t luck; it was God’s faithfulness. Implementation: tell this testimony to at least one person. Brothers and sisters, once a testimony is spoken out loud, faith turns from a memory into a strength.

That’s exactly what David did. Standing before Saul, he counted off the lion and the bear, and then said, “he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.” The lions and bears of your past are the preparatory course for today’s Goliath.

Practice 2: Practise saying to God every day, “I believe your word!”

Each day, find one of God’s promises and declare, “Lord, I believe your word!” Not relying on feelings, not relying on circumstances — relying only on his word.

How do you go deeper? Evaluation: each evening, look back — today, did I live by this word, or by my circumstances? Correction: if you find you’ve been calculating all day, hand that matter back to God before you go to sleep. Repetition: declare the same verse for at least seven days; don’t swap it for a new one every day. Brothers and sisters, faith doesn’t run on novelty; it runs on repetition. Romans 10:17 says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” Hearing once isn’t enough; we need to hear it every day.

This is exactly Peter’s lesson. What he needed was not a new word, but to hold on to that one word, “Come!”, and not let go.

Practice 3: Face your present challenge and make your decision by faith

Think of something you’ve been hesitating over recently. Is it because you’ve been “relying on the brain too much”? Try to stop analysing, start trusting God’s promise with your heart, and take a step of faith.

How do you go deeper? First, discern: is this a case of “God hasn’t spoken yet” or “God has spoken and I won’t do it”? If God hasn’t spoken yet, wait quietly — that’s wisdom. If God has spoken and I won’t do it, that’s unbelief, and I need to repent at once. Proverbs 3:5–6 says, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.”

Then comes Multiplication: once you’ve taken this step and experienced God, go and walk alongside someone else who is still in the boat, too afraid to get out. The last of the eight stages is not “success” but “multiplication”. Faith that stops with you is a museum specimen; faith passed on to the next person is life.

The Lesson’s Gentle Reminders

First, faith is not about how much you can control, but about how much you trust God.

Second, sincere faith needs no proof; it only needs eyes for Jesus alone.

Third, the simpler you are, the more genuine your faith; the more you analyse, the hollower your faith.

Fourth, don’t doubt God’s word because your circumstances are talking; let God’s word prevail over everything.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, faith is not measured by how much you know or how much you understand, but by whether you simply trust Jesus. Sincere faith is trust that doesn’t calculate, obedience that doesn’t waver.

May you be like Peter, daring to step out of the boat — because what holds you up is not the water but that one word, “Come!”

May you be like Caleb, seeing God’s promise — because however tall the giants, they are never taller than the God who promised.

May you be like David, full of confidence in God — because the battle is Yahweh’s.

Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord isn’t asking you to become more impressive; the Lord is asking you to give up the throne. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

1 Samuel 16:7 says, “for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” 2 Chronicles 16:9 says, “For Yahweh’s eyes run back and forth throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him.” This morning, too, God’s eyes are searching. He is not looking for the most gifted person; he is looking for a heart that is simply turned towards him.

Are you willing, today, to take off the mask? To pour away that watered-down faith and draw a fresh bucket of faith that is pure, simple and turned towards Jesus alone?

If you do, you will be a person who “relies on the heart”, and God himself will surely do great things for you.

keyVerses: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith,” (1 Timothy 1:5)
“having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois, and your mother Eunice, and, I am persuaded, in you also.” (2 Timothy 1:5)
declarations: Please declare with me: I do not look at my circumstances; I trust only in Jesus. I do not rely on my brain to analyse; I rely on my heart to trust his word!
practices: Recall a time when your faith “stepped across”
Practise saying to God every day, “I believe your word!”
Face your present challenge and make your decision by faith
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, you know our hearts. You see all that is mixed in us — faith led around by circumstances, godliness propped up by social pressure, obedience weighed and haggled over again and again by reason. Lord, forgive us. So often our mouths say we believe while our hearts are calculating; so often we sing loudly before you, then go back to daily life and do things our own way.
Lord, give us a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith. Take away our masks, and let us be real before you.
Lord, take hold of us as you took hold of Peter. When we begin to sink, remind us to turn our eyes to you.
Lord, give us a spirit like Caleb’s — “another spirit” — so that we hold on to your promise and do not let go, even for forty-five years.
Lord, give us a mouth like David’s and feet like David’s, so that what we say agrees with what we believe, and what we believe agrees with what we do.
Lord, we give up the throne of our hearts. Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 14:30 says, “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” Share: what “storm” has recently drawn your eyes away from Jesus? How do you plan to turn your focus back?

Numbers 14:24 says, “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and has followed me fully, him I will bring into the land into which he went. His offspring shall possess it.” Share: what promise has God given you that you’ve been waiting on for a long time? What concrete way will you use this week to declare to God, “I believe your word”?
l030.title: A Sincere Faith
l030.subtitle: How to Measure Whether We Rely on the Heart
l030.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: Your First Thought in the Morning
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Please be still for three seconds and think back to the moment you opened your eyes this morning — what was the first thought that came into your heart?

For some, the first thought was: “Here we go — today’s going to be a tough fight.” For others, the first thought was: “That thing he said yesterday — why did he have to talk to me like that?” For some, the first thought was a list: what time the meeting is, what time to pick up the kids, which bill still hasn’t been paid. And for some, the first thought was: “Good morning, Lord. Today I belong to you.”

The same morning, the same six o’clock, the same kind of Christian — so why is what’s going on inside so different?

In the last lesson we saw that what God values is not our brain but our heart. The Bible says, “for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). We have also understood that rely on the brain and you’ll have worry; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy; and that the wellspring of life flows from the heart (Proverbs 4:23).

But, brothers and sisters, understanding a truth is one thing; living it out is something else entirely. Many people hear “rely on the heart and not the brain”, go home, and carry on worrying, carry on complaining, carry on tossing and turning at night, calculating. Why? Because they treat “relying on the heart” as a slogan rather than a practice.

So the title of this lesson is not “The Doctrine of Relying on the Heart” but “Putting the Heart into Practice”.

“Relying on the heart” is not an abstract idea; it is a state of life that can actually be practised and lived out. Once we understand that what God values is our “heart”, the question follows: how do we genuinely “rely on the heart”?

The answer will probably come as a relief to many — and a real surprise to many others: “relying on the heart” does not depend on human effort, still less on the analysis of the brain. What truly enables us to rely on the heart is the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

Without the Holy Spirit, our hearts are dead and cold, and we can only live by the brain. A person can use their brain to memorise a hundred verses and still not have a single verse enter their heart; a person can use their brain to analyse ten methods of prayer and never once truly meet God. But when the Holy Spirit lives in us, he awakens our hearts and brings them to life, and helps us to love God with our hearts and to do his will.

This lesson sets out to lead us into a crucial practice: letting the Holy Spirit guide our hearts, so that we live a life of “relying on the heart”.

We’ll look at three things together. First, relying on the heart is a life “guided by the Holy Spirit”. Second, circumstances are the tool God uses to test whether we are “relying on the heart”. Third, those who rely on the heart are willing to let God search and renew their hearts.

One is the source, one is the examination hall, one is the turning back. The source is the Holy Spirit; the examination hall is our circumstances; the turning back is repentance. Put the three together and you have “putting the heart into practice”.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Books, Two Situations, One Heart
sections.html:
To stand firm in this lesson, let’s first set out the background to our two key passages.

The author of Romans 8 is the apostle Paul. He wrote this letter in the winter of around AD 56–57 in Corinth, in Greece, as he prepared to take the collection to Jerusalem and then travel on via Rome to Spain (Romans 15:24–28). The church in Rome that received it had not been founded by Paul. It included both Jewish and Gentile believers, and there was frequent tension between the two groups over the law, food and festivals.

In Romans 7, Paul describes with searing honesty the agony of a person trying to do good by their own willpower and failing: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18) Chapter 7 ends with a cry: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24)

Chapter 8 is God’s answer to that cry. In the chapter’s thirty-nine verses, the word “Spirit” appears nearly twenty times — the densest chapter on the Holy Spirit in the whole Bible. Paul wants to tell the brothers and sisters in Rome that the way out of failure is not to try harder, but to change the source of power for our lives — from “relying on our own flesh” to “relying on the indwelling Holy Spirit”.

Notice that when Paul wrote Romans 8, the Christians in Rome were living in a highly unstable situation. A few years earlier, the emperor Claudius had ordered the Jews out of Rome (Acts 18:2), and believers had only just begun to return; a few years later, the fires of Nero’s persecution would blaze. So chapter 8 is not armchair speculation; it is a guide to life for a group of people who might lose everything at any moment. No wonder Paul says in the same chapter: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us.” (Romans 8:18)

As for Psalm 139, its superscription says it is “for the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David.” David knew the wilderness of the shepherd and the wilderness of the fugitive, the temptations of the palace and the pain of a son’s betrayal. The psalm opens: “Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me.” (Psalm 139:1) From verse 1 to verse 18, David marvels at God’s knowledge, presence and power — God knows when he sits down and when he rises up; God saw him before he was formed.

Then, at verse 19, David suddenly turns and asks God to destroy the wicked. And in the last two verses of the psalm he does something remarkable: he swings the searchlight of judgement away from others and back onto himself. “Search me, God, and know my heart.” (Psalm 139:23)

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the watershed between “relying on the heart” and “relying on the brain”. Those who rely on the brain turn the spotlight on others; those who rely on the heart turn the spotlight on themselves.

There is a third piece of background: Deuteronomy 8. On the plains of Moab, Moses preached his final sermons to the new generation of Israelites about to cross the Jordan. Their parents had fallen in the wilderness; they themselves were the generation born and raised there. Moses looked back over the forty years of the journey so that, once they entered Canaan and grew prosperous, they would not forget God. “You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to test you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.” (Deuteronomy 8:2)

Romans 8 speaks of the source, Deuteronomy 8 of the examination hall, Psalm 139 of the turning back. Three books, three situations, all pointing to the same heart.

sections.heading: 1. Relying on the Heart Is a Life “Guided by the Holy Spirit”
sections.html:
1. Two Kinds of People, Two Ways of Setting the Mind, Two Outcomes

The Bible says, “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit.” (Romans 8:5)

Notice Paul’s wording. He doesn’t say the world is divided into “good people” and “bad people”; he says there are two kinds of people: “those who live according to the flesh” and “those who live according to the Spirit”. The dividing line isn’t how well we perform morally, but where the power for our lives comes from.

Those who rely on the heart are people guided by the Holy Spirit; those who rely on the brain are people steered by themselves.

“Set their minds” here is the Greek phroneō (φρονέω), meaning “to think about, to be intent on, to set one’s mind on something”. It doesn’t mean thinking about something now and then; it means the habitual direction of a person’s life, where their mind is fixed. Paul uses the same word in Philippians: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)

So “setting our minds on the things of the Spirit” doesn’t mean thinking about spiritual topics every second of the day. It means that the compass of our mind has been reset by the Holy Spirit.

Then comes the outcome: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:6)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: Paul isn’t saying here “you will die one day”. He is speaking in the present tense — the mind of the flesh “is” death. If a person keeps relying on the brain and on themselves — calculating, scheming, comparing, defending — they don’t have to wait for the future; inside, they are already dried up, worn out, without peace. On the other hand, the mind of the Spirit “is life and peace”. Life and peace are not prizes earned by effort, but fruit that grows naturally from following the Spirit.

2. The Holy Spirit Brings Dead Hearts to Life

So what enables us to set our minds on the things of the Spirit? Determination? Self-discipline? Neither.

The Bible says, “And because you are children, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father!’” (Galatians 4:6)

Notice the direction of movement in this verse: it’s not our hearts straining to climb up and find God, but God sending the Spirit of his Son “into” our hearts. “Abba” is the Aramaic word a child in a Palestinian home used for their father — the most intimate form of address, the equivalent of today’s “Dad”. A slave would never call his master that; only a son would. And what enables us to cry out “Abba” is not our eloquence but the Holy Spirit within us.

Paul also says, “But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.” (Romans 8:11)

The One who raised Jesus from the tomb now lives in you and me. If he can raise the dead, can he not set a cold heart on fire again?

As far back as Ezekiel’s day, God promised: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them.” (Ezekiel 36:26–27)

What is the difference between a heart of stone and a heart of flesh? A stone also has shape and weight, and can even look sturdier than flesh; but a stone has no feeling, no response, no blood flowing through it. Those who rely on the brain are like a heart of stone — all the right doctrine, but nothing moves. Those who rely on the heart are like a heart of flesh — a gentle touch of the Holy Spirit, and it softens, it weeps, it obeys.

So without the Holy Spirit, our hearts are dead and cold, and we can only live by the brain. But the Holy Spirit lives in us, and he awakens our hearts and brings them to life. He lets us see the beauty of Jesus; he helps us respond to God’s promptings; he strengthens our faith.

3. Those Who Raise a Sail Don’t Row

Jesus said to Nicodemus, “The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” (John 3:8) The single Greek word pneuma (πνεῦμα) means both “wind” and “spirit”.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a beautiful picture. There are two kinds of boat at sea: one runs on its own engine, the other on the power of the wind. The motorboat goes fast, but it constantly needs refuelling; when the fuel runs out, it stops in the middle of the ocean. The sailing boat doesn’t seem to decide its own speed, yet it can cross oceans, because the power that drives it is not inside the boat but outside it.

A life that relies on the brain is a speedboat frantically refuelling; a life that relies on the heart is a sailing boat that has learned to raise its sails. A sailor cannot make the wind, but a sailor can open the sails. Prayer, reading Scripture, stillness and obedience are how we open our sails. When the wind comes is the Holy Spirit’s sovereign choice; whether the sails are open is our responsibility.

4. A Man Whose Brain Was Intact but Who Could Not Live

Here I want to mention a real case from modern neuroscience as corroboration.

In his 1994 book Descartes’ Error, the American neuroscientist Antonio Damasio recorded a patient he called “Elliot”. Elliot had been a successful professional until surgery for a brain tumour removed part of his ventromedial prefrontal cortex. After the operation, his IQ scores were still above normal, and his memory, language and logical reasoning were all intact — but his emotional responses had almost disappeared.

The result? He could not make decisions. Just choosing “whether to use a blue pen or a black pen today”, or “which folder this document should be filed in”, could have him analysing back and forth for hours. In the end he lost his job, his marriage broke down and he went bankrupt. From this Damasio proposed the “somatic marker hypothesis”: pure reason is not enough to guide a person’s life.

Brothers and sisters, I’m not trying to use science to prove the Bible — the Bible doesn’t need science to prove it. I simply want to say this: even the bodies God made bear witness that a person with nothing but a brain cannot live. How much more is that true of spiritual life?

The seventeenth-century mathematician and thinker Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) left a famous line in his Pensées: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” A genius who laid the foundations of probability theory finally admitted that the deepest things in life lie beyond the reach of reason.

“Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned.” (1 Corinthians 2:14)

5. Applying the 321 Vision: The Holy Spirit Is My Guide

The third of 321’s Three Foundations is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. This lesson turns that foundation into everyday life.

“Led” uses the Greek word agō (ἄγω): “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14) This is the passive voice — it’s not we who lead the Holy Spirit; it’s we who are led by the Holy Spirit.

Relying on the brain and ourselves is the self-centred life; relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit is selflessness. Self-centred people sit in the driver’s seat of their own lives and want the Holy Spirit to be their satnav; selfless people move out of the driver’s seat and let Jesus be King.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus. Paul could not put it more clearly: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) My calculations are limited; the Holy Spirit’s guidance is limitless. My strength runs out; the Holy Spirit’s power never runs out.

So those who rely on the heart are willing to obey the Holy Spirit and set their minds on the things of God; those who rely on the brain lean on reason and are self-centred, and the result is death and emptiness. A true life of “relying on the heart” is a life of “walking with the Holy Spirit”.

Paul sums up this practice in two very practical sentences: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)

Receiving life is the Holy Spirit’s work, and walking must also be by the Holy Spirit. Beginning by grace but trying to carry on by our own effort — that was the old weakness of the Galatian church, and it is the old weakness of many Christians today.

sections.heading: 2. Circumstances Are the Tool God Uses to Test Whether We Are “Relying on the Heart”
sections.html:
1. Relying on the Heart Is Not Something We Get to Declare

We often think we’re “relying on the heart” very well. We sit in church singing, tears roll down our faces, and we say, “Lord, I truly love you.” But genuinely relying on the heart is not something we get to declare for ourselves; it is proven through our circumstances.

The Lord Jesus quoted Isaiah to rebuke the religious people of his day: “These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.” (Matthew 15:8) Lips are the cheapest instrument; the heart is the costliest altar.

Jeremiah puts it even more searchingly: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9) We can’t even read our own hearts accurately. So what do we do? The very next verse gives the answer: “I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart.” (Jeremiah 17:10)

God reveals our hearts in two ways: one is his direct light shining on us; the other is the circumstances he permits.

2. Forty Years in the Wilderness, to Know What Was in Your Heart

When God brought Israel out of Egypt, he did not take them straight into the Promised Land. From Rameses to Canaan along the coastal highway was no more than an eleven-day journey (Deuteronomy 1:2 says it is eleven days from Horeb to Kadesh Barnea), yet God had them wander in the wilderness for forty years.

Why? Moses gives the answer:

“You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to test you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.” (Deuteronomy 8:2)

There are two key Hebrew words in this verse.

“Humble” is ʿānâ (עָנָה), meaning “to bring low, to afflict”. Its purpose is not torment but the demolition of pride. When things go smoothly, it’s hard to know how proud we are; step into the wilderness and you find out.

“Test” is nāsâ (נָסָה). The emphasis of this word is not “to lure someone into falling” but “to examine, to prove”. It’s like a quality inspector putting a product through a stress test — not to break it, but to find out its true strength. God never tempts anyone to sin (James 1:13), but God does test people, so that what is hidden in the heart comes to light.

Moses goes on: “He humbled you, allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know, that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.” (Deuteronomy 8:3)

So even the manna was an exam. God said, “the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.” (Exodus 16:4) They could gather only one day’s portion each day; any extra bred worms and stank. What was the lesson? The lesson was “you can’t stockpile; you can only trust”. People who rely on the brain can’t stand that, because they want security, reserves and control; people who rely on the heart learn to look to God day by day.

The hardships of the wilderness exposed the unbelief and grumbling inside the Israelites. At Marah they complained because the water was bitter (Exodus 15:23–24); in the Wilderness of Sin they said they would rather have died in Egypt (Exodus 16:3); at Rephidim, when there was no water, they tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us, or not?” (Exodus 17:7) And at Kadesh Barnea, the ten spies brought back an evil report and the whole congregation wept all night.

But in the same wilderness, over the same forty years, two men walked out with a completely different ending. God said of Caleb, “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and has followed me fully, him I will bring into the land into which he went.” (Numbers 14:24)

Brothers and sisters, notice that God didn’t say Caleb had another “brain”; he said he had another “spirit” — in the Chinese Union Version, another “resolve” of the heart. The same wilderness, the same pot of manna, the same giants — some saw death, and some saw God. The difference wasn’t in the circumstances; it was in the heart.

So the wilderness was also God’s opportunity for them to learn to follow him by truly “relying on the heart”.

3. Trees Without Wind Fall Down

From 1991, in the Arizona desert in the United States, a famous scientific experiment called “Biosphere 2” was carried out. Researchers built a huge sealed glass structure containing rainforest, ocean, grassland and farmland, with plenty of sunlight, water and nutrients — lacking only one thing: wind.

The result was surprising: the trees inside grew fast and tall, but their trunks were weak, and many of them sagged or even fell over before they reached maturity. The researchers later discovered that trees need to be shaken by the wind in order to grow denser “stress wood” where the strain falls; trees without wind have weak trunks, and the taller they grow, the sooner they fall.

Brothers and sisters, this is the principle of the wilderness. We ask God for a greenhouse with no wind, but God knows that trees without wind cannot stand.

“Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance. Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.” (James 1:2–4)

Sitting in the ashes, Job spoke a golden line: “But he knows the way that I take. When he has tried me, I will come out like gold.” (Job 23:10)

4. What Psychology Says: Growth After Crisis

Psychology has observed something similar. In 1996, Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun of the University of North Carolina at Charlotte put forward the concept of “post-traumatic growth”. Their research found that many people, after going through a major crisis, change for the better in five areas: new possibilities in life, deeper relationships, discovering they are stronger than they thought, a greater appreciation of life, and spiritual growth.

In addition, research published in 2007 by Angela Duckworth, a psychologist at the University of Pennsylvania, showed that the strongest predictor of a person’s long-term achievement is often not IQ but “grit” — sustained passion and perseverance towards long-term goals.

Please note: this research cannot save anyone, nor can it take the place of the Holy Spirit’s work. It simply confirms, from one angle, what God was doing in the wilderness: God is not wasting our time; God is forging our hearts.

The English writer C. S. Lewis, in The Problem of Pain (1940), wrote a line that is often quoted: “God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world.”

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus Is the Focal Point, Not Our Circumstances

Our lives, too, will have many “wilderness” seasons — wildernesses of health, of finances, of relationships, of ministry. All of these are God’s grace. He allows hardship to come in order to reveal whether we are truly “relying on the heart”.

Will we choose to complain and retreat, or choose to believe and persevere? These choices reveal our heart towards God.

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The lesson’s gentle reminder puts it perfectly: those who rely on the brain look at their circumstances; those who rely on the heart look at Jesus.

Peter is the most vivid example. “He said, ‘Come!’ Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:29–30)

Notice that the wind didn’t start blowing after he began to sink; the wind had been there from the start. What changed was not the circumstances but the focus. His eyes moved from Jesus to the waves, and his heart fell from faith into fear.

This is also the shift of perspective 321 speaks of: from the human perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The same wilderness, seen with earthly eyes, is a disaster; seen with heavenly eyes, it’s a school. Seen with temporary eyes, it’s loss; seen with eternal eyes, it’s glory.

That is how Paul saw it: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us.” (Romans 8:18)

And, brothers and sisters, the wilderness is the most real training ground for the 920 practice. 920 says that everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”, and with them we practise living out the selfless “0” and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. The family member who upsets you most, the colleague who makes you most want to quit, the co-worker in ministry who discourages you most — that person is the exam question God has placed in your wilderness. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — which of them doesn’t grow through friction?

Patience doesn’t grow in an empty wilderness; patience grows only beside the people who make you impatient.

sections.heading: 3. Those Who Rely on the Heart Are Willing to Let God Search and Renew Their Hearts
sections.html:
1. David’s Prayer: Turning the Searchlight on Himself

David was a man who relied on the heart. God himself testified of him: “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.” (Acts 13:22)

A man after God’s heart is not a man who never fails. David committed terrible sins — numbering the people, taking another man’s wife, having a man killed by another’s sword. But the greatest difference between David and Saul was not who sinned less; it was who would hand over his heart when the light shone on him.

David often prayed like this: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

These two verses also contain two very vivid Hebrew words.

“Search” is ḥāqar (חָקַר), whose root meaning is “to dig, to explore”. It’s what a miner does — not standing on the surface for a glance, but drilling, going down the shaft, digging layer after layer deeper until the seam is found. David was asking God: Lord, don’t just look at my surface; please dig down.

“Try” is bāḥan (בָּחַן), a term from metalworking — putting metal in the furnace and melting it so the dross rises to the surface and is skimmed off, leaving pure gold. David was asking God: Lord, burn what needs burning, skim off what needs skimming.

Brothers and sisters, do you dare pray like that? Most people’s prayers go: “Lord, please search my boss.” “Lord, please shine your light on my husband.” “Lord, please deal with that co-worker of mine.” But David said, “Search me.”

Those who rely on the brain shine the searchlight on others; those who rely on the heart put the searchlight in God’s hands and say, “Shine it on me.”

2. Saul and David: Two Responses to Being Corrected

Scripture sets these two kinds of heart side by side, and the contrast is stark.

Saul disobeyed God’s command and did not completely destroy the Amalekites. When Samuel came to confront him, what was his first reaction? Self-justification. “Saul said to Samuel, ‘But I have obeyed Yahweh’s voice, and have gone the way which Yahweh sent me.’” (1 Samuel 15:20) He blamed the people, and even presented the sheep and cattle he had kept as an offering for God. In the end he did say, “I have sinned,” but immediately added: “yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel.” (1 Samuel 15:30) What he really cared about was saving face.

And David? When Nathan pointed straight at him and said, “You are the man,” David’s first reaction was just one short sentence: “David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against Yahweh.’” (2 Samuel 12:13) No explanation, no shifting the blame, no press release.

Then he wrote Psalm 51: “For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.” (Psalm 51:3) “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10) “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

Brothers and sisters, this is the watershed.

Those who rely on the heart are not people who never fail, but people who are willing to let God’s light shine on them, willing to repent and turn to God. If they find their hearts have drifted, their motives have become impure, or they have grown cold towards God, they don’t use their brains to find excuses; they turn back at once and give their hearts to God afresh.

When those who rely on the brain are corrected, they say, “You don’t understand what I’m up against.” When those who rely on the heart are corrected, they say, “Lord, it’s me.”

3. God’s Word Is the Most Precise Scalpel

What does God use to search us? His main tool is his word.

“For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. There is no creature that is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open before the eyes of him to whom we must give an account.” (Hebrews 4:12–13)

“Piercing, dividing” is the language of surgery. Brothers and sisters, when we go for a health check and lie in a scanner, do we feel violated? No, because we know the doctor isn’t taking X-rays to condemn us but to heal us.

It’s the same when the Holy Spirit holds up Scripture to our hearts. He isn’t trying to humiliate us; he wants to heal us. Satan’s accusation drives people to despair and makes them hide; the Holy Spirit’s conviction makes the heart ache but makes us run towards God. This is the simplest way to tell the two voices apart: one voice pushes you away from the cross, the other draws you closer to the cross.

And then there is the promise we can lean on every day: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

“Confess” in Greek is homologeō (ὁμολογέω), literally “to say the same thing” — that is, to stop defending ourselves and say the same thing God says: you call this sin, and I call it sin too.

4. We Know Ourselves Less Than We Think

On this point psychology gives us a very humbling reminder.

A team led by the organisational psychologist Tasha Eurich published research in the Harvard Business Review in 2018 showing that about 95 per cent of people believe they are self-aware, but by objective measures only 10 to 15 per cent actually are.

In other words, nine and a half people out of ten overestimate how well they know themselves.

As early as the sixteenth century, the Reformer John Calvin said in the very first sentence of his Institutes of the Christian Religion (in its final 1559 edition) that nearly all the true and sound wisdom we possess consists of two parts — the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves. And he went straight on to point out that the two are bound together: a person who does not know God will not truly know himself either.

Brothers and sisters, when we look at ourselves in a mirror, we see what we want to see; only when we look at ourselves in God’s light do we see the truth. So what we need is not more self-analysis but more of God’s light shining on us. Self-analysis is relying on the brain; being searched by God’s light is relying on the heart.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Old Self to the Selfless New Self

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem.

What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and trying to take God’s place. That’s what Saul did — he wanted to hold on to his throne, his face, the people’s support. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. That’s what David did — he put himself back in the creature’s place and said, “You are God, I am a man, and I was wrong.”

“Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.” Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. A heart willing to be searched is the heart Satan can do least about, because his most powerful weapon is accusation, and accusation has no effect at all on someone who has already confessed and been washed clean.

This also brings out 321’s fivefold change: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes.

Notice the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people go the other way round — they charge into ministry first, patch up relationships afterwards, and only last think about their life. The result is that the bigger the ministry, the emptier the heart. What God cares about is first having a renewed heart.

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

And what is the result of that renewal? Becoming more and more like Jesus: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

This is “putting the heart into practice”: letting God keep searching our hearts, and being willing in every circumstance to examine ourselves, repent and be renewed, until our hearts draw ever closer to God’s heart.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Relying on the Heart Means Handing Our Lives Back to God
sections.html:
Put these three points together and we find they fit exactly into the 321 framework.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. In the Garden of Gethsemane, the Lord Jesus prayed: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42) That was the most wholehearted prayer ever prayed. He didn’t pretend it didn’t hurt; he laid his true feelings completely open before the Father, and then laid down his own will. Relying on the heart doesn’t mean being emotionally worked up; relying on the heart means genuinely giving your heart to the Father.

The Bible is my standard. David asked God to search him, and God searches with his word (Hebrews 4:12). Promptings need to be tested; impressions need to be checked; no genuine “leading of the Holy Spirit” will ever contradict the Scripture already written. “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” (Psalm 119:11)

The Holy Spirit is my guide. This is the heart of this lesson. “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14) It’s not we who drag the Holy Spirit along; it’s the Holy Spirit who leads us.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King. The heart is the throne room within us, and the throne has room for only one. If “I” am still sitting on it, the Holy Spirit can only be an adviser; if Jesus is sitting on it, we have direction. Putting the heart into practice comes down, in the end, to giving up the throne every morning.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The meaning of the wilderness is not to prove how strong I am, but to show what Paul spoke of — that we are only clay vessels, “that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7). If we can stand, the glory goes to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A person guided by the Holy Spirit, searched by God and still trusting in the wilderness is a living stone in God’s system. The system isn’t built by piling up institutions; it is built from heart upon heart willing to rely on the heart.

The Path of Serving and the Priority of Relationships

321’s Path of Serving is: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. This lesson stands especially at the first station: Spirit. If a person skips “Spirit” and rushes straight to “Service”, ministry becomes drudgery.

The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. The three points match it exactly — Point 1 is about God (being guided by the Holy Spirit), Point 3 is about ourselves (being searched by God), and Point 2 is about others and things (being proven in our circumstances). Get the order wrong and the effort is wasted.

920 and 235

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. With them we practise living out the selfless “0”, so that the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit can grow from within us. The hardest person to get along with in your wilderness is the very ninefold training ground God has prepared for you.

The 235 relationships: becoming a “2” with someone who is selfless, being honest with each other and praying for each other; establishing the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that life is passed on; and finally becoming the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, building together.

Brothers and sisters, if you don’t dare face the wilderness alone, then don’t face it alone. Find your “2”. Anyone willing to be searched by God also needs a companion with whom they can speak the truth to each other. God never meant us to walk the wilderness road alone.

Four Shifts of Perspective

From the human perspective to God’s: people say, “Why me?” God says, “I want to know what is in your heart.”

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly: the earth sees lack; heaven sees provision.

From the temporary perspective to the eternal: what is temporary is suffering; what is eternal is glory.

From the worldly perspective to the godly: the world looks at success or failure; God looks at whether it pleases his heart.

A person who relies on the heart is a person who has been given a new pair of eyes.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Making “Relying on the Heart” a Daily Action
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We are going to put them into action one by one using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication.

Practice 1: Be still for five minutes each day and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on your heart

Each day, be still for five minutes and ask yourself before God: “Did my reactions, words and choices today come from the heart, or were they worked out by the brain?”

Information: first, take hold of this lesson’s truth — relying on the heart doesn’t come by effort but by the guidance of the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:5).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this truth from your head into your heart, so that in one specific situation you “see” yourself relying on the brain.

Conviction: stop arguing, and admit that your natural instinct is to rely on the brain, to rely on yourself.

Implementation: set a fixed time and place. Morning is best, because your first thought in the morning sets the direction of the day. Put your phone well out of reach. Five minutes is enough — don’t start by committing to thirty.

Evaluation: before bed, ask: did I do those five minutes today? When I did, was I going through the motions, or did I really open my heart?

Correction: if you keep failing, shorten the time again, fix the place more firmly, or switch to a different time of day. Don’t force yourself on with guilt — guilt is relying on the brain; grace is relying on the heart.

Repetition: forty days in a row. Forty days is not a superstitious number; it’s the reminder God gives us through the forty years in the wilderness and Jesus’ forty days in the wilderness: the lessons of the heart take time.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister, invite them to do it with you, and check in with each other once a week.

Practice 2: Write down how you reacted the last time you faced difficulty

Take a pen and paper and write down the most recent thing that upset you. Then ask honestly: at that moment, was I trusting or complaining? Was I responding to the Holy Spirit’s prompting, or doing things my own way? Then dig one layer deeper: behind that reaction, what was I really protecting? My face? My sense of security? My control?

Information: circumstances are the tool God uses to test whether we are relying on the heart (Deuteronomy 8:2).

Revelation: ask God to show you that this was no accident but an exam question.

Conviction: admit, “I was relying on my brain then,” without making excuses.

Implementation: write it down. Writing it down matters, because self-examination that isn’t written down is usually diluted by emotion.

Evaluation: compare yourself with Caleb — “another spirit” (Numbers 14:24). If you could do it again, what would a heart-led response look like?

Correction: confess to God, and apologise to others where necessary. If you’ve hurt someone, go and repair the relationship — life first, then relationships, and only then ministry.

Repetition: from now on, every time you face a difficulty, write it down again. After a year, you’ll have your own wilderness notebook.

Multiplication: share one of those testimonies. Your wilderness will become a spring of water for someone else.

Practice 3: Memorise Psalm 139:23 and use it as a prayer

Each day, say to God: “Search me, God, and know my heart.” (Psalm 139:23)

Information: read Psalm 139:23–24 until you know it well, and memorise it together with the next verse: “See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.”

Revelation: as you memorise, say it slowly, and let the two pictures of “search” (digging) and “try” (refining gold) rise up before you.

Conviction: be genuinely willing to be dug into and refined, rather than treating it as just a nice-sounding prayer.

Implementation: pray this line first thing when you get up in the morning, and pray it again before you go to sleep.

Evaluation: watch whether, within a week, God answers you through people, through circumstances or through a passage of Scripture.

Correction: the moment God shines his light, respond at once — don’t let it carry over to the next day. “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath.” (Ephesians 4:26)

Repetition: make it your breath prayer — you can say it once in a traffic jam, waiting for a lift, standing in a queue.

Multiplication: teach your children and your small-group members to memorise it with you. One verse that enters a family can change three generations.

The Lesson’s Gentle Reminders

A life of relying on the heart does not run on willpower but on the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

God allows difficulties to come not to make you fall, but to test whether you are “relying on the heart”.

Those who rely on the brain look at their circumstances; those who rely on the heart look at Jesus.

Let the wilderness become the place where you bear witness to loving God with your heart.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call: Let Jesus Reign as King in My Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, “relying on the heart” is not a choice made in a moment but a practice of a lifetime.

The Holy Spirit living in us is the foundation that makes a life of relying on the heart possible. What great grace this is — God didn’t hand us a checklist and say, “Go and try hard”; God put his Spirit within us and said, “I will walk with you.”

So let us learn to set our minds on the things of the Spirit in everything, and let him lead us in the will of God. Whether in good times or in the wilderness, we are willing to let God test our hearts, so that we become people who follow him with all our hearts.

I want to issue a call to three kinds of brothers and sisters.

First, if you are in the wilderness right now, today’s message is to tell you: you have not been abandoned; you are being proven. God led Israel into the wilderness not because he had forgotten the Promised Land, but because he wanted a people with hearts for him to go in. Please don’t spend your time in the wilderness only complaining. Lift up your head and see whether the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire are still there — he has been there all along.

Second, if things are going well for you right now, today’s message is also a reminder: good times are a test too. The verses that follow in Deuteronomy 8 warn the Israelites that when they have eaten their fill, built fine houses and seen their silver and gold multiply, they must take care lest their hearts be lifted up and they forget Yahweh (Deuteronomy 8:12–14). The wilderness tests our faith; abundance tests our faithfulness.

Third, if you feel that your heart has been cold for a long time, today is the day to turn back. Don’t use your brain to analyse why you’ve grown cold; just come before the Lord with your heart and say: “Lord, it’s me. Search me.” God never despises a broken and contrite heart (Psalm 51:17).

Finally, let us hand the throne of our hearts back to him. May Jesus reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory go to Jesus. For we rely on the heart not to become better versions of ourselves, but so that he may receive within us the place and the glory that are rightfully his.

keyVerses: “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit. For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace;” (Romans 8:5–6)
“Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:
“Lord, I will follow you with my heart every day. May my heart always be searched by you, and always be guided by the Holy Spirit!”
practices: Be still for five minutes each day and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on your heart
Write down how you reacted the last time you faced difficulty
Memorise Psalm 139:23 and use it as a prayer
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we come before you and confess that we are far too used to relying on the brain, far too used to relying on ourselves. We analyse you with our heads but do not love you with our hearts; we honour you with our lips, but our hearts are so often far from you. Lord, forgive us.

Thank you for giving us the Holy Spirit. Lord, without your Spirit our hearts are dead and cold; but you have promised to take away our hearts of stone and give us hearts of flesh. Begin your work in us today. Awaken our hearts and bring them to life, so that we can hear your still, small voice and be willing to obey.

Lord, we thank you for the wilderness too. Help us to stop complaining about our circumstances and, in every difficulty, to turn our eyes to Jesus. Make us like Caleb, with another spirit, following you fully.

Lord, we ask you in the words of David’s prayer: search me, and know my heart; try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way. Whatever you point out, we will repent of at once; whatever you want to refine, we will not hide.
Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit.” (Romans 8:5) Share: in your life this past week, was there something you clearly handled by “relying on the brain”? If you could do it again, how would handling it by “relying on the heart” be different?

“You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to test you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.” (Deuteronomy 8:2) Share: in a “wilderness” season you’ve been through, what did God reveal about your heart? Looking back today, what grace of God can you see?
l031.title: Putting the Heart into Practice
l031.subtitle: Let the Holy Spirit Guide Our Hearts
l031.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: Your Eyes Are Deciding Your Direction
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re going to look together at a lesson that seems simple, yet decides which way our whole life will go: fixing our eyes on Jesus.

Let me begin with something that really happened. In July 1999 John F. Kennedy Jr., son of the former American president, was flying his own small plane over the waters of the Atlantic when it went down into the sea in the dark. All three people on board were killed. After its investigation, the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) concluded that the probable cause was that the pilot, flying at night over water with no horizon to use as a reference, lost control of the aircraft — what the aviation world calls “spatial disorientation”.

What is spatial disorientation? When a person loses any reliable reference point outside himself, the balance sense of the inner ear begins to lie. The plane is plainly descending, yet the body feels it climbing; the wings are plainly banking, yet your senses tell you everything is fine. A pilot who trusts his feelings will fly, “feeling great” all the way, straight into the sea. So flight training has an iron rule: when you enter cloud or darkness, don’t trust your feelings — trust your instruments.

Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life is just like that. When our life flies into cloud, flies into darkness — a doctor’s diagnosis, a redundancy notice from the company, a child’s betrayal, a marriage gone cold, a long wait in prayer with no answer at all — that’s when our feelings start to lie. Feeling says: God has probably forgotten me. Feeling says: this time there really is no way through. Feeling says: did I believe the wrong thing?

And in that moment the easiest, most natural thing for us to do is to turn our eyes away from Jesus and onto our circumstances. Once the eyes turn, the heart turns with them; once the heart turns, doubt, fear and wavering come one after another, and in the end we give up.

The Bible records a scene that acts this truth out to the full. In Matthew 14, in the wind and waves of the Sea of Galilee, Peter called to the Lord, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.” The Lord said, “Come!” Peter stepped down from the boat and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. Then Scripture says: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:30)

Notice the wording: “when he saw that the wind was strong”. The wind had been strong all along; it didn’t suddenly whip up at that moment. What changed was not the wind but Peter’s eyes. At first he was looking at Jesus; then he was looking at the wind and the waves. While he looked at Jesus, the water became a road; when he looked at the waves, the road became an abyss.

Brothers and sisters, this is what today’s lesson wants to say to us: what you see decides where you go.

One sister described her hardest year like this: “It wasn’t that I couldn’t pray. It was that the moment I opened my eyes, my head was full of those few things. Every day I was reviewing my troubles, and I was hardly ever meditating on my Lord.” Then she made a decision — a very small one, but a crucial one: every morning, before opening her phone, she would open her Bible first. Her circumstances didn’t change straight away, but she herself was made new.

In this lesson, the very attitude to life we want to practise is this: however hard the circumstances, our eyes see only Jesus.

The lesson divides this practice into three levels, matching three of life’s hardest situations:

First, in a dead end, still believe — Jesus is real.

Second, in the waiting, still trust — Jesus doesn’t lie.

Third, in the chaos, still obey — Jesus makes no mistakes.

Real. Doesn’t lie. Makes no mistakes. Brothers and sisters, if these three sentences get into our hearts, there is no circumstance that can knock us down.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Group of People About to Give Up, and a Word That Saves
sections.html:
To truly grasp the weight of the words “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith”, we first need to get to know the letter to the Hebrews.

First, the author. Hebrews is the only letter in the New Testament that carries no name. Most of the early Church Fathers in the East attributed it to Paul, while the Western church long had its doubts. The famous interpreter of church history, Origen, once said something very honest: who actually wrote this letter, only God truly knows (his words are recorded by the church historian Eusebius in Book Six of his Ecclesiastical History). Today most evangelical scholars think the author was a Jewish Christian leader in Paul’s circle, well educated in Greek and deeply versed in the Old Testament sacrificial system. The author is uncertain, but the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the message are beyond doubt.

Second, the date and the recipients. The book repeatedly speaks of the priests’ “offering” of sacrifices as still going on, using the present tense — for example in Hebrews 8:4 and 10:11. This is usually taken as a clue that it was written before the Jerusalem temple was destroyed in AD 70. So the book is generally dated to the AD 60s. As for the recipients, both the title and the content point to a group of Jewish Christians.

What situation were they in? The author tells us plainly: “But remember the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle with sufferings; partly, being exposed to both reproaches and oppressions; and partly, becoming partakers with those who were treated so. For you both had compassion on me in my chains, and joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have for yourselves a better possession and an enduring one in the heavens.” (Hebrews 10:32–34)

Brothers and sisters, here was a group of people who had once been on fire, who had once paid the price, and who were now worn out. They had been slandered, plundered, pushed out; believing in the Lord hadn’t made their days better — it had made them harder. So something in their hearts began to loosen: let’s go back — back to the temple, back to the sacrifices, back to the familiar old system; at least it’s safe. That’s why the whole letter to the Hebrews has just one theme: Jesus is better. He is better than the angels, better than Moses, better than Aaron’s priesthood; his covenant is better, his sacrifice is better. The author isn’t arguing theology; he is rescuing a group of brothers and sisters who are on the point of giving up.

Next, the context before and after. Chapter 11 is the famous “hall of faith” — Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Rahab … The author names them one after another in a single breath, and at the end says, “These all, having had testimony given to them through their faith, didn’t receive the promise” (Hebrews 11:39). Then chapter 12 picks it straight up: “Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses …”

There’s something here that’s often misunderstood. Many people imagine that “cloud of witnesses” as spectators sitting in the stands of heaven, watching us run our race. But the Greek word for “witness” is martys, and the point of the word is not “someone who watches” but “someone who testifies” — it is the very root of our later word “martyr”. They are not sitting in the stands handing out scores; they are standing beside the track holding up signs that testify: I’ve run this road; God can be trusted; you can make it!

The author is using an image from the arena that everyone at the time knew well. The runner must “lay aside every weight” — in the original, “weight” means excess bulk, not necessarily sin; it may be a good thing, yet it slows us down. And he must cast off “the sin which so easily entangles us” — “entangles” means wraps tightly around, trips the feet.

Then comes the climax of the whole passage: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.”

“Looking to” translates the Greek aphoraō, which is made of two parts, “away from” and “look at”. It means to take your eyes off other things and gaze steadily, intently, at one object. So it isn’t a quick glance, or a look in passing; it is “turn your gaze away from there, and fix it here”. Brothers and sisters, true looking to Jesus always includes an act of “turning away” — if we don’t take our eyes off our circumstances, we can never really fix them on Jesus.

“Author and perfecter” are two words. “Author” is archēgos, meaning the pioneer, the leading commander, the first one to travel this road; “perfecter” is teleiōtēs, the one who makes complete, who brings to the finish. Put together, they mean: Jesus is the one who starts our faith off and the finishing line of our faith; he ran this road first, and he will surely bring us to the end of it.

Then the author tells us how he finished the race: he “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” The Lord Jesus himself came through the cross by “fixing his eyes” — he fixed his eyes on the joy set before him.

Brothers and sisters, so today’s theme verse is not a motivational slogan; it’s a lifeline thrown to people who are about to give up. Its logic is this: don’t look at how tired you are from running; look at the Lord who has already run the whole course and now sits at the right hand of the throne.

sections.heading: 1. In a Dead End, Still Believe: Jesus Is Real
sections.html:
When nothing turns out as we expected and there seems to be no hope, we have to go back to the most basic question of faith: is Jesus real?

Brothers and sisters, don’t think it’s unspiritual to ask that. Quite the opposite — the greatest saints in the Bible asked questions like it. From prison, John the Baptist sent his disciples to ask Jesus, “Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3) Job, sitting in the ashes, asked God why. The psalmist cried out too: “How long, Yahweh? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1) The issue is not whether we have questions, but where we take them — whether we take them before our circumstances and brood over them alone, or bring them before Jesus and ask him to make himself known.

1. The risen Lord is real, and he is alive today

The Bible’s answer is unequivocal: yes, Jesus is real. He rose from the dead, and he is alive today.

When the apostle John fell at his feet like a dead man on the island of Patmos, the Lord appeared to him and said: “Don’t be afraid. I am the first and the last, and the Living one. I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. I have the keys of Death and of Hades.” (Revelation 1:17–18)

Notice the order here: first the Lord says “Don’t be afraid”, and then he immediately explains why there’s no need to be afraid — because “I was dead, and behold, I am alive”. In the original, “the Living one” is a present participle; it describes not a historical event but an ongoing state: he is the one who goes on living. He didn’t just live once; he lives.

Hebrews sums it up in one sentence too: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.” (Hebrews 13:8) He is Lord of history, Lord of the present, and the Lord who will never change in all the future.

Paul goes further and stakes the whole weight of the faith on the resurrection: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins.” (1 Corinthians 15:17) But he goes straight on to declare: “But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruits of those who are asleep.” (1 Corinthians 15:20)

Brothers and sisters, this is the most fundamental difference between the Christian faith and every religion and philosophy. Jesus is not a moral symbol, not a set of life principles, not a portrait hanging on the wall. He is a Saviour who is still alive today and still walks with us.

2. Joseph: thirteen years of darkness, held only by the heart’s conviction that “God is real”

The lesson mentions Joseph, and the example could hardly be more fitting.

At seventeen Joseph had two dreams and received God’s promise (Genesis 37:2 records that he was seventeen at the time). But what happened between receiving the promise and seeing it fulfilled? He was envied by his brothers, thrown into a pit, sold into Egypt, made a slave in Potiphar’s house, falsely accused by his master’s wife, thrown into prison, interpreted the cupbearer’s dream and then was forgotten for two years. By the time he stood before Pharaoh, Scripture says, “Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt.” (Genesis 41:46)

From seventeen to thirty: thirteen whole years.

In those thirteen years, did Joseph ever once complain that God had deceived him? Scripture records nothing of the kind. Instead, it writes down the same sentence twice: “Yahweh was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian.” (Genesis 39:2) “But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him, and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.” (Genesis 39:21)

Notice that “Yahweh was with Joseph” appears once when he was a slave and once when he was in prison. God’s presence doesn’t mean favourable circumstances; God’s presence is what is real in the middle of adverse ones.

A psalm adds a profound footnote to this period of Joseph’s life: “until the time that his word happened, and Yahweh’s word proved him true.” (Psalm 105:19) The Chinese Union Version reads, “the word of Yahweh tested him.” Brothers and sisters, so it wasn’t only that Joseph was being tested in the waiting; it was “Yahweh’s word” that was testing Joseph. God’s promise was like a fire, burning away all the fleshly pride in Joseph, until the seventeen-year-old who loved to show off his dreams became the thirty-year-old prime minister who could carry the survival of a nation.

Many years later, Joseph spoke those great words to his brothers: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.” (Genesis 50:20)

It wasn’t that Joseph felt no pain. It was that, in the pain, he still held fast: God is real.

3. Brutal facts, and unshakeable faith

There is a very important balance here. “Believing that Jesus is real” doesn’t mean denying reality or pretending nothing’s wrong.

The American admiral James Stockdale was taken prisoner during the Vietnam War and spent eight years in a prisoner-of-war camp, enduring torture. The management writer Jim Collins interviewed him for his book Good to Great and asked him: who didn’t make it out? Stockdale’s answer is startling: the optimists. They said, “We’ll be out by Christmas”; Christmas came and went. Then they said, “We’ll be out by Easter”; Easter came and went. In the end they died of a broken heart. Stockdale himself said he never lost faith that he would get out, and that he would in the end turn the experience into the defining turning point of his life; but at the same time he would never compromise with the most brutal facts in front of him. Collins called this principle “the Stockdale Paradox”.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what biblical faith is. Faith isn’t burying your head in the sand and saying, “It’s fine, it’s fine.” Faith is opening your eyes wide to see clearly how hard things are, and then lifting your head and saying: my God is bigger than this.

The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl lost his wife and his parents in the Nazi camps, and after the war wrote Man’s Search for Meaning. He observed that those who held on were often not the physically strongest, but those who still held a “why” in their hearts; quoting Nietzsche, he said that someone who has a “why” to live for can bear almost any “how”. Brothers and sisters, our “why” is firmer than anyone’s — because our hope doesn’t rest on whether our circumstances improve, but on the Lord who rose from the dead and is alive today.

4. Applying the 321 vision: Jesus is the focal point, not our circumstances

The first of the Three Foundations of the 321 vision is: Jesus is my role model.

What does it mean to take Jesus as our role model? Hebrews 12:2 tells us that he “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame”. The Lord Jesus walked the road of the cross not by gritting his teeth and forcing his way through, but by fixing his eyes on the joy the Father had prepared. His eyes saw the resurrection first; then his feet could climb Golgotha.

So the 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, we can check ourselves honestly: when I woke up this morning, where was my focus? If our focus is on ourselves, we fall into self-pity; if it’s on other people, we fall into bitterness; if it’s on our circumstances, we fall into fear. Only when our focus is on Jesus do we have peace.

This is also the shift in perspective the 321 vision talks about: from man’s perspective to God’s, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. Paul put it well: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Joseph’s thirteen years were temporary; God’s promise is eternal. Your troubles today are temporary; your Lord is eternal.

sections.heading: 2. In the Waiting, Still Trust: Jesus Doesn’t Lie
sections.html:
The first question was “Is Jesus real?” The second question hurts even more: Jesus is real — but might he forget me? The things he promised — might they not count?

Brothers and sisters, what wears us down most in life is often not suffering itself but waiting. Suffering at least sometimes gives us something definite to push against; waiting is a slow drain with no end in sight.

1. God is not a man, that he should lie

The Bible’s answer to this question is one of the most ringing sentences in the Old Testament. Balak had hired Balaam for a great fee to curse the Israelites, but God made it so that only blessing could come out of his mouth. Balaam said: “God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?” (Numbers 23:19)

This verse uses two contrasts: God doesn’t lie as man does; God doesn’t go back on his word as a son of man does. People lie because they are limited, because they’re afraid, because they change; people regret because they don’t know what tomorrow holds. God is bound by no limit and knows how everything ends; he has no reason ever to lie, and never needs to revise a decision.

Paul says it too: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ, our Lord.” (1 Corinthians 1:9) Notice what the evidence of his faithfulness is here — that “you were called”. Since he was willing to call you, he will take responsibility for you to the very end.

In his letter to Titus, Paul even gives God a title: “God, who can’t lie” (Titus 1:2). And Hebrews ties this attribute directly to our perseverance: “let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful.” (Hebrews 10:23)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the logic: we can keep from wavering not because our willpower is strong, but because he who promised is faithful. Our certainty doesn’t rest on how big our own faith is, but on how reliable the one we believe in is. The thickness of the ice matters far more than how brave the person standing on it is.

In Old Testament Hebrew, the root of “faithful” is aman, whose basic meaning is “firm, reliable, able to bear the weight”. The “Amen” we say at the end of every prayer comes from this root. So “Amen” doesn’t just mean “end of prayer”; it means “this can be relied on; I’m putting my whole weight on it”.

2. The Red Sea: God brings people to a dead end in order to open a new way

The lesson mentions the Israelites at the shore of the Red Sea — the most classic “dead end” in the whole Bible.

Let’s spread out the map of the moment: in front, the Red Sea; behind, Pharaoh with “six hundred chosen chariots, and all the chariots of Egypt” (Exodus 14:7); on either side, the wilderness. The Israelites’ reaction was utterly human. They said to Moses, “Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness?” (Exodus 14:11)

What they doubted wasn’t really the road; it was the God who was leading them on it.

But notice one thing: who brought them to the shore of the Red Sea? “Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night.” (Exodus 13:21) In other words, this dead end was one that God himself led them into.
