God is never late and never gets it wrong. He lets us walk into a dead end not to disappoint us, but to show that he can open a new way that didn’t exist before.

At that moment Moses fixed his eyes firmly on Yahweh and declared to the people: “Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today; for you will never again see the Egyptians whom you have seen today. Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still.” (Exodus 14:13–14)

“Stand still”, “see”, “be still” — brothers and sisters, by human logic these three verbs are the three most useless things you could do. In a dead end, what people most want to do is run, shout, find a way out. But God says: stand still, see, be still. Because when people stop relying on themselves, God begins to fight for us.

Later Isaiah summed up God’s works in one line: “Yahweh, who makes a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters” (Isaiah 43:16). The way wasn’t there to begin with; the way is one God opens.

3. Supporting evidence from psychology: hope is a “pathway”

In 1991 C. R. Snyder, a psychologist at the University of Kansas, put forward his well-known “hope theory”. He pointed out that hope is not a good mood but a cognitive capacity made of two components: first, “pathways thinking” — believing there is a route to the goal; second, “agency thinking” — believing you have the drive to keep going along it. Research found that people with higher hope are less likely to collapse when they meet setbacks, because they believe that “if this road is blocked, there’s another”.

Brothers and sisters, psychology puts it well, but Christian hope goes a layer deeper: our hope isn’t “I can still think of another way”; it is “the one who opens the way is still here”. At the Red Sea, no amount of pathways thinking could have come up with a plan to part the waters. True hope lies not in our imagination but in God’s mighty power.

Remember the spatial disorientation from the introduction? The pilot’s lifeline is this: don’t trust your feelings; trust your instruments. Brothers and sisters, circumstances can deceive our feelings, but God never lies. God’s word is our instrument panel.

4. Applying the 321 vision: the Bible is my standard; rely on the heart and not the brain

The second of the Three Foundations of the 321 vision is: the Bible is my standard.

When do we most need a standard? When our feelings and the facts are fighting each other. In good times we don’t much need a standard, because feelings and truth seem to agree; in hard times, feeling shouts out loud and truth seems silent, and if we have no standard then, we will certainly go astray.

That’s why the 321 vision often says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. This isn’t telling us not to think. It’s saying that if the starting point of our thinking is our own analysis and calculation, the conclusion will always be worry, because our resources are never enough; but if we rely on the heart to trust the Holy Spirit and God’s word, we’ll be glad, because God’s resources never run short. Proverbs says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Brothers and sisters, in the waiting, we have a choice to make every day: today, will I listen to the broadcast of my feelings, or to the broadcast of God’s word?

This is also what the 321 vision calls the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. We often get the order backwards — we deal with things first; when we can’t, we take it out on people; then we blame ourselves; and only last of all do we think of God. Turn the order round, align yourself with God first, and you’ll find that the people are still the same people and the things are still the same things, but you yourself are completely different.

sections.heading: 3. In the Chaos, Still Obey: Jesus Makes No Mistakes
sections.html:
The third question goes deepest, and few people dare to say it out loud: could God have got it wrong?

Very often it isn’t that we don’t believe God exists, or that we don’t believe God is faithful; we just can’t make sense of his arrangements. Why does this person get cancer? Why does that wicked man prosper instead? Why has the door I’ve prayed about for three years stayed shut? In the deepest corner of our hearts, a thought now and then pops up: God, did you get it wrong this time?

1. His thoughts are thoughts of peace

Scripture answers this question head-on, and the people it answers are precisely people whose lives had been smashed to pieces.

Jeremiah 29 is a letter the prophet Jeremiah wrote to the people of Judah who had been carried off to Babylon. Their city had been breached, the temple destroyed, their homes all lost, and they had been marched over a thousand kilometres to a foreign land. In exactly that situation, God said through Jeremiah: “For Yahweh says, ‘After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, I will visit you and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place. For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,’ says Yahweh, ‘thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.’” (Jeremiah 29:10–11)

Brothers and sisters, please don’t cut verse 11 off from verse 10. God says his thoughts are thoughts of peace, but in the same breath he says: seventy years. In other words, God’s “peace” does not mean “immediate escape”. For most of the adults there at the time, seventy years meant they would die in a foreign land; those who went back would be their children and grandchildren.

So were God’s thoughts still good? Yes. Because God sees much further than we do. In fact, the seventy years of exile became a turning point in Israel’s history: from then on they broke completely with their ingrained habit of idolatry; the synagogue arose during the exile; and the Old Testament scriptures were treasured and preserved in the exile. God used what looked like a disaster to heal a nation’s sickness of a thousand years.

“Thoughts” in Hebrew is machashabah, a word that also carries the sense of “plan, design, something carefully woven”. God hasn’t sketched your life with a careless stroke; he has carefully designed it.

And Isaiah voices the humility we must learn: “‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.’” (Isaiah 55:8–9)

Brothers and sisters, the word “higher” is very important. God’s thoughts are not “opposite” to ours; they are “higher”. He isn’t deliberately working against us; he simply sees further than we do. That’s why Paul could say: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28)

2. David: no calculating the odds, only the conviction that God never fails

The lesson takes David facing Goliath as its example, and this is the most vivid picture there is of “God makes no mistakes”.

First, see how absurd the situation was. Goliath’s “height was six cubits and a span” (1 Samuel 17:4); reckoning a cubit at about 45 centimetres, he stood nearly three metres tall. His armour weighed about five thousand shekels of bronze, and his spearhead six hundred shekels of iron. Scripture says, “When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid.” (1 Samuel 17:11) Even the king who “from his shoulders and upward … was taller than any of the people” (1 Samuel 9:2) didn’t dare go out to fight.

Then David arrived. He did no analysis of the odds. His first question was not “Can I win?” but: “For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” (1 Samuel 17:26)

Do you see it? The whole camp was comparing height, armour and weapons — they were looking at how big Goliath was; David was looking at how big God was. The same battlefield, the same giant, different eyes — and a completely different conclusion.

So David spoke words that have echoed through history: “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.” (1 Samuel 17:45) And he said: “and that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn’t save with sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh’s, and he will give you into our hand.” (1 Samuel 17:47)

Brothers and sisters, David won not by skill but by faith; not by calculation but by conviction.

The lesson has a line that puts it superbly: those who “rely on the brain” calculate the odds; those who “rely on the heart” believe that God never fails.

3. What you look at is what you crash into

There’s a fascinating phenomenon here that can help us see why our “eyes” matter so much.

In motorcycle and racing-driver training, one of the things instructors repeat most is called “target fixation”: if a rider on a bend sees a fallen rock in the middle of the road and stares fixedly at it, he will almost certainly ride straight into it, because the body involuntarily follows the focus of the eyes. So the first lesson instructors teach is: don’t look at what you don’t want to hit; look at where you want to go.

Psychology has made the same discovery. In 1999 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, then at Harvard University, ran the famous “invisible gorilla” experiment. Participants were asked to count how many times the players in white passed a ball in a video. Of those concentrating on counting passes, about half completely failed to notice that, partway through the video, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the picture, thumped their chest and walked out again. The phenomenon is called “inattentional blindness”.

Brothers and sisters, these two examples point to the same truth: wherever your attention is, that’s all you can see — and that’s where you’ll go. Someone who spends all day meditating on their own troubles will find it hard to see God’s work at the same time; it isn’t that God isn’t working, it’s that their eyes are already full.

The Dutch sister Corrie ten Boom is generally credited with saying something like this: look at your circumstances and you’ll be troubled; look at yourself and you’ll be discouraged; look at Christ and you’ll find rest. She lost her sister in a Nazi concentration camp, yet after the war went out to preach forgiveness; coming from her lips, these words carry particular weight.

4. Applying the 321 vision: obedience is returning to our originally intended position

The third of the Three Foundations of the 321 vision is: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

In the chaos, what we need most isn’t more information but a guide. Because the very nature of chaos is too much information, clues too tangled, judgements too hard to make. If a person insists on thinking everything through before he will obey, he will never obey, because no one can ever think God through.

The 321 vision says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to replace God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, when we wonder whether God might make a mistake, we’re actually doing something: we’ve climbed onto the judge’s bench and summoned God into the dock. That is leaving our originally intended position. Obedience is stepping down from the judge’s bench, returning to our originally intended position as creatures, and saying: Lord, I don’t understand, but I believe you don’t make mistakes.

This is what the 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. The first lie Satan told humanity in the Garden of Eden was meant to make them doubt whether God’s heart toward them was really good — “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1) From that day on, every time we doubt God’s good intentions in the chaos, that ancient serpent stands by smiling.

And the way to overcome him isn’t to argue harder; it’s to obey humbly. Our role model is the Lord himself: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8)

Brothers and sisters, emptying himself is selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out without limit.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, have you noticed something beautiful? The lesson’s three key points correspond exactly to the Three Foundations of the 321 vision.

First, Jesus is real — that is “Jesus is my role model”. He is alive; he has walked this road; he is waiting for us up ahead. Hebrews calls him the “author” and the “perfecter” of our faith.

Second, Jesus doesn’t lie — that is “the Bible is my standard”. What he has said will certainly stand, so when our feelings and our circumstances are both lying to us, we have a ruler that never bends out of shape.

Third, Jesus makes no mistakes — that is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. We don’t have to understand the whole picture before we’re willing to walk, because the one who guides us never fails.

Once the Three Foundations stand firm, the Two Core Values naturally emerge.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory

What does it mean to let Jesus be King? It means that on the throne of my heart, he is the one seated there — not my circumstances, and not me.

Brothers and sisters, let’s be honest: anxiety is really a secret coronation. When we lie awake all night, running through every possibility again and again, we are playing a role we cannot play — ruler of the universe. Fixing our eyes on Jesus is handing the throne back to him, and then lying down to sleep in peace. The psalm says: “I laid myself down and slept. I awakened; for Yahweh sustains me.” (Psalm 3:5)

And when he truly reigns as King, the result is bound to be that he receives all the glory. When Joseph was brought out of prison and Pharaoh asked him to interpret his dream, Joseph’s first words were: “It isn’t in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.” (Genesis 41:16) Thirteen years of darkness refined just this one sentence: “It isn’t in me.”

The Goal: establish God’s system

God saves us not only so that we as individuals may have peace, but even more to establish God’s system.

The 321 vision speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

The main battlefield of this lesson is the first link — mindset. “Fixing our eyes on Jesus” sounds like a behaviour, but it is really a change of mindset: from “I have to solve this problem” to “I will look to this Lord”; from man’s, earthly, temporary and worldly perspectives to God’s, heavenly, eternal and godly perspectives.

When the mindset turns, the life changes. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) This is moving from the self-centred life to selflessness.

The 321 vision also reminds us of the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Only someone whose eyes are fixed on Jesus can have healthy relationships; someone who is chased around by his circumstances will spill his anxiety even onto those closest to him.

The 920 practice and 235 relationships

The 920 practice is this: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out a selfless (0) life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, notice that several of these nine graces are exactly the ones only a person whose eyes are fixed on Jesus can bear: joy, peace, patience. Someone whose eyes are glued to the wind and waves can try very hard to fake joy, but he can’t bear real joy — because fruit grows; it isn’t stuck on.

235 relationships means: becoming a “2” with someone who is selfless, being spiritual companions to each other; establishing the “3”, the passing on of life from spiritual parents to spiritual children; and going on to become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

This echoes exactly the “cloud of witnesses” surrounding us in Hebrews 12:1. Brothers and sisters, no one can keep their eyes fixed alone. When my eyes grow blurred, I need a spiritual companion beside me to say: lift up your head — the Lord is still here. When your “2” is in the storm, you are the cloud God has placed beside them.

The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God

The 321 vision sums up the path of serving in five steps: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, you see, the starting point of this path isn’t “doing” but “seeing”. First comes the Spirit’s guidance and the light of the word, then life, then service. Today’s lesson is driving in the first stake on that path: setting our eyes straight.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them one at a time, and use the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deeper.

Practice 1: Meditate on three questions

Please quiet yourself, ask yourself honestly, and write your answers down, or speak them out loud in prayer:

Is Jesus real?

Would Jesus deceive me?

Can Jesus make a mistake?

Brothers and sisters, these three questions aren’t a knowledge test; they’re a check-up for the heart. We all know the head’s answers: yes, no, no. But the heart’s answers are often different. That’s why we write them down and say them out loud — because what the mouth speaks out is what the heart truly believes: “that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” (Romans 10:9)

Now let’s apply the eight stages to this practice:

Information — first gather God’s word. Copy Revelation 1:18, Numbers 23:19 and Jeremiah 29:11 onto a card, one for each of the three questions.

Revelation — don’t just read them; ask the Holy Spirit to “open” these words up in you. Ask the Lord to show you: which line do you find hardest to believe? That line is often where you most need healing.

Conviction — move from “I know” to “I believe”. Conviction is the surrender of the heart; it’s putting your whole weight on that word and saying a heartfelt “Amen”.

Implementation — put it to use today. Today, when that old question rises up in your heart again, declare at once: Jesus is real, Jesus won’t deceive me, Jesus makes no mistakes.

Evaluation — in the evening, be quiet for three minutes and look back: how many times today did I turn my eyes to my circumstances? How many times did I turn them back to Jesus? Don’t condemn yourself; just see clearly.

Correction — identify the triggers that most easily knock you out of focus: is it scrolling your phone late at night? A particular phone call? The moment you open your bank account? For that moment, prepare a verse to be your instrument panel.

Repetition — once doesn’t count; do it every day. Psychology calls this forming a habit; the Bible says, “Exercise yourself toward godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7).

Multiplication — take these three questions to your “2”. The road you’ve walked becomes someone else’s handrail.

Practice 2: Find the most recent moment you “doubted God”

Think back: when was the last time doubt about God arose in your heart? Over what?

Then ask honestly: in that moment, where were my eyes? Was it because my eyes weren’t fixed on Jesus that I was overwhelmed by my circumstances?

Brothers and sisters, the key to this practice isn’t self-blame but “seeing clearly”. At the moment Peter began to sink, the Lord didn’t scold him for his unbelief first. Scripture says: “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matthew 14:31) The Lord reached out first and spoke afterwards; his rebuke came only once his hand had already taken hold of us.

So now, please make the choice again: take that matter, that person, that diagnosis, that figure, and one by one ask them to step down from the throne of your heart. Then say: Lord Jesus, I choose again to fix my eyes on you.

Here the emphasis among the eight stages is Correction and Repetition. Correction means finding the pattern that keeps tripping you up; Repetition means admitting you’ll fall again, but turning your eyes back more quickly each time. Spiritual maturity isn’t never losing focus; it’s that the time it takes to turn back after losing focus gets shorter and shorter.

Practice 3: Write down a testimony of God opening a way for you

Please write down a time when you walked into a dead end but God opened a way for you. You can record it in your devotional journal, or share it with others so it encourages one another.

Brothers and sisters, why write it down? Because the human memory is especially good at suffering and especially poor at grace. The Israelites crossed the Red Sea, sang songs and danced; yet three days’ walk later they came to Marah, the water was bitter, and they grumbled at once (Exodus 15:22–24). Three days. The memory of the miracle lasted three days.

That’s why, after Joshua led the people across the Jordan, God told them to take twelve stones from the river and set them up as a sign, so that when their children later asked, “What do you mean by these stones?”, the parents could tell them the works of God (Joshua 4:6–7). Brothers and sisters, your testimony is the twelve stones of your life.

And this is the last of the eight stages: Multiplication. The testimony you write down isn’t only your own reminder; it will become a cloud for someone else. Every darkness God brings us through is so that we can become a torch for the next person. Paul says that God is the one “who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.” (2 Corinthians 1:4)

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson sums up its heart in a single sentence: what you see decides where you go.

When we fix our eyes on our problems, our lives head towards anxiety, bitterness and giving up; when we fix our eyes on Jesus, our lives head towards light, hope and a victorious ending.

Remember the picture of the race in Hebrews 12. You aren’t the first to run this road — a cloud of witnesses stands beside the track testifying for you. Nor are you someone who has to finish it on your own — the Lord, the author and perfecter, has already run ahead and has already sat down at the right hand of the throne.

This morning the Lord wants to speak to several kinds of people.

If you’re in a dead end right now and feel it’s all over — the Lord says: I was dead, and behold, I am alive. Not even death could stop me, and the thing in front of you can’t stop me either.

If you’re in a long wait right now and about to give up — the Lord says: God is not a man, that he should lie. I am never late; it simply isn’t time yet.

If you’re in chaos right now and can’t make sense of what God is doing — the Lord says: my thoughts are higher than your thoughts. You don’t have to understand; you only have to follow.

Brothers and sisters, let’s make a decision today: give the throne of our hearts back to Jesus. No longer let circumstances be king, no longer let fear be king, no longer let ourselves be king. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

May you no longer be led around by your problems, but let faith lead you to look to Jesus and go forward with courage.

keyVerses: “Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith (or: looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of the faith), who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” (Hebrews 12:1–2)
declarations: Faith is not an emotion but a choice — the choice to fix our eyes on Jesus in the midst of chaos.

Brothers and sisters, this sentence deserves to be engraved on the tablet of our hearts. Emotions rise and fall with blood sugar, sleep, the weather and our notifications; if our faith is built on emotion, it will be as unreliable as the weather forecast.

True faith is a choice of the will. “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.” (Hebrews 11:1) In the original, the words behind “assurance” and “proof” both carry the sense of “a foundation you can stand on” and “legal title or evidence”. Faith isn’t feeling good; faith is holding the evidence.
So we don’t wait for things to improve before we believe; right in the storm, we declare that he is Lord.
Let’s declare it together, out loud:
Jesus is real, Jesus is faithful, Jesus never makes a mistake.
I choose to fix my eyes on him in hardship, not to be dragged away by my circumstances, and to believe firmly that he reigns to the very end.
practices: Meditate on three questions
Find the most recent moment you “doubted God”
Write down a testimony of God opening a way for you
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We bow down before you. We confess that in these days our eyes have so often left you and landed on our circumstances, on other people, on ourselves. One look at the wind and waves and we’re afraid; one look at the numbers and we’re anxious; one thought of tomorrow and we can’t sleep. Lord, forgive us.

Lord, today your word has come to us. You said you are the Living one, that you were dead and now are alive — so we believe you are real. You said God is not a man, that he should lie — so we believe you will not deceive us. You said your thoughts are thoughts of peace, to give us hope and a future — so we believe you make no mistakes.

Lord, please heal our eyes. Holy Spirit, help us, at every moment when we want to turn our heads to look at our circumstances, to turn our eyes back to you. Make us no longer rely on the brain and ourselves, but rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit; no longer be led around by our problems, but be led by faith to look to you.

Lord, we pray too for the brothers and sisters around us. Some are standing at the edge of the Red Sea; some are sitting in Joseph’s prison; some are standing before Goliath. Show them your presence, and let them know that you are with them, just as you were with Joseph.
We give all the glory to you. May you reign as King in our hearts for ever and ever.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 14:30: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” Please share: what has recently been your “wind and waves”? How did it steal your eyes away? What concrete step do you plan to take to turn your eyes back to Jesus?

Genesis 50:20: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.” Think back to a dead end you once walked through. Looking back now, what was God’s good purpose in it? Write it up as a testimony and share it with one another in your small group.
l032.title: Fix Your Eyes on Jesus
l032.subtitle: In Desperate Straits, in Waiting and in Chaos, Look to the Lord Who Is Real, Faithful and Never Late
l032.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: “You Never Once Asked Me How I Was”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we open today’s lesson, I’d like to ask you to be still for thirty seconds and picture a scene.

There was a small-group leader who ran his group like clockwork. Meetings started on time, the study never fell behind schedule, attendance records were handed in every single week, and there was even someone assigned to the tea and snacks. In everyone’s eyes this was a “very successful” group. But one day a brother who had quietly given himself to that group for three years suddenly, and just as quietly, withdrew. The leader was taken aback and pressed him for the reason. The brother thought for a long time, and then gave just one sentence in reply: “Leader, for the past six months, every time you’ve spoken to me, the first thing you’ve said is, ‘How’s that job going?’ You never once asked me — how I was.”

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is like a fine needle that pierces the heart of many who serve. It isn’t that we’re not serious; we’re often too serious. It isn’t that we don’t love the Lord; it’s that, without noticing, we have quietly swapped “loving the Lord” for “getting the Lord’s work done”. We treat people as channels for getting ministry done, and forget that people themselves are what is on God’s heart. We fill our planners to the brim, and leave people’s hearts empty.

In 1958 the psychologist Harry F. Harlow of the University of Wisconsin ran an experiment that later shook the whole field of psychology. He placed newborn rhesus monkeys between two “surrogate mothers”: one was made of wire and fitted with a feeding bottle, so it gave milk; the other was made of soft cloth, soft and warm, but without a single drop of milk. According to the behaviourist theory then in fashion, the infant monkeys ought to have attached themselves to the one “with milk”. The result was the exact opposite: apart from running over to the wire mother for a few hurried gulps when they were hungry, the infants spent almost the whole day clinging tightly to the cloth mother; and the moment they were frightened, they rushed to the cloth mother without the slightest hesitation. Harlow called this phenomenon “contact comfort”.

That experiment told us something that surprised even the scientists: life’s deepest need is not to be fed but to be held; not to be supplied but to be connected.

People are the same. The deepest longing of the human heart is not to be managed but to be understood; not to be directed but to be cared for. A person can be in a team that does everything beautifully and feel so lonely that he wants to leave; and a person can be in a small group with meagre resources and a shabby meeting place and, because someone genuinely remembers his name and remembers that his mother is still in hospital, decide to put down roots there for life.

This is what today’s lesson wants to say to us. The lesson’s theme is just a single short line, yet it is the whole lesson of serving:

Rely on the heart, and you will win the heart; win the heart, and you will win revival.

“Relying on the heart” is not only what God asks of us; it is the key to our entering revival. Only when we treat people and treat God with sincerity and from the heart can we win people’s hearts and win the Lord’s pleasure, and only then can we bring renewal of life and revival. Do you want the people you lead to be built up? Do you want your service to truly bear fruit? Then you must learn this lesson.

In the 321 vision this is called “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. We often turn the order upside down: charge into ministry first, talk about relationships afterwards, and think about life last of all. The result is that the ministry grows bigger and bigger while the life grows drier and drier; more and more people gather, while their hearts drift further and further apart. This morning, let’s put the order right again.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Eras Behind Two Verses
sections.html: Of today’s two theme passages, one comes from the wisdom literature of the Old Testament, and the other from the most crucial turning point of the kingdom of Israel. Once the background is clear, the force of these verses becomes something altogether different.

sections.heading: (1) The Background of Proverbs 23:26
sections.html:
The principal author of the book of Proverbs is King Solomon (Proverbs 1:1; 10:1); its writing and collecting span the period of the kingdom of Israel, and its final editing was completed in the time of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The verse we read today sits within the long section from Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22. That section has a distinctive heading: “Turn your ear, and listen to the words of the wise” (Proverbs 22:17), which is why interpreters through the ages have called it “the Words of the Wise”.

The style of this section is distinctive: it is no longer one free-standing couplet after another, but a series of earnest exhortations, in a tone like a father sitting by the lamp, holding his son’s hand as he speaks. Scholars have also noticed that its structure bears a formal resemblance to the wisdom instructions handed down in ancient Egypt — a sign that the Holy Spirit used a literary form everyone of that age knew well, placing the truth in a vessel people could understand.

And at the high point of this whole section comes this line: “My son, give me your heart; and let your eyes keep in my ways.” (Proverbs 23:26)

Brothers and sisters, notice the weight of these words. The father doesn’t ask his son for results, doesn’t ask him for property, doesn’t ask him for performance. He asks for only one thing — your heart.

The Hebrew for “heart” is לֵב (lēb) or לֵבָב (lēbāb). In Hebrew thought, the “heart” is never only the seat of the emotions; it is also the centre of the mind, the will, decision and conscience — a person’s “innermost self”. So when the father says “give me your heart”, what he wants is not a part of his son but the whole of him.

The verb “give” in Hebrew is תְּנָה (tenāh), whose most basic meaning is simply “give”. It is in the imperative — “Give me your heart.” The first gift God asks of us has never been our abilities, our time or our offerings, but our heart. Because once the heart is given, everything else naturally follows; if the heart isn’t given, everything else is just going through the motions.

sections.heading: (2) The Background of 1 Samuel 16:7
sections.html:
The second passage takes us to Bethlehem around 1025 BC. King Saul had been rejected by God for his rebellion, and the aged prophet Samuel’s heart was full of grief. God told him to fill his horn with oil and go to Jesse of Bethlehem, because God had provided himself a king among Jesse’s sons (1 Samuel 16:1).

Samuel arrived and saw Jesse’s eldest son, Eliab: tall and imposing, every inch what people imagine a “king” should look like. Samuel said in his heart, “Surely Yahweh’s anointed is before him.” (1 Samuel 16:6) At that very moment God spoke words that pierce through three thousand years:

“For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

In the original Hebrew these words are very direct: man looks at “what the eyes see”; Yahweh looks at “the heart”. Man’s eyes stop at the surface; God’s eyes go down into the depths.

In the end it was the youngest son, David — left out in the sheepfold and not even called to the feast — who was anointed king. God’s verdict on David was not “he is the most capable” but “a man after my heart” (1 Samuel 13:14; Acts 13:22).

Brothers and sisters, put these two verses side by side and you will see a thread that runs through the whole Bible:

God looks at the heart, so God wants our heart; and because God wants our heart, God also wants us to rely on the heart to win other people’s hearts.

sections.heading: (3) Echoes in the New Testament
sections.html:
When this thread reaches the New Testament, it becomes two pictures.

One is the charcoal fire on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:9), where the Lord Jesus asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” He didn’t hold him to account for his failure; he asked only about love.

The other is the ship about to sink on the Mediterranean (Acts 27), where those on board threw all the cargo and tackle into the sea just to save the two hundred seventy-six lives on board (Acts 27:37).

One is about winning the heart; the other is about valuing people. Today’s three key points follow exactly along this line.

sections.heading: 1. Only by Relying on the Heart Can We Win People’s Hearts
sections.html:
Scripture

“For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

“My son, give me your heart; and let your eyes keep in my ways.” (Proverbs 23:26)

The deepest human longing

The lesson hits the mark exactly: the deepest longing of the human heart is not to be managed but to be understood; not to be directed but to be cared for.

We put far too much energy into “managing”: managing time, managing schedules, managing manpower. Management isn’t a bad thing, but management can only ever touch people’s behaviour; it can never touch their hearts. You can manage someone into turning up on time, but you can’t manage anyone into being willing from the heart; you can direct a highly efficient team into being, but you can’t direct a band of disciples whose lives have been set on fire.

Behaviour can be demanded; the heart can only be won.

And how is a heart won? The answer is just one phrase: rely on the heart.

Jesus was exactly this kind of person

The lesson says, “Jesus was exactly this kind of person.” These words deserve careful meditation.

The Lord Jesus was not like the Pharisees, who cared only about rules. The Pharisees carefully counted out a tenth of their mint, dill and cumin to offer, but the Lord said to them, “and have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith.” (Matthew 23:23) They measured the small things with great precision, and lost people’s hearts completely.

The Lord Jesus, by contrast, went among the crowds with sincerity. Scripture says: “But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.” (Matthew 9:36) The Greek word for “moved with compassion” is σπλαγχνίζομαι (splanchnizomai), whose root means “the inward parts, the bowels”; it means “to be churned up in your very insides”. This is not polite sympathy; this is being shaken to the depths.

In the town of Nain he met a widow whose only son had died, and Scripture says: “When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said to her, ‘Don’t cry.’” (Luke 7:13) He saw the person first, and then worked the miracle.

He looked at the rich young ruler, so eager yet unable to let go of his wealth, and Scripture records a deeply tender detail: “Jesus looking at him loved him” (Mark 10:21). Even though the man turned and walked away in the end, the Lord still loved him.

As he passed through Jericho, he looked up at the chief tax collector in the tree, the man everyone despised, and said: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” (Luke 19:5) That very day Zacchaeus stood up and said he would give half of his goods to the poor. The Lord didn’t rebuke him first; the Lord first came into his house and into his heart.

So the lesson is right: Zacchaeus, Mary, the tax collectors and the prostitutes didn’t follow Jesus because of “miracles”; they followed him because they were moved by his love — a love that came from the heart.

Miracles make people marvel; love makes people follow.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: God has always asked for the heart first

Read the whole Bible as one, and you’ll find that from the first page to the last, God wants the same one thing.

On the plains of Moab Moses said to the Israelites: “You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.” (Deuteronomy 6:5) The Lord Jesus named it the first of the commandments: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” (Matthew 22:37)

The prophet Hosea conveyed God’s heart: “For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” (Hosea 6:6; the Chinese Union Version reads “goodness”, with “mercy” as an alternative rendering)

Isaiah put God’s heartache even more bluntly: “Because this people draws near with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught” (Isaiah 29:13). The Lord Jesus quoted these words again in Matthew 15:8 to rebuke the religious leaders of his day.

In his deepest repentance David saw this clearly: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

And Proverbs distils it into a single line to live by: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Brothers and sisters, do you hear it? The wellspring of life doesn’t flow from your diary, or from your gifts, or from your network of contacts; it flows from the heart. Get the heart right and the fruit comes naturally; get the heart wrong and even the most impressive ministry is just a beautifully crafted exhaustion.

An example from life: the doctor who crouched down

There was a senior paediatrician who had a habit at every consultation: instead of sitting up high in his chair to examine, he would crouch down until his eyes were a little lower than the child’s, and only then begin to speak. When someone asked him why, he said: “A frightened child will only tell you where it really hurts when he doesn’t have to look up at you.”

Brothers and sisters, that is “relying on the heart”. The same diagnosis, the same prescription — said crouching down or said standing up — has a completely different effect. Because what people receive is never only the content; it’s also the attitude.

How long has it been since we lowered ourselves a little for someone’s sake?

Supporting evidence from psychology

Carl R. Rogers, a founder of humanistic psychology, argued in a classic paper published in 1957 that for real personality change to happen, certain conditions are necessary in the relationship, the two most crucial being “unconditional positive regard” and “empathic understanding”. In other words, people aren’t changed by being persuaded; people change within relationships in which they are accepted.

The employee engagement survey long used by Gallup (the Q12) contains one item that is remarkably plain and yet remarkably predictive: “At work, someone cares about me as a person.” Research shows that the answer to this item correlates strongly with employees’ engagement and their intention to stay.

Brothers and sisters, even the workplace confirms it: people aren’t kept by systems; people are kept by being cared for. How much more the church — how much more the body of Christ.

The American president Theodore Roosevelt is commonly credited with saying: “People don’t care how much you know until they know how much you care.” Though where the saying comes from is disputed, the truth it expresses is exactly what the Lord Jesus lived out all his life.

Applying the 321 vision

In the 321 vision, relationships have an order that must not be reversed: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

The reason we’re in such a hurry to “get things done” is often that the first three relationships have gone hollow. When our relationship with God goes hollow, we need the results of our ministry to prove we’re still standing. When our relationship with ourselves goes hollow, we need other people’s approval to fill us up. When our relationship with others goes hollow, all we can do is keep order with a schedule.

The first step in relying on the heart to win people’s hearts is actually not to put our heart into people, but first to give our heart to God. Proverbs 23:26 says, “Give me your heart” — that comes first. When our heart has first been given to God, God gives us his way of seeing; and with God’s way of seeing, we no longer look at people’s outward appearance, but see heart after heart that God treasures.

This is the Three Foundations of the 321 vision worked out in daily living: Jesus is my role model — however he treated people from the heart, so I treat people; the Bible is my standard — I measure people by God’s word, not by my own feelings; the Holy Spirit is my guide — I love by the Holy Spirit’s prompting, not by holding on through my own fleshly strength.

The lesson also reminds us that relying on the heart is the everyday version of the 920 practice. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”. Whom will you meet this morning? The sister who has been silent in the group chat for a long time, the brother who is always the last to leave, the family member who cooks for you every day and has never once been thanked — they are your “2”. Live out a selfless (0) life before them, and let the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — flow out of you naturally. That is relying on the heart.

sections.heading: 2. Only by Relying on the Heart Can We Influence People’s Hearts
sections.html:
Scripture

“We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19)

“You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you.” (John 15:16)

Winning the heart is not the finishing line but the starting line

The lesson says: we win people’s hearts not merely to win their approval, but even more to influence them, and to bring about the passing on of life.

That sentence pulls us back from a very great danger. There is a kind of “winning hearts” that is for ourselves: I want people to like me, follow me, affirm me, be unable to do without me. That isn’t shepherding; it’s buying people. It isn’t influence; it’s control. The 321 vision says it very plainly: that is the self-centred life doing the serving.

Truly winning a heart means winning that heart back and then placing it in Jesus’ hands. John the Baptist put it most beautifully: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) We rely on the heart to win people’s hearts so that in the end those hearts turn to Christ, not to ourselves.

That is why the Lord Jesus said: “You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.” (John 15:16) Notice the word “remain”. The Greek μένω (menō) is the very word “remain” that recurs again and again throughout John 15. What the Lord wants is not a brief, flash-in-the-pan excitement, but fruit that can last and be handed on.

The charcoal fire by the Sea of Tiberias

The lesson gives the example of Peter, the most moving restoration in the whole Bible.

Let’s get the facts right first. John 21:14 records: “This is now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.” In this appearance the Lord asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?”

The background is this. Only a few days earlier, in the high priest’s courtyard, Peter had denied the Lord three times. Luke 22:61–62 records: “The Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word … He went out, and wept bitterly.”

Now notice a detail that is often overlooked. On the night Peter denied the Lord, Scripture says: “Now the servants and the officers were standing there, having made a fire of coals, for it was cold. They were warming themselves. Peter was with them, standing and warming himself.” (John 18:18) And by the Sea of Tiberias, when the disciples came ashore, “they saw a fire of coals there” (John 21:9).

The Greek for “fire of coals” is ἀνθρακιά (anthrakia). In the whole New Testament this word appears only twice — once in the courtyard where Peter fell, and once on the shore where Peter was restored.

Brothers and sisters, do you see the Lord’s heart in this? The Lord brought Peter back to the same smell, the same warmth, the same scene, and healed him right there. The Lord didn’t pretend it had never happened; the Lord walked right into it and redeemed it.

And how did the Lord ask? He didn’t say, “Why did you deny me?” He didn’t say, “Do you know how much you disappointed me?” He only asked: “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15)

Three denials; three questions about love. The lesson puts it well: he exchanged a true heart for a true heart.

In passing: some interpreters have noticed that the Lord’s first two questions use the verb ἀγαπάω (agapaō), Peter answers with φιλέω (phileō), and the third time the Lord switches to φιλέω. Some take this as the Lord stooping to Peter’s weakness; other scholars caution that John habitually alternates synonyms, so we shouldn’t read too much into it. Either way, one thing is clear: what the Lord was pressing Peter about was not his performance but his heart.

When the heart is won back, the life is changed

And the result? The Peter who had sworn with curses in front of a servant girl stood up on the day of Pentecost with the eleven apostles and preached at the top of his voice (Acts 2:14). Scripture says: “Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, ‘Brothers, what shall we do?’” (Acts 2:37) And “there were added that day about three thousand souls” (Acts 2:41).

From three denials to three thousand coming to the Lord — and what lay in between was one breakfast, one charcoal fire, and three times “Do you love me?”

The lesson says: Jesus knew that when a person’s heart is won, their life will naturally be renewed, and their influence will flow far and long. This is exactly the fivefold change the 321 vision speaks of: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

We often try to start with the last link — to change the ministry directly. The result is twice the effort for half the result. But the Lord started with the first link, changing Peter’s mindset about himself, about the Lord and about failure — and so the four links after it all turned with it.

Paul treated people this way too

Not only the Lord Jesus, but Paul as well. This apostle, who wrote thirteen letters, said of his ministry in Thessalonica:

“But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8)

Notice: “not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls.” You can preach the gospel and give only doctrine; but someone who relies on the heart gives himself away as well.

To the church in Corinth he also said: “for I seek not your possessions, but you.” (2 Corinthians 12:14)

This is the secret of passing life on. Paul said to Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) Four generations of spiritual inheritance under one roof — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others — and what passes between each generation is not only the content of the truth, but a life that has been loved.

Supporting evidence from science and psychology

In the 1990s a research team led by Giacomo Rizzolatti at the University of Parma discovered “mirror neurons” in the brains of macaque monkeys: when a monkey performed an action itself, certain neurons fired; and when it merely watched someone else perform the same action, the very same neurons fired too. Later research suggested that a similar mirroring mechanism exists in the human brain, and it is thought to be connected with our understanding of other people’s intentions and our capacity for empathy.

In other words, when God made human beings, he built into our brains a design that “catches” what others carry. Your sincerity will be “mirrored” in the other person’s life; and so will your half-heartedness.

In his long-term research at the University of Washington, the marriage researcher John Gottman put forward his famous “magic ratio”: in stable, happy relationships, positive interactions outnumber negative ones by about five to one. One rebuke takes five sincere affirmations to balance it.

Brothers and sisters, think back to the Lord with Peter — that breakfast, that charcoal fire, those three “Do you love me?”s — and not one word of rebuke. The Lord understood this ratio long ago.

Mother Teresa once said: “Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love.” What influences people has never been how big the things we do are, but how true the heart is with which we do them.

Applying the 321 vision

The 321 vision speaks of 235 relationships: becoming a “2” with someone who is selfless — spiritual companions; establishing the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and going on to become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Notice: 235 is not an organisation chart; it is a map of hearts joined together. What existed between the Lord and Peter was exactly a “3” relationship — spiritual parent and spiritual child. The Lord first became Peter’s spiritual father, and only then could Peter become a spiritual father to three thousand.

And where is the key to being spiritual parents? In selflessness. The old self is self-centred, so we want people to depend on us; the new self is selfless, so we bring people to Jesus. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out without limit — because when I step back, Christ can live out his life in me, and he is without limit.

Rely on the heart to win people’s hearts, and then hand those hearts to Jesus. That is influence; that is the passing on of life.

sections.heading: 3. Winning the Task Is No Match for Winning the Heart; Only by Winning the Heart Can We Win Revival
sections.html:
Scripture

“If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:3)

“This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.” (John 15:12)

The world looks at efficiency; the Lord looks at the heart

The lesson says: this world prizes “getting things done efficiently”, but Jesus prizes “winning people’s hearts” far more.

Every person who serves should copy that sentence out and stick it above their desk. Efficiency isn’t a sin; efficiency is a steward’s virtue. But when efficiency becomes the highest standard, people turn into costs, relationships turn into resources, and shepherding turns into a production line.

The Lord Jesus’ itinerary would fail any efficiency expert’s assessment: for the sake of one Samaritan woman, he sat by a well for half the day (John 4); on his way to Jairus’ house to save a dying girl, he actually stopped to find the woman who had touched the fringe of his garment (Mark 5:25–34); for the sake of one demon-possessed man of Gerasa, he crossed the whole Sea of Galilee, cast out the demons, and went back again (Mark 5:1–20).

In man’s eyes it was waste; in God’s eyes it was mission. For “the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10) — and what he came seeking was never “tasks” but “people”.

The ship that was about to sink

The lesson cites the example of Acts 27. Let’s get the background clear.

Paul was being taken to Rome as a prisoner. After the ship passed Crete, it was caught by a violent wind called the “Euroclydon” (Acts 27:14). The storm was so fierce that Scripture records:

“As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.” (Acts 27:18–19)

Notice that it was the sailors and the others on board who actually threw out the cargo and the tackle; but the judgement of value this revealed was precisely the one Paul held to throughout the voyage: people matter more than cargo. When everyone had sunk so far into despair that “all hope that we would be saved was now taken away” (Acts 27:20), Paul stood up and said:

“Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.” (Acts 27:22)

In the end, “In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship” (Acts 27:37), and every one of them came safely ashore (Acts 27:44).

The cargo was gone, the tackle was gone, and the ship was broken to pieces. But of those two hundred seventy-six people, not one was missing.

Brothers and sisters, this is the value system of the kingdom of heaven. Tasks will sink, people will live; tasks will pass away, people will remain for ever.

The Lord Jesus asked a question that still makes people break into a sweat today: “For what does it profit a man, to gain the whole world, and forfeit his life?” (Mark 8:36) We can turn it into a version for those who serve: what does it profit a person to make his ministry known throughout the whole world, and forfeit the hearts of the people around him?

The ultimate sacrifice without love

1 Corinthians 13 is a passage Paul wrote right in the middle of the “quarrel over gifts”. The church in Corinth lacked nothing — eloquence, knowledge, every kind of gift (1 Corinthians 1:5–7) — yet it split into factions and fought among itself. So after dealing with gifts in chapter 12, and before dealing with order in chapter 14, Paul inserted “a most excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12:31).

He says: “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:3)

Look carefully: this isn’t about “not doing enough”; it’s about “doing the very utmost”. Giving away every possession, even laying down your life — on anyone’s scorecard that’s full marks. Yet Paul says: it profits me nothing.

The Greek οὐδὲν ὠφελοῦμαι literally means “I gain no benefit at all”. Not “less benefit”, but “zero”.

Why? Because God looks at the heart, not the quantity. The deeds can be very great, while the heart is utterly empty.

So the Lord gives just one command: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.” (John 15:12) He didn’t say, “This is my suggestion”; he said, “This is my commandment.”

Revival starts from the heart

The lesson says: when we too learn to value people like this, respect people, love people, and nurture people from the heart, we will see people built up, relationships restored and teams renewed — and this is the beginning of revival.

What is revival? Revival isn’t the attendance graph going up, or a lively atmosphere in the meetings, or more and more events. Revival is what God has promised:

“I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 36:26)

A heart of stone becoming a heart of flesh — that is revival. Stone is hard, durable and highly efficient, but it feels nothing; a heart of flesh can hurt, can soften, can weep for others. What God wants is people whose hearts ache for others.

And revival has never been built up by piling on methods: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6)

The Welsh Revival of 1904–1905 is one of the best-known revivals in modern church history. The man God used was Evan Roberts, a young man in his twenties who had worked down the mines. What he preached was astonishingly simple — chiefly four appeals: confess and deal with every unconfessed sin; put away everything doubtful from your life; obey the Holy Spirit’s leading completely; confess Christ publicly. There was no vast organisation and no ornate preaching — only hearts turned around by the Holy Spirit, confessing to one another and forgiving one another. During the revival, the moral climate in many parts of Wales changed noticeably, as the newspapers and church records of the time consistently report.

Brothers and sisters, revival has never begun from the pulpit; it begins from hearts renewed one by one.

Supporting evidence from psychology

Self-Determination Theory was put forward in the 1980s by Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan of the University of Rochester. They pointed out that people have three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. If a team meets only the need for “competence” — that is, getting things done well — and neglects “relatedness”, its members’ intrinsic motivation will gradually dry up.

The Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed the same group of people for over eighty years, making it one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in history. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, has distilled its conclusion into one sentence: what truly keeps people healthy and happy throughout life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, even secular research has taken eighty years to reach this conclusion. And the Bible said it three thousand years ago: “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

In The Little Prince the French writer Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote the line now quoted all over the world: “It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.”

Applying the 321 vision

Why do we “win the task but not the heart”? The 321 vision gives a very sharp diagnosis: the self-centred life.

When a self-centred person serves, people become my stage, my results, my proof. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to replace God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When I press people with a schedule, I have already left my originally intended position as a servant and sat down in the master’s seat.

And what is the result of pride? Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. You push hard, he pushes back; the more you demand, the more he withdraws; in the end the task isn’t done and the hearts have scattered too.

What is the result of humility? Humility sets off humility, and both sides win. You lower yourself first, and he softens; you listen to him first, and he becomes willing to listen to you. This isn’t a technique; it’s a spiritual law: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5)

The Lord himself said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Notice that when the Lord describes himself, he speaks not of his power but of his heart — “I am gentle and humble in heart”.

The secret of winning hearts, when all is said and done, is selflessness. Selflessness overcomes Satan; humility overcomes pride.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s three key points within the whole picture of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. All through today’s lesson we’ve been watching how Jesus treated people: he had compassion on the harassed and scattered crowds; he loved the rich young ruler who turned and walked away; he stayed in Zacchaeus’ house; he restored Peter beside the charcoal fire. Treating people from the heart isn’t a set of interpersonal skills; it is following Jesus’ example.

The Bible is my standard. We don’t define what “loving people” means by our feelings. The Bible says, “Keep your heart with all diligence” (Proverbs 4:23); the Bible says, “love one another, even as I have loved you” (John 15:12). The standard lies in the Bible, not in our temperament.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Relying on the heart will run dry — unless that love doesn’t come from me. “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) The order of love is always: first receive, then pour out. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. The greatest temptation in winning people’s hearts is to keep those hearts for ourselves. True shepherding brings people’s hearts before the King, letting Jesus reign as King in their lives, rather than letting me reign as king in their lives.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. When someone is moved by the heart you’ve shown them, you must immediately turn the glory away from yourself: it isn’t that I love you; it’s that the Lord first loved me, and only so can I love you.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. A system isn’t a set of regulations; it’s a network of lives joined to lives. Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others (2 Timothy 2:2) — that is the system. And every joint in that system is a heart that has been won by someone relying on the heart. If the hearts aren’t won, the system is only an empty organisational structure.

The fivefold change and the order of serving

Today’s lesson walks precisely the road of the fivefold change: mindset (people matter more than tasks) → life (from the self-centred life to selflessness) → daily living (how I speak to the people around me) → relationships (small groups, families and co-workers restored) → ministry (revival comes naturally).

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If today you find you can’t put your heart into people, don’t blame yourself for being cold just yet; go and check the first relationship — is your heart still with God these days?

A shift in perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective: man looks at the outward appearance; God looks at the heart.

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly one: cargo and tackle will sink; people’s souls will remain for ever.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal one: no one will remember this quarter’s report next year; the tears you shed for one person today will be remembered for ever.

From a worldly perspective to a godly one: the world asks, “What have you achieved?”; God asks, “Whom have you loved?”

920 and 235

The 920 practice: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”. Before them we live out a selfless (0) life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Today’s assignment is very concrete — choose one “2” and put your heart into them.

235 relationships: once a heart is won, we must enter into a connection of life. Become a “2” with someone who is selfless, establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and in the end become the “5” of a fivefold-ministry team. The Lord with Peter is the finest model.

The Path of Serving

Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory).

Notice the order of this path: Spirit first, Understanding first, Life first, and only then Service. We often skip the first three stops and go straight to “Service” — no wonder we’re exhausted. Relying on the heart means walking the path again from the first stop.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three questions and one action. Let’s use the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take it deeper.

Stage 1: Information

Today you have already received the information: man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7); the first gift God asks of us is the heart (Proverbs 23:26); the ultimate sacrifice without love still profits me nothing (1 Corinthians 13:3).

Please copy these three verses onto paper, or set them as your phone wallpaper. Information that doesn’t land will be gone by tomorrow.

Stage 2: Revelation

Information belongs to others; revelation is your own. Please quiet yourself, let the Holy Spirit shine his light, and answer the lesson’s three questions honestly:

First, in what things have I lately wanted only to “get the job done”, while neglecting “people’s feelings”?

Second, has anyone been hurt because I was in a hurry to finish a task? Am I willing to go and show I care, apologise and repair the relationship?

Third, how can I treat the members of my small group, my family or my colleagues “from the heart”, so that they feel the love of Jesus?

Brothers and sisters, don’t rush past this. Revelation often comes with a little sting. When a certain face comes to mind, a certain remark, a certain sharing you cut short — that’s the Holy Spirit speaking.

Stage 3: Conviction

Conviction is saying to God in your heart: “Lord, you are right, and I am wrong.”

Conviction isn’t agreeing with an idea; it’s surrendering a position. I used to believe “getting things finished matters most”; now I am convinced that “people matter more than tasks”. If this step isn’t taken, everything after it is forced.

Stage 4: Implementation

The assignment the lesson gives is very concrete: write down one person you will treat “from the heart”, and plan to reach out to them once this week — not for the sake of a task, but for the sake of the person.

Please write it now. Write down the name, write down what you’ll do, write down when.

I suggest three principles. First, bring no agenda: this contact isn’t for discussing ministry, assigning work or asking about progress. Second, listen before you speak: ask one real question, then close your mouth and listen for a full three minutes. Third, remember specifics: bring up some small thing they once told you — their mother’s illness, their child’s exams, that difficulty they mentioned last time. To be remembered is to be loved.

Stage 5: Evaluation

At the end of this week, find a quiet moment and ask yourself: did I really do it? While I was doing it, what was going on in my heart? Was I truly loving them, or was I completing my “rely on the heart” homework? How did they respond? Was there any disappointment in me, any resentment that they didn’t appreciate it?

Evaluation isn’t condemnation; it’s looking in the mirror.

Stage 6: Correction

If you find you’ve once again treated people as tools, go back to the cross, confess it and make a fresh adjustment. Corrections are often small: slow your tone down a little; swap “How’s that job going?” for “How have you been lately?”; hold a word of rebuke for three days before you say it.

If someone has been hurt by you, go and apologise. An apology needs no explanation; just say: “I was in too much of a hurry that day. I didn’t consider how you felt. I’m sorry.” The spiritual power of that one sentence far exceeds ten perfect sermons.

Stage 7: Repetition

Relying on the heart once is a moment of being moved; relying on the heart again and again is life.

Behavioural science tells us that forming a habit takes a good deal of repetition over time; the Bible says it more directly: “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). Please turn “caring for one person a week” into a long-term rhythm, not just homework for this lesson.

Stage 8: Multiplication

The last step, and the most crucial: pass on what you have received.

When the brother or sister you’ve treated from the heart has had their heart restored, take them with you to treat the next person from the heart. That is “Multiplication”; that is the four-generation inheritance of 2 Timothy 2:2; that is establishing God’s system.

We win hearts not to keep people, but to multiply love.

A Gentle Reminder

Don’t treat people “as tools”, neglecting their hearts for the sake of getting something done.

Paul once said with deep sorrow: “For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you. For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 2:20–21) He also urges us: “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:4)

Jesus never “used people”; he only “loved people”. He didn’t treat the twelve disciples as a team for expanding his ministry; he called them friends (John 15:15). He didn’t treat the five thousand as a support base; what he saw were people like sheep without a shepherd, and he had compassion on them (Mark 6:34).

Follow Jesus’ example, and treat every heart from the heart.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson closes with a beautiful line: winning the task is easy, winning the heart is hard; but only by winning the heart can we win people, and only by winning people can we win the kingdom.

Winning the task is easy, because tasks have a model answer, and when they’re done you feel a sense of achievement. Winning the heart is hard, because there are no shortcuts to the heart; it can only be won with time, with tears, with watching and waiting again and again and asking nothing in return.

But remember: this is exactly how God himself won us. He didn’t press us down with authority; the Word became flesh and lived among us (John 1:14). He didn’t force us with the law; he laid down his life for us: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). He spent the whole of the cross just to win one heart that would not otherwise turn back — your heart.

How could anyone who has been loved like that bear to treat people half-heartedly?

So this morning I want to issue this call to you: from today, lay down the anxiety of “doing the right things”, and learn to “become the right person” — someone willing to serve the Lord and serve people with sincerity, humility, and from the heart.

Laying down anxiety isn’t laying down responsibility. It’s handing over the voice that has been driving you on, and taking up instead the Lord’s gentle and humble yoke (Matthew 11:29). It’s letting Jesus reign as King over your diary, reign as King in your small group, reign as King in your family. It’s this: when someone’s heart has been won through you, you give that heart, and all the glory, to Jesus without a moment’s hesitation.

Revival begins with one sincere heart.

Beginning with your heart. Beginning this morning.

keyVerses: “My son, give me your heart; and let your eyes keep in my ways.” (Proverbs 23:26)
“For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)
declarations: Please join me with one heart and read the lesson’s declaration aloud:

Lord, I want to learn to treat people from the heart as you do, and to win their hearts. I will be a vessel that moves people, influences people and builds people up. Starting with me, relying on the heart, I will bring revival!
practices: Ask yourself every day: today, did I only want to get the job done, or did I also consider people’s feelings?
If anyone has been hurt because I was in a hurry to finish a task, take the initiative to show I care, apologise and repair the relationship.
This week, treat one small-group member, family member or colleague from the heart, so that they feel the love of Jesus.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you that you don’t see as man sees — man looks at the outward appearance, but you look at the heart. Thank you that while we were still unlovely, you loved us from the heart, and won our hearts through the cross.

Lord, forgive us. We are so often busy getting things done that the people around us get hurt by our efficiency. We treat people as helpers for completing tasks, and forget that they are your children, bought with your precious blood. We honour you with our lips, while our hearts are so often far from you.

Lord, take away our hearts of stone and give us hearts of flesh. Give us your way of seeing people, so that we can see the longing, the pain and the hope within them. Take away our self-centredness and our pride; let us learn your gentleness and humility, and return to our originally intended position as servants: let man be man and let God be God.
Lord, we give our hearts to you. Reign as King within us, and grant that every person we lead, through our relying on the heart, may in the end see you, follow you and glorify you.
May revival begin in my heart, in my home, in my small group.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7) Please share: has there been a time recently when you saw only someone’s “outward appearance” — their performance, their progress, their attitude — and failed to see the real need in their heart? If you could do it over, what would you do?

Question 2: “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:3) Please share: in your present service or family life, is there something you are “doing very well, but perhaps without love”? This week, which “2” do you plan to put your heart into? What is your concrete plan?

l033.subtitle: Winning the Task Is Not as Good as Winning the Heart; Only Winning Hearts Brings Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: What Is Thrown Overboard in the Storm, and What Is Kept
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin with a question for all of us: if the ship you were on were sinking, and you could save only one thing, what would you save?
