In the small hours of 15 April 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. She was the most luxurious, most advanced feat of engineering of her day, and her holds were loaded with priceless cargo, mail, fine china and paintings. Yet when the sea began pouring in, not one person ran back down to the hold to rescue those paintings. On that night the more than two thousand two hundred people on board were left with only one question: could one more person squeeze into a lifeboat? In the end about one thousand five hundred perished in the icy sea, and only a little over seven hundred were saved. What people have argued about for more than a hundred years has never been how valuable the cargo on the seabed was, but whether one more person might have been saved that night.

Storms put things in order for us. In the calm days we often weigh tasks and people on the same scale — and without realising it we even let the tasks weigh more. But once the storm hits, the truth about value rises to the surface: the cargo can be thrown overboard, the tackle can be thrown away, but people cannot be thrown away.

But brothers and sisters, we have to be honest: we don’t need to wait for a storm to make this choice. In fact, we are making it every single day.

A sister once told me about a large evangelistic rally her church held, with her as the lead organiser. That night the programme ran smoothly, the worship was moving, and the number of people who made a decision for Christ went beyond all expectations. Afterwards everyone applauded and said it was the most successful meeting in years. But three days later she realised that the brother who had run the sound desk had stopped coming to church altogether. The reason was simple: during the rehearsal he had been half a beat late, and in front of everyone she had said, “If you can’t even do something this simple, do I have to do it myself?” The task was done, and the man was gone. Later, with tears in her eyes, she said, “I won that meeting, but I lost a brother.”

In our ministry, our work and our dealings with people, we often face a very deep choice: do we “get the task right”, or do we “win the person”? Brothers and sisters, please notice: this is not a question of technique but of values; not a matter of better or worse methods, but of the direction of our mindset. Methods can be learned, but a mindset has to be renewed — and once the mindset is renewed, the life is renewed along with it.

The ministry of Jesus reveals a truth to us: he did not merely pursue results in ministry; he cared far more about whether people’s hearts had been touched by love and renewed by truth. When he won a person’s heart, he gained an eternal harvest for the kingdom of God. In this morning’s devotion we will learn this lesson together: winning the heart matters more than getting the task done.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Storm That Exposes the Order of Our Values
1. Author, Date and Audience
sections.html:
The author of Acts is Luke, the one Paul calls “Luke the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). He also wrote the Gospel of Luke, and both books were written to a man named Theophilus (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1). In Greek the name “Theophilus” is Θεόφιλος (Theophilos), meaning “one who loves God” or “one loved by God”. With the careful hand of a historian, Luke records how the gospel travelled from Jerusalem to Rome.

Chapter 27 belongs to the final “voyage to Rome” section of Acts. There is something very striking about this section: Luke uses “we”, the first person plural. “When it was determined that we should sail for Italy” (Acts 27:1). This tells us that Luke himself was on that ship. He is not passing on hearsay; he lived through it. So every detail in this chapter — the name of the wind, the handling of the ship, the order in which things were thrown overboard, the number of people aboard — is an eyewitness record.

sections.heading: 2. Historical and Cultural Setting
sections.html:
Shipping on the Mediterranean in those days was strictly bound by the seasons. The Romans counted summer as the safe sailing season; once the autumn equinox had passed the sea turned treacherous, and from November to March shipping almost entirely stopped. Luke takes care to note: “When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous, because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished them…” (Acts 27:9). “The Fast” here refers to the Jewish Day of Atonement, which falls roughly between late September and early October. In other words, this ship put out to sea at the most dangerous time of year.

Not long after the ship left Crete, “before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon” (Acts 27:14). “Euroclydon” was the sailors’ name for this kind of north-easterly gale. The ship was driven before the wind; for many days they saw neither sun nor stars (Acts 27:20), and they drifted at sea for fourteen whole days (Acts 27:27, 33). Luke honestly records the despair of that moment: “all hope that we would be saved was now taken away.” (Acts 27:20)

sections.heading: 3. Literary Context
sections.html:
It is in exactly this situation that today’s key passage appears: “As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.” (Acts 27:18–19)

Notice the order in these two verses: first the cargo goes overboard (the Chinese Union Version says it plainly — “the cargo”), then the tackle. The cargo was the purpose of the voyage — this was a grain ship of Alexandria (Acts 27:6, 38), and the grain was the profit, the very reason the voyage existed. The tackle was the means of fulfilling that purpose. When the storm drove them far enough, they threw away the “purpose”, and they threw away the “means” too. And from beginning to end, not one person suggested throwing anybody overboard.

Even more beautiful is what follows — the heart of God. Paul stood up and said, “Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.” (Acts 27:22) The angel had said to Paul, “Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.” (Acts 27:24)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to God’s arithmetic: the ship was lost; the cargo sank; the tackle was gone. What God granted Paul was not the ship, not the cargo, but “all those who sail with you”. In the end Luke records: “In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.” (Acts 27:37) Two hundred and seventy-six people — and not a single one was missing (Acts 27:44).

A whole shipload of cargo went down, and two hundred and seventy-six hearts came ashore alive. In God’s ledger, that voyage turned a great profit. This is the biblical foundation for “winning the heart matters more than getting the task done”: in God’s eyes, people are always more precious than tasks.

sections.heading: 1. Jesus Cared About Winning the Heart More Than Getting the Task Done
sections.html:
(1) He Could Have Dazzled the World with Miracles, Yet He Chose to Walk with People

“He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach” (Mark 3:14).

This verse is the master plan of how the Lord Jesus built his disciples. Notice the order of the two verbs: first “that they might be with him”, and only then “that he might send them out to preach”. The Greek is ἵνα ὦσιν μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ (hina ōsin met’ autou), literally “in order that they might be with him”. Being with him is the purpose; being sent is the fruit. Being with him is the root; ministry is the fruit. The Lord Jesus did not first hand his disciples a job; he first gave them a relationship.

If Jesus had only wanted to “get the task done”, he could easily have dazzled the world with signs and wonders. This isn’t our imagination — it is exactly the plan Satan actually put to him in the temptation in the wilderness. “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” (Matthew 4:3) — solve the problem of hunger overnight, and the whole world would follow him. “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” (Matthew 4:6) — leap from the pinnacle of the temple and land without a scratch, and all Jerusalem would fall at his feet. “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” (Matthew 4:9) — no need to walk the road of the cross; take the glory of all the kingdoms directly.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Satan’s three temptations are really one temptation: use the fastest way to “get the task done”, and bypass the narrow road of “winning the heart”. Three times the Lord Jesus answered with Scripture, and three times he refused the shortcut. He chose the slowest road of all — living for three and a half years with twelve ordinary men, walking step by step along the dusty roads of Galilee, putting up with their rivalry, answering their foolish questions, washing their feet.

(2) What Is the “Heart” in the Bible?

The Hebrew word for “heart” is לֵב (lēb) or לֵבָב (lēbāb), and it appears more than eight hundred times in the Old Testament. It means far more than emotion; it is the centre of a person’s whole inner life, including thought, will, conscience and decision. The Greek καρδία (kardia) is the same. So when the Bible says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23), it means that the heart is the source of your whole life — only when the spring is clear can the river run clear.

And that is exactly why God never looks first at a person’s performance; he looks first at the heart. “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7) People look at CVs, results and numbers; God looks at the heart hidden within, the heart no one else can see.

And what God wants is precisely our heart. “My son, give me your heart; and let your eyes keep in my ways.” (Proverbs 23:26) Brothers and sisters, listen: God did not say, “My son, give me your achievements”, nor did he say, “Give me your ministry.” He said: give me your heart.

(3) He Did Not Despise Weakness — He Won Hearts

Jesus’ aim was not to train a group of people who “could get things done”, but to win a group of people “with a heart”. So he did not despise his disciples’ weakness or rebuke them for being slow; instead, again and again, he accepted them, encouraged them and taught them.

Look at Peter. The Lord knew full well that Peter would deny him three times, yet he said beforehand: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” (Luke 22:31–32) Brothers and sisters, notice the Lord’s words: not “if you turn again”, but “when once you have turned again”. Before Peter ever fell, the Lord had already prepared a place for him to rise again.

After the resurrection, on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, the Lord lit a charcoal fire, grilled fish, and waited for that failed fisherman to come ashore. He did not ask, “Why did you fall?” He asked: “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15) Three denials, three questions about love. He was not investigating a task; he was restoring a heart.

“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) The Lord first let people see his heart, and only then did they dare to entrust their hearts to him.

“But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.” (Matthew 9:36) “Moved with compassion” in Greek is σπλαγχνίζομαι (splanchnizomai), whose root refers to a person’s inner organs, the bowels — it means “to be churned up inside”. This is not polite sympathy; it is being seized, body and soul, by another person’s plight. When Jesus saw the crowds, it wasn’t his brow that moved; it was his very insides.

(4) Confirmation from Psychology: Security Comes First, Then Productivity

In 1999, Professor Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School put forward the concept of “psychological safety”: team members’ confidence that they can admit mistakes and raise questions without being humiliated or punished. She had expected the best-performing medical teams to make the fewest mistakes, but the data showed the opposite: the best-performing teams actually “reported” the most mistakes — because they dared to speak up.

Better known still is Google’s “Project Aristotle”. Beginning in 2012, the company spent several years analysing more than a hundred of its own teams, trying to find what effective teams have in common. The conclusion was unexpected: it wasn’t the members’ IQ, nor their experience, nor who was friends with whom. The number one factor was precisely “psychological safety”.

Brothers and sisters, this confirms, from another angle, exactly what the Lord Jesus did. Over three and a half years he created a safe place for the hearts of his twelve disciples — so safe that Peter dared to say the wrong thing in front of him, Thomas dared to voice his doubts before him, and John dared to lean against his chest. Once the heart is safe, life dares to grow; once life has grown, it can bear the weight of ministry.

(5) The Fruit of Winning the Heart: They Gave Everything for Him

Precisely because Jesus had won his disciples’ hearts, even after his ascension they were still willing to pay any price for him, so that the gospel spread throughout the world. Church history records that the great majority of these Galilean fishermen and tax collectors eventually died as martyrs for the Lord. Not one of them was bound by an institution; they had been won by a heart.

The nineteenth-century missionary James Hudson Taylor is generally held to have said: “If I had a thousand pounds, China should have every penny. If I had a thousand lives, China should have every one of them.” Brothers and sisters, someone who can say that is not driven by a task; he has been won by love.

(6) Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus Is My Role Model

The first of the Three Foundations of the 321 vision is “Jesus is my role model”. In this lesson his example could not be clearer: life first, then relationships, then ministry. He first was with his disciples, building life; then he walked with them, building relationships; and only last did he send them out to accomplish ministry.

Yet we so often turn the order upside down: first we give people work, then we demand their cooperation, and only last do we grudgingly show a little concern for their life. The result is that the bigger the ministry grows, the faster people leave. Brothers and sisters, the order turned upside down is not efficiency; it is demolition.

sections.heading: 2. Do We Care About “Getting the Task Done” or “Winning the Heart”?
sections.html:
(1) The Storm Forces Out Our True Values

“As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.” (Acts 27:18–19)

For the act of “throwing overboard” the Greek original uses ἐκβολήν ἐποιοῦντο, literally “they began to make a jettison”, which carries the sense of an ongoing action — not everything thrown out at once, but day after day, item after item. On the first day it was the cargo, the profit of the voyage; on the next it was the tackle, the very gear of the ship. Luke deliberately writes “with their own hands” so that we can see how hard it was to let go: these were things the sailors threw into the sea one by one with their own hands.

Why would they rather throw away the cargo and the tackle than throw away people? Because when life and death are at stake, everyone knows one thing by instinct: people are worth more than tasks.

The Lord Jesus stated this truth in no uncertain terms: “For what will it profit a man, if he gains the whole world, and forfeits his life? Or what will a man give in exchange for his life?” (Matthew 16:26) Brothers and sisters, can the whole world be traded for one person? The Lord says: no. Then can one event, one set of figures, one flawless programme be traded for a brother’s heart? The answer is even more obvious.

(2) Yet Today We Often Do the Opposite

Yet today we often do the opposite — to “get the task done” we sacrifice people; to complete the mission we ignore people’s feelings, and even let them leave wounded.

It’s the same at home. Parents “get the task done” on their child’s grades — and one sentence, “How can you be so stupid?”, earns them the sound of a bedroom door closing. Husband and wife “get the task done” on dividing the housework — they win the argument and lose the warmth of a whole evening. Co-workers “get the task done” on some detail of ministry — the messages fly back and forth, the arrangements get made, but the relationship goes cold.

The apostle Paul put it superbly: “for I seek not your possessions, but you.” (2 Corinthians 12:14) Brothers and sisters, that sentence ought to hang on the heart of everyone who serves. It is you I seek — not your attendance, not your giving, not your willingness to cooperate, but you yourselves.

(3) Why Is Hurt So Hard to Repair?

Psychology has made a very important discovery that helps us grasp the weight of the saying “once a heart is broken, it is hard to mend.” In 2001 the social psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a classic paper entitled “Bad Is Stronger Than Good”. Reviewing a large body of research, they showed that in human psychological experience, negative events generally have a greater impact than positive events of the same strength. One wounding word takes many warm words to make up for.

The marriage researcher John Gottman, after long years of observing couples interact at the University of Washington, proposed his well-known “five-to-one” ratio: in stable marriages, positive interactions outnumber negative ones by roughly five to one or more. Brothers and sisters, this figure reminds us that damage comes retail, but repair comes wholesale. Hurt someone once, and it takes five acts of tenderness just to break even.

In his 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, Daniel Goleman coined the phrase “amygdala hijack”: when we feel threatened, the brain’s emotional centre takes over the whole body before rational thought has even started up. That explains why the brother who was rebuked in front of everyone at the meeting can’t remember a word of what you said afterwards — he only remembers the feeling of humiliation.

God’s word said the same thing long ago, and more simply and powerfully: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1)

(4) The New Commandment Is Not “Do the Job Well”

The world teaches us to look at results, but Jesus teaches us to look at relationships. The new commandment he gave is not “do the job well” but “love one another”.

“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:34–35)

Notice that the Lord did not say, “If you do things beautifully, by this everyone will know that you are my disciples.” The mark by which the world recognises us as the Lord’s disciples has never been our efficiency; it is our love for one another.

In 1 Corinthians 13 Paul says it all: “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal. If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing. If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:1–3)

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at Paul’s list: tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith, giving to the poor, martyrdom — every one of them an astonishing way of “getting things done”! Yet without love, the verdict comes in three phrases: sounding brass, I am nothing, it profits me nothing. In God’s eyes, “winning people’s hearts” is true success.

(5) Applying the 321 Vision: The Priority of Relationships Must Not Be Reversed

sections.heading: The 321 vision teaches us an order of the utmost importance: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.
sections.html:
People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. But the self-centred old self always turns this order upside down — because what the self-centred person really cares about is not the task itself, but “if this gets done, I gain face; if this goes wrong, I lose face.” So in the end, we don’t hurt people for the sake of the task; we hurt people for the sake of “self”.

Pride is the root of the problem. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When I crush a co-worker with a single sentence, his pride is stirred up too. He may say nothing at the time, but go home and decide never to come back. That is how both sides lose.

Humility, on the other hand, is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:3–4)

Brothers and sisters, this morning allow me to ask a question that cuts deep: the last thing you insisted on to the bitter end — was it really for the kingdom of God, or for being right yourself?

sections.heading: 3. Win the Heart and You Win the Person; Win the Person and You Win the Kingdom
sections.html:
(1) Temporary Results and Eternal Influence

The results of “getting the task done” are temporary; the influence of “winning the heart” is eternal.

Paul says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18) Tasks can be seen; hearts cannot. What can be seen will pass away; what cannot be seen lasts for ever.

Someone who only gets the task done without winning the heart may complete the mission, but cannot build up life; whereas someone who wins people wholeheartedly, who wins their hearts, enables life to multiply life.

(2) Barnabas: One Man Who Won Hearts Changed Church History

The Bible gives us a perfect example of this: Barnabas.

When Saul had just come to faith, no one dared go near him. “When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.” (Acts 9:26–27)

Later, when the church in Antioch needed people, “Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul. When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.” (Acts 11:25–26)

Brothers and sisters, if Barnabas had not been there that day, the church might never have had Paul; without Paul, the New Testament might have been short of thirteen letters, and the gospel might have reached Europe many years later. Barnabas never left behind a single letter, but he left behind a Paul. That is the fruit of winning the heart.

And Barnabas did it a second time. Over Mark he argued with Paul, so sharply that they parted company (Acts 15:37–39). At the time it looked like “something that hadn’t gone well”. Yet many years later, shortly before his martyrdom, Paul wrote: “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.” (2 Timothy 4:11) The young man who had once turned back went on to write the Gospel of Mark.

Brothers and sisters, if no one back then had been willing to stake his own reputation on a “useless” young man, today we would have one Gospel fewer. Win one person’s heart, and you may win a whole generation.

(3) Life Multiplies Life

“The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) There are four generations in this verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Ministry that wins hearts multiplies; ministry that only gets tasks done merely accumulates.

How did Paul win people’s hearts? He tells us himself: “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8) Not only the gospel, but his own life as well. That is the price of winning the heart.

And what is the reward of winning the heart? “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Isn’t it even you, before our Lord Jesus at his coming? For you are our glory and our joy.” (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20) Paul’s crown was not the number of churches he had planted; it was the people who stood firm.

(4) A Vivid Picture and a Reminder

The American pastor Robert H. Schuller is generally credited with saying: “Anyone can count the seeds in an apple, but only God can count the apples in a seed.” Getting tasks done is like counting the seeds in an apple — you can count them all; winning hearts is like counting the apples in a seed — you never can.

Nature gives us the same reminder. Among the many kinds of bamboo, some show almost no sign of life above ground for the first few years after planting, because they pour all their strength into the root system underground. Once the roots are firmly established and the shoots begin to rise, they grow at an astonishing speed. Ministry that wins hearts is just like that: for the first few years you often can’t see any “results”, because God is putting down roots; but once the roots run deep, nothing can hold back the fruit.

So in every act of service we must learn to remind ourselves: we do the task not in order to finish it, but in order to win the person. A task can be done over again, but once a person’s heart is broken, it is hard to mend. If we are willing to value people as Jesus did, we can become true vessels in God’s hands.

(5) Applying the 321 Vision: The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

How do we win people’s hearts? The 321 vision gives us two very concrete practices.

The first is “the 920 practice”. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out a life of selflessness (0) before them, we will surely bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice: not one of these nine graces is for “getting things done”; every one of them is for how we treat people. The fruit God apportions to us was prepared for relationships from the start.

The second is “235 relationships”. With a selfless person, become a “2” — spiritual companions; build up a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–12). Barnabas to Paul was a “3”; Paul to Timothy was also a “3”; the team the church in Antioch sent out was a “5”. Win the heart and you win the person; win the person and you win the kingdom — this is how we establish God’s system.

When we value people’s growth and their building up in the spirit, we will see the fruit of revival come naturally.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
sections.html:
(1) The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

Jesus is my role model — he cared about winning the heart more than getting the task done; he was first with people, and only then did he send them out.

The Bible is my standard — it is not the efficiency manual that has the final say, but “Keep your heart with all diligence” (Proverbs 4:23).

The Holy Spirit is my guide — “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies (Zechariah 4:6). Winning people’s hearts has never been a technique; it is the work of the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — in every tug-of-war between “people and tasks”, hand the decision back to him; let Jesus receive all the glory — when the task is accomplished, the glory goes to him; when a person is won, the glory still goes to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system is built out of people, not piled up out of tasks.

(2) From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

When I run someone over in order to get a task done, I am really taking God’s place as that person’s lord. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) Brothers and sisters, only a selfless person can truly see another person’s heart; for when “I” fill the whole room, there is no space left for anyone else.

(3) The Fivefold Change and a Shift in Perspective

When the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. This is the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

So what today’s lesson sets out to change is not our methods of service but our mindset. From man’s point of view to God’s point of view; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

“Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) Earthly things are measured by results; the things above are measured by life.

(4) Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

Rely on the heart and you find joy; rely on the brain and you find worry. Those who serve with their brains see progress charts, gaps and problems; those who serve with their hearts see the person who is harassed and scattered.

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
This lesson has three practices. We will set them within the eight stages of changing our mindset, so that the practice is not merely a moment of being moved, but real change. The eight stages are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication.

Practice 1: Look Back and Confess

Look back over this week’s service or work. Was there a moment when, to “get the job done right”, you overlooked someone’s heart? Confess it to the Lord and ask him to help you change.

Information: today’s teaching and scriptures are the information God is giving us — people matter more than tasks.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine this truth into your concrete situation. Don’t stop at “I know that now”; ask the Lord to point out “that day, that sentence, that person”.

Conviction: conviction is not admitting that you were wrong; it is believing that God’s way is better than mine. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

Implementation: today, write down that person’s name and pray for him or her for three minutes.

Practice 2: Take the First Step to Repair the Relationship

Take the initiative to seek out someone who was hurt by your demands or your impatience, and repair the relationship with sincerity and care.

Evaluation: honestly examine what you really cared about at the time — was it the task, or your own face?

Correction: make your apology specific. Don’t say, “If I made you uncomfortable, I’m sorry.” Say, “What I said to you in that meeting the other day hurt you. I was wrong. Please forgive me.”

“In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor preferring one another” (Romans 12:10). Brothers and sisters, the one who takes the first step is not the one who loses; it is the one who is like the Lord.

Practice 3: Make Choices Through the Lord’s Eyes

Whenever you face a choice, meditate on this question: “If Jesus were me, what would Jesus do?” Let the Lord’s love and the Lord’s eyes guide what you do.

Repetition: turn this question into a switch you can press at any moment. Before you send that message, before you open your mouth to correct someone, pause for three seconds and ask it.

Multiplication: once you have tasted the joy of winning someone’s heart, bring another person along to practise with you. “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

A Gentle Reminder

A task can be done again, but a heart once lost is hard to win back. What the Lord cares about is not efficiency but relationships; not how much we have completed, but how much we have loved.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
“Winning the heart matters more than getting the task done” is a kingdom way of seeing, and it is also a life choice.

Let us no longer measure success by results, but measure influence by the depth of our love. When we learn to win people’s hearts, the kingdom of God is established in those hearts — because when the heart is right, the person is right; and when the person is right, the task is right.

Brothers and sisters, come back with me to that ship. The cargo sank, the tackle was gone, the ship itself broke apart — yet of the two hundred and seventy-six people, not one was missing. What God wanted Paul to see that night was exactly his own eternal scale of values.

The Lord Jesus said: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.” (Luke 19:10) He came not to complete a task but to seek out a people. And the first call he spoke to Peter was not “I will make you get things done well”, but: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.” (Matthew 4:19)

So this morning I want to issue this call to you, brothers and sisters: let Jesus be King over the way you rank what matters. When people and tasks collide, let him decide; when your face and a brother’s heart collide, let him decide. And give all the glory to him — for every heart that is won was bought with his precious blood; it is not our achievement.

May we all become people like Barnabas: perhaps leaving no writings behind, but leaving people; perhaps leaving no numbers behind, but leaving life. For on that last day we will not be able to take a single task with us; all we can take with us are the people the Lord has won.

keyVerses: “As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.” (Acts 27:18–19)
“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)
“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” (John 13:34)
declarations: Lord, teach me to be like you — seeking not only to get the task done but, even more, to win people. May love be the starting point of everything I do; may I serve wholeheartedly, become a fisher of people, and be a vessel fit for your use!
practices: Look back and confess
Take the first step to repair the relationship
Make choices through the Lord’s eyes
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we are quiet before you.

Lord, we confess that we have often loved tasks more than people, and results more than life. We have done many things in your name, yet in doing them we have hurt the very people you love. Please forgive us.

Lord, please give us your heart. When you saw the crowds you were moved with compassion; let our insides, too, be stirred for people. You prayed for Peter; teach us, too, to keep hope alive for those who are weak.

Holy Spirit, help us to lay down the pride of the self-centred life and live out a life of selflessness. Let us bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions in every relationship, walk together with our spiritual companions, and be built up into your system.
Lord, we give our hearts to you. Reign as King in our homes, our workplaces and our ministry; may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.” (Acts 27:18–19) In your present life or ministry, what “cargo” or “tackle” is God asking you to throw overboard for the sake of people?

“He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach” (Mark 3:14). In your ministry, has the order of “being with” and “being sent” been reversed? This week, for whom can you set aside some time with no agenda, simply to be with them?
l034.title: Winning the Heart Matters More Than the Task
l034.subtitle: Win People’s Hearts and You Win God’s Kingdom
l034.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: Introduction: That Night, It Wasn’t Only the Car Door That Got Dented
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, I’d like you to step into a scene with me first.

A father had saved for several years and finally bought a car. His son had just passed his driving test, and in high spirits he borrowed the car and went out. That night, a little after eleven, the doorbell rang. The son stood at the door with his head bowed, the keys clutched in his hand, his voice trembling: “Dad… the car… I dented it.”

The next three seconds would decide the relationship between that father and son for the next ten years.

The first kind of father looks at the garage first. He rushes out, walks all the way round the car, runs his fingers along the dent, then turns back and lets fly: “I told you so! Do you ever listen? Do you know how much this is going to cost to fix?” — And the result? The car goes to the panel beater, and two weeks later it’s fixed; you can’t even tell it was in an accident. But after that night, the son comes home later and later, and says less and less. The car was repaired, but a hole had been dented into his heart.

The second kind of father looks at his son first. He puts down what he’s holding, walks over, and his first words are: “Are you hurt?” The son shakes his head, and the tears start to fall. The father reaches out, holds him, and says: “As long as you’re all right, that’s what matters. The car is made of metal, and metal can be beaten back into shape; you’re my son, and I only have one son.” Only when the boy has calmed down does the father sit down with him, go through the insurance papers together, work out the cost of the repair, and teach him, sentence by sentence, how he should have judged that junction. — And the result? The car still gets fixed, and that night the father won his son’s heart.

Brothers and sisters, the same incident, the same dent — two reactions, two outcomes. The first father got the task done and lost the heart; the second father won the heart and didn’t lose the task either.

Let’s take this scene, exactly as it is, and carry it into the church.

The Sunday service is over. The pianist played two wrong chords, the slides came up half a beat late, and the welcomer forgot to bring a newcomer to the welcome desk. At the review meeting afterwards, what are our first words? Is it “How could so many things go wrong today?” or “Thank you, everyone, for all your hard work this month”? Are we in a hurry to make the procedures more detailed and the rules more rigid, or do we first see the sister who played the wrong chords — whose family had just gone through a crisis this week, and who sat down at the piano with tears in her eyes?

In the previous lesson we saw together that winning the heart matters more than getting the task done. Jesus cared about winning the heart more than getting the task done; people are worth more than tasks; win the heart and you win the person, win the person and you win the kingdom. This is the second talk, and we’re going to bring that truth somewhere closer to home — into the atmosphere of our church, into those three seconds of our emotional reaction, and into God’s own example.

Because if our focus is in the wrong place, then without noticing it we will replace a relationship of love with the pressure of law. We’ll do more and more, get more and more tired, and end up with fewer and fewer people. The attendance figures may not drop, but one by one, hearts will close their doors to each other.

Jesus did not come to set up more rules; he came to restore relationships and win hearts. For only love can make service a joy rather than a burden.

Today we will look at three things together. First, a church that values getting tasks done is like a company; a church that values winning hearts is like a family. Second, look at your reactions and you’ll know whether what you care about is the task or the heart. Third, God’s own example — what he pursues has never been tasks, but hearts.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Verses, One Father’s Heart
sections.html: Our two key passages today come one from the very front of the Bible and one from the centre of the New Testament; one from the day humanity fell, the other from the summit of the revelation of salvation. Taken together, they point to the same thing: what God wants is the human heart.

sections.heading: 1. The Background to Genesis 3:9
sections.html:
Genesis has traditionally been held to have been written by Moses. It records the history from creation to the patriarchs, and it was God’s foundational revelation to his people as Israel journeyed out of Egypt towards Canaan. Chapter 3 records the fall of humanity.

Notice the order of events on the day of the fall. “They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8)

God was “walking in the garden” — that is a relational act. God did not hand down a verdict from far away in heaven; he walked into the garden to look for the man.

Then came the call that has echoed through history: “Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)

Brothers and sisters, this is the first question God asks a human being in the whole Bible. Think about it: God knows everything. Did he not know which tree Adam was hiding behind? Of course he did. So “Where are you?” is not a question of geography; it is a question of relationship.

The Hebrew אַיֶּכָּה (‘ayyekkah) literally means “where are you?”, but as the Bible uses it, a call like this often carries a sense of searching, of summoning, of an aching heart. God did not first ask, “What have you done?” He first asked, “Where are you?” — where have you, you yourself, gone? How did things between us come to this?

In fact, it is only afterwards that God asks: “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?” (Genesis 3:11) The deed he will still deal with; sin he will never wink at. But his order is this: first find the person, then deal with the deed.

sections.heading: 2. The Background to Romans 5:8
sections.html:
The apostle Paul wrote Romans around AD 56–57, at the end of his third missionary journey, while he was staying in Corinth. It was addressed to the church in Rome — a group of believers Paul had never yet met, both Jews and Gentiles.

In Romans 1–4 Paul builds his case layer by layer: the Gentiles have sinned, the Jews have sinned, all the world has sinned; by works, by the law, by circumcision, not one person can be justified before God. The only way out for humanity is justification by faith.

When he reaches chapter 5, Paul walks out of the courtroom and into the family home. He no longer speaks only of our “standing”; he begins to speak of “love”. “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

“Commends” in Greek is συνίστημι (sunistēmi), which carries the sense of “to prove, to recommend, to set right before someone’s eyes so they can see it”. Paul is saying: God’s love is not a slogan. God has set his love out on the cross, set it right before your eyes, and proved it to you.

Notice the timing — “while we were yet sinners”. Not once we’ve done things right, not once our performance is up to standard, not once we’ve passed the assessment. God loves first, and then we change; it is not that we change first, and then God loves.

Brothers and sisters, put these two verses together and you have the foundation of this lesson: God first asks, “Where are you?” — and while we were yet sinners, he died for us. From Eden to Golgotha, God has been doing one and the same thing all along — winning the human heart.

sections.heading: 1. A Church That Values Getting Tasks Done Is Like a Company; a Church That Values Winning Hearts Is Like a Family
sections.html:
1. The Logic of a Company: Performance, Rules, Replacement

If in church we value only “getting the task done”, the church will slowly turn into a company.

What is the logic of a company? A company focuses on performance and results. If results are poor, hold a review; if the review doesn’t help, set up a system; if the system doesn’t help, raise the standards; if the standards still don’t help, replace the person. In business this logic works, because a company exists in the first place to produce.

The problem is: what happens when that logic is carried into the church?

First, service becomes “duty”. What began as “I’m willing” becomes “I ought to”; what began as a response to grace becomes the obligation of a post.

Second, people live in comparison. Whose small group is biggest, whose ministry gets noticed, who is up on the platform, who is pushed to the back — rankings begin to appear among brothers and sisters.

Third, people live under pressure and in weariness. Because you can clock off from a company, but you can’t clock off from church; performance at a company earns a bonus, but performance at church only earns the next, higher standard.

Fourth, and most painful of all — people begin to be afraid of making mistakes. A community afraid of making mistakes is a community that doesn’t dare speak the truth; and a community that doesn’t dare speak the truth can no longer grow real life.

In Galatians Paul has some hard words for a church that is “looking more and more like a company”: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision amounts to anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.” (Galatians 5:6) It wasn’t that the Galatian church lacked zeal. They were extremely zealous — so zealous that they wanted to use rules to keep everyone in line. Paul says: that amounts to nothing.

He also says: “who also made us sufficient as servants of a new covenant, not of the letter, but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6) Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the letter kills. Not that the letter is unimportant, but when there is only the letter and no life, the letter will crush people to death.

2. The Logic of a Family: Relationship, Shared Burdens, Willing Hearts

But if we value “winning the heart”, the church will be like a family.

What is the logic of a family? A family focuses on relationships and on being bound to one another. When a child at home breaks a bowl, we don’t dismiss him for “insufficient productivity”. It isn’t that a family makes no demands — a family disciplines too; but in a family, discipline happens within the relationship, rather than the relationship being traded for performance.

The Bible plainly says the church is a family. “So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). And Paul says to Timothy: “God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.” (1 Timothy 3:15)

Deeper still is Romans 8:15: “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’”

Brothers and sisters, nail this verse to your heart. The spirit of bondage — the Chinese Union Version calls it “the heart of a slave” — is marked by fear; the Spirit of adoption — “the heart of a son” — is marked by the cry “Abba! Father!” A company culture breeds the heart of a slave; a family culture breeds the heart of a son. When you serve in church, is there fear in your heart, or sweetness? That question tells you whether you are in a company or a family.

Jesus himself drew this line: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” (John 15:15) The Lord tells us what is on his heart — that is how you treat family.

Peter puts it even more directly to the elders of the church: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.” (1 Peter 5:2–3) Not under compulsion, but voluntarily; not lording it over, but being an example. That is how a family is governed.

When we are willing to carry burdens for one another, to pay a price for others, to be patient for our brothers’ and sisters’ growth, relationships are built up layer upon layer. And by then, service is no longer a burden but a joy — because everyone is doing it gladly and willingly, from the heart.

3. Confirmation from Psychology: Intrinsic Motivation and Psychological Safety

This is not only a spiritual principle; it is also the way human beings are made.

From the 1980s onward, the American psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan developed “Self-Determination Theory”. After more than forty years of research, they point out that people have three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. When someone acts out of intrinsic motivation, their engagement, creativity and staying power are at their highest; conversely, the more external control, monitoring, rewards and punishments there are, the more intrinsic motivation is actually weakened.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the greatest danger of a “corporatised church”: we use more rules to make up for the loss of passion, and the more rules we make, the faster the passion drains away.

Another line of research comes from Professor Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School. In 1999 she put forward the concept of “psychological safety”: in a psychologically safe team, members believe they can admit mistakes and raise questions without being humiliated or punished. Later, Google’s “Project Aristotle”, carried out from 2012 to 2015, analysed more than a hundred of the company’s own teams and concluded that the most decisive factor in a team’s effectiveness was not how clever or how senior its members were, but psychological safety.

A church that will stop and ask, “Are you hurt?” is a church with psychological safety. In a church that always asks first, “How could a mistake like this happen?”, people will leave one by one in their hearts, even while their bodies are still sitting in the pews.

But brothers and sisters, remember the order: it is not that the Bible is right because psychology says so; rather, because this is how God made human beings, even psychology has to admit it. The Bible is our standard; science only nods along behind it.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

sections.heading: The 321 vision has a saying that hits this point exactly: life first, then relationships, then ministry.
sections.html:
A company’s order is upside down: ministry first; when the ministry doesn’t go well, add rules; when the rules can’t push people, replace them — life and relationships are never on the agenda. A family’s order is this: life comes first, then relationships, and when the relationships are right, the ministry grows naturally out of them.

There’s another saying: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. That night, the son mattered more than the car; that Sunday, the sister at the piano mattered more than two chords.

The 321 vision also reminds us of the fivefold change: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. Notice that ministry comes last — not because ministry is unimportant, but because ministry is the fruit, not the root. If we spend all day shaking the fruit, the tree will die; if we water the root, the fruit will come of itself.

Brothers and sisters, this morning you can ask yourself a very simple question: in the community I serve, are people more afraid of making mistakes, or more willing to speak the truth? The answer tells you whether your church, right now, is a company or a family.

sections.heading: 2. Look at Your Reactions and You’ll Know Whether You Care About the “Task” or the “Heart”
sections.html:
1. Our Reactions Are the Outlet of the Heart

What a person really cares about is seen not in what he says from the pulpit, but in what his first reaction is in the three seconds after something goes wrong.

When someone else gets something wrong, our first reaction reveals our focus. If we get angry, criticise and rebuke, that shows we value the “task”; if we choose to be forbearing, to understand and to teach, that shows we value the “heart”.

Why is the “first reaction” the most accurate? Because rehearsed words can be polished, but a reaction that bursts out unbidden doesn’t lie. The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) The mouth is the heart’s outlet pipe; the moment the water gushes out, you know what’s in the tank.

That is why Proverbs says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The wellspring of life flows not from our diary, not from our abilities, but from the heart.

2. That Dent: Two Fathers, Two Outcomes

The lesson text gives a very fitting example: a child accidentally crashes the car.

If we value the “task”, we will scold him first and lose our temper. And the result? The car gets fixed, but we lose the child’s trust. The thing is restored to how it was, but the relationship can’t go back.

If we value the “heart”, we will first make sure the child isn’t hurt, be willing to bear the consequences together with him, and then teach him. And the result? The car gets fixed, and the child’s heart is won as well.

Notice that the father who valued the heart did not skip the teaching. He still has to teach his son to read junctions, to work out costs, to take responsibility. The only difference is the order — deal with the person first, then the task; give a sense of safety first, then instruction.

Paul puts it with great precision: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Galatians 6:1) The word “restore” in Greek is καταρτίζω (katartizō), a term originally used for setting broken bones and mending fishing nets. Brothers and sisters, someone setting a bone needs hands that are steady, gentle and precise, because what they are touching is a person who can feel pain. When we correct someone, are we setting a bone, or hammering it?

Paul adds one more phrase: “looking to yourself”. Those who are quick to rebuke others have mostly forgotten that they could fall too.

3. A Choice in Ministry: Correct, or Shepherd?

It’s the same in ministry. When a co-worker makes a mistake, are we in a hurry to correct, or do we seize the chance to shepherd?

A true leader knows how to turn failure into an opportunity to “win the heart”, so that people feel loved and grow as a result.

One of the most beautiful scenes in the Bible takes place on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias. Peter had denied the Lord three times; judged by “performance”, he should long since have been replaced. Yet after the resurrection, Jesus first lit a charcoal fire for them and grilled the fish, and only then did he speak. He didn’t say, “Why did you do that?” What he asked was: “do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15) Three denials, three questions; three failures, three commissions: “Feed my lambs.” (John 21:15)

Brothers and sisters, if Jesus had only wanted to “get the task done” that day, church history would never have had Peter preaching at Pentecost. Because the Lord won his heart, he won his whole life.

In the same way, with the woman caught in adultery, the crowd stood with stones in their hands, ready to use the law to wrap the matter up neatly. But Jesus said: “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:11) He did not condone sin — “sin no more” is not ambiguous in the slightest; but first he rescued the person from under the stones, and then he talked about how she should walk from here.

And then there is Martha. To host the Lord she bustled in and out; she did the most work, and her heart was the most bitter. What did the Lord say? “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” (Luke 10:41–42) Brothers and sisters, the Lord did not despise Martha’s service; his heart ached over Martha’s anxiety. Many things, and the one thing needed — this is exactly the watershed between “getting the task done” and “winning the heart”.

4. Confirmation from Psychology: The Three Seconds of Emotion, and Five to One

Why do those three seconds matter so much?

In his 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, the American psychologist Daniel Goleman drew on neuroscience to coin the phrase “amygdala hijack”: when we are threatened or provoked, the brain’s amygdala takes control of the body a step ahead of the rational prefrontal cortex, before it has time to weigh things up, producing a fight-or-flight response. By the time reason returns, the words have already been spoken and the damage has already been done.

So the letter of James gave us a prescription long ago: “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Swift to hear, slow to speak — this is exactly putting the brakes on the amygdala, handing those three seconds over to the Holy Spirit rather than to our emotions.

In addition, the social psychologist Roy Baumeister and colleagues published a well-known paper in 2001 entitled simply “Bad Is Stronger Than Good”. Having reviewed a large body of research, they showed that the psychological impact of negative events is generally stronger than that of positive events of the same degree. A single rebuke often takes several words of affirmation to make up for.

The marriage researchers John Gottman and Robert Levenson, observing couples’ interactions over many years from the 1970s onward, found that in stable, happy marriages the ratio of positive to negative interactions is about five to one. Brothers and sisters, this figure reminds us that relationships are not usually destroyed by one big explosion, but worn away by small unkindnesses piling up day after day; nor are they mended by one grand speech, but nursed back by small kindnesses piling up day after day.

So before that rebuke leaves your mouth, give yourself three more seconds. Those three seconds may be a person’s whole life.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus Is the Focal Point; Rely on the Heart, Not the Brain

sections.heading: The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.
sections.html:
When we lose our temper, our focus is really on ourselves: my face, my plans, my time, my loss. The mark of the old self is the self-centred life. Touch a self-centred person and he immediately springs back; touch a selfless person and what comes out of him is the reaction of Christ. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

The 321 vision also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you find worry, rely on the heart and you find joy. In those three seconds, the person who relies on the brain is calculating the loss; the person who relies on the heart sees a human being.

And the 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When a co-worker makes a mistake and I accuse him in a proud tone, he defends himself with a proud attitude; the problem isn’t solved, and the relationship breaks first — that is how both sides lose. But when I humble myself first and show concern for him as a person first, his heart softens and he says of his own accord, “I’m sorry — I slipped up.” The problem is solved and the relationship is deeper — that is how both sides win.

Brothers and sisters, our reactions are our sermons. People may not remember what we’ve preached, but they will remember for the rest of their lives how we looked at them on the day they fell.

sections.heading: 3. God’s Example: What He Pursues Is Not Tasks, but Hearts
sections.html:
1. The First Question in the Garden of Eden

After Adam and Eve sinned, God’s first words were not “What have you done?” but “Where are you?”

“Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)

Brothers and sisters, in that question lies the deepest tenderness in heaven and earth. Man hid himself, yet God came walking into the garden to look for him. Man broke the relationship, yet God took the initiative to come and repair it. What concerned him was not a checklist of behaviour but the rupture in the relationship; what mattered to him was not Adam’s wrongdoing in itself, but whether Adam’s heart was still willing to come back before him.

Look at one more detail: “Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.” (Genesis 3:21) Man covered his shame with fig leaves — that was man’s solution, and it wouldn’t last three days; but God slaughtered an animal and made garments of skin. This is the first shedding of blood in the Bible, foreshadowing the atonement to come on the hill of Golgotha. After pronouncing judgement, God sewed clothes for them with his own hands — that is not how a company deals with an employee; that is a father’s heart towards his children.

2. The Supreme Expression on the Hill of Golgotha

In the same way, Jesus’ love is just like this. Paul says: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

God did not wait until we had done things right before he loved us; while we were still unworthy, he laid down his life for us. He showed by his actions that what he wants is not “getting it right” but “the heart coming home”. This is the supreme expression of love prevailing over law.

Please don’t misunderstand: love prevailing over law does not mean abolishing the law. Paul says: “Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law.” (Romans 13:10) Love is not the enemy of the law; love is the fulfilment of the law. The law can draw boundaries, but it has no power to give anyone a new heart; only love can make a person willing from within.

The Lord Jesus quoted the prophet Hosea: “But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you wouldn’t have condemned the guiltless.” (Matthew 12:7) Sacrifice is the “task”; mercy is the “heart”. Once religion is reduced to nothing but tasks, it begins to condemn; for being right without love always ends up wounding.

Paul also says: “If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:2) Power, knowledge, faith — all three are the very peaks of “getting things done”; without love, God’s verdict is: I am nothing.

3. Three Parables of God Seeking People

In Luke 15 the Lord tells three parables in a row: the lost sheep, the lost coin, the prodigal son. Three parables, one theme — God wants to find and bring back what was lost.

“Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep, and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?” (Luke 15:4) By a company’s arithmetic this doesn’t pay: leaving ninety-nine per cent behind for the sake of one per cent. But by a family’s arithmetic it goes without saying: if the one who went missing were your child, would you go and look?

The scene of the prodigal’s homecoming paints God’s heart even more vividly: “He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” (Luke 15:20)

Brothers and sisters, look at this father. He “saw him” — which means he had been watching every day. He “ran” — in the Middle Eastern culture of the time, for an elder of standing to hitch up his robes and run was undignified, but the father didn’t care about his own dignity; he cared only about his son coming home. First he embraced him, first he kissed him, and only then did he hear out the confession his son had rehearsed.

Notice: the father did not settle accounts first. It wasn’t that he didn’t know his son had squandered the family’s wealth; he won the person first, then dealt with the matter. And the elder brother — sullen, every sentence a reckoning of accounts — was the one who stayed at home yet lived like an employee: “Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours” (Luke 15:29). That is the classic picture of living in a family as though it were a company.

Paul goes straight to the heart of it: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4) What leads people to repentance is not intimidation, but kindness.

4. Confirmation from Facts and Famous Sayings

Human beings were made, from the very beginning, longing to be loved, not longing to be graded.

In the 1950s the psychologist Harry Harlow carried out his famous experiments with rhesus monkeys. He gave infant monkeys two “surrogate mothers”: one made of wire, fitted with a feeding bottle that supplied food; the other made of soft cloth, with no milk at all, but soft and warm. The result: the little monkeys went to the wire mother only when they were hungry, and as soon as they had fed they went straight back to the cloth mother, clinging to her for more than ten hours a day; and whenever they were frightened, they always rushed to the cloth mother. Harlow’s conclusion shook the academic world of his day: the comfort of contact, more than the supply of food, is the foundation of attachment.

Brothers and sisters, if the church is only a “wire mother” — fully functional, with complete procedures and an unfailing supply of milk — people will feed and leave. If the church is a “cloth mother” — with warmth, with open arms — people will make their home there.

Then there is Harvard University’s Study of Adult Development, launched in 1938, which has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has summed up its clearest finding many times: what truly makes people healthy, happy and long-lived is not fame, wealth or achievement, but good relationships.

Eighty years of research, boiled down to a single sentence: relationships are the greatest asset of a person’s life. Isn’t that exactly what the Bible has been saying all along?

Mother Teresa is generally held to have said: “If you judge people, you have no time to love them.” Brothers and sisters, we have twenty-four hours a day. Spend them judging, and there’s no time left for love; spend them loving, and many of the things that seemed to need judging resolve themselves.

In his Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Augustine left us a famous saying: “Love, and do what you will.” He did not mean anything goes; he meant that when there is truly love in a person, what he does will naturally not harm others. Love is the deepest standard of all.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

sections.heading: The first of the Three Foundations of the 321 vision is this: Jesus is my role model.
sections.html:
The third point of this lesson sets that very role model before our eyes. As God treated Adam, so we treat the brother who has fallen; as the father ran towards the prodigal, so we run towards the one who has left the church; as Jesus asked Peter by the lake, “Do you love me?”, so after a co-worker makes a mistake we first ask, “Are you all right?”

The second foundation: the Bible is my standard. Not my emotions, not my habits, not that old Chinese mindset, “Beating is affection and scolding is love.” The Bible says, “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” — that is the standard.

The third foundation: the Holy Spirit is my guide. In those three seconds, we can’t hit the brakes in our own strength; only the Holy Spirit can. Among the fruit the Holy Spirit bears are “patience, kindness, goodness, … gentleness, and self-control” (see Galatians 5:22–23) — every one of them exactly what we lack most in that moment.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. When I let Jesus reign as King in those three seconds, my reaction is no longer my temper but his character; and when someone is restored because of how I reacted, the glory goes to Jesus, not to my “principles”.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system is not a beautifully engineered machine of procedures, but a family of flesh and blood who love one another.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From a Company Culture Back to a Family Culture
sections.html:
1. The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

Why does a church turn into a company without noticing? Because inside each of us there is a “self”.

When we are self-centred, we value results above people, because results can prove me; when we are self-centred, we can’t bear others making mistakes, because their mistakes will drag me down; when we are self-centred, we rush to correct, because I need to show that I’m right. Pride is the root of the problem; the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall.

The 321 vision puts it very clearly: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Adam fell because he wanted to leave his originally intended position, seize rights and take the place of God; whereas humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When a co-worker slips up and I lay down my own face first, I am returning to my originally intended position as a human being; when I trust the Holy Spirit to work in his heart, I am letting God be God.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Only a selfless person can say, at the very moment someone has dented the car, “As long as you’re all right, that’s what matters.”

2. The Priority of Relationships: First with God, Then with Ourselves, Then with Others, and Last of All with Things

sections.heading: The 321 vision reminds us of the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.
sections.html:
A company’s order is exactly the reverse: things first; when things won’t move, deal with people; when people can’t be dealt with, deal with yourself; and only last of all, in the dead of night, think of God. No wonder we are so busy, so tired and so empty.

Put the order back the right way round: early in the morning, align yourself with God first; then allow yourself to be a limited human being; then see the people around you; and only last of all look at the task. You’ll be surprised to find that it’s often not as big as you thought.

3. A Shift in Perspective

From man’s point of view to God’s point of view; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

From man’s point of view, a car is money; from God’s point of view, a child is a heritage. From an earthly point of view, a botched Sunday is a failure; from a heavenly point of view, it is an opportunity to shepherd. From a temporary point of view, all that matters is getting the job done; from an eternal point of view, it is people’s hearts that will be carried into eternity.

Brothers and sisters, the results of “getting the task done” are temporary; the influence of “winning the heart” is eternal. A task can be done over again, but once a person’s heart is broken, it is hard to mend.

4. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

The 920 practice: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”. Before them, I practise living out the “0” — a life of selflessness — and let the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in me in all nine of its expressions: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (see Galatians 5:22–23).

Look: not one of these nine graces is “efficiency”; not one is “performance”. The fruit God wants all grows within relationships. When a co-worker makes a mistake, patience and kindness have a chance to come into play; when family members disappoint us, gentleness and self-control have a training ground. It turns out that God allows those difficult people into our lives precisely so that we will bear fruit.

235 relationships: with a selfless person, become a “2” — spiritual companions; build up a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, not one of these three layers of relationship is built by systems; every one of them is built by “winning the heart”. A company can only give you colleagues; only a family can give you spiritual parents and spiritual children.

5. The Path of Serving

The 321 Path of Serving is: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. First let the Holy Spirit guide; then let Scripture shine its light so that we gain understanding; understanding enters into life; life brings forth service; and finally all the glory is given to God.

Notice that “Service” comes fourth. We often put it first, and so we end up with service but no life, ministry but no relationships. Today’s lesson is asking us to put the order back the right way round.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. The 321 vision reminds us that changing our mindset follows eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. Let’s use these eight stages to take the three practices deeper.

Practice 1: Ask the Holy Spirit to Shine on Your True Focus

Think back to the last thing that made you angry or disappointed — were you valuing the success or failure of the task, or that person’s heart? Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on your true focus.

Information: first, write down what happened. The time, the place, who was involved, what happened, what I said, what my tone was like. Don’t comment; just record.

Revelation: bring that piece of paper before God, be still for three minutes, and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: in that moment, what was my heart really protecting? Was it God’s house, or my own face?

Conviction: admit that I really do often value tasks above people. Admitting it is not beating myself up; admitting it is agreeing with God’s view.

Implementation: this week, when a similar situation comes up again, silently count to three first, and first ask: “Are you all right?”

Evaluation: at the weekend, look back: how many times this week did I see the person first? How many times did I see the task first again?

Correction: identify the times and settings where you are most likely to slip — usually when you’re tired, when you’re pushing to meet a deadline, or over the things you care about most. Prepare in advance for those moments.

Repetition: don’t do this for just one week. For a mindset to become life, we have to walk the same road again and again.

Multiplication: tell a brother or sister about your experience, and invite them to practise with you. Only those who have been won will go and win others.

Practice 2: Take the Initiative to Respond in Love to Someone Who Has Disappointed You

Find someone who has disappointed you, and take the initiative to respond to them in love. Not to correct them, but to restore the relationship.

Information: in your heart, write down that name. Not a long list — just one.

Revelation: ask God to let you see their situation — what were they carrying at the time? Why did they act that way? Much of what we take for malice is really someone else’s heavy burden.

Conviction: believe the Lord’s word: “And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.” (1 Peter 4:8)

Implementation: this week, take one concrete action. A phone call, a breakfast together, a sincere message. Don’t bring up the past, don’t slip in any correction; simply express your care.

Evaluation: after you’ve acted, note down what you felt inside. You’ll find that the first heart to soften is often your own.
