Correction: if the other person responds coldly, don’t give up, and don’t push hard either. Love is patient and enduring; it isn’t a lightning campaign.

Repetition: let caring become a habit, not a one-off special effort.

Multiplication: when the relationship is restored, the two of you become a testimony to others — broken relationships really can be mended.

Practice 3: If Jesus Were Me, What Would Jesus Do?

When you face pressure in ministry, meditate on this: “If Jesus were me, what would Jesus do?” Learn to replace rules with love, and demands with relationship.

Information: write your biggest pressure in ministry right now as a single sentence.

Revelation: read the Gospel accounts of how Jesus dealt with failure and weakness — questioning Peter by the lake (John 21), treating the woman caught in adultery (John 8), speaking to Martha (Luke 10). See how he did it.

Conviction: believe that Jesus’ way is not only more loving but also more fruitful. In three and a half years he won the hearts of twelve men, and those twelve men turned the world upside down.

Implementation: at your next team meeting, make the first item on the agenda “How are you doing this month?”, and put the review after it.

Evaluation: watch your co-workers’ faces and what they say. Has the atmosphere changed? Has anyone begun to speak honestly?

Correction: if there are things you really must require, require them after the relationship has been built; and when you do, explain the reasons rather than simply issuing orders.

Repetition: let “ask about the person first, then about the task” become your team’s culture.

Multiplication: when your co-workers begin treating others the same way, the family culture is multiplying.

The Lord Jesus said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30) Brothers and sisters, if our service makes people’s loads heavier and heavier, we may already have swapped his yoke for another.

A Gentle Reminder

The law can make people do the right thing; only love can make people live out the right heart.

When the church turns from a “company culture” back to a “family culture”, service will once again be full of vitality and joy.

The early church was just such a family: “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.” (Acts 2:46–47) Notice the order: first glad and sincere hearts, then the favour of all the people, and then the Lord adding to their number day by day. People were not added by systems; they were drawn in by love.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Choose Love, Choose Relationship, Choose to Win the Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s walk back over today’s road once more.

First, a church that values getting tasks done is like a company; a church that values winning hearts is like a family. A company runs on rules; a family runs on love. A company breeds the heart of a slave; a family breeds the heart of a son.

Second, look at your reactions and you’ll know whether what you care about is the task or the heart. Those three seconds don’t lie. A true leader knows how to turn failure into an opportunity to win the heart.

Third, God himself is our example. In Eden he asked, “Where are you?” At Golgotha he proved that “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” What he wants is not “getting it right” but “the heart coming home”.

“Getting the task done” may make people admire you, but “winning the heart” makes people trust you. God’s purpose is not to build a perfect system, but to restore broken relationships.

So this morning I want to issue a call to you, brothers and sisters: let Jesus be King in your reactions.

Let him reign as King in the three seconds before you open your mouth; let him reign as King in your team meetings; let him reign as King at your dinner table and in the tone of voice you use with your children. When Jesus is King, the family comes back; when the family comes back, the people come back; and when the people come back, the task gets done of itself.

May all the glory go to Jesus. Not to our systems, not to our results, but to the Lord who loved us first, while we were still unworthy.

Let us learn from his example: choose love, choose relationship, choose to “win the heart” — for only by winning hearts can we truly win the heart of God.

keyVerses: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
“Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)
declarations: Lord, I want to learn your ways — no longer valuing results and performance, but valuing people’s hearts. Give me eyes of compassion, so that in every act of service I may win people’s hearts and win your pleasure.
practices: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on your true focus
Take the initiative to respond in love to someone who has disappointed you
If Jesus were me, what would Jesus do?
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

In Eden you did not first ask us what we had done; you first asked, “Where are you?” On the hill of Golgotha you did not wait for us to become good; while we were yet sinners, you died for us. Lord, when you love us, it is our hearts you love first.

Please forgive us. We have often run your house like a company — replacing relationship with rules, replacing love with demands, measuring the worth of our brothers and sisters by results. And often, when others have fallen, we have seen the incident first, and not the person.

Lord, give us a heart of compassion; give us the wisdom to be slow to anger; give us the strength, in those three seconds, still to fix our eyes on you. Holy Spirit, bear in us the fruit of patience, kindness and gentleness.

Help us to put life first, then relationships, then ministry; let it be no longer we who live, but Christ who lives in us. Reign as King in our homes, our church and our teams, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9) God’s first question after humanity sinned was a question about relationship, not about the deed. Think back to the last time you dealt with someone else’s failing: what were your first words? If you could do it again, what would you say?

“For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15) In the community you serve, which areas are more like a “company”, and which are more like a “family”? This week, what one concrete thing could you do to make it more like a family?
l035.title: The Church Is a Family, Not a Company
l035.subtitle: Winning the Heart Matters More Than the Task (Part 2)
l035.partTitle: Unit 3 · The Beginning of Revival — Revival Starts from the Heart

sections.heading: 2. Introduction: The Day They Wanted to Stone Him
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Before we open the Bible, I’d like you to close your eyes and let me take you into a scene.

Dusk in the wilderness. A weary, dust-covered column of men crests the last ridge. Three days on the road, grimy from head to foot, yet their hearts are light — in another quarter of an hour they’ll be home. Home means a wife, children, hot soup, a lamp in the window.

Then they look up, and they freeze. The town is gone. Where the walls should stand there are only blackened ruins; where the cooking smoke should rise, there is the black smoke of embers still smouldering. Scripture records that moment in the plainest of words: “When David and his men came to the city, behold, it was burned with fire; and their wives, their sons, and their daughters were taken captive.” (1 Samuel 30:3)

The next verse gives us one of the most heartbreaking pictures in the whole Old Testament: “Then David and the people who were with him lifted up their voice and wept until they had no more power to weep.” (1 Samuel 30:4)

Brothers and sisters, these were six hundred men who had been to war and seen blood. They were not weak men. Yet that day they sat on scorched earth and wept until there was no weeping left in them. Even David’s own two wives had been carried off (1 Samuel 30:5). This was not someone else’s crisis. This was David’s own.

And worse was still to come. When the weeping ran dry, it turned into a roar. Scripture says, “David was greatly distressed; for the people spoke of stoning him.” (1 Samuel 30:6a)

Who was saying this? Not the Philistines, not Saul’s pursuing troops — it was his own brothers. The old guard from the cave of Adullam, the men who had nowhere left to go, whom he had taken in and personally shaped into warriors. These very men now stood with stones in their hands, ready to kill their own leader.

When people are in unbearable pain, they need someone to carry that pain. The handiest target is often the one standing nearest, standing highest, and loving us most. When crisis strikes, the first person to have stones thrown at them is often the one who has given the most.

If the story stopped there, it would be the tragedy of a leader devoured by his own followers. But right in the middle of this verse, Scripture places one small turning word — “but”.

“But David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.” (1 Samuel 30:6b)

Brothers and sisters, that little word “but” is the doorway into this lesson. On one side of the door lie collapse, blame, and more than a decade of relationship wiped out overnight. On the other side lie pursuit, recovery, a team bound closer than ever — and, a few years later, all the tribes of Israel coming to him at Hebron and saying, “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh.” (2 Samuel 5:1)

One crisis, two possible endings. The dividing line was not the circumstances; it was where his heart turned in that moment.

There’s a widely quoted saying: adversity doesn’t build character, it reveals it. That is half right. From the Bible’s point of view, adversity doesn’t only reveal our heart; it also forms our heart — because in adversity our heart is forced to make a choice: to turn towards God or to turn in on ourselves; to throw a rope, or to throw a stone.

That is why today’s lesson is called “A Crisis Is an Opportunity to Win the Heart”. Winning the heart here has three layers: in the crisis, we win back our own heart; in the crisis, we win the hearts of others; and in the end, in the crisis, we win the heart of God.

Brothers and sisters, the crisis you are going through right now — that misunderstanding, that quarrel, that relationship that keeps you awake at night, that trouble with no way out in sight — God has allowed it to come to you not to destroy your relationships, but to rebuild them right there. A crisis is not the end of a relationship; a crisis is a turning point in a relationship.

Today we will look at three things together: first, a crisis is an opportunity to win people’s hearts; second, in a crisis, whether we throw stones or throw a rope — our response decides the relationship; third, those who pay the price of loving from the heart will in the end win people’s hearts.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Background: A Fugitive, a Ragtag Band and a Burned-Out Town
sections.html:
To understand 1 Samuel 30, we first need to stand back a little and get a clear view of the lie of the land in this stretch of history.

[Author and Composition] First and Second Samuel were originally one book; they were divided into two only in the Septuagint. 1 Chronicles 29:29 says, “Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the history of Samuel the seer, and in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the history of Gad the seer.” Tradition has therefore held that the book’s material comes from the records of these three prophets. The book covers roughly the mid-eleventh century BC to the early tenth century BC — exactly the turning point when Israel passed from the time of the judges into the age of the kings.

[Audience and Purpose] This book is not a flattering court chronicle; it is “theological history”. It sets out to answer a sobering question: Israel asked for a king “like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5) — and what came of it? Saul was the ideal king in the people’s eyes, tall and imposing; David was the king after God’s own heart. Scripture spelled out the difference between the two kings long beforehand: “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7b)

Brothers and sisters, please remember that sentence. It is the key to the whole of Samuel, and it is the key to this lesson too. From beginning to end, the book is saying one thing: what God wants is the heart.

[Historical Setting] After Saul became king he increasingly went his own way, and God sent Samuel to anoint a young man from Bethlehem named David. David killed Goliath and won great victories in battle, but what he earned in return was Saul’s jealousy and Saul’s spear. From chapter 21 onwards, David enters roughly ten years as a fugitive. He flees first to Nob, then to Gath, where he feigns madness, and then he hides in the cave of Adullam.

Adullam lies in the Shephelah, the foothills of Judah, a dozen or so kilometres south-west of Bethlehem, a hill country riddled with limestone caves. It was in that cave that something happened which would shape the history of Israel: “Everyone who was in distress, everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was discontented, gathered themselves to him; and he became captain over them. There were with him about four hundred men.” (1 Samuel 22:2)

[Ziklag] Later, to escape Saul, David took six hundred men and went over to Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, and Achish gave him the border town of Ziklag (1 Samuel 27:6). It lay close to the wilderness and was easy prey for nomadic raiders. David lived there for a year and four months, the darkest stretch of his life — living under another man’s roof, guarding every word, covering every move.

[The Amalekites] In the very days when David had marched north with the Philistine army and then been sent back by the Philistine commanders, the Amalekites seized their chance and plundered Ziklag. They were Israel’s age-old enemy, who on the road out of Egypt had made a practice of attacking the weary stragglers at the rear (Deuteronomy 25:18). But this time they killed no one; they only took people captive as slaves — God’s providence is often hidden in details that look like mere chance.

[Context] Chapter 30 is sandwiched between two great events: before it, Saul, at the end of his rope, goes to the medium at Endor (chapter 28); after it, Saul falls in battle on Mount Gilboa (chapter 31). The contrast is glaring: at the same time, in the same land, Saul in his extremity consults a spirit of the dead, while David in his extremity inquires of Yahweh. Saul lost a kingdom; David won back hearts.

Brothers and sisters, both men met a crisis. The crisis did not decide how their stories ended; where their hearts turned in the crisis decided it.

Around 1010 BC Saul died in battle, and David became king of Judah at Hebron; seven and a half years later he became king over all Israel. Yet the true foundation of his throne was not the anointing oil at Hebron but the scorched earth of Ziklag — the choice he made on that field of ruins.

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 1: A Crisis Is an Opportunity to Win People’s Hearts
sections.html:
1. David’s Kingdom Was Built on Human Hearts

Brothers and sisters, let’s begin with a question: what was David’s kingdom built on?

Not on military force — at most he had six hundred men under him. Not on power — after he was anointed he waited more than ten years for the throne, and for much of that time he didn’t even have a town to call his own. Not on family background — he was the youngest son of a shepherd family in Bethlehem.

David’s kingdom was built on winning people’s hearts.

Scripture records that beginning very clearly: “Everyone who was in distress, everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was discontented, gathered themselves to him; and he became captain over them. There were with him about four hundred men.” (1 Samuel 22:2)

All three of these terms are heavy in Hebrew. “In distress” is מָצוֹק (matsoq), a situation of being oppressed, pushed into a corner, unable to breathe. “In debt” refers to people saddled with debts, hounded by creditors, liable at any moment to see their whole family sold into slavery. “Discontented” is מַר־נֶפֶשׁ (mar nephesh) in the original, literally “bitter of soul” — not a passing bad mood, but a bitterness built up over long years, bitter to the bone.

In other words, the people who gathered in the cave of Adullam were the bottom rung of that society, the people nobody wanted. In today’s terms: the indebted, the accused, the abandoned, the depressed, the angry. A crowd like that, thrown together, usually turns into a band of outlaws.

Yet years later, these people had become the famous “mighty men of David”, their names recorded one by one in 2 Samuel 23 and still read aloud to this day.

What happened in between?

Nothing else. Just this: there was one man who welcomed them at their very worst, who slept beside them in the cave, went hungry with them, fled with them, wept with them, and knew every one of them by name. He won their hearts, and so he won their whole lives.

2. A Crisis Is a Chance for Heart to Meet Heart

Brothers and sisters, please notice something: David’s bond with these men was not built in good times; it was built in crisis.

Good times don’t make people love one another; good times only make people get along. What really welds two hearts together is usually the hardship they have walked through side by side. This is a spiritual principle, and it is also something psychology has confirmed.

In 2000, Shelley E. Taylor, a psychologist at the University of California, Los Angeles, and her colleagues put forward the “tend-and-befriend” theory. Until then, research on the stress response had spoken only of “fight or flight”; Taylor pointed out that under stress people have another path open to them: to look after those around them and to form alliances with others.

This explains why a crisis is so often a watershed for a relationship. The very same pressure can push people towards “fight or flight” — attacking the other person or walking away from them; or it can push them towards “tend and befriend” — drawing near to the other person and holding them up. The pressure itself is neutral; our heart decides which way it goes.

Another, even weightier, line of research is the “post-traumatic growth” described in 1995–1996 by Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun of the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. They found that a significant proportion of people, after a major trauma, do not merely “recover” but actually grow beyond their former selves in five areas — and the second of these is deeper relationships with others.

A crisis will tear some relationships apart, and it will weld others fast. The only difference is how we respond in the crisis. When a grain of sand gets inside an oyster’s shell and the oyster cannot expel it, it secretes layer upon layer of nacre to wrap up the irritation; year after year, the place that hurt most becomes the smoothest place of all. Brothers and sisters, the oyster can’t choose whether the sand gets in; it can only choose how to respond to it. So it is with you and me.

3. Ziklag: First He Won Back His Own Heart

Now back to the scorched earth of Ziklag. What was David’s first move?

“But David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.” (1 Samuel 30:6b)

“Strengthened himself” is a single word in Hebrew: חָזַק (chazaq), meaning to take firm hold, to make strong, to make firm. And here it is in the reflexive stem (Hitpael), so it reads literally: “David made himself strong in Yahweh his God.”

That word tells us three things. First, this is an action, not a feeling; what David felt at the time was “greatly distressed”, not strong at all. Second, it is an active choice; no prophet, no priest, no friend came to comfort him — he had to lift himself up. Third, this strength has a definite location — “in Yahweh his God”, not in his own willpower, nor in his past victories.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the 321 vision means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. David did not first go and quell the mutiny, did not first explain that “this isn’t my fault”, did not first count how many fighting men he had left. He dealt first with his relationship with God; he first let his own heart stand firm in God.

The priority of relationships is this: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Skip the first step and go straight to handling people and things, and all you will produce is a bigger mess — a person whose own heart is in turmoil cannot steady anyone else’s.

His second move was also crucial: “David inquired of Yahweh, saying, ‘If I pursue after this troop, will I overtake them?’ He answered him, ‘Pursue; for you will surely overtake them, and will without fail recover all.’” (1 Samuel 30:8) Stand firm first, then inquire, and only then act. Brothers and sisters, the crisis is never the problem; the direction we take in the crisis is the problem.

4. He Won Back What Was Lost — and Won Back Hearts

David caught up with the Amalekites, fought them for a day and a night, and recovered every captive and every possession. Scripture stresses that nothing was missing, small or great, sons or daughters or spoil (1 Samuel 30:18–19). God had said “you will without fail recover all”, and truly not one was lost.

But the really remarkable part is what happened on the way back.

During the pursuit, two hundred men had been too exhausted to go on, and they stayed by the brook Besor to guard the baggage. When the victorious army returned, “Then all the wicked men and worthless fellows, of those who went with David, answered and said, ‘Because they didn’t go with us, we will not give them anything of the plunder that we have recovered, except to every man his wife and his children, that he may lead them away, and depart.’” (1 Samuel 30:22)

Do you see it? Brothers who had only just wept together and fought together turned round in an instant and drew a line among their own: you don’t deserve it.

David’s reply is one of the finest things he ever said: “Who will listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down to the battle, so shall his share be who stays with the baggage. They shall share alike.” (1 Samuel 30:24)

Then Scripture adds a footnote rich with meaning: “It was so from that day forward, that he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this day.” (1 Samuel 30:25)

Feel the weight of that sentence. A decision one man made in the aftershocks of a crisis became the law of a nation for centuries. Our response in a crisis never affects only that one day; it becomes a family’s way of life, a team’s culture, a church’s constitution.

That day David taught his people three things: we are one body, not an interest group; faithfulness behind the lines is as precious as courage on the front line; and the spoil is what Yahweh has given, not what we have earned (1 Samuel 30:23).

Those three things are what the 321 vision means by “people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things”. However great the treasure, it was not worth as much as the hearts of those two hundred brothers. David recovered the treasure, and more than that, he recovered people’s hearts. This crisis turned him from “a captain with six hundred men” into “a king with six hundred hearts”.

Brothers and sisters, the crisis you are walking through may be God’s opportunity for you to win a heart. What God wants you to win back there may not be that sum of money, that position or that sense of justice, but a person’s heart.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 2: Throw a Stone or Throw a Rope — Our Response Decides the Relationship
sections.html:
1. Our Most Natural Response Is to Throw Stones

Brothers and sisters, notice the action in 1 Samuel 30:6 that was never carried out: “the people spoke of stoning him.”

A stone is the handiest thing in a crisis. It lies right at your feet; no learning, no practice, no money needed — just bend down and pick it up. And throwing a stone brings an instant rush of relief — the pain in my heart gets passed on to someone else.

Of course, today we don’t literally throw stones. What we throw is a remark that drags up the past, a cold look, a forwarded message, a deliberate silence. The stone has changed its shape, but not its purpose — it’s all meant to make the other person hurt, to let them know they are the one in the wrong.

From the 1970s onwards, the psychologists John Gottman, of the University of Washington, and Robert Levenson, of the University of California, Berkeley, recorded married couples’ conflict conversations in the laboratory and analysed facial expressions, tone of voice and heart rate second by second. Research they published in 1992 showed that simply by observing a couple’s patterns of interaction during conflict, they could predict with considerable accuracy whether that couple would later divorce.

They identified four especially destructive responses, which they called “the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse”: criticism (attacking the person rather than addressing the issue), contempt (eye-rolling, sarcasm, looking down on the other), defensiveness (I’m not wrong, it’s all you), and stonewalling (simply refusing to talk and shutting the other person out).

Brothers and sisters, these four things are four kinds of stone. And you’ll notice that on that day at Ziklag, all four stones flew at David: they criticised him, they despised him, they pinned the blame on him, and in the end they wanted to finish the conversation with stones.

Another important finding of Gottman’s is the “five to one” ratio: in stable relationships, positive interactions outnumber negative ones by roughly five to one. Throw one stone, and it takes five moments of warmth to make up for it. Brothers and sisters, what a costly price. We often spend three seconds throwing a stone, and then three years repairing the damage.

2. Why It Is So Easy to Throw Stones in a Crisis

Physiologically, this is not hard to understand. In the 1990s the New York University neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux showed that sensory signals can take a “shortcut”, bypassing the cerebral cortex and going straight to the amygdala, so that we react before we have thought anything through; in his 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, the psychologist Daniel Goleman called this phenomenon “amygdala hijack”.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us an important reminder: in a crisis, the one thing you can least rely on is your brain in that moment.

The 321 vision has a very down-to-earth saying: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. The moment a crisis hits, the brain runs faster than anyone — it analyses for you who is right and who is wrong, drafts the indictment for you, and works out exactly how much you’ve been short-changed. The faster the brain spins, the colder the heart grows.

In that moment David did not rely on his brain; he relied on his heart. “Strengthened himself in Yahweh his God” is not an act of thinking; it is an act of turning. He turned his heart away from six hundred angry faces and towards the face of God.

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The word “keep” carries the Hebrew sense of guarding, of keeping watch at a city gate. When a crisis comes, the most important thing is not to save face, not to win the argument, but to guard the gate of your heart and not let bitterness in.

3. Those Who Rely on the Heart Choose to Throw a Rope

Brothers and sisters, “throwing a stone” and “throwing a rope” look very alike from the outside — both involve bending down, reaching out and throwing something towards the other person. There is only one difference: once a stone is thrown, it’s gone; when a rope is thrown, this end is still held tight in my hand.

That is the cost of throwing a rope: you have to hold on and not let go, you have to be pulled and strained, you have to keep your footing, and your palms may even be rubbed raw. When you save someone who is falling, this end of the rope is bound to hurt.

Jesus is the one who throws a rope better than anyone. A crowd shoved a woman caught in adultery in front of him, their hands full of stones. Jesus said, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” (John 8:7b) One by one the stones dropped to the ground. Finally he said to her, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:11b)

On the cross, with stones thrown at him to the very limit, what he threw back was still a rope: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” (Luke 23:34a)

Paul spells out the technique of this rope in fine detail: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:1–2)

Two Greek words here are worth remembering. “Restore” is καταρτίζω (katartizō); in Matthew 4:21 it is used of fishermen “mending” their nets, and in medicine it was used of setting a dislocated joint back in place. It means not condemning, not cutting off, but mending, putting back, making something usable again.

“Gentleness” is πραΰτης (prautēs). In ancient Greek, this word described a spirited horse that had been tamed — its strength not diminished in the least, only brought entirely under its master’s control. Gentleness is not weakness; gentleness is strength that refuses to abuse its strength.

Brothers and sisters, the one who throws stones often feels very powerful, but in fact he has simply lost control; the one who throws a rope looks as though he is giving way, but in fact his strength is held in the hand of God.

Japan has a craft for repairing ceramics called “kintsugi”, which joins broken pieces with lacquer mixed with powdered gold. Kintsugi does not hide the cracks; instead it traces them out in lines of gold, so that the bowl, because it was once broken, becomes more precious than it was before it broke. This is how God repairs relationships too: he doesn’t pretend the cracks aren’t there; he traces them out in the gold of grace. The place of breaking becomes the place that bears witness to grace.

4. Pride Leaves Both Sides Wounded; Humility Lets Both Sides Win

The 321 vision puts it bluntly: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Why does throwing stones never win? Because stones draw stones. I throw one, he throws two; I drag up the past once, he drags it up five times. When this battle is over there is no winner, only two wounded people and a relationship that can’t go back to what it was. This is the inevitable end of the self-centred life — I have to prove I’m right, and the price is losing a person.

Humility is not admitting that I was wrong; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position: let man be man and let God be God. The authority to judge belongs to God, not to me; the work of changing hearts belongs to the Holy Spirit, not to me. My only job is to throw the rope.

Paul says, “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” (Romans 12:21) Peter says, “not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.” (1 Peter 3:9) And Solomon sums up the whole technique in one sentence: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1) Whether anger dies down or flares up often depends on the very first sentence out of our mouths.

In Strength to Love, published in 1963, Dr Martin Luther King Jr wrote, “Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.” Those words still speak today to everyone who is holding a stone.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, please think of one specific person. The one who disappointed you, the one who misunderstood you, the one who embarrassed you in the group chat. What are you holding in your hand right now — a stone, or a rope?

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 3: Those Who Pay the Price of Loving from the Heart Will in the End Win People’s Hearts
sections.html:
1. Water from the Well by Bethlehem’s Gate

Brothers and sisters, 2 Samuel 23 records a small incident. So small that it changed the course of no battle, yet Scripture solemnly devotes three verses to it.

At that time David was in the cave of Adullam, and the Philistine army was garrisoned at Bethlehem — the town where he grew up. In the heat and the weariness, David murmured a few words:

“David longed, and said, ‘Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!’” (2 Samuel 23:15)

It was only a homesick man talking to himself — not an order, not addressed to anyone, hardly even a request. But three men heard it.

Without a word, those three men broke through the Philistine camp, fought their way to the well by Bethlehem’s gate, drew water from it, fought their way back again, and carried the water to David (2 Samuel 23:16). For one sentence. For one cup of water.

David took the water, but he would not drink it. He poured it out before Yahweh and said, “Be it far from me, Yahweh, that I should do this! Isn’t this the blood of the men who risked their lives to go?” (2 Samuel 23:17a)

Brothers and sisters, this short account hides two very deep lessons.

2. Why Were They Willing? Because He Loved from the Heart First

The first lesson: why were they willing to do this?

No one forced them; there was no reward, no promotion, and the price of breaking through that camp could well have been death. They were willing for only one reason — this man had once treated them the same way.

They were that very group from the cave of Adullam — the distressed, the indebted, the bitter of soul. It was David who first took them in, first stayed with them, first wept for them on the scorched earth of Ziklag, pursued the enemy for them and divided the spoil equally among them. David loved them first, so they loved him. What they were repaying was not his position; it was his heart.

The apostle John put this principle in one sentence: “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19)

Love never appears out of nowhere; love is a response. The heart you sow into someone today will come back to you at a time you don’t expect and in a way you don’t expect.

But notice this: when David took them in back in the cave, he had no idea that one day someone would break through an enemy camp to fetch him water. If he had known, that wouldn’t have been loving from the heart; that would have been an investment.

“My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18) Loving from the heart is something you do, and very often you do it when no one is watching.

3. He Did Not Drink the Water: Giving People’s Love Back to God

The second lesson goes deeper still: why wouldn’t David drink it?

That cup of water was something he himself had wanted, something others had given him of their own free will; he had every right to drink it. But the moment he looked at that cup, he saw three lives — the water was too heavy, so heavy that only God was worthy of it.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the 321 vision calls “let Jesus receive all the glory”.

For someone who serves, the most dangerous moment is not when stones are being thrown at you; it is when people adore you. Stones hurt when they hit you, and they wake you up; applause tastes sweet when it lands on you, and it lulls you to sleep. How many of God’s servants have stood up under persecution, yet could not stand up under adulation.

What David did was this: the love people brought to him, he passed straight on and poured out before God. He did not refuse that love; he “redirected” it.

This is selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is not grasping. It is not refusing to receive; it is not keeping for ourselves what we receive. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

And again: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:5–7) “Emptied himself” translates the Greek κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to pour oneself out”. Being emptied does not mean becoming zero; it means making room for God to fill.

4. Not Everyone Will Be Moved

And yet, brothers and sisters, we must be honest.

The lesson text says it plainly: even so, not everyone will be moved.

Jesus truly loved his disciples, loved them to this extent: “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” (John 13:1b) “To the end” is the Greek εἰς τέλος (eis telos), which can mean “to the very last” and can also mean “to the utmost, to the limit”. Both meanings are true: he loved to the end of time, and he loved to the very limit of love.

That night he knelt and washed his disciples’ feet one by one, Judas’s feet included. And he knew full well: “When Jesus had said this, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, ‘Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.’” (John 13:21)

In the garden of Gethsemane, Judas came with men armed with swords and clubs and kissed him. The first thing Jesus said to him was: “Friend, why are you here?” (Matthew 26:50a) Right to the last moment, the Lord still called him friend.

Brothers and sisters, winning a heart is a two-way response. We can only take responsibility for our own end — to love with all our heart, all our mind, all our strength. Whether the other person reaches out and takes hold of the rope is their freedom, and it is the work of the Holy Spirit.

“you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.” (Mark 12:30b) Please notice that the measure of love is “all”, not “success”. What God measures in us is whether we have given everything we have; whether it succeeds is God’s business.

So the lesson text puts it well: the purpose of loving from the heart is not to be repaid, but to let God’s love be seen in our relationships.

If you have ever treated someone with a true heart and been let down; ever thrown a rope and had it flung away; ever shed tears for a family or a church and received only cold words in return — brothers and sisters, your love has not been wasted. For “You count my wanderings. You put my tears into your container. Aren’t they in your book?” (Psalm 56:8)

5. Relationships Are Our Most Precious Inheritance

Science, too, bears witness to this spiritual principle.

Since 1938, Harvard University has been running the Harvard Study of Adult Development, now more than eighty years old, tracking the lifelong health and happiness of several hundred participants and their descendants. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, sums up its conclusion very simply: good relationships are the strongest predictor of whether a person will be healthy and happy in later life — stronger than wealth, stronger than fame.

Barbara Fredrickson, then a psychologist at the University of Michigan, proposed the “broaden-and-build” theory between 1998 and 2001: negative emotions narrow a person’s field of vision down to the threat right in front of them, while positive emotions — love, gratitude, joy — broaden the range of a person’s thinking and acting, and over time build up their psychological and social resources. This is exactly the difference between throwing stones and throwing a rope: when we throw stones, our world shrinks to nothing but that person’s fault; when we throw a rope, our world opens up again.

Here’s another picture, this time from nature. When a bone breaks, the body does not grind the break smooth; it grows a “callus” at the fracture, wrapping the break layer upon layer, so that during healing that section is thicker than before, and then it is slowly remodelled into bone that can bear weight. This is also how God repairs relationships: the crack is not erased, but in Christ, deeper understanding, truer humility and firmer trust grow right there.

“We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28) Brothers and sisters, “all things” includes that crisis, and it includes the person who hurt you.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set this lesson back into the framework of the 321 vision, and you’ll see a complete picture.

[The Three Foundations] Jesus is my role model — stones were thrown at him, yet he threw back a rope; he prayed for those who crucified him; he loved his disciples to the end, including the one who would betray him. The Bible is my standard — in a crisis we don’t go by feelings, by arguments or by public opinion, but by the word of God: “not rendering evil for evil”, “overcome evil with good”, “a gentle answer turns away wrath”. The Holy Spirit is my guide — in those three seconds when the amygdala is hijacked, what can stay our hand is not self-cultivation but the Holy Spirit.

[The Two Core Values] Let Jesus be King — in a crisis, the hardest thing to hand over is the “right to judge”; we always feel we have at least the right to decide who is right and who is wrong, and letting Jesus reign as King means putting that authority back into the Lord’s hands. Let Jesus receive all the glory — David would not drink that cup of water but poured it out before Yahweh; he did not take the repair of relationships as his own achievement.

[The Goal] Establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, please notice 1 Samuel 30:25: “It was so from that day forward, that he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this day.” One choice made in one crisis became the institution of a whole nation. This is how a system is born. God’s system does not begin with an organisational charter; it begins with one person making a choice after God’s own heart in a crisis, and then that choice becomes an example, the example becomes a culture, and the culture becomes a system.

[The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless] At the core of throwing stones is the self-centred life — my grievances, my face, my arguments, my sense of justice. At the core of throwing a rope is selflessness — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living that fullness out; for only when I no longer need to prove myself am I truly free.

[Humility Overcomes Pride; Selflessness Overcomes Satan] Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. On the scorched earth of Ziklag, David did not take God’s place and pass judgement on the men holding stones; he returned to his originally intended position: a man who relies on Yahweh. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

[The Fivefold Change] Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. The mindset this lesson sets out to change comes down to one sentence: a crisis is not the end of a relationship; a crisis is an opportunity to win the heart. If this mindset truly gets inside you, your life will grow soft, your daily living will be full of gentle answers, your relationships will be restored one by one, and God’s ministry will grow naturally out of those restored relationships.

[Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry] David’s order on that scorched earth is crystal clear: first he relied on Yahweh (life), then he calmed and treated the people well (relationships), and only last did he establish the kingdom (ministry). People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. How much service gets the task done but drives the people away.

[A Shift in Perspective] From a human point of view, Ziklag was an utter failure; from God’s point of view, it was the foundation ceremony of David’s dynasty. From an earthly point of view, he lost a town; from heaven’s point of view, he gained six hundred hearts. From a temporary point of view, those were the darkest days of his life; from an eternal point of view, those days were written into Scripture and have given strength to countless people for three thousand years. “For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory.” (2 Corinthians 4:17)

[The 920 Practice] Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. In a crisis, that “2” is often at their least lovable. The 920 practice means living the selfless (0) life at precisely that least lovable moment, letting the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in us: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23a) Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that each of these nine graces is exactly what is most needed in a crisis — and hardest to produce? Fruit doesn’t grow in easy times; fruit is borne under pressure.

[The 235 Relationships] David’s life is the best picture of 235. In the cave of Adullam, he and that group of desperate men became one another’s “2” — spiritual companions suffering together. The three mighty men who broke through the camp for him were the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, entrusting their lives to one another and able to carry life onwards. The six hundred finally became “David’s mighty men”, and that is the “5” — a team of spiritual comrades, each in their own role, fighting side by side. And the starting point of that whole team was a cave and a crisis.

“For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” (Ecclesiastes 4:10) Brothers and sisters, God never intended you to walk through a crisis alone.

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three practices. Let’s take them deeper using the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Towards the Person Who Disappointed You, Throw a Rope, Not a Stone

Facing someone who has disappointed or misunderstood you, choose to “throw a rope” rather than “throw a stone” — take the initiative to care, to listen and to repair the relationship.

Information: Today, first write down a name — the person whose name makes your heart tighten the moment you think of them. Then write down what kind of stone you are holding — criticism, contempt, defensiveness or stonewalling?

Revelation: Read Galatians 6:1–2 three times, and ask the Holy Spirit to let you see that God’s heart for this person is to “restore”, not to “deal with”. When you can shed a tear for them, revelation has come.

Conviction: Admit one thing — I am not this person’s judge; I am this person’s brother or sister. Hand the right to judge back to the Lord.

Implementation: Within this week, take one concrete step. No need for big speeches — a message saying hello, a cup of coffee, or a simple “About what happened last time — did I hurt you?” is a rope.

Evaluation: Afterwards, get quiet and ask yourself: was I doing this to repair the relationship, or to prove I’m more mature than they are? When I spoke, was there a stone hidden in my tone?

Correction: If you find a stone still tangled in the rope, throw it again. Correction is not failure; correction is growth.

Repetition: Don’t expect it to work the first time. Gottman’s research reminds us that one negative interaction takes roughly five positive ones to make up for. Keep throwing the rope until it becomes a habit.

Multiplication: When the people around you see that you no longer throw stones, they will learn too. Share your experience with your “2”, and let throwing ropes become the culture of your home and your small group.

Practice 2: Look Back on Your Crises and Count What God Did in Them

Think back on the crises you have been through: didn’t God use them, too, to teach you to love people more deeply? Thank the Lord and respond to him.

Information: Take a sheet of paper, draw a timeline, and mark the three biggest crises of your life.

Revelation: Beside each crisis, write down the people who were around you at the time — who gave you a hand up? And whom did you help up? Ask God to let you see the hand that was there all along.

Conviction: Believe that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28) is not a comforting phrase but a fact.

Implementation: Write a short thank-you today — first to God, then to someone who held you up in a crisis.

Evaluation: Ask honestly, too: is there a crisis for which I am still blaming someone to this day? How long have I been holding that stone?

Correction: In prayer, set them down one stone at a time. Setting it down doesn’t mean they weren’t wrong; it means I am no longer collecting a debt on God’s behalf.

Repetition: Keep this timeline, and every quarter take it out and add a new line. You will see God’s hand more and more clearly.

Multiplication: Share a crisis you have walked through with your small group. Your scars will become someone else’s map.

Practice 3: Keep a Soft Heart Under Pressure

Ask the Holy Spirit to help you keep a soft heart even under pressure, not defending yourself with anger but defusing conflict with love.

Information: Get to know your own “trigger points”. What kind of words, what tone of voice, what kind of situation is most likely to make your face change within three seconds?

Revelation: Understand the truth about those three seconds — when our emotions are triggered, we are relying on the brain and ourselves, not on the heart and the Holy Spirit. Rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled; only by relying on the heart will you be glad.

Conviction: Accept the standard of Proverbs 4:23: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” Guarding your heart matters more than guarding your face.

Implementation: Set yourself a “David’s three seconds”. When someone hits a sore spot, don’t open your mouth yet; say in your heart, “Lord, I turn my heart towards you.” This is what it means to “strengthen yourself in Yahweh your God”.

Evaluation: Every evening, look back: how many times today did I hold the line, and how many times did I lose it? No condemnation — just keep a record.

Correction: Where you lost it, go and apologise that same day. A timely “I’m sorry, I spoke too harshly just now” is worth more than a hundred explanations after the fact.

Repetition: Practise this for forty days in a row. Softness is not an inborn personality trait; softness is a habit the Holy Spirit wears into us day by day.

Multiplication: Teach this “three-second practice” to your children and your co-workers. If a household learns these three seconds, its whole atmosphere will change.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that scorched earth.

A crisis exposes our heart, and it also forms our heart. It is like a fire that burns away our pretences; it is also like a kiln that fires the vessel of our heart until it is stronger.

The lesson text gives us a very warm little reminder: a crisis is not the end of a relationship but the starting point of its renewal. When you choose to respond by relying on the heart rather than on the brain, God can use your softness to win people’s hearts.

So when others throw stones at us, if we are willing to throw a rope, God can turn the relationship around in that very instant and win back people’s hearts.

But, brothers and sisters, I want to take this one step further. We don’t win people’s hearts so that we ourselves can be popular, well connected and admired. What David was truly commended for was not how many hearts he won, but this: “Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart.” (1 Samuel 13:14b) And in the book of Acts God bears witness to him once again: “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.” (Acts 13:22b)

The purpose of winning people’s hearts is to bring people to the Lord who alone is worthy of their hearts. Every rope should, in the end, be tied to the cross.

So this morning, I want to issue a call to you.

First, let Jesus reign as King in your crisis. Not waiting until the crisis is over before letting him reign, but handing him the sovereignty in the most chaotic, most painful, most unwilling moment.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When relationships are restored and hearts are won, don’t drink that cup of water — pour it out before Yahweh.

Third, from today on, be someone who throws a rope. In your home, in your workplace, in your small group, in your church, be the one who reaches out first.

Brothers and sisters, those who love from the heart will in the end win hearts; and those who win hearts will in the end win the heart of God.

May we all, like David, see in every crisis the opportunity God has prepared.

keyVerses: 1 Samuel 30:6

“David was greatly distressed; for the people spoke of stoning him, because the souls of all the people were grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters; but David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.”
Proverbs 4:23
“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”
declarations: Lord, I want to learn, like David, to rely on you in crisis and still to choose love in hardship. Grant me wisdom and courage, so that in every challenge I may become someone who wins people’s hearts.
practices: Towards the one who disappointed you, throw a rope, not a stone
Look back on your crises and count what God did in them
Keep a soft heart under pressure
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
Thank you that through the scorched earth of Ziklag you have shown us that a crisis is not your absence; a crisis is your invitation.

Lord, forgive us. So often under pressure we pick up a stone first, protect ourselves first, look for someone to blame first. We rely on the brain and ourselves, and our hearts grow harder and our relationships grow more distant.

Holy Spirit, help us, when we are misunderstood, not to justify ourselves; when we are let down, not to hold a grudge; and in those three seconds when we most want to throw a stone, to strengthen ourselves in you, as David did.

Lord, we ask you to give those broken relationships back into our hands one by one, and give us the courage to reach out first and throw that rope. Heal, too, the places in our own hearts that are still bleeding, and with your golden thread trace the cracks into marks of glory.

May every heart we win in our lifetime be given to you; may every affliction we suffer in our lifetime work for us an eternal glory. Let Jesus reign as King in our relationships; let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 1 Samuel 30:6: “David was greatly distressed; for the people spoke of stoning him, because the souls of all the people were grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters; but David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.” Please share: what was the most recent crisis that left you “greatly distressed”? In that moment, did you turn first to people, to yourself, or to God? If you could do it again, what would you do?

Galatians 6:1–2: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” Take a quiet minute and think of the person you most want to throw a stone at right now. This week, what kind of rope could you throw to them? Name one specific action, and ask the group to pray for you.
