sections.heading: Introduction: Sand in the Hand, and the Seed in Your Palm
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. In this morning’s devotion, let’s begin by doing a small experiment together.

Please hold out one hand and imagine that you have a handful of fine sand in your palm. If you open your hand and turn your palm upward, the sand rests there, safe and still. But if you are afraid of losing it and clench your five fingers tight, the sand slips out between your fingers, grain by grain, until it is all gone. The tighter you hold it, the faster you lose it. It is a very simple law of physics, and yet it is a very deep spiritual lesson.

I have seen a very real kind of pain in the church. A small-group leader walked with a brother who was new to the faith for three years. He read the Bible with him, stood by him through the loss of his job, stood by him through the lowest point of his marriage, took his calls in the middle of the night and prayed for him in the early morning. After three years, this brother was moved by God and went to another city to pioneer gospel work. By rights, this was the happiest of news. But when the small-group leader came home, there was an empty place in his heart. In prayer he said to God, “Lord, I gave so much — why, in the end, does someone else get to have him?”

That one sentence had already given away where his heart was really anchored. Deep down in his heart, he had always expected that the one who would “have him” would be himself.

Brothers and sisters, I want to say this very gently: this is not the thinking of a wicked person. It is a very common way of thinking, and also a very dangerous one. It shows up in pastors, it shows up in small-group leaders, it shows up in parents, it shows up in everyone who has ever truly given of themselves. The more we give, the more justified this thinking feels. We say, “But I love him!” Yet whether love is real or false usually depends not on how much we have given but on why we gave it; not on how many hearts we have won, but on where we put a heart once we have won it.

On the journey of serving, “winning people’s hearts” is a crucial ability. A servant who cannot win people’s hearts may preach the finest sermons and run the most events, and still be unable to move anyone’s life. But, brothers and sisters, there is a question even more crucial than winning hearts: why do we want to win people’s hearts at all? If we win people’s hearts only for influence, for a sense of achievement, for a sense of security, or for control, then this “love” has already, quietly, gone bad. It still looks very much like love, it still talks very much like love, but its core has been switched from “giving” to “possessing”.

The example of Jesus points us in a completely different direction: he won people’s hearts not to possess them but to complete them. He won us so that we would be restored, would grow and mature, and in the end would become people who can complete others in turn.

So that handful of sand in your palm should not really be treated as sand. It should be treated as seed. Sand is only worth something while you hold it in your hand; seed is only worth something once it is sown in the ground. The Lord Jesus said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) A clenched hand can only keep a single grain; only an open hand can fill the barn at harvest.

True love is not grasping but releasing; truly winning a heart is not possessing but completing.

In this morning’s devotion we will look at three things together: first, we win people’s hearts not to possess them but to complete them; second, we win people’s hearts to help them fulfil what God has entrusted to them; third, a ministry that wins hearts with the heart is light, and a joy.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A “Book of Completing” Sent from a Prison
sections.html:
Our key passage today comes from Ephesians chapter 4. To understand these words, we first need to stand where the writer stood and look around for a moment.

The author of Ephesians is the apostle Paul. The letter opens by saying, “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 1:1). At the start of chapter 3 Paul says, “For this cause I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles” (Ephesians 3:1); and at the start of chapter 4 he says again, “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called” (Ephesians 4:1). By chapter 6, he even calls himself “an ambassador in chains” (Ephesians 6:20).

In other words, this letter — which the church down the ages has called “the summit of the doctrine of the church”, a letter brimming in every line with glory and fullness — was written by Paul as he sat in prison. On the view generally held by evangelical scholars, it was written around AD 60 to 62, during Paul’s first imprisonment in Rome, and together with Philippians, Colossians and Philemon it belongs to the “Prison Epistles”.

It was addressed to the saints in Ephesus. Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, one of the most prosperous cities in the Mediterranean world of that day, and the home of the temple of the goddess Artemis — a temple counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Acts chapter 19 records that the fruit of Paul’s ministry in Ephesus was so great that it shook the idol trade, so much so that Demetrius the silversmith stirred up the whole city in uproar. Paul later said to the elders of Ephesus, “Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.” (Acts 20:31)

Brothers and sisters, please notice this detail: three years, night and day, with tears without ceasing. This is “winning hearts with the heart”. Paul was not a guest speaker parachuted in, not an adviser directing things from a distance; he was a man who shed his tears on the streets of Ephesus. He won the hearts of the Ephesians.

But having won people’s hearts, what did Paul do next?

The structure of Ephesians is very clear. Chapters 1 to 3 speak of “what God has accomplished for us in Christ” — election, redemption, resurrection, being seated with him, unity, unsearchable riches; chapters 4 to 6 speak of “how, therefore, we should walk”. And chapter 4 is exactly the turning point. Paul first speaks of unity (4:1–6), then of gifts (4:7–10), quoting Psalm 68 to say that when Christ ascended on high, he “gave gifts to people” (Ephesians 4:8). And then comes our key passage: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–12).

Here there is an exegetical point of the greatest importance. The ascended Christ gave the fivefold ministry — but for what purpose? Not so that these five kinds of people would do all of the ministry while the whole church sits and watches them perform, but “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving”. The order in the original is this: the saints are perfected, so that the saints will do the work of serving, and the result is that the body of Christ is built up. Pastors do not serve in the saints’ place; pastors equip the saints to serve.

The word “perfecting” (the Chinese Union Version’s “completing”) is καταρτισμός (katartismos) in Greek, and its verb is καταρτίζω (katartizō). The way this word appears in the New Testament is fascinating. Matthew 4:21 says that James and John were “in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets” — that word “mending” is this very word. Galatians 6:1 says, “even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” — that word “restore” is this word too. And in the medical language of ancient Greece, the word was also used for “setting a dislocated bone back in its place”.

Brothers and sisters, put these three pictures together and you have the full definition of what it means to complete someone: mending a torn net, restoring a person who has strayed, setting a dislocated bone back in its place. Have you noticed? Every picture of completing is about putting the other person back in the place where he was always meant to be — not about putting him in my pocket.

The net is mended so it can go back to sea and catch fish, not so it can hang on the wall as a decoration. The bone is set so the hand can work again, not so it can lean on my shoulder for the rest of its life.

This is the lesson we are learning today.

sections.heading: 1. We Win Hearts Not to Possess but to Complete
sections.html:
1. To win our hearts, Jesus paid with his life

To win our hearts, Jesus paid the price of his own life.

Paul says, “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved” (Ephesians 2:4–5). And again, “But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

Please notice the verbs in these two passages: “made us alive” and “reconciled us to himself”. Jesus won our hearts not so that we would become his property, but so that we would come alive out of death and be reconciled out of separation. He does not need us to do anything for him — “He isn’t served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath, and all things” (Acts 17:25) — what he wants is for us to be restored and built up, to become the whole person he has in his heart.

The Lord Jesus himself put it as plainly as it can be put: “even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28)

Brothers and sisters, please say that sentence over quietly to yourself once. He came not to be served. This Lord, who has every right to receive the worship of all peoples, in his work of winning hearts laid down first of all the right “to be served”. John 13:1 says, “Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” And what he did next was take off his outer garment, wrap a towel around himself, kneel down and wash his disciples’ feet.

The highest form of winning hearts is kneeling down.

2. Two ways of winning hearts: Absalom and David

There is a passage in the Bible that describes “winning hearts in order to possess” in a way that makes your heart pound.

2 Samuel chapter 15 records that David’s son Absalom rose early every morning and stood beside the road at the city gate. Whenever anyone had a dispute to bring to the king for judgment, Absalom would call him over, reach out and take hold of him, kiss him, and say to him, “Behold, your matters are good and right; but there is no man deputized by the king to hear you.” And the Bible gives its verdict: “Absalom did this sort of thing to all Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” (2 Samuel 15:6)

Where the Chinese Union Version says Absalom “secretly won the hearts” of Israel, the Hebrew uses the verb גָּנַב (ganav), whose basic meaning is simply “to steal”. The same word appears in the Ten Commandments: “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20:15). So, taken literally — as the World English Bible renders it — this sentence says: Absalom stole the hearts of Israel.

Brothers and sisters, look closely at Absalom’s methods: he stood at the city gate, he took people by the hand, he kissed them, he listened to their grievances, he said exactly what their hearts most wanted to hear. On the outside, all of this looked so much like shepherding, so much like pastoral care, so much like “winning hearts with the heart”. Yet the Bible calls it “stealing”. Why? Because his aim in winning people’s hearts was to seize the throne. What he wanted was not for the people to be completed; what he wanted was for the people to be possessed by him.

And the result? Absalom died hanging in an oak tree, Israel shed the blood of many innocent people, and David wept bitterly in the chamber over the city gate. Pride provokes pride, and both sides are destroyed — this is one of the most sobering warnings of Kingdom 321, and Absalom’s story is its footnote.

His father David, though, took the completely opposite road. We will see it in detail in the second key point: David also won people’s hearts, but he turned and offered those hearts to God.

The same act — winning hearts; two motives — possessing or completing; two endings — destruction or revival. Brothers and sisters, motive is never a small thing.

3. Paul’s self-restraint: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ”

When we win people’s hearts in the church, our aim too should be to “complete”, not to “possess”.

While serving the church in Corinth, Paul said, “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1)

If you read only the first half of that sentence, it sounds arrogant; but the second half is the brake on the whole sentence, and its steering wheel too — “even as I also am of Christ”. Paul is like a mirror: he does not hold on to the light; he reflects the light onto Christ. He did not want people to follow him; he wanted people to follow Christ through him.

In fact, Paul was extremely alert to the danger of “being possessed” by people. As soon as factions appeared in the Corinthian church, he said at once and in no uncertain terms, “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:12–13)

Brothers and sisters, for many who serve, the greatest temptation of their whole lives is not committing some great sin; it is enjoying other people’s dependence on them. When someone says, “I couldn’t live without you,” our hearts secretly taste something sweet. But Paul says: Was Paul crucified for you?

John the Baptist kept this sense of proportion even more beautifully. When his disciples ran to report that everyone was going over to Jesus, John answered, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) Truly godly ministry helps people draw nearer to Jesus through us, not become more dependent on us.

The pastor is the matchmaker, not the bridegroom. Paul says, “For I married you to one husband, that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ.” (2 Corinthians 11:2) If the matchmaker falls in love with the bride himself, the wedding is ruined.

4. Psychology bears witness: the sculptor effect and two kinds of love

Psychological research, from another angle, bears witness to the truth of the Bible.

In 1999, the American psychologists Stephen Drigotas and Caryl Rusbult, with their colleagues, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology their well-known study of the “Michelangelo phenomenon”. They found that in close relationships, when one partner, like a sculptor, can see and support the other’s “ideal self”, helping the other move step by step towards becoming that person, both the couple’s satisfaction with the relationship and each person’s own growth rise significantly; whereas when one partner tries to sculpt the other into “the person I want you to be”, the quality of the relationship actually declines.

Brothers and sisters, the difference between these two is precisely the difference between “completing” and “possessing”. Completing sculpts the other person into the shape God designed; possessing sculpts the other person into the shape I need.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in Life Together, distinguished two kinds of love: human love longs to possess the other person and needs the other’s response to feed itself; spiritual love, though, gladly hands the other person over to Christ and lets Christ be Lord in that person’s life. Human love produces dependence; spiritual love sets people free.

C. S. Lewis, in The Four Loves, said something very honest: to love at all is to be vulnerable. Brothers and sisters, completing has a cost. If you really let go, it will certainly hurt. But that pain is the pain of the grain of wheat falling into the ground, the pain of childbirth — not the pain of loss.

5. Applying 321: from the self-centred life to selflessness

Here the vision of Kingdom 321 gives us the most direct answer.

The root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life, and pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

“Winning hearts in order to possess” is the subtlest form of pride. It isn’t glaring like a fit of temper, it isn’t ugly like greed for money — it even wears the cloak of love. But what it does is take a seat, in someone else’s heart, on the throne that only Jesus is worthy to occupy. That is leaving our originally intended position; that is taking God’s place.

“Winning hearts in order to complete”, on the other hand, is the most practical form of humility. What it does is lift the other person’s heart out of our own hands, place it reverently back before the throne of Jesus, then step aside and say: He must increase, but I must decrease.

Jesus is our role model: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:5–7) “Emptied himself” is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen) in Greek, which means “to pour oneself out”. This is selflessness.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Brothers and sisters, only when we no longer need other people’s dependence to prove our own worth are we truly free. Then you will discover that a ministry of “winning hearts” is free and joyful, because the focus is not on ourselves but on helping others fulfil what God has entrusted to them.

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. That is the conclusion of our first key point.

sections.heading: 2. We Win Hearts to Help People Fulfil What God Has Entrusted to Them
sections.html:
1. Why we rarely see “David’s mighty men” today

Brothers and sisters, let’s face a question that cuts deep: why, in the church today, do we so rarely see people willing to commit themselves, to serve and to lay down their lives for the Lord the way David’s mighty men did?

Some say the times have changed; some say there are too many temptations. There is some truth in both. But the deeper reason, more often than not, is this: no one has truly won their hearts.

When people are driven by a system, all they can act from is duty; but when they are moved by love, they act from the heart. Duty can get someone to turn up on time, but it cannot draw a single tear from him; duty can produce a beautiful serving rota, but it cannot produce a single willing heart. Peter’s exhortation to the elders in 1 Peter 5:2–3 addresses exactly this: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.”

Not under compulsion, but voluntarily. Brothers and sisters, this is what God has always asked of service. And willingness cannot be bought; willingness can only be awakened by love.

2. The cave of Adullam: from four hundred failures, David’s mighty men arise

David was able to raise up mighty men because he treated them sincerely, stayed alongside them, accepted them, and walked with them through hardship.

Let’s look at what this group was like at the start. 1 Samuel 22:1–2 says, “David therefore departed from there, and escaped to Adullam’s cave. When his brothers and all his father’s house heard it, they went down there to him. Everyone who was in distress, everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was discontented, gathered themselves to him; and he became captain over them. There were with him about four hundred men.”

Look at that list: those in distress, those in debt, those who were discontented. In today’s language: people at the end of their rope, people buried in debt, people who were depressed and wounded. This was no elite training programme; these were people on the margins of society. And please note that David himself was a fugitive at the time, hunted by Saul, with no idea what the future held. He had no wages to pay, no positions to hand out, no prospects to promise.

He had only one thing to give — his heart.

Then we turn to 2 Samuel chapter 23. Here thirty-seven mighty men are listed by name, and three of them are the ones who came down to David at the cave of Adullam (2 Samuel 23:13); many from that company in the cave were completed in ranks like these: one who killed eight hundred at one time; one who stood alone in a field full of lentils and struck down the Philistines; one who went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion.

Brothers and sisters, this is one of the greatest stories of “completing” in the Old Testament. Between the cave of Adullam and the roll of mighty men lay not a training course but a heart that truly won their hearts.

David did not change where they came from, but God, through David, changed who they were. This is completing: not keeping people at my side, but bringing them up to the height they were meant to reach.

3. A cup of water he would not drink: winning hearts, yet giving those hearts to God

David’s true greatness lay not in winning the hearts of his mighty men, but in what he did once he had won them.

2 Samuel 23:15–17 records: “David longed, and said, ‘Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!’ The three mighty men broke through the army of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate, and took it and brought it to David; but he would not drink of it, but poured it out to Yahweh. He said, ‘Be it far from me, Yahweh, that I should do this! Isn’t this the blood of the men who risked their lives to go?’”

Brothers and sisters, picture the scene. A scorching wilderness, a parched king, three mighty men who risked death to cross the enemy camp, and a cup of clear water beaded with drops. That water was loyalty at its height, the sweetest fruit of “winning hearts”. Any leader, at that moment, would have felt loved beyond all measure.

What did David do? He poured the water out on the ground.

Not because he wasn’t thirsty, not because he was ungrateful, but because he knew that loyalty like this was too precious — so precious that it was fit to be offered only to God. He did not dare drink that water down himself, because that would have been like swallowing the blood of his mighty men into his own glory.

This is the supreme demonstration of “winning hearts in order to complete”. David won people’s hearts, yet he did not take possession of those hearts; he poured them out before Yahweh and gave them back to God.

Brothers and sisters, how much “water” is carried to us today? Other people’s trust, other people’s admiration, other people’s dependence, other people’s devotion. Do we drink it down, or do we pour it out before Yahweh?

4. Jesus’ intention: that they would do greater things than these

Jesus raised up his disciples with the same heart. He said, “Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father.” (John 14:12)

Please notice the Lord’s words: “he will do greater works than these”. He was not afraid that his disciples would surpass the scale of the work he had done; on the contrary, he hoped they would. What teacher in the world hopes his students will surpass him? What master craftsman hands over every last secret of his trade? Only someone who puts “completing” above “possessing” can do that.

Paul was the same. He said to the Galatians, “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). What he wanted was not for “Paul to be formed in you” but for “Christ to be formed in you”. He said to the Colossians, “We proclaim him, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus; for which I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me mightily.” (Colossians 1:28–29)

To present every man perfect, bringing each one before God — before God, not before me. That sentence ought to be engraved on the heart of everyone who serves.

And Paul’s words to Timothy late in his life carry completing on to a fourth generation: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others — four generations of handing on, in a single verse. This is multiplication.

We win people’s hearts not so that they will do things for us, but so that they can accomplish greater things for God.

5. Science and psychology: the secure base and intrinsic motivation

Contemporary psychology has reached quite consistent findings about “what makes people truly commit”.

In 1985 the American psychologists Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan put forward Self-Determination Theory, which holds that people have three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness; only when these three are met do people develop lasting intrinsic motivation. As early as 1971, Deci had found in an experiment that giving external rewards to people who were already freely engaged actually lowered their willingness to engage of their own accord.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the difference between being “driven by a system” and being “moved by love”. Pressure can push people a little way; only inner drive can carry people for a lifetime.

Gallup’s 2023 State of the Global Workplace report found that only about 23 per cent of employees worldwide are “engaged”; and Gallup’s surveys over many years have shown again and again that “someone at work genuinely cares about me as a person” is one of the strongest predictors of engagement. The church is not a company, but the human heart is the same: if no one genuinely cares, no one will genuinely commit.

Another piece of research comes even closer to the heart of “completing”. Attachment theory, put forward by the British psychiatrist John Bowlby, shows that children who have a “secure base” are actually bolder about leaving their mother to explore the world; children without a secure base become either clingier or more withdrawn.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this finding: the purpose of security is to give people the courage to go out, not to keep them where they are.

The Bible said this long ago with an even more beautiful picture: “As an eagle that stirs up her nest, that flutters over her young, he spread abroad his wings, he took them, he bore them on his feathers.” (Deuteronomy 32:11) The eagle deliberately stirs up the nest so that the eaglets cannot stay comfortable, forcing them to try to fly; but when an eaglet falls, the eagle spreads her wings beneath it and catches it. She stirs the nest so that it will fly; she catches it so that it will dare to fly again. The eagle never means to keep her young in the nest for ever.

The nineteenth-century missionary Hudson Taylor said something that has been quoted far and wide: “If I had a thousand pounds China should have it — if I had a thousand lives, China should have them.” He gave himself away completely, and the result was that the China Inland Mission sent out hundreds upon hundreds of missionaries. Those who truly give themselves away, God gives more people to.

6. Applying 321: the 235 relationships and spiritual multiplication

Kingdom 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Very often our order is upside down: first there is a ministry need, and only then do we go looking for people. The result is that people become parts for getting the ministry done rather than lives to be completed. David’s order was right — he first lived in the cave with those four hundred men and fled with them, building life and relationships first, and the ministry of the mighty men grew naturally out of that.

The “235 relationships” of 321 are a concrete path for completing: with a selfless person you become a “2” — spiritual companions who hold each other up; then you go on to build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on from generation to generation; and finally you become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, building up the body of Christ together.

Brothers and sisters, please notice: neither the 2, the 3 nor the 5 is about drawing people into my circle; each is about sending people out to the place where they are meant to stand. The greatest joy of spiritual parents is not that their children cling to them all their lives, but that their children become spiritual parents themselves.

“We win hearts in order to complete”, in the language of 321, means this: the purpose of winning is multiplication; we hold someone close so that one day we can let go and watch him step out onto his own battlefield.

sections.heading: 3. A Ministry That Wins Hearts with the Heart Is Light, and a Joy
sections.html:
1. Serve with the brain and you’ll be anxious; serve with the heart and you’ll enjoy it

When we serve relying on the brain, we become anxious; when we serve relying on the heart, we enjoy it.

Why? Because when we rely on the brain, the focus is on performance and control; when we rely on the heart, the focus is on love and completing.

Someone who relies on the brain asks: How many people came to the meeting this time? Did I preach well? What do people think of me? These questions share one subject — “I”. Someone who relies on the heart asks: Why was he so quiet today? Has his load been too heavy lately? What is God’s plan for his life? These questions also share one subject — “he”.

Brothers and sisters, it is the same service, but change the subject of the sentence and the weight is completely different.

Kingdom 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. This has its basis in Scripture: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The brain is in charge of calculating; the heart is in charge of life. Calculating wears you out; life grows.

The invitation the Lord Jesus himself gives is this: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

“Light” in Greek is ἐλαφρόν (elaphron), meaning light, not heavy. Please notice: the Lord did not say, “You don’t have to bear a yoke”; what the Lord said was, “My yoke is easy.” Serving still has a yoke, still means walking the road, still makes us sweat; but when we share one yoke with the Lord who is gentle and humble, the weight falls on him, and we simply walk with him.

Heaviness usually comes not from the size of the ministry, but from our carrying things that don’t belong to us — other people’s success or failure, other people’s opinion of us, whether other people will always need us. None of these is the yoke the Lord gives.

2. The picture of parents: hard work, yet joy

When parents look after their children, it is hard work, but in their hearts there is joy.

Getting up in the middle of the night to feed the baby, washing their hands ten times a day, putting up with crying that makes no sense — parents can be exhausted to the point of falling apart. Yet very few parents would say, “I get no sense of achievement from looking after my child.” Why? Because they know that everything they give is so that their child will grow up, mature and be blessed. Once our giving has a direction, our hard work has meaning.

Paul used exactly this picture to describe his ministry: “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8)

When a mother nurses her child, she is feeding it not just milk but her own body. Paul says: not the Good News only, but our own souls as well. This is winning hearts with the heart.

And the father in Luke chapter 15 takes “completing” to its very height. The younger son took his share of the estate, went far away and squandered everything, yet the father sent no one to drag him back. When the son came to his senses and returned, the Bible says, “But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” (Luke 15:20)

In the Near Eastern culture of the time, an elder of standing did not run; to run he had to hitch up his long robe, which was utterly undignified. But this father ran. He laid aside his own dignity just so that he could embrace his son before the son could open his mouth to apologise.

Brothers and sisters, when this father first let his son go, that was respect; when he later ran to meet him, that was compassion. Letting go is not the same as giving up; completing is not the same as indifference. True completing lets him go and fly, and also lets him know that the door of home is always open to him.

3. Psychology bears witness: exhaustion, broadening, and the joy of helping

In 1981 the American social psychologist Christina Maslach set out three dimensions of “burnout”: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment.

The one we most need to watch for is the second — “depersonalisation”, in which helpers begin to treat the people they serve as “cases”, as “numbers”, as items to be processed, and no longer as persons. Brothers and sisters, isn’t that a clinical description of “serving with the brain”? Once people become tasks in our eyes, burnout begins. Turn it the other way: once tasks become people again in our eyes, joy comes back.

On the other side, the “broaden-and-build theory” put forward by the American psychologist Barbara Fredrickson shows that positive emotions broaden the range of people’s thinking and action, and build up lasting physical, mental and social resources. Love and joy don’t just make people feel good; they let people see further and do more.

Harvard’s Study of Adult Development has followed its participants continuously from 1938 to the present day, making it one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in human history. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, sums the study up like this: what truly keeps people healthy and happy throughout their lives is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, this is how God made people when he created us. He did not make us machines that run on performance; he made us people who live by relationships. So when we serve others by winning hearts with the heart, we are not only blessing others; we ourselves are living within the design we were created for — and that is why serving with the heart is something we enjoy.

4. A cycle that multiplies

Serving by winning hearts with the heart not only brings fulfilment to the one who serves; it also lets those who are served feel loved and respected.

People who have been treated sincerely carry a special kind of strength. They have been encouraged and restored, and once that thought in their hearts — “So someone like me is worth loving too” — has been set alight, they turn around and love and serve others in the same way.

John put it most simply: “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) Love has always been caught, not demanded.

When a cycle like this takes hold in the church, it brings real revival. Revival is not a big rally; revival is a group of people who have been completed beginning to complete others; it is spiritual parents bringing forth spiritual children, and spiritual children becoming spiritual parents in turn.

This is exactly the “920 practice” of 321: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; in front of every “2” we practise living out a selfless (0) life; and the result is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, please notice: joy is the second of the nine graces. Joy is not a by-product of serving; joy is the fruit of the Spirit, the natural outcome of a selfless life. The Lord Jesus said, “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:11)

Serving by winning hearts with the heart is a sweet season of working together with God. “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35) is not a moral exhortation; it is a fact of life.

5. Applying 321: the fivefold change begins with the mindset

Kingdom 321 says the fivefold change is in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

In today’s lesson, the first step is a change of mindset.

I used to think: successful ministry means people stay by my side. Now I see: successful ministry means people are sent to where God wants them to go.

I used to think: winning someone’s heart means getting them to need me. Now I see: winning someone’s heart means helping them no longer need me, but need only Jesus.

I used to think: letting go means losing. Now I see: letting go means harvest.

A shift of perspective happens here too: from man’s perspective to God’s — man’s perspective sees “I’ve lost a co-worker”, God’s perspective sees “the kingdom has gained a worker”; from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Brothers and sisters, once the mindset changes, the burden lifts. Because you finally understand: that person was never yours; he is God’s. You are only the wings that bear the eaglet up for a while.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message back within the whole picture of Kingdom 321.

The Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide

Jesus is my role model. He won the hearts of his disciples, yet at the Last Supper he knelt down to wash their feet; he won the hearts of the crowds, yet when they were about to take him by force to make him king, he withdrew to the mountain (John 6:15). He never exploited people’s love for him.

The Bible is my standard. Ephesians 4:12 defines the purpose of ministry — “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ”. We judge whether a ministry is healthy not by its popularity or its size, but by whether the saints are being perfected.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Motives are something no one else can search out; only the Holy Spirit can shine his light on them. “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9) So every day we must ask the Holy Spirit to search us: Lord, the kindness I showed this person today — was it to complete him, or to possess him?

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory

The problem of “winning hearts in order to possess” is, at bottom, a question of the throne. A heart can have only one king. When we get people to depend on us, we are competing with Jesus for the throne of that heart.

To let Jesus be King means: I bring people to Jesus, then I step aside. To let Jesus receive all the glory means: when that person bears fruit, the applause goes not to me but to the Lord.

David pouring out that water before Yahweh is the most vivid Old Testament foreshadowing of “let Jesus receive all the glory”.

The Goal: establish God’s system

All our completing must, in the end, flow into one Goal — to establish God’s system.

Human systems are held together by structures; God’s system grows by the multiplying of life. Human systems need people to stay; God’s system sends people out.

When we win hearts in order to complete, we are establishing God’s system; when we win hearts in order to possess, we are building our own kingdom — even if that kingdom has a church sign hanging over its door.

The self-centred life and selflessness

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of our problems.

When it comes to “winning hearts”, the self-centred life shows itself in very concrete ways: needing to be needed, fearing being replaced, feeling a pang when someone we’ve led praises another pastor. Every one of these reactions is evidence that “self” is still alive.

Selflessness is not having no feelings; it is not suppression, still less indifference. Selflessness is “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. Only when “self” no longer needs to be fed do we have room left over to truly love others.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan does best is quietly turn, in the middle of our service, “the Lord’s work” into “my work”, and “God’s people” into “my congregation”. The way to resist him is not to try harder but to be humbler — to lay down our rights, return to our originally intended position, and let man be man and let God be God.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry

People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Someone whose relationship with God is secure doesn’t need to find security in other people’s dependence; someone at peace with himself doesn’t need to control others to prove his worth. When the first three layers of relationship are right, ministry becomes light.

In the cave of Adullam, David had life first, then relationships, and only last of all ministry. Get the order right, and the fruit comes naturally.

920 and 235

The 920 practice faces inward: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; in front of every “2” we practise living out a selfless (0) life, and we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

The 235 relationships face outward: with a selfless person you become a “2”; you build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and you become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

First practise selflessness, and then you can truly complete others; once people are truly completed, God’s system grows up generation after generation.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared three practices for us. Let’s combine them with the eight stages of changing our mindset in Kingdom 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that the practices really take root.

Practice 1: Examine your motive for “winning hearts”

Think about your motive for “winning hearts” in your service or your relationships — is it to complete, or to possess? Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on it.

Information: today you have heard two ways of winning hearts — Absalom “stealing hearts” and David “pouring out the water”. Keep these two pictures in your heart.

Revelation: be still for five minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to place one specific name on your heart. Don’t think vaguely about “what my motives are like”; ask specifically: towards him, what is my motive?

Conviction: if the Holy Spirit shines his light on you and lets you see that you really do enjoy being needed, please don’t make excuses, and don’t beat yourself up either. Admitting it is the beginning of overcoming.

Implementation: today, do one “completing” thing for this person — perhaps a word of affirmation, perhaps an opportunity, perhaps letting go.

Evaluation: at the weekend, ask yourself: this week, did my words hint that “nothing works without me”?

Correction: change “You need me” into “We both need the Lord”.

Repetition: for forty days in a row, pray for the same person once every morning.

Multiplication: find a companion in ministry, share this lesson of self-examination with him, and invite him to practise it with you.

Practice 2: Pray for someone you have influenced, and encourage him to rely more on God

Choose someone you have influenced; take the initiative to pray for him and bless him, and encourage him to rely more on God rather than depend on you.

Information: true completing brings people before God, not before me (Colossians 1:28).

Revelation: think about it — when this person hits trouble, who is the first person he calls? If it is always you, perhaps God wants you to take a step back.

Conviction: believe that God loves him more than you do, and is better able to help him than you are.

Implementation: this week, send him a message that includes at least this sentence: “I’m praying for you, and I believe God will speak to you himself.”

Evaluation: after sending the message, is there a little sense of loss in your heart? That loss will tell you how much “self” is still left.

Correction: next time he comes to you for help, pray with him first and give advice afterwards; ask first, “How do you think God sees this?” before you say, “I think…”.

Repetition: put him on your prayer list and keep watch over him in prayer for the long haul.

Multiplication: encourage him to go and shepherd someone too, moving up from “the one being cared for” to “the one who cares”.

Practice 3: Serve people with a parent’s heart

Serve people with the heart of a parent who loves a child; listen and walk alongside with your heart, and help them discover God’s plan for their lives.

Information: Paul says that among the believers he was “like a nursing mother” cherishing her own children (1 Thessalonians 2:7).

Revelation: ask God to let you see that person as he will be “twenty years from now” — what is God’s blueprint for his life?

Conviction: believe that God has entrusted something to every single person; no one is surplus.

Implementation: this week, arrange one conversation that is not about ministry but only about life. Keep your own talking to no more than a third of the time.

Evaluation: think back over that conversation — did you find yourself unable to resist handing out answers, guidance or verdicts?

Correction: learn to ask one more question: “And then what happened?” “What were you feeling inside?” Let the other person finish what he has to say.

Repetition: make this kind of conversation a monthly habit.

Multiplication: once he has been listened to like this, he has learned how to listen to others. Ask him to go and walk alongside a newcomer too.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Winning hearts is not the goal; completing people and bringing them back to Jesus is the true meaning of service.

Serving with the heart will let you enjoy it, because it is a sweet season of working together with God.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s come back to where we started.

Jesus won people’s hearts not to build his own glory, but to complete his disciples and bring them into God’s plan. After his resurrection, by the Sea of Tiberias, he said to Peter, who had denied him three times, “Feed my lambs.” (John 21:15) He did not say, “You must keep following me around”; he said, “Go and feed.” He took a disciple who had failed and set him back in the place of a shepherd. “He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick.” (Isaiah 42:3) Our Lord is just such a Lord, one who completes people.

Today he calls us to do the same — to love with the heart, and to complete with love. So, brothers and sisters, I want to invite you to make three decisions this morning:

First, open your hand. The person you have been holding on to so tightly — today, in prayer, hand him back to the Lord. He is not yours; he is God’s.

Second, pour out the water. The trust, the admiration and the thanks you have received — don’t swallow them into your own glory; pour them out before Yahweh and say: This is too precious; it is fit to be offered only to you.

Third, hand over your heart. Stop serving with the brain; stop proving yourself by your performance. Come back to the heart, back to the guidance of the Holy Spirit, back under the yoke of the Lord who is gentle and humble.

When we serve like this, we will discover that truly “winning hearts” is not holding on to others but letting their lives take flight because of you; and then serving is no longer a burden but a joy.

May Jesus reign as King in every one of our relationships, and may all the glory be his.

keyVerses: Ephesians 4:11–13

“He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.”
1 Corinthians 11:1
“Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.”
declarations: Lord, teach me to be like you: to love people with my heart, not to possess them but to complete them.
May every person I serve, because of me, love you more, become more like you, and fulfil what you have entrusted to them.
practices: Examine your motive for “winning hearts”
Pray for someone you’ve influenced; encourage him to rely more on God
Serve people with a parent’s heart
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you. To win our hearts you paid the price of the cross; you won us not to possess us, but to make us alive, reconcile us to God and make us whole.

Lord, forgive us. In our service we so often treat your sheep as our own sheep and your glory as our own glory. We enjoy being needed and fear being replaced; we wrap a heart that wants to possess in a cloak of love. Shine the light of your Holy Spirit on every motive within us.

Lord, give us the heart of David — to win people’s hearts, yet pour that cup of water out before you. Give us the heart of Paul — seeking not that people follow us, but only that Christ be formed in their hearts.

Lord, make our service heavy no longer. Teach us to rely on the heart and not the brain; to rely on the Holy Spirit and not on ourselves. May every person we shepherd go beyond us, to places we cannot reach, and glorify your name.
Reign as King among us, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 2 Samuel 15:6: “Absalom did this sort of thing to all Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” On the outside, what Absalom did looked very much like sincere shepherding. Please share: in your service or your relationships, what subtle motives have there been that “look like love but really want to possess”? How will you ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on them and correct them?

John 14:12: “Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father.” The Lord Jesus hoped his disciples would do greater things than he did. Please share: who is the one person you most want to complete right now? What might God have entrusted to him? What is one concrete act of “completing” you can do for him this week?
